Hydrogen internal combustion engine CHP in decentralized energy systems: Towards TEA-LCA in an open-source framework
abstract: Hydrogen-based decentralized energy systems (H 2 -DES) are gaining prominence as potential solutions for local decarbonization of heat and power supply. This paper presents a life cycle assessment (LCA) of a H 2 -DES using an internal combustion engine for combined heat and power (ICE-CHP), grounded on a techno-economic analysis (TEA) model implemented in OpenModelica. The study addresses the relative underexploration of H 2 -ICE-CHP technologies in the LCA literature, offering a comprehensive analysis based on real hourly demand data of buildings in Offenburg (Germany), a municipality involved in the Franco-German Interreg CO2InnO project. Scenarios families were developed with varying configurations and dimensioning (PV, wind, battery, H 2 storage). The results of the TEA model were interfaced with the Brightway2 framework for LCA through custom Python-based routines and manual implementation. Monte Carlo simulations and global sensitivity analysis were conducted in the Activity-Browser software to evaluate uncertainty and parameter influence. Results show that impacts are strongly dependent of the scenario family and selected system boundaries. The H 2 sub-system components showed modest impacts to climate change but not in other environmental categories, while PV significantly affected environmental assessment overall, depending on excess electricity consideration. These findings highlight the necessity of careful system design and boundary comparison in policy and environmental reporting. This work also contributes methodologically towards the development of an open-source TEA-LCA workflow. While still requiring manual data adaptations, it forms the foundation for future automation efforts. The approach offers actionable insights for local policymakers and researchers aiming for transparent, reproducible, and multi-criteria sustainability assessments of H 2 -DES.

title: Performance-efficiency trade-off for multiple reagent dosage regulation using lightweight deep reinforcement learning in full-scale drinking water treatment plant
A novel model to assess the hydrogen storage capacity in depleted gas reservoirs considering dynamic geo-bio-chemical reactions
Integrating catalytic performance and life cycle assessment for a γ-valerolactone biorefinery design from biomass
abstract: γ-Valerolactone (GVL) is a renewable platform molecule with applications as a greener solvent and fuel additive. This study couples catalytic experiments, process simulation, and cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment (LCA) to guide lower-impact GVL production from lignocellulosic residues via levulinic acid (LA) hydrogenation. Vapor-phase continuous tests over Cu–Ni/SiO 2 catalysts used LA diluted in isopropanol (IPA) with H 2 co-feed; under these conditions, IPA acts as a solvent and contributes as a hydrogen donor alongside molecular H 2 through transfer-hydrogenation pathways, improving conversion and stability versus IPA-free operation. The best formulation (6Cu–14Ni/SiO 2 ) sustained 79% average LA conversion and 91% GVL selectivity over 50 h. Experimental results parameterized an Aspen Plus model to generate mass and energy requirements for an attributional LCA with selective system expansion (functional unit: 1 kg GVL) across three Colombian residues. Baseline impacts (9.30 ± 1.55 –11.37 ± 2.14 kg CO 2 -eq kg −1 GVL) were dominated by fossil IPA and process heat. Switching to bio-based IPA, green H 2 , and renewable heat reduced impacts by up to 87%. Sensitivity analysis showed a near-linear dependency of impacts on LA conversion (SR > 0.9), highlighting catalytic efficiency as the primary lever for environmental improvement. Overall, coupling catalytic performance with LCA enables early identification of hotspots and supports low-carbon design choices for bio-based chemical production. • Integrating LCA into biorefinery design supports low-carbon chemical pathways. • LA hydrogenation over CuNi/SiO 2 can deliver relevant GVL yields over time. • LCA identifies isopropanol and fossil heat as main environmental hotspots. • Green routes reduce climate impact by up to 87% and eutrophication by 96%. • Sensitivity analysis identified LA conversion as the dominant environmental driver.

title: Carbon intensity assessment and fuel pathway optimization under the international maritime Organization's new regulations

Corrigendum to “Assessing microbial internal drivers of nitrogen–cycle functional potential in lakeside wetlands: insights from random forest modelling and co-occurrence network analyses” [J. Clean. Prod. 541 (2026) 147519]
Drivers and barriers of transformation towards a sustainable food system in Warsaw
abstract: Despite the growing body of research on sustainable food systems (SFSs), empirical and locally grounded studies examining the drivers and barriers of urban food system (FS) transformation in Central and Eastern European cities remain limited, particularly from the dual perspectives of citizens and organized initiatives. Urban SFSs have significant potential to improve both public and planetary health. Therefore, this study aims to identify the drivers and barriers to a SFS in Warsaw from the perspectives of households and transition initiatives, following the SysOrg project framework. Data were collected using a mixed-methods approach, combining a household survey (HHS) (N = 449) and semi-structured interviews (SSI) with local initiatives (N = 5), across three key dimensions: sustainable and healthy diets, organic food and farming, and food waste reduction. The results indicate that all three domains share common barriers, including budgetary constraints, limited awareness and knowledge, insufficient institutional support, and data gaps, with outcomes significantly influenced by gender, age, income, and education. Key drivers identified include awareness-raising, improved availability and infrastructure, and policy support, particularly at the municipal level. The findings highlight the interconnectedness of the three project perspectives—diet (D), organic food and farming (O), and food waste (W)—and identify critical leverage points for sustainable transformation, such as targeted policies and incentives, green public procurement, education, and supportive food infrastructure. This study addresses the existing knowledge gap in urban FS research and provides actionable insights for policymakers, municipalities, and local initiatives in Warsaw. Furthermore, it serves as a preliminary resource for other European cities engaged in the development of food policies, particularly for less-explored municipalities in the field of SFS that share similar dynamics with the Polish capital, such as those within the Visegrad Group.

Can photovoltaic retrofit redefine heritage value? Practical and theoretical evidence from meta-analysis and multi-criteria evaluation of 133 international case studies over 35 years
abstract: This paper investigates the role of photovoltaic (PV) systems in accelerating the energy transition of built heritage through the comparative analysis of 133 international case studies realized between 1991 and 2026. Covering a wide range of climatic zones, regulatory frameworks, building functions, and heritage protection levels, the study adopts a mixed-method research framework that integrates archival analysis, policy review, technological assessment, quantitative energy evaluation, and critical architectural interpretation. The case studies enable the identification of performance patterns, temporal trends, and critical innovation thresholds, offering an evidence-based understanding of how aesthetic, technical, and energy performance goals negotiated in practice the trade-offs between decarbonization policies, technological feasibility, cultural values, product innovation, and social acceptance of PV adoption in historical environments. From a regulatory perspective, 47% of the analyzed buildings are formally listed, while others are subject to indirect heritage constraints, demonstrating that PV integration is not confined to weakly protected contexts. Case studies span from the 14th to the 20th century, and PV adoption is most frequent in residential, religious, office, and rural buildings, while cultural, educational, and institutional uses confirm the growing penetration of PV systems into public and highly symbolic building types. Crystalline silicon cells dominate due to reliability and availability, while glass-glass, frameless, and chromatically treated panels emerge after 2018 as enablers of higher architectural and energy integration. The PV fraction covering annual primary energy consumption ranges from approximately 10% to 149%, with a mean value of 60.7% and a median of 58.5%. More than 42% of the cases achieve coverage above 50%, while 21% reach full or surplus energy balance (≥100%). The temporal analysis identifies three evolutionary phases: experimental applications (1991-2001), visually subordinate and concealed solutions driven by conservative guidelines and early EU directives (2002-2017), and context-sensitive architectural integration (2018-2026) aligned with higher energy targets and technological maturation. Building on these findings, a data-driven design taxonomy was structured around emerging retrofit paradigms ( concealment, mimicry, transparency, and expression ) as guidance to inform future policy strategies, technological development, decision-making and design practices. This approach challenges and reinterprets the traditional principles of “ authenticity ” and “ reversibility ” from architectural conservation, adapting them to the language and design logic of PV retrofit. • Dataset of 133 international cases on photovoltaic retrofit of heritage buildings. • Cross-disciplinary framework balancing heritage, technological and energy measures. • Photovoltaic design taxonomy derived from real-world implementations.

Waste activated sludge derived biopolymer amelioration for desert sand: Impact on moisture retention, vegetation growth and microbial community
From monitoring to scenario-based predictive planning: What-If rollouts for a commercial broiler-house microclimate
abstract: Commercial broiler production is increasingly operated as sensor-informed process in which ventilation-related actions shape indoor air quality, thermal stability, and operational efficiency. A persistent gap is that many analytics pipelines stop at point forecasting or single-variable alerts, while deployment decisions are made in discrete multi-hour windows and must be reliable across flock episodes and seasonal drift. This study develops a decision-scale framework for scenario-based predictive planning in one commercial broiler house, aiming to reduce high-ammonia exposure time without incurring disproportionate thermal penalties or excessive control effort. Operational records from one commercial broiler house were organized into four consecutive production cycles (306 days; 7344 hourly observations) and transformed into 6-h decision blocks. Season-adaptive, quantile-based thresholds were used to derive an operational RiskState label from thermal load and ammonia, while an interpretable Adaptive Agro-Environmental Efficiency Index (AAEEI) combined thermal burden, air-quality burden, and control burden into bounded efficiency score. RiskState identification was learned using a bagged-tree classifier and evaluated with leave-one-cycle-out testing to reflect strict episode-level transfer. A multi-output neural surrogate was trained for 6-h-ahead forecasting of ammonia (NH3_next6h), indoor–outdoor temperature gradient (dT_next6h), and AAEEI_next6h, enabling multi-step what-if rollouts under hypothetical inlet interventions. Cycle-wise evaluation showed high accuracy can coexist with modest class-balanced performance, highlighting the importance of macro-averaged sensitivity for risk prevention. Short-horizon forecasts provided useable fidelity for coupled endpoints, and rollout experiments revealed regime-dependent trade-offs where ammonia reductions may be offset by thermal-gradient penalties and reduced efficiency. A MATLAB dashboard was developed as an output to translate forecasts and rollouts into an auditable what-if scenario for practical decision support.

Carbon- and lifecycle-aware tariff design for solar-battery prosumers: A mean-field modeling framework for cleaner electricity production
abstract: Rooftop solar paired with behind-the-meter storage can either reduce or shift environmental burdens, depending on how tariffs reward charging, discharging, and exports. This study examines when decentralized prosumer battery operation aligns with decarbonization and lifecycle resource efficiency in a California-calibrated mean-field modeling framework. The model combines reflected battery-state dynamics, hourly carbon intensity, and a convex battery-wear proxy, and it distinguishes posted residential tariffs from a scenario-specific dynamic settlement adder. Flat-rate and time-of-use cases therefore follow exogenous posted tariffs, while endogenous load feedback appears only in a stylized dynamic-settlement scenario used to diagnose congestion feedback. We evaluate six policy scenarios using daily attributable CO 2 emissions, integrated battery-wear proxy, electricity-bill savings, and duck-curve metrics. Conventional time-of-use pricing increases emissions by 3.2% relative to the flat-rate benchmark because low off-peak prices synchronize charging in high-carbon nighttime hours. Carbon-intensity pricing reduces emissions by 22.1% but raises modeled battery wear by 2.1%. Combining carbon-intensity pricing with a lifecycle-preserving incentive delivers the strongest joint outcome in the base calibration: emissions fall by 24.6%, the integrated wear proxy falls by 13.6%, and electricity-bill savings reach $2.78 per prosumer-day. Carbon-aligned tariffs shift charging toward lower-emission hours, while lifecycle incentives moderate excessive cycling. In this calibration, the strongest joint emissions–wear outcome requires carbon-aligned tariffs together with lifecycle-preserving incentives.

title: A transformer-reinforcement learning framework integrating acoustic thermometry for multi-pollutant prediction and control in a full-scale WtE plant in China
Heatwaves intensify microplastic-driven greenhouse gas emissions from soil by modulating microbial abundance
Achieving system-level decoupling in intensive agriculture via zoning-based cleaner production strategies: Insights from the Huang-Huai-Hai plain
Evaluating the environmental impact for lettuce production in vertical farming through LCA
abstract: Vertical farming represents a promising innovative solution to the challenges of sustainable food production, reducing land consumption and optimizing production. This agricultural system relies on vertical spaces and advanced technologies to grow plants in controlled environments, although it is typically associated with high energy consumption. However, to assess its actual environmental sustainability, a Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) approach is applied, enabling the evaluation of impacts across the entire life cycle, including production, energy use, transportation, and end-of-life stages. This study considers the LCA of a productive pilot site at the National Agriculture University of Athens, which has been used to produce Valerianella locusta and Lactuca sativa . The LCA analysis primarily takes into consideration and compares vertical farming to the open field production of Valerianella locusta and Lactuca sativa . Upscaling and improved scenarios of vertical farm production have been studied to evaluate the environmental impact trends of this technology based on specific set up variations also assessing the pros and cons of the production method. The study shows that, despite the high energy consumption for lighting and climate control of indoor production, vertical farming can outperform open-field production in several important environmental categories, depending on the crop-specific productivity. For Lactuca sativa , reductions in water consumption (−41%), marine eutrophication (−86%), freshwater ecotoxicity (−91%), and land use (−95%) compared to open-field production were observed primarily in the baseline scenario. However, freshwater eutrophication increased significantly (+425%) in the VF baseline scenario, mainly driven by upstream emissions associated with electricity production. Therefore, VF does not systematically outperform open-field systems across all impact categories. The situation is different for Valerianella locusta , which, due to lower crop yields, shows higher impacts, although these are comparable to those of lettuce under different energy supply choices and increased yields, with an unchanged system setup. The integration between vertical farming and LCA allows identifying optimization strategies, promoting technological and policy innovations that favor resilient and sustainable transition to sustainable urban agriculture.

title: Evaluating CO2 mitigation strategies in SAF biorefineries: Techno-economic and life cycle analysis
abstract: The aviation sector requires scalable decarbonization strategies, and lignocellulosic sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) represents a promising pathway. This study comparatively evaluates the techno-economic analysis and life cycle assessment (LCA) of three CO 2 management strategies integrated within a U.S.-based gasification–Fischer–Tropsch SAF biorefinery: (i) catalytic hydrogenation of captured CO 2 to methanol, (ii) geological CO 2 sequestration, and (iii) mineralization to sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO 3 ). Techno-economic analysis indicates that methanol synthesis requires approximately 26% higher capital investment and 33% higher operating costs than mineralization. Although methanol co-production generates the highest gross revenue, NaHCO 3 production reduces the SAF minimum selling price by approximately 38% relative to both methanol synthesis and geological sequestration pathways, reflecting a more balanced cost allocation through mineral co-product valorization. Geological sequestration lowers operating costs by nearly 50% compared with methanol synthesis but remains highly dependent on carbon credit mechanisms. LCA reveals substantial divergence in climate performance. Relative to methanol synthesis, sequestration improves net greenhouse gas performance by approximately 163%, transitioning the system from net-positive to net-negative emissions. Mineralization further enhances carbon mitigation, achieving roughly 85% greater carbon reduction than sequestration and over sixfold improvement relative to methanol synthesis within the defined system boundary. Sensitivity analysis identified hydrogen price, co-product market value, and process emissions as dominant drivers. Under baseline assumptions, CO 2 mineralization is found to offer the most balanced pathway.

Fast solvent-free hydroprocessing of waste cooking oil to produce green diesel over Ru/NbOPO4 catalysts
abstract: Climate change has significantly increased demand for renewable fuels, especially those derived from waste, such as waste cooking oil (WCO). However, highly efficient catalytic systems are needed to convert these low-quality feedstocks completely. In this context, we presented a rapid, solvent-free, and efficient process for WCO upgrading to produce green-diesel-range hydrocarbons, using Ru/NbOPO 4 catalysts. The in situ activation of needle-like RuO 2 nanocrystals promoted the complete conversion of WCO within 30 min, achieving 96% green diesel selectivity and 78 wt% liquid yield, with a catalyst containing 2.4 wt% Ru. The presence of oxophilic NbO x acid sites facilitated deoxygenation reactions in nitrogen (N 2 ) atmosphere; however, their effectiveness was reduced under hydrogen (H 2 ) conditions. Conversely, the metallic Ru 0 nanocrystals significantly enhanced hydrogenation and hydrogenolysis reactions, in the presence of H 2 , thereby minimizing the undesirable cracking of free fatty acids. Regardless of the atmosphere (H 2 or N 2 ), niobium-based catalysts favored the decarboxylation and decarbonylation reactions, resulting in the C n-1 hydrocarbons. The strong synergy between Ru and NbOPO 4 enabled the development of a rapid process for converting low-quality waste feedstocks into drop-in biofuels, thereby supporting the decarbonization of the industrial sector. • Fast solvent-free deoxygenation of WCO to green diesel production in 30 min. • Ru/NbOPO 4 catalyst delivers 96% green diesel selectivity with 78 wt% liquid yield. • NbOPO 4 drives catalytic deoxygenation under N 2 via oxophilic NbO x sites. • Higher Ru loading enhances hydrogenation reactions, increasing C n-1 hydrocarbons selectivity. • NbOPO 4 intrinsically promoted DCO x regardless of Ru loading or reaction atmosphere.

title: The plastic pulse: How global water consumption behaviors shape exposure to nano- and microplastics from single-use plastic water bottles
abstract: Understanding how everyday hydration behaviors contribute to human exposure to nano- and microplastics (NMPs) is an emerging public health priority. This study examines the extent to which personal water consumption habits, especially reliance on single-use plastic (SUP) water bottles, influence potential NMP exposure. Using a global dataset of 15,143 respondents from 81 countries collected via ArcGIS Survey123, we assessed consumption frequency, recycling habits, situational triggers, and awareness of environmental and health impacts. Multivariate analyses, including logistic regression, principal component analysis, and factor analysis, revealed strong associations between consumption behaviors and demographic variables such as age, education, gender, and race. Younger respondents and those with higher education levels reported greater consumption and recycling, whereas older adults more frequently used refillable bottles. Motivations for SUP water bottles use varied across behavioral clusters, with convenience, travel, and social influence emerging as key predictors. Awareness of microplastic contamination was high: 75% of participants believed that SUP water bottles contain microplastics, and 70% perceived a link to cancer risk. Preferences for sustainable alternatives, such as filtered water and glass containers, were closely aligned with environmental awareness. Infrastructure limitations and advertisement exposure further shaped consumption patterns. By integrating environmental science, behavioral analysis, and public health perspectives, this study identifies behavioral exposure pathways that can inform targeted risk communication, sustainable consumption strategies, and evidence-based policy. SUP water bottles were examined due to their unique role as a direct ingestion pathway for microplastics, distinguishing them from other single-use plastics whose exposure routes are less behavior-dependent.

title: Restructuring metabolic networks and hydrogen-mediated electron transfer to enhance methanogenesis process through microelectrolysis
Resource efficiency and circularity under rapid urbanization: Insights from dynamic material stock–flow analysis in Vietnam
abstract: Emerging economies face major data gaps in modeling material transitions, especially for building stocks and demolition. This study develops a lifespan-differentiated, stock-driven dynamic material flow analysis for Vietnam's residential sector (1986–2050), integrating socio-economic decomposition and circular-economy assessment under data scarcity. Using the Residential Building Material Metabolism and Efficiency Assessment Framework, we reconstruct material inflows, in-use stocks, and demolition outflows; identify socio-economic drivers through Logarithmic Mean Divisia Index decomposition; and compare legacy-stock circular-economy scenarios. Results reveal a pronounced shift toward long-lived, cement-intensive housing and indicate that demolition outflows are likely to peak in the 2040s due to accumulated stock inertia and lifetime structure. Although material inflows show partial decoupling from GDP, floor-area expansion and service-level improvement remain dominant drivers of long-term stock growth. The scenario analysis is intentionally bounded to the accumulated residential stock under a no-new-inflow-after-2023 condition. Within this boundary, selective dismantling–based recovery (SD) is more effective for landfill reduction, whereas lifetime extension (LE) yields stronger embodied-CO 2 mitigation by reducing replacement demand; combining SD and LE provides the strongest overall result. These findings should be interpreted as comparative conditional estimates rather than forecasts, indicating that slowing-loop and closing-loop strategies affect different components of the stock–flow system. The results further indicate that housing-service expansion and structural upgrading reinforce upstream material demand and contribute to long-term stock-related lock-in in the residential system. The study contributes a typology-resolved, lifespan-differentiated framework for analyzing residential material dynamics under data scarcity and offers bounded comparative insights for stock-driven circular-economy assessment in emerging economies.

Stimulatory and inhibitory nutrient effects on methane emissions from farm dams in southeast Australia: Field evidence to inform management
abstract: Small freshwater systems play a disproportionate role in global methane (CH 4 ) budgets, yet the drivers of their emissions remain poorly resolved. High nutrient concentrations are often associated with elevated CH 4 emissions, typically by stimulating primary production that increases organic matter inputs and promotes sediment anoxia. However, most studies focus on broad indicators like total nitrogen (TN) and phosphorus (TP), overlooking the roles of other solutes (e.g., iron, sulphate) and physicochemical factors (e.g., dissolved oxygen, turbidity). The role of warming in amplifying these effects also remains unclear, especially in small agricultural ponds. Here, we conducted a two-year field study across 89 temperate small agricultural ponds (commonly referred to as farm dams) spanning 1,498 km in southeastern Australia. We collected water chemistry data alongside 36,408 hourly CH 4 flux measurements (diffusive + ebullitive) to identify which water quality parameters stimulate or suppress methane emissions, and whether there are any interactive effects with temperature. These fluxes averaged 262 kg CH 4 ha −1 yr −1 , more than double the mean reported for temperate reservoirs and nearly four times higher than fluxes from lakes and small ponds. We found that TN, dissolved iron (Fe), and turbidity are strong positive drivers of CH 4 flux in farm dams while sulphate and DO have inhibitory effects. Temperature had a consistent positive main effect on microbial metabolism but showed no interactive effects with any nutrient, DO, or turbidity, challenging assumptions from laboratory studies that warming amplifies nutrient-driven emissions. By identifying turbidity and temperature, both of which can be measured using satellite remote sensing, as key predictors of CH 4 flux, our findings highlight a promising opportunity for future landscape-scale monitoring of emission hotspots and provide useful insight for water-quality management. This study provides field-based evidence that CH 4 dynamics in farm dams are shaped by the complex and multivariate effects of nutrients and water-quality parameters.

Scoring social sustainability of food products: A framework based on national-level data
abstract: This study presents a new framework for assessing social risks in the food system through a social sustainability score, aiming to enable more socially responsible decision-making among consumers, producers and policymakers. The framework was designed to apply to both domestic and imported food, based on quantifiable open-source data, and combining multiple indicators into a single weighted score. Relevant categories were identified through stakeholder engagement, followed by the selection of suitable indicators and the collection of reliable open data. To simplify interpretation and reduce data redundancy, the initial set of indicators was reduced using correlation analysis, cluster analysis and principal component analysis. Eleven categories were retained: child labour, forced labour, poverty alleviation, animal welfare, non-fatal injuries, equal opportunities for women, fair salary, smallholders’ production conditions, agricultural infrastructure, public sustainability and local employment . Weighting is unavoidable when aggregating multiple dimensions into a single score. Weighting factors were developed using an expert panel assessing the relative importance of categories, incorporating both normative and sector-specific considerations. A scoring scale with threshold values was then established. To avoid situations in which high risk on critical indicators (e.g. child labour) was compensated by low risk on others, a non-compensatory approach was applied to two critical human rights categories, resulting in a capped total score regardless of performance in other categories. An optional reward for domestic production was tested to integrate the proposed category of national self-sufficiency and food security. Sensitivity analysis showed that methodological choices affected the results. To strengthen validity, the selected categories were compared with established European and global frameworks, showing substantial overlap.

Carbon fixation and material improvement through CO2 treatment of coarse recycled concrete aggregates: Experimental insights and projections for Brazil by 2050
abstract: Alternatives for carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) have applications in the treatment of recycled concrete aggregates (RCA) in a process known as CO 2 mineralization. This study evaluates the influence of CO 2 treatment on RCA's physical and microstructural properties and the CO 2 fixation potential of RCAs until 2050 in the Brazilian scenario, considering the projected population growth and concrete waste generation. To produce recycled coarse aggregate, source concretes were prepared using different cement types (CP IV-32 and CP V) and water/cement (w/c) ratios (0.55 and 0.65). Following crushing and screening, the coarse particles were selected for CO 2 treatment in a carbonation chamber (RH 65%, CO 2 15%, time 24 h). CO 2 fixation by the RCA was determined through thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). Additionally, specific gravity, water absorption, X-ray microtomography (μCT), scanning electron microscope (SEM), and Vickers microhardness tests were conducted to evaluate physical and microstructural changes after treatment. Results indicate that aggregate carbonation was partial, with the w/c exerting a greater influence on CO 2 diffusion than the cement type. The RCA produced with CP IV-32 and a 0.65 w/c ratio, achieved the highest CO 2 fixation (29.10 kgCO 2 /ton), projecting a total fixation of 77.50 ktCO 2 per year in the 2050 scenario. This treatment led to the most significant physical improvements, including a 3.03% increase in specific gravity and a 7.32% reduction in water absorption. Although X-ray microtomography (μCT) confirmed a general decrease in porosity and microhardness improved, SEM analysis indicated that carbonation remained superficial and did not reach the adhered mortar near the interfacial transition zone (ITZ). Ultimately, the treatment improved RCA physical and microstructural properties and promoted CO 2 utilization and fixation, contributing to circularity and decarbonization in construction through a promising process for large-scale application. • The influence of CO 2 treatment on carbon fixation and RCA properties was evaluated. • CO 2 mineralization increased specific gravity and reduced water absorption and porosity of RCA. • Microstructural analyses (μCT, SEM, microhardness) confirmed partial carbonation and improved surface quality. • Up to 29.10 kg of CO 2 per ton of RCA was uptake in 24 h of CO 2 exposure. • The average annual CO 2 fixation potential of RCAs in Brazil until 2050 is 77.50 ktCO 2 .

title: Spatiotemporal prediction and differentiated governance of coal mining subsidence in the desert-loess transition region
Upcycling of pyrolytic char waste as a filler for circular asphalt pavement infrastructure
abstract: Incorporating industrial waste into road pavements is a key strategy for advancing asphalt decarbonisation. This manuscript reports the first study into the potential use of a byproduct (defined as PMMA-char) from the industrial pyrolysis of commercial poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) plastic as a sustainable alternative to conventional mineral fillers, namely limestone and hydrated lime, in the asphalt mastic part of an asphalt mixture. Physicochemical characterisation revealed that PMMA-char contained calcite, barium sulfate, and amorphous carbon, exhibiting mineralogical similarities to limestone, which supports its potential as a substitute filler. Various asphalt mastic combinations were prepared by replacing traditional fillers with PMMA-char from 0 to 100% levels, and their rheological properties were evaluated. The overall findings showed that the optimum PMMA-char replacement level depended on the rheological performance metric considered. For limestone-based mastics, the high-temperature Performance Grade (PG) critical temperature peaked at 25–50% replacement, while the fatigue life reached its maximum at 75% replacement. For hydrated lime-based mastics, a 25% replacement level enhanced the high-temperature mastic performance, whereas fatigue life decreased progressively with increasing PMMA-char content. These differences are likely due to variations in microstructure, void ratio, and specific surface area among the fillers, affecting the mastic's effective bitumen fraction. Given that PMMA-char is an industrial byproduct with low economic value, it offers significant promise as a viable low-carbon filler replacement for pavements when compared to current commercial mastic using traditional mineral fillers, which generate significant environmental impact, including high energy consumption, resource depletion, and associated CO 2 emissions. • First use of poly(methyl methacrylate) pyrolytic char as a sustainable asphalt filler. • Its mineral and microstructural features support its suitability as a viable filler. • Replaces up to 75% of limestone while maintaining strong rheological performance. • Microstructural features of the char yield a balanced binder–filler system in mastics.

title: A novel and intelligent system for ciprofloxacin sensing by molecularly imprinted polymers loaded graphitic carbon nitride-based municipal wastewater sludge

Enabling degrowth through entrepreneurial ecosystems: Exploring key factors influencing degrowth decisions for SMEs
abstract: While entrepreneurial ecosystems are traditionally viewed as engines for growth-centric innovation, the intensifying pressures of climate change and resource depletion have catalyzed interest in degrowth as a viable alternative paradigm. This study investigates the factors influencing the adoption of degrowth strategies among Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) within the entrepreneurial ecosystem of Quebec, Canada. Based on a 2024 survey of 1416 entrepreneurs, our analysis focuses on the 512 respondents who implemented degrowth strategies in subsequent years, revealing that motivations such as personal work-life balance, economic constraints, and a lack of adequate ecosystem support were more influential than environmental concerns. These findings highlight a significant misalignment between existing ecosystem structures and the practical needs of sustainability-oriented entrepreneurs. Ultimately, this research argues that integrating degrowth principles into the broader entrepreneurial framework can foster greater inclusivity, resilience, and ecological responsibility, offering critical insights for policymakers and stakeholders seeking to bridge the gap between individual decision-making and systemic sustainability.

title: Outdoor cultivation of an extremophilic cyanobacteria in desertic environment for phycobiliprotein and biobased bitumen analogue production
abstract: Native extremophilic marine cyanobacteria strains from Qatar represent promising candidates for large scale outdoor cultivation in desert environments, taking advantage of the local solar, seawater and CO 2 resources. In this study, a recently isolated pigment producing Pleurocapsa sp. strain was successfully cultivated in open ponds using urea as an inexpensive local nitrogen source, producing biomass with up to 12% dry weight of phycobiliproteins, predominantly phycocyanin. Following pigment extraction, the residual biomass was valorized via hydrothermal conversion, demonstarting the feasibility of obtaining bitumen-like oil fractions. However, this result that opens perspectives for optimized biorefinery, was shown to require a pigment extraction process allowing the simultaneous reduction of the ash content in the biomass, which is about three-fold higher than that of a spirulina biomass reference cultivated in France. Indeed, the reduction in biomass ash content had a significant impact on the hydrothermal conversion oil yield, but also on the oil's chemical composition in terms of molecular mass distribution, and on the resulting material's rheology. The bitumen-like thermo-rheological behavior of the oils appears to be associated with the presence of a significant fraction of molecules above 1000 g/mol, in addition to a dominant population around 300 g/mol. It was further validated by the successful fitting of experimental data using a rheological model originally developed for conventional petroleum bitumen. These findings highlight the potential of Qatar's native extremophillic cyanobacteria for integrated pigment production and optimized algal biorefineries in arid regions.

Multi-objective evaluation framework of live transport parameters for leopard coral grouper (Plectropomus leopardus): Balancing survival, energy efficiency, and carbon footprint via LCA
abstract: The live transport of high-value marine fish is a critical link in the aquaculture supply chain; however, it has long been plagued by issues such as severe physiological stress during transport, unstable survival rates, and significant environmental impacts. Most existing studies have focused on optimizing single factors such as temperature or oxygen supply, lacking a comprehensive and systematic analysis of the coupled relationship between fish physiological responses and environmental impacts. This study used the leopard coral grouper as the subject to construct a multi-objective evaluation framework that integrates in vivo physiological responses with life cycle assessment. Through low-water live transport experiments conducted under varying temperature gradients and oxygen-to-nitrogen ratios, key physiological indicators such as antioxidant capacity, metabolic stress, and tissue damage were systematically measured. A survival rate prediction model was then established and integrated with life cycle assessment results for analysis. The results indicate that the combination of 18 °C and 75% O2–25% N2 represents the optimal transport conditions, achieving a transport survival rate of approximately 95% while maintaining good physiological stability. Compared to traditional transport methods, the low-water controlled-atmosphere mode significantly reduces energy consumption and carbon emissions at the unit-product level (by 26.8% and 25.8%, respectively). Furthermore, by introducing survival rate as a linking variable, this study established a quantitative correlation pathway between “physiological state—survival performance—environmental impact,” demonstrating that improvements in physiological state can directly reduce the environmental cost per unit of effective biomass by up to 40.4%. This study proposes a comprehensive evaluation method that establishes, for the first time, a quantitative coupling framework between physiological responses and life cycle assessment in the transport of leopard coral grouper, providing a data-driven pathway for optimizing green transport and a generalizable framework for other aquatic species.

title: Achieving superior tribological performance and extended cutting life of multilayer coated cutters during high-speed dry cutting of Ti-6Al-4V
Visualization approach on the industrial hydrogen-enriched blast furnace for low-carbon ironmaking
abstract: Injecting hydrogen from the tuyere of the blast furnace (BF) is one of the most viable green-steel innovations for traditional BF ironmaking. However, the black box characteristic of the BF complicates the direct assessment of hydrogen's impact on fossil fuel replacement and the intricate events occurring within the furnace. This study employed a novel 2-D digital twin technology for an industrial hydrogen-enriched BF, establishing a coke-ore layered structure that facilitated distinct chemical reactions in the two solid layers of the BF shaft, while enabling the mixing of the two-phase solids throughout their descent. Based on the mathematical model considering mass and heat transfers, and chemical reactions, the impact of hydrogen content on the physical and chemical alterations was examined. The calculation domain covers the industrial scale region of BF from the lower throat to the bosh. The final results indicate that as the quantity of hydrogen injection increases from 0 to 40 and 100 m3/thm, (1) the carbon emissions decrease by 7.5 and 31.6 kg/thm, respectively; (2) The reduction of hematite accelerates by 19.98% and 25.61%, respectively; (3) The reduction of magnetite (Fe3O4→FeO) surpasses its production (Fe2O3→Fe3O4) during the same period, and the reduction of magnetite totally accelerates by 4.21% and 5.07%, respectively; (4) The wustite generates (Fe3O4→FeO) more than it consumes (FeO→Fe) simultaneously, resulting in a 65.71% and 99.92% deceleration in reduction, along with an enhancement of 4.43% and 9.68% in iron production, respectively; (5) The coke consumption at the shaft does not follow the expected trend of monotonic attenuation with the increase of hydrogen injection’ due to the complicated competition reactions in furnace. In conclusion, this research presents a digital and visual methodology for understanding and improving the hydrogen-enriched low-carbon ironmaking process.

The limits of “Win–Win” transitions: Understanding tensions between resource nationalism and just transitions
abstract: Rare earth elements (REEs) underpin clean energy and defense technologies, and recovering REEs from coal-related wastes is widely cast as a “win–win” that advances resource security, energy transitions, remediation, and regional development. Using a framework of the four tenets of energy justice (procedural, recognitional, distributional, and restorative justice), this paper interrogates the “win-win” claim by examining how resource nationalism and just transitions interact in U.S. efforts to extract REEs from coal ash, tailings, and acid mine drainage. Existing scholarship treats resource nationalism and just transitions as analytically separate. This paper addresses that gap by synthesizing both literatures and using a case study of rare earth element (REE) extraction from mining waste to examine their tensions in practice. Using a qualitative case study design, the analysis draws on 22 semi-structured interviews with expert stakeholders across government, academia, industry, and civil society. Findings show that national security and competitiveness concerns strongly shape research agendas and early implementation decisions, often privileging state-led priorities over community participation and transparency. Stakeholders identify risks that costs and environmental burdens will fall disproportionately on local communities and that site selection will prioritize economic viability over restorative justice needs. The study shows justice outcomes depend on explicit policy design. • Resource nationalism shapes REE extraction decisions across the innovation cycle. • Resource nationalism does not inherently conflict with just transition goals. • Tensions emerge across procedural, recognitional, distributional, and restorative justice. • Win–win outcomes require policy design to constrain nationalist priorities. • Competing narratives create risks of climate obstruction.

A framework for assessing material Circularity: Integrating key performance indicators across the building life cycle
abstract: Material Circularity (MC) is increasingly recognised as a critical strategy for reducing resource depletion, minimising construction and demolition waste, and promoting sustainable practices in the built environment. Effective assessment of MC requires integration across the Building Life Cycle (BLC), with Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) providing measurable insights into material selection, design strategies, sourcing, construction, use, and end-of-life processes. Despite growing interest, current literature lacks a comprehensive, stage-specific framework linking MC criteria and KPIs, leaving practitioners with limited tools to operationalise circularity across all BLC stages. Thus, this study aimed to develop a framework for assessing MC across the stages of the BLC. Under an interpretivist philosophy, using a qualitative choice, the Delphi technique was applied over three rounds with 21, 18 and 17 experts respectively, followed by code-based content analysis to refine criteria and ensure practical applicability. The study identified six BLC stages: Design, Material Sourcing, Construction, Use, End-of-Life, and Beyond-the-Life, and established 10 Main Criteria with 32 Sub-Criteria linked to 40 KPIs. Key findings include reframing material specification as circular material selection, introducing adaptive reuse and closing cycles as new main criteria, and aligning KPIs such as recoverability, predictive maintenance, and supplier engagement to lifecycle stages. The proposed framework enables stage-wise evaluation of circular practices, supports data-driven decision-making, and enhances accountability in MC implementation. This study contributes to the industry by offering a practical assessment tool, to academia by advancing lifecycle-integrated MC evaluation, and to society by promoting sustainable resource flows, reducing material waste, and supporting environmentally responsible construction. • Framework links MC criteria and KPIs across six Building Life Cycle stages. • Delphi method with experts refines 10 criteria, 32 sub-criteria, and 40 KPIs. • Introduces adaptive reuse and closing cycles as new MC assessment criteria. • Supports stage wise evaluation for measurable and accountable MC practices. • Framework offers scalable applicability beyond Sri Lanka to other contexts.

Quantifying future post-demolition concrete in Germany: A multi-model projection until 2080
abstract: To meet climate targets, the environmental impacts of concrete production must be reduced, particularly those associated with cement manufacture. While recycled aggregates primarily contribute to resource conservation, secondary cementitious materials derived from recycling offer direct CO 2 mitigation potential. Post-demolition concrete (PDC) represents a critical secondary resource for both substitution pathways. Reliable projections for future availability are therefore essential for climate-oriented material and circular construction strategies. This study aims to quantify and spatially resolve future availability of PDC in Germany at district level until 2080. A novel multi-model approach is applied, integrating concrete waste statistics, material stocks modelling of buildings and infrastructure, and historical concrete production data. Findings based on the production-based approach indicate that by 2040 approximately 50 million tons of PDC will become available as a secondary raw material, with the highest volumes concentrated in urban regions such as Hamburg and Berlin. Despite its considerable recycling potential, PDC is currently predominantly landfilled or used in low-value applications, indicating substantial underutilization. In parallel, landfill capacity is decreasing, while certain primary raw materials required for concrete production face increasing supply constraints. The projected PDC volumes provide a quantitative basis for assessing future substitution potentials in concrete production. Under the assumption of 35% replacement of primary aggregate and 30% substitution of Portland cement, the annual production of recycled concrete could reach up to 165 million tons annually by 2080. Overall, the results highlight the strategic relevance of PDC for advancing circular material cycles, reducing CO 2 emissions, and mitigating pressure on primary resources.

title: Barriers to sustainability engagement – Evidence from dual universities
abstract: Dual universities integrate theory and practice into their organizational structure and study design. Due to the inclusion of additional stakeholders and perspectives, dual universities may face unique challenges and opportunities when implementing sustainability. This study, based on a survey of stakeholders at a well-established dual university in Germany, examines barriers to sustainability engagement within the context of dual studies. Qualitative content analysis and quantitative correlation analysis reveal a consistent and comprehensive approach by stakeholders toward sustainability. The results indicate a generally high commitment to sustainability on the part of stakeholders. At the same time, the findings show that the intensive study model and the involvement of multiple stakeholders may create additional constraints when it comes to sustainability engagement. Time restrictions and competing priorities appear particularly pronounced in the dual university context. The analysis also reveals a high degree of consistency in how different stakeholder groups perceive sustainability barriers. Based on these findings, the study highlights the importance of developing a sustainability-informed vision and establishing dedicated organizational structures and responsibilities to support sustainability implementation in dual universities.

abstract: This paper analyzes whether firms specialize in specific dimensions of environmental corporate social responsibility (ECSR). We assume that ECSR includes firms' investment in emission reductions and analyze whether environmental concerns should also be incorporated into production decisions. Firms' choices depend on both the extent of their environmental concern and the existence of strategic interaction between governments. In a single country setting, where no strategic interaction between governments arises, firms do not consider ECSR in their production decisions in equilibrium, resulting in a narrow scope of ECSR. However, this result may change when strategic interaction between governments is present. In this case, when environmental concern is low, firms incorporate ECSR into both production and emission reduction decisions, leading to a broad ECSR scope. By contrast, when environmental concern is high, firms choose a narrow scope. Thus, the strategic behavior between governments increases the likelihood that firms adopt a broad ECSR compared to the single country case. From a welfare perspective, joint social welfare is maximized when firms adopt a narrow ECSR in both national and international settings. Therefore, in international markets, alignment between firms' strategies and government objectives arises only when firms display a sufficiently high level of environmental concern, highlighting the importance of policies that shape firms’ environmental incentives.

Operationalizing collaborations between universities and municipalities for place-based sustainability transitions
abstract: Even though many cities and regions pledge to become more sustainable and/or carbon neutral, actionable platforms that would enable the needed place-based transformation are not yet in place. In this study, we argue that successful university-municipality collaborations can play a key role in accelerating the uptake of sustainability innovations, with direct benefits for the region. We propose pathways that include operational mechanisms for universities and municipalities to co-develop institutional capacity for local/regional sustainability transitions. The study explores how higher education institutions that have developed relevant sustainability competencies, succeeded in connecting to local processes of sustainability transitions. We pursue the following research question—- Under which contexts could higher education institutions (HEIs) productively contribute to sustainability transitions locally or regionally, and how could such a mandate become institutionalized within universities that choose to do so? In the selected case studies, we identify multiple entry points for regions to tap into university sustainability competencies, capabilities and skillsets. Based on our findings, we initially propose university-region collaborations in methodological integration of cross-disciplinary research in sustainability planning and transdisciplinary practice. Next we recommend institutionalizing university-municipality engagement and configure specific operational mechanisms to make the engagement actionable and effective. Finally, we outline potential benefits and opportunities for the region, including impacts on sustainability transitions or specific sustainable development goals. The study contributes to research on (i) concepts of smart specialization for sustainable development, (ii) theoretical models of higher education institutions, and (iii) policy frameworks that envision universities as key contributors to regional sustainability innovation and sustainability transitions.

Environmental determinants and spatial patterns of soil antibiotic resistance gene diversity across Europe using interpretable geographically weighted machine learning
abstract: The dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in soils poses significant threats to ecosystems and public health. Their diversity is associated with a complex interplay of environmental factors and exhibits pronounced spatial heterogeneity. However, the spatial patterns and key associated factors remain insufficiently characterized. In this study, ARGs data from the topsoil of 649 sites across Europe, obtained from the 2018 Land Use/Cover Area frame statistical Survey (LUCAS, 2018), were used to develop an interpretable geographically weighted machine learning model. The model was used to quantify the relative importance of environmental factors associated with soil ARG diversity and to characterize spatial distribution patterns. The results indicate that by incorporating spatial heterogeneity in ARG diversity is associated with improved model performance, with geographically weighted machine learning models outperform conventional machine learning models. In particular, the geographically weighted extreme gradient boosting (GW-XGBoost) model achieved a higher R 2 and lower RMSE than the other models, with the test set R 2 improving by 22.3% compared to XGBoost. Soil pH showed the highest relative importance, accounting for 41.3%, with lower ARG diversity observed under neutral to alkaline conditions (pH > 6.7). Both pH and precipitation showed strong direct associations with ARG diversity, whereas land cover, temperature, and elevation were associated with ARG diversity through indirect pathways related to soil properties. Spatial mapping revealed higher ARG diversity in northern Europe, particularly Sweden and Finland, and lower ARG diversity in southern regions, including Spain and Italy. This study characterizes the environmental factors associated with soil ARG diversity and their spatial patterns, providing a scientific basis for soil management and public health protection, and offering a useful reference for modeling in environmental studies.

Pricing strategies on ride-hailing platforms: The role of carbon point reward program for electric vehicle services
abstract: To reduce carbon emissions, ride-hailing platforms have introduced electric vehicle (EV) services. Platforms have two pricing strategy choices between gasoline vehicles (GS) and EV services: Uniform pricing and differentiated pricing (DP). Additionally, to increase the EV demand, the platform implements a carbon point reward (CPR) program, which affects pricing strategy choices and further affects carbon emissions. In this paper, we develop a game-theoretic model with the platform as the leader and consumers and drivers as the followers to examine how pricing strategies and the CPR program impact stakeholders (consumers, drivers, and a platform) and the environment. The results show that the platform always prefers the DP strategy. And when the environmental impact of one trip (EI) is moderate and range anxiety is small or the EI is small, the DP strategy can achieve a win-win-win situation for the platform, the environment, and EV drivers if the number of consumers without a coupon is large and the economic value of carbon points is small. Furthermore, when the economic value of carbon points is small, the CPR program may increase the platform's profits while exacerbating total environmental impacts under the DP strategy. Therefore, this study provides valuable insights for ride-hailing platforms to optimize pricing strategies and promote green travel.

title: Towards a state-of-art co-utilization for multiple solid wastes by integrating deep reinforcement learning
Green ammonia: A techno-economic supply chain optimization
abstract: Green ammonia is emerging as a strategic intermediary within green energy supply chains, serving effectively as both industrial commodity and hydrogen carrier. This study provides a techno-economic analysis of green ammonia supply chains, compares cost-effective procurement strategies from global production to European consumers, and evaluates ammonia alongside alternative hydrogen carriers. Therefore, a global Well-to-Border import pricing model was coupled with a spatially explicit Border-to-Consumer optimization to complement import prices with inland distribution costs into supply costs across heterogeneous consumer locations. Gaseous hydrogen consistently remains the most economical import option for Europe, though ammonia holds a narrowing cost advantage over liquid hydrogen (from 16 % in 2030 to 10 % by 2040). Competitive ammonia suppliers, notably Morocco, the United States, and the United Arab Emirates, benefit from low renewable energy costs, with marginal costs reaching 123 €/MWh for ammonia, 137 €/MWh for liquid hydrogen and 84 €/MWh for gaseous hydrogen in 2040. Optimal transport modes vary by consumer demand and distance: trucks are ideal for low demands at all distances, rail for medium ranges, and pipelines for high-demand scenarios. By 2040, ammonia will primarily serve direct-use applications, as hydrogen consumers increasingly shift to direct hydrogen supplies. Policymakers should prioritize pipeline infrastructure for hydrogen distribution, cautiously invest in ammonia's short-to medium-term infrastructure advantages, and limit long-term reliance on ammonia as a hydrogen carrier to mitigate stranded asset risks.

title: Production of green inventory in EU metropolitan regions: The roles of collaboration networks and knowledge networks
The nonlinear link between AI and energy poverty: Empirical evidence from global data
abstract: Despite the burgeoning literature on artificial intelligence (AI) and sustainable development, cross-country panel research on AI and energy poverty has predominantly assumed a linear association, potentially obscuring stage-dependent dynamics. We examine whether this relationship is instead nonlinear, using a balanced panel of 64 countries from 2000 to 2019. Employing two-way fixed effects and system GMM estimations with Lind and Mehlum U-shape tests, we document a robust inverted U-shaped relationship: industrial-robot adoption is initially associated with higher energy poverty at low penetration levels but with alleviation beyond a critical threshold of approximately 358 industrial robots per million employees. Heterogeneity analysis shows that countries with stronger human capital and institutional quality exhibit flatter inverted-U curves; they are buffered from both the early adverse phase and the subsequent alleviation phase, while maintaining consistently lower energy poverty levels across the AI distribution. Mechanism tests provide suggestive evidence for two supply-side channels, namely energy efficiency enhancement and renewable energy transition. Results are robust to alternative measures, Bartik IV, and spatial lag models. Estimates should be interpreted as robust conditional associations rather than identified causal effects, and they primarily characterize middle- and high-income economies undergoing industrial transformation, with limited applicability to Sub-Saharan Africa. We organize the findings through an interpretive framework labelled the “conditional curse-remedy transformation”.

Configurational product life-cycle management (PLM) for sustainability: Embedding carbon-aware decision rules in product design
abstract: Industrial firms face a dual challenge: delivering highly customized products while meeting ambitious decarbonisation targets. Although product configurators accelerate variant definition and quoting, sustainability metrics are rarely integrated into configuration logic, leaving life-cycle impacts unaddressed at the point of design choice. This paper asks: How can sustainability objectives be embedded as executable decision logic within product configurators? We introduce integrated configurational PLM, a governance approach that embeds life-cycle carbon metrics directly into configurator rule systems, linking configuration logic, PLM traceability, and module-level LCA data. Empirically, we combine a multi-firm field study with a quasi-experimental digital twin to evaluate how carbon-aware rules influence configuration outcomes. Across 1000 synthetic orders, sustainability-aware rules reduce embodied (A1–A3) emissions by 10–20% and increase module reuse by 15–25%, with a modest increase in processing time (+18%). Monte Carlo analysis indicates that these effects remain robust under realistic LCA uncertainty. The findings demonstrate that configurators can evolve from feasibility tools into multi-criteria decision systems that operationalize carbon-aware design. The paper contributes (i) a mechanism for embedding sustainability into configurator rule logic, (ii) empirical evidence of its impact on variant outcomes, and (iii) design principles for integrating and governing LCA data within PLM-enabled configuration environments.

title: Study on the interaction mechanisms of urban flood risk driving factors based on explainable machine learning: A human-centered assessment framework
Innovation quality trade-offs in transport decarbonization: Evidence from EU environmental regulation and national resilience

Valorization of waste tire pyrolysis residues in sustainable asphalt pavements: Anti-UV mechanisms and eco-efficiency assessment
Integrated dynamic, regulatory, and economic assessment of onboard carbon capture systems
abstract: The decarbonization of maritime transport is a key objective of IMO greenhouse gas strategy, requiring reductions in CO 2 emissions. Carbon Capture Systems (CCS) offer a promising onboard mitigation solution; however, most existing assessments rely on steady-state assumptions and fail to capture ship operations variability. Also, Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) evaluation methods do not fully reflect operational impact of CCS, including changes in net emissions and transport capacity. To address this gap, this study develops a novel integrated dynamic framework combining real operational data with physics-based models of engines and chemical absorption-based carbon capture. The framework simulates CCS performance under time-varying conditions, develops an enhanced CII evaluation method, and performs techno-economic analysis, including sensitivity analysis of key parameters. The framework was applied to a container ship emitting 63,547 tCO 2 annually, with 42.65 GWh of recoverable waste heat, evaluating four exhaust-integration scenarios and design capacities of 2–16 t/h. CO 2 avoidance increased from 19% at 2 t/h to 74% at 16 t/h when all engines were integrated, while fuel penalties increased from 2.2% to 15.5%. CCS reduced CII from 5.1 gCO 2 /t·nm (without CCS) to 1.44 gCO 2 /t·nm (16 t/h configuration), achieving A-ratings across all scenarios. Considering technical, regulatory, spatial, and economic performance, the integrated optimal configuration is 10 t/h, capturing from all exhaust sources, achieving 70.1% CO 2 avoidance, sustaining IMO A-rating compliance, displacing 242 TEU (1.62% of capacity), and a CO 2 avoidance cost of 171.5 $/tCO 2 . The results indicate that CCS delivers substantial emission reductions while maintaining regulatory compliance and economic and spatial feasibility.

Sustainable Intensification Index: A flexible strategy for assessing the role of process intensification in achieving the 2030 agenda and beyond
abstract: Sustainability is decisive when designing, evaluating, and modifying new or existing chemical processes. One of the promising approaches in the chemical and biochemical processing plants that consider this factor is Process Intensification (PI). An intensified process could decrease the energy consumption and waste generation while improving its cost-effectiveness and safety. Even though there are several methods that include a the sustainability dimension to assess the performance of a chemical process or different intensified equipment, most of them do not explicitly aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals and usually are difficult to compare it with other metrics. Therefore, this work proposes the Sustainable Intensification Index (SII) as a new multifactorial strategy to assess technology performance based on the United Nations (UN) Sustainable Development Goals (SDG). The SII is obtained from three independent methodologies. One of the main advantages of the SII is that it can be a comparable metric across different methodologies which can be used to define an Overall Sustainable Intensification Index (OSII) that to try to dampen the inherited bias that each method might have. The proposed SII and OSII methods were applied to evaluate different alternatives for lactic acid production from previously reported data as a case study. The obtained SII and OSII results showed which technologies could be adopted to improve the process sustainability and aided in identifying opportunity areas of the evaluated technologies. Finally, the SII and OSII are powerful tools in the decision-making process for enhancing existing technologies in sustainability or developing new ones.

Beyond heavy metals: Integrating safety and agronomic performance in the classification of organic amendments
abstract: Nutrient-containing organic amendments, such as compost, have gained attention as sustainable alternatives to conventional fertilizers, aligning with global efforts to promote a circular economy and sustainability principles. However, classification of organic amendments in the European Union generally focuses on heavy metal concentrations. Thus, the nutritional quality of the products is generally not considered, and information regarding the fertilizing capacity is therefore incomplete, despite being important. This paper reports a study of the heavy metal concentrations of organic amendments registered in Spain between 2007 and 2024. Multivariate chemometric analysis, including principal component analysis and hierarchical cluster analysis, revealed significant variability in the metal concentrations and fertilizing potential among the 338 amendments considered. Most of the products had intermediate concentrations of heavy metals; however, the overlap in concentrations in many of the categories indicates the need for criteria that also include information on the fertilizing capacity. Therefore, a new three-component product identification code (3c-ID) is proposed to classify organic amendments by integrating fertilizing potential (C, N, P, K), C:N ratio and heavy metal concentrations. Based on the results obtained, the application of this code reveals that only 18.05% of amendments exhibit high fertilizing capacity (Fertility score = 3), while 40.24% and 41.72% show medium (Fertility score = 2) and low capacity (Fertility score = 1), respectively. In addition, 77.81% of amendments present balanced C:N ratios (10–20). Moreover, a clear overlap in heavy metal concentrations among regulatory classes was observed, indicating limited discriminatory power of the existing classification. These results demonstrate that the proposed system enables a more differentiated and function-oriented classification of organic amendments, improving the identification of products with similar safety profiles but contrasting agronomic potential. Moreover, the use of the new, updated classification system for amendments will contribute to improving soil health and reducing dependence on synthetic fertilizers.

Coupling renewable energy and storage technologies with hydrogen-based steel production: A design and scheduling optimization approach
abstract: The decarbonization of energy-intensive industries is essential to achieve global greenhouse gas emission reduction targets. Steel production, responsible for approximately 7% of global CO 2 emissions, requires innovative low-carbon alternatives. One promising option is the use of renewable electricity and green hydrogen in the Direct Reduced Iron (DRI) process. In this study, an integrated energy system to supply renewable electricity and hydrogen to a DRI-based steel plant is analyzed. The proposed network combines two renewable power generation technologies (solar photovoltaic and onshore wind) with three complementary storage solutions (batteries, compressed hydrogen, and Liquid Organic Hydrogen Carriers (LOHCs)). A mathematical optimization framework is developed to determine both the optimal sizing and operational strategy of the system. The methodology is applied to the provinces of mainland Spain as a case study. Results highlight the critical role of integrating multiple generation and storage technologies to ensure a continuous supply of electricity and hydrogen. They also reveal a strong dependence on geographical location for design and technology selection, driven by variations in renewable resource availability. The energy cost per ton of steel is estimated at 500–600 €/t. It exceeds five fold current costs but is expected to decline significantly with future technology improvements. Hence, these integrated renewable systems are regarded to be a technically feasible and economically competitive option in the future. Overall, it represents a key enabler for the deep decarbonization of the steel sector.

Microaerobic pretreatment and engineered Schizochytrium converts food waste into single-cell protein: A sustainable solution to global protein crisis
abstract: The global challenge of food waste (FW) management and protein scarcity necessitate innovative valorization strategies. This study presents a two-stage FW bioconversion integrating microaeration/thermal pretreatment to enhance biodegradation into organic acids (OAs), including volatile fatty acids (VFAs) and lactic acid, followed by their utilization by Schizochytrium limacinum SR21 for single-cell protein (SCP) production. The optimized pretreatment conditions achieved an OAs yield of 37.0 g/L at an organic loading rate (OLR) of 20 gVS/L, producing 258.23 kg of total organic acids (wet weight) from one ton of FW (25.82% conversion). S. limacinum SR21 demonstrated efficient OAs consumption, with 90% OAs degradation within 48 h under optimal conditions. Genetic engineering via lactate oxidase overexpression further enhanced strain performance, resulting in 17.46 g/L biomass, 14.87% lipid content, and 6.53 g/L protein yield, which were 14.19% and 12% greater than those of the wild-type strains for biomass and protein, respectively, alongside a 107.1% increase in lipid content. The recombinant strain SdLDH achieved 46.72 kg SCP per ton of dry FW (18.18% conversion). Life cycle assessment (LCA) revealed 67.5-73.4% lower impacts compared with soybean protein and 27.2-59.0% compared with soybean meal, and 18.3% lower impacts than conventional FW treatment, including 90.3% lower global warming potential and lowering land-use impacts to ∼1% of soybean-based production. This research establishes a sustainable circular economy pathway for FW-to-protein conversion, offering a low-carbon solution to address global protein deficits and waste management.

title: Producing purple bacteria in a membrane bioreactor for fish feed: Enhancing growth, immunity, and survival of GIFT tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus)
Strategic analysis of E-waste management in Switzerland: Stakeholder dynamics and pathways for the implementation of a nationwide reuse strategy
abstract: This study analyses the role of reuse strategies in e-waste management in Switzerland and documents the system itself to promote sustainable alternatives to recycling. It examines the interests and incentive structures of stakeholders, identifies barriers and drivers, and assesses unintended consequences of reuse. The methodology is based on literature review, interviews, and systems thinking. The findings reveal that reuse offers significant ecological and economic potential but is constrained by regulatory, technical, and social challenges. Barriers include unclear regulations, lack of infrastructure. Political measures, technological innovations, and awareness campaigns can foster implementation. Recommendations involve standardized certifications, modular design, and financial incentives. Stronger cooperation between policymakers, industry, and recycling companies is essential to leverage synergies between reuse and recycling and to advance sustainable e-waste system.

Comparative cradle-to-application life cycle assessment of hydrogen pathways: Role of ethanol purity and end-use efficiency in SOFCs and hydrogen engines
abstract: This study presents a cradle-to-application life cycle assessment (LCA) of hydrogen energy systems, evaluating ethanol as a renewable hydrogen carrier and solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) as high-efficiency end-use technologies. Fossil-based pathways (grey and blue hydrogen via steam methane reforming, and coal gasification) are compared with renewable ethanol-derived pathways using corn and municipal solid waste (MSW), including an integrated ethanol-fed SOFC configuration. Environmental impacts are quantified across seven midpoint categories using OpenLCA, Ecoinvent v3.12, and ReCiPe 2016 Midpoint (H), with results normalized to both hydrogen production and useful energy delivered in SOFCs and hydrogen internal combustion engines (H 2 -ICE). Results show that end-use efficiency is a dominant driver of life cycle performance, with SOFCs reducing global warming potential (GWP) by 35–45 % compared with H 2 -ICE across all pathways. Among renewable options, MSW-derived ethanol exhibits the lowest impacts, achieving 0.89 kg CO 2 -eq/MJ in SOFC systems and 0.72 kg CO 2 -eq/MJ in integrated ethanol-fed SOFC configurations. Ethanol purity shows a non-linear effect, where moderate dilution (50–75 vol %) minimizes impacts by reducing dehydration energy demand while maintaining reforming efficiency, whereas excessive dilution (25 vol %) introduces additional thermal penalties. Integrated ethanol-fed SOFC systems further reduce GWP by 9–13 % by eliminating hydrogen purification, compression, and transport stages. These results highlight the importance of jointly optimizing feedstock selection, ethanol purity, and end-use efficiency. Waste-derived ethanol and integrated SOFC systems offer a promising pathway for low-emission and resource-efficient hydrogen energy applications, particularly in emerging distributed energy contexts such as data centers and AI-driven electricity demand, where high-efficiency and low-emission systems are increasingly required.
