Mild thermal pre-treatment of waste activated sludge combined with hydrogen peroxide and iron addition
abstract: This work investigates the effects of mild thermal pre-treatment combined with hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ) and iron(II) chloride (FeCl 2 ) dosing on WAS (waste activated sludge) disintegration to boost anaerobic digestion and subsequent energy recovery potential. A two-stage thermal approach was applied, where sludge was first treated at 55 °C with and without chemical additives, followed by further processing at 70 °C. All pre-treatments significantly increased soluble chemical oxygen demand (SCOD), with the highest solubilisation observed under combined FeCl 2 and H 2 O 2 addition, suggesting an observable effect of chemical addition on sludge solubilisation. This increase in SCOD was further supported by extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) analysis, which showed a shift from tightly bound to soluble fractions. Additionally, hydrogen production was observed during pre-treatment at 55 °C, with higher yields in the presence of FeCl 2 addition. Overall, the results indicated that mild thermo-chemical pre-treatment, particularly with FeCl 2 addition, enhanced WAS hydrolysis while enabling hydrogen production, highlighting its potential to improve sludge energy recovery and support more resource-efficient wastewater treatment operations.

title: A sustainable approach for the functionalization of lyocell nonwovens by hardwood kraft lignin
abstract: Eucalyptus kraft lignin (EKL), a side product of pulp-and-paper industry, was proposed as an environmentally sustainable multifunctional agent for the modification of needle-punched nonwovens produced from regenerated lyocell fibres. Functionalization was attained by impregnating the nonwoven in a lignin solution (5-100 g/L) in 1-5% ammonia using the padding process followed by hot pressing of the dried mat at 180 °C for 2 min at 2 bar. This heat treatment carried out above the glass transition temperature of lignin allowed its better dispersion and adhesion to the fibre surface, particularly evident in the hydrophobicity of the nonwoven fabric and its resistance to leaching during washing. Tuneable nonwoven colour (from beige to dark brown), water contact angle (from 120° to 160°), improved tensile strength in machine direction, enhanced UV protection (UPF >50+), programmable thermal management response, and variable antimicrobial resistance against Gram-positive bacteria Staphylococcus aureus can be achieved while varying the amount of the retained lignin in the needle-punched structure. Although EKL imparts enhanced integrity to lyocell nonwovens fabrics during biodegradation, lignin-modified nonwovens still retain biodegradability and demonstrate the absence of concomitant phytotoxic effects. All-round balance of nonwoven fabrics properties was attained with a lignin content in the fabric of approximately 2.5%. This study positions EKL as a reliable bio-based multifunctional additive, enabling the development of sustainable, high-performance lyocell nonwovens aligned with circular economy principles through an environmentally responsible approach thus avoiding the hazardous functional agents originating from fossil resources.

title: A macro–micro nested coupling framework for assessing water resources carrying capacity in the Gansu section of the Yellow River Basin
Enhancing anaerobic digestion yield of agro-industrial residues using solid–liquid extraction: a microbiome assessment
abstract: Valorizing industrial agro-residues such as tomato pomace (TP) and potato peel (PP) within circular economy frameworks is crucial to reducing environmental burdens while recovering valuable compounds and bioenergy. This study investigates the potential of solid–liquid extraction (SLE) of TP and PP, applied before anaerobic digestion (AD), to enhance the associated microbial community and the biogas yield. Ethanol was employed as the extraction solvent to maximize the recovery of value-added compounds (e.g. phenolic molecules). The residual biomass post-extraction is significant (>90%) and was then used as substrate in batch AD tests to evaluate its biochemical methane potential (BMP). Microbiome analysis was also performed to elucidate the bacterial communities associated with the observed changes in AD performance following SLE. Chemical characterization of both extracts revealed a recovery of 1.1 and 2.3 mg gallic acid equivalents - GAE/g dried sample of PP and TP, respectively. BMP assays demonstrated that extracted biomass yielded higher methane production (>1.5x) relative to raw materials, suggesting that residual ethanol present in the extracted material positively influenced methane yield and biogas quality. Indeed, the microbiome revealed significantly different patterns, indicating that extracted materials promote the growth of specific microbial species. The AD of extracted materials containing residual ethanol exhibits lower microbial diversity, with the class Bacilli accounting for around 50% of the overall community. This result reflects significant microbiome adaptation to the altered substrate composition. The results support the implementation of valorization pathways that simultaneously generate value-added compounds and optimize biogas production, advancing the transition toward sustainable, circular bio-based systems.

title: A multi-dimensional circular economy maturity assessment framework for construction organisations
abstract: Recent advances in construction research have produced multiple circularity assessment frameworks that focus from material to whole-scale projects, covering various life cycle stages. These frameworks have been valuable for quantifying project-level outcomes, offering a short-term perspective, while overlooking the long-term circular economy (CE) transition. Recent studies therefore advocate shifting assessment to the construction organisational level, targeting the process improvement to generate consistent CE outcomes across projects. The maturity assessment framework is a promising approach, as it captures and guides organisational processes from initial to a desired state, thereby supporting long-term CE transition. Hence, this study aims to develop a multi-dimensional CE maturity assessment framework for construction organisations. To achieve the aim, three objectives were formulated: i) define the relevant Key Process Areas (KPAs), ii) determine the level of importance and categorise the KPAs, and iii) define the suitable assessment attributes to assess/operationalise the KPAs. Initially, the conceptual KPAs and assessment attributes were formulated based on previous studies on CE indicators for construction organisations. Subsequently, two Delphi-based expert forums were conducted. Forum 1 focused on verifying the suitability of conceptual KPAs and assessing their importance, while Forum 2 focused on verifying the suitability of assessment attributes. The results yielded 19 KPAs and 62 assessment attributes. Critical KPAs include material circularity improvement, circularity in building design and construction, waste circularity improvement, and greenhouse gas emissions reduction. Theoretically, this study addresses the organisational-level circularity assessment gap; in practice, it guides construction professionals toward circularity adoption by focusing on appropriate KPAs and assessment attributes.

title: Fluorite tailings derived NaA@MoS2 core-shell composites for efficient visible-light photodegradation of rhodamine B: performance and mechanism insights
A pore-structure-informed multiphysics carbonation model enabling evaluation of durability and CO2 sequestration potential of sustainable cementitious materials
Sustainable lithium extraction from low-grade aqueous resources via reverse Li/Mg separation enabled by hydrated cation-π interaction
How different acceptability modelling approaches influence sustainable diet solutions: an overview of methods and a case study
abstract: Diet optimisation modelling is increasingly used to design sustainable diets that meet nutritional and environmental goals. However, adequately capturing (cultural) acceptability in these models remains a major challenge. While most studies rely on a few common methods to address acceptability – defined as distance to observed diets – their impact on model outcomes is not well understood. This study systematically evaluated the extent to which different acceptability modelling approaches affect sustainable diet solutions. First, we reviewed existing strategies to incorporate acceptability into diet optimisation models. Second, we applied a selection of the most frequently used approaches in two models (iOTA Model® and SHARP Model) under consistent data and parameter conditions. Sixteen combinations of acceptability approaches were tested, covering different model components (algorithm, decision variables, objective function and constraints). Results showed that the choice of acceptability approach substantially influenced both the quantitative and qualitative outcomes of the models, although some consistent patterns emerged. Strong agreement was observed for meat (decreased consumption from 20% greenhouse gas emissions reduction onwards) and directional agreement for cereals, fish and seafood, fruits, legumes, nuts and seeds, potatoes, and vegetables (maintained or increased consumption). Minimal agreement was found for dairy products or substitutes, eggs, fats and oils, meat substitutes, and sugar-rich or salty foods. These findings underscore that methodological choices regarding acceptability influence sustainable diet solutions, with important implications for dietary recommendations and food policy. To enhance robustness and relevance, future studies should explicitly justify acceptability modelling choices and test multiple approaches to assess the sensitivity of model outcomes.

title: High-value recycling of waste PET/TPEE blends via supercritical CO2 foaming: Enhanced toughness and thermal insulation for lightweight applications
Carbon footprint analysis and its underlying drivers in a mega-urban region: Evidence from the Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei urban agglomeration
abstract: Achieving global climate targets under a shrinking carbon budget requires understanding not only where urban emissions occur, but how they are transmitted across intercity supply chains. Existing studies often quantify urban carbon footprints or decompose emission drivers separately, yet lack an integrated diagnostic framework capable of comparing structural emission dependence across cities within metropolitan regions. This study analyzes embodied carbon flows among 13 cities in China's Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei (BTH) urban agglomeration for 2012 and 2017 using environmentally extended input–output (EEIO) accounting combined with structural decomposition analysis (SDA). To translate complex supply-chain information into policy-interpretable diagnostics, we introduce two indicators: Coverage Rate (CR), measuring the breadth of sectoral amplification, and Resource-Chain Coverage (RCC), measuring dependence on upstream resource-intensive production chains. Results reveal a stable upstream–downstream production structure in which emission-intensive material production is spatially separated from final demand. Construction and service activities act primarily as demand-inducing sectors, generating large upstream emissions despite low direct emission intensity. Structural decomposition shows that efficiency improvements reduce emission intensity, but expanding consumption and investment scale offset these gains through supply-chain amplification along a materials–energy–construction corridor. Consequently, emission growth is driven less by local technological inefficiency than by intercity economic specialization and demand-induced production. The proposed CR–RCC framework links carbon accounting to coordinated mitigation planning by identifying structurally dependent cities and sectors rather than isolated emitters. Because it relies on benchmark input–output data rather than long time series, the approach is transferable to other urban agglomerations where supply-chain-driven emissions complicate city-level climate governance.

title: AI agent for carbon emission accounting and uncertainty analysis of Shanghai's electricity consumption
abstract: Accurate carbon emission accounting underpins decarbonization strategy development. However, the current manual methods for carbon emission accounting and uncertainty analysis are tedious, time-consuming, and costly. To solve these problems, an AI agent for carbon emission accounting consisting of reasoning-capable large language models (LLMs) and external tools was developed in this study. Using Shanghai's electricity consumption as a case study, the agent was adopted to quantify the electricity's carbon emissions, average carbon emission factors ( EF ele ), and their uncertainties, reconciling data from various sources. The total carbon emissions from electricity in Shanghai rose from 64.7 (95% confidence interval: 52.2-77.4) Mt CO 2 e yr −1 in 2000 to 110.3 Mt CO 2 e yr −1 in 2023 along with the increasing electricity consumption. Meanwhile, EF ele dropped from 1.1580 kg CO 2 e kWh −1 to 0.5966 kg CO 2 e kWh −1 owing to the increase in renewable electricity imported from other provinces. The agent could also automatically execute the pedigree matrix method to evaluate the uncertainty of the raw data. The quality control framework, consisting of three LLMs, achieved higher accuracy in raw data uncertainty analysis than individual LLMs across ten independent runs, demonstrating the reliability and reproducibility of the approach in the case study. The case study explores the possibility of a paradigm shift from manual calculation to an artificial intelligence-driven approach with an explicit verification process.

Barriers and drivers on the pathway to a future of localised circular fashion systems in the UK
abstract: Fast fashion has a detrimental impact on people and the planet, consuming excessive amounts of water, polluting the atmosphere, depleting resources and often operating in ways that exploit workers’ rights. Interest in the circular economy has been gaining momentum, a model capable of reducing resource use and pollution through ensuring that materials and products are used effectively and efficiently throughout the lifecycle, including life extension through practices like reuse, repair and upcycling. Although barriers and drivers to circularity in fashion are described in the literature, they focus on the present and are not holistic enough for the kinds of complex systems-wide temporal changes needed to be made into the future. The aim of this research is to uncover possible system-wide barriers and drivers anticipated to occur between now - 2025, and future - 2050, that can be influential in the development of a future UK-wide distributed network of localised clothing circular supply chains - the alternative to the global linear supply chain that exists today. Futures method - backcasting, was used to work backwards from a desirable future of localised circular fashion systems to determine a feasibility of that future based on events required to occur in order to reach it. Six workshops, involving a total of 22 participants, were conducted with stakeholders from the fashion industry who have experience across the supply chain, discussing and mapping barriers and drivers on a temporal scale of 25 years. These were distilled, identifying 15 social, political and economic barriers, and 15 corresponding drivers, distributed across the following categories: time; emotions; group dynamics and connectivity; knowledge and skills; consumer decisions and legislation; government structure; legislating industry; existential threats; financial budgets; infrastructure; systems thinking; materials innovation; capitalism, companies and currency; dominant narratives and access. The barriers, drivers are further presented across three parallel but interconnected temporal pathways across the social, political and economic subsystems. They form a network of anticipated events anticipated between 2025 and 2050 that can potentially hinder and support the society reaching a preferable future where localised circular fashion is the norm in the UK. The results help to foresee hurdles in the process of transitioning to a more sustainable and socially equitable local economy, offering opportunities to counteract and overcome them, and presenting a clear pathway of anticipated events. This research provides foundational knowledge for the development of a robust, comprehensive and actionable roadmap, thereby enabling the localised industry and policymakers to plan their collective action for a systemic industry-wide change.

title: Turning green under the spotlight? Environmental information disclosure, legitimacy manipulation, and green total factor productivity
A novel biological core material from Agave sisalana flower stalks for bio-based composite sandwich panels
abstract: Among plant-grown lignocellulose-based core materials, balsa wood remains unique for its combination of low density and high mechanical properties, making it the predominant natural alternative to petrochemical rigid foams in sandwich panels for low-density and structural applications. The flower stalk of Agave sisalana P. exhibits a rigid, foam-like cellular structure in its core, with densities lower than those of conventional balsa wood (57–84 kg/m 3 ). Given the growing demand for sustainable and circular material solutions, this work introduces this underutilised by-product of the sisal fibre production as a novel bio-based core material. This study presents a multi-scale characterisation using SEM and μCT to establish a relationship between cellular architecture and performance. This is supplemented by mechanical tests and analyses that assess structural, property, and sustainability performance indicators. The compressive properties demonstrate highly anisotropic behaviour. Flexural testing of the composite sandwich panels demonstrates that the agave core material has competitive strength (57.9 ± 4.3 MPa) and effective stiffness (94.35 ± 5.8 Nm 2 ), offering a sustainable alternative to balsa and petrochemical rigid foams such as PU, XPS, or rPET. Overall, the novel core material exhibits a lower performance-related environmental impact than balsa. Its lower density and comparable mechanical performance make it a promising sustainable core material for mass-efficient applications.

title: Impact of polysaccharides, proteins, lipids, and humic-like substances on thermal stability and flammability of wastewater sludge extracellular polymeric substances
abstract: The current study investigates the application of extracellular polymeric substances (EPS), recovered from municipal wastewater sludge, as sustainable flame-retardant materials. While EPS show significant fire-safety potential, their compositional complexity requires a clear understanding of fire performance. The primary objective of this research is to elucidate how key EPS components, such as proteins (PN), polysaccharides (PS), lipids (LP), and humic-like substances (HS), govern thermal decomposition and flammability. Thermogravimetric analysis reveals that PN and HS have higher activation energies than those of other components, enhancing EPS thermal stability. PS yield the highest char residue (48.7% at 900 °C), while PN achieve the highest graphitisation degree, highlighting their crucial roles in char formation of EPS. Pyrolysis gas analysis indicates that PN and HS are main sources of nitrogenous compounds, diluting oxygen. Moreover, flammability tests show PS have the lowest peak heat release rate (29.7 W/g), underlining the important role in increasing flame-retardancy of EPS. However, TGA-FTIR analysis indicates lipid as a primary source of combustible gases likely due to their hydrocarbon chains. This study provides valuable insight into the role of major EPS components in the flame-retardant properties and suggest a sustainable approach to enhance flame retardancy through targeted component optimisation.

Influence of post-consumer recycled polypropylene on the mechanical performance of glass fiber-reinforced polypropylene
abstract: Glass fiber-reinforced polypropylene (GFR-PP) is widely used for its excellent mechanical properties and low weight. However, sustainability concerns arise due to its reliance on virgin polymers and the difficulty of incorporating post-consumer recycled polypropylene (PCR-PP). This study investigates the effect of increasing PCR-PP content in GFR-PP composites. Particular attention is given to titanium dioxide (TiO 2 ), a common pigment in white polypropylene products that remains in post-consumer streams and becomes a contaminant in glass-fiber-reinforced compounds. To isolate its role, reference compounds were produced using virgin polypropylene with controlled additions of TiO 2 . Results reveal that TiO 2 is the primary driver of tensile performance loss due to its high hardness and sharp-edged particle morphology, which induce abrasive wear on the glass fibers during high-shear melt processing. This abrasive interaction caused a 22% reduction in average fiber length even at low concentrations (0.1–0.2 wt%), directly decreasing tensile strength from 77 MPa to 63 MPa. In contrast, impact strength declined progressively from 15.2 to 8.2 kJ/m 2 as recycled content reached 70%, indicating degradation mechanisms driven by matrix heterogeneity and incompatible polymer inclusions. These findings demonstrate that TiO 2 contamination governs fiber breakage and tensile loss, while matrix heterogeneity primarily controls impact resistance. By isolating these contributions, this study provides critical insights into mechanical property loss mechanisms in GFR-PP with rPP and highlights the need for improved sorting and filtration practices to enable higher recycled content in structural applications.

title: Within-industry heterogeneity of emission productivity: Evidence from Portuguese manufacturing firms
Investment intensity, technical efficiency and carbon emissions under the CAP: a conditional DEA analysis of the agricultural sector
abstract: Investment is crucial for farm modernisation, production processes, and profitability in agriculture. However, farm-level evidence remains limited, mainly due to data constraints and a predominant focus on the determinants of investment adoption (an input-oriented perspective), rather than on how annual investment effort relates to output-oriented efficiency outcomes across heterogeneous farm structures. This leaves an important gap in understanding the performance implications of investment behaviour within the CAP context. This study examines the conditional association between annual new fixed investment and output-oriented technical efficiency in Italian agriculture using a conditional Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) approach applied to farm-level data from the Italian Farm Accountancy Data Network (2011–2020). New investment effort measured the annual value of new fixed investments and reflects farms’ yearly efforts to renew and strengthen their productive capital base. Findings show that younger farm holders and larger farms invest more on average, whereas smaller farms achieve larger efficiency improvements relative to their investment levels. In addition, a descriptive assessment of carbon emission intensity suggests that farms characterised by higher conditional efficiency tend to display lower emission intensity, indicating potential environmental co-benefits associated with investment-related efficiency improvements.

title: Terrain-constrained functional zoning and driver attribution for resource-efficient sustainability governance in a mountain urban agglomeration
Continuous plastic film mulching reduces global warming potential (GWP) in greenhouse soil biosolarization by regulating microbial carbon and nitrogen metabolism
Sustainable nitrogen management in maize: environmental benefits of integrating microbial biostimulants and nitrification inhibitors
abstract: Biostimulants and nitrification inhibitors are promising tools to improve nitrogen dynamics in agricultural soils and reduce associated environmental impacts. In Europe, these solutions are increasingly promoted to improve nitrogen use efficiency and losses, yet farm-level evidence of their combined environmental performance in maize remains limited. This study evaluated whether applying a microbial biostimulant (Methylobacterium symbioticum SB23) with a nitrapyrin-based nitrification inhibitor can mitigate the environmental impacts of maize in Italy. A cradle-to-farm-gate LCA was performed on 14 farms, comparing a conventional scenario (CS) with an alternative scenario (AS) applying the two products while reducing mineral N fertilization. Three functional units were assessed: 1 tonne maize grain (14% moisture), 1 tonne high-moisture corn (25% DM), and 1 tonne fresh chopped maize (35% DM). Inventory modelling combined primary on-farm data from questionnaires and interviews with secondary data, including Brentrup's N balance for N emissions. Across farms and functional units, AS generally lowered nitrogen-driven categories, climate change, acidification, particulate matter formation, and terrestrial eutrophication, reflecting reduced mineral N inputs and inhibited nitrification. For grain, 10 of 11 impact categories decreased (−2% to −50%); for high-moisture corn, 8 of 11 decreased (−1% to −87%); and for silage, 10 of 11 decreased (−1% to −83%). Trade-offs emerged: marine eutrophication occasionally increased where fertilizer reductions were limited and the biostimulant enhanced soil N availability, increasing NO3 - leaching. Contribution analysis confirmed category hotspots: NH 3 volatilization for acidification, particulate matter, and terrestrial eutrophication, N 2 O for climate change, NO 3− leaching for marine eutrophication, and crop protection products for freshwater ecotoxicity. Overall, integrating a microbial biostimulant with a nitrification inhibitor can substantially reduce most impacts of maize cultivation.

title: Assessment of installable offshore solar power capacity in Spain based on maritime spatial planning
abstract: The growing demand for electricity highlights the need for new renewable energy solutions beyond land-based systems. Floating offshore photovoltaic technology has emerged as a promising alternative, offering large available areas and improved efficiency due to the cooling effect of seawater. However, its deployment is strongly constrained by marine spatial planning regulations, which are not yet specifically defined for this technology. This study aims to estimate the maximum installable offshore solar potential in Spain by integrating technical constraints with planning-based restrictions. A spatially explicit methodology is developed using the Merganser floating platform as a reference and adapting existing regulatory criteria currently defined for offshore wind. Two scenarios are analyzed: (i) areas compatible with offshore wind development, representing a technically favorable context, and (ii) areas subject to broader spatial restrictions, including environmental protection and competing marine uses. Although Scenario 2 presents a substantially larger available area (15,574.5 km 2 ) compared to Scenario 1 (3127.4 km 2 ), the estimated installable potential is lower, reaching 4.45 GW versus 6.48 GW. This result is explained by the prevalence of spatially constrained areas in Scenario 2 that do not meet the minimum surface requirements for the installation of individual platforms, thereby limiting the effective use of the available area and reducing platform density. These findings highlight the importance of jointly considering technical and planning-based constraints when assessing offshore solar potential and provide a methodological framework to support realistic large-scale deployment of this emerging technology in Spain.

Income-segmented intention-to-adoption pathways for organic food in Lima, Peru: A survey-informed system dynamics analysis
abstract: Organic food uptake in unequal urban markets often remains below stated consumer interest, especially among lower-income groups. This matters for sustainable consumption and cleaner production because broader demand is one condition under which more sustainable food systems can move beyond niche markets. This study presents a survey-informed, scenario-based System Dynamics analysis of income-segmented intention-to-adoption pathways for organic food in Lima, Peru. Drawing on an archived survey of 509 valid millennial respondents and segment-specific weights derived through the Analytic Hierarchy Process, the model tests five mechanism-specific scenario families across segments D, C, and A-B over a 30-month horizon: social influence, subsidy-based reductions in economic effort, their joint dynamic activation, knowledge of benefits and environmental awareness, and ethical-value activation. The results are clearly segmented. The largest end-of-horizon improvement appears in segment D when affordability relief and social reinforcement operate jointly (ΔP = 0.123), followed by social influence alone (ΔP = 0.087) and subsidy-based relief (ΔP = 0.051). Knowledge of benefits and environmental awareness in segment C produces a more modest gain (ΔP = 0.012), while ethical-value activation in segment A-B provides bounded directional evidence (ΔP = 0.020). These findings suggest that intention-to-adoption pathways under urban inequality are better understood as dynamic, non-additive, and segment-specific than as the outcome of a single common driver. All results should be read as scenario-based evidence on differentiated modeled pathways, not as direct observation or external validation of real purchasing behavior.

title: The spatial impact of pixel scale PM2.5 driven by policy dissemination. New evidence from a super urban agglomeration

Mapping business ecosystems using AI: A case study on energy transition
abstract: This study explores the application of artificial intelligence (AI) for mapping business ecosystems, particularly in the context of the energy transition, a phenomenon of global significance that requires the interaction of multiple industries, nations, technologies, innovations, and regulatory frameworks. An AI-driven method is introduced to process large-scale textual data and construct business ecosystems as social networks. By analyzing datasets from academic papers, online news, regulatory documents, and a combined dataset, the scalability and accuracy of these ecosystems were assessed. The validity of the method was tested through an expert survey involving 90 professionals across 9 countries, multiple industries, and diverse roles. Regression analysis revealed a statistically significant relationship between network centrality scores and expert assessments, demonstrating the robustness of the method. The combined dataset provided the highest model fit but required significant computational effort. In contrast, academic papers offered a more efficient and interpretable alternative, achieving similar accuracy with significantly lower processing demands and noise. The findings suggest that AI-driven methods can standardize, automate, and enhance real-world ecosystem mapping, reducing analyst subjectivity and improving scalability. This type of mapping is useful in both theory and practice because it enables scholars and decision-makers to identify structural dependencies, coordination patterns, and bottlenecks that may not be visible through manual analysis, thereby informing strategic positioning, diversification, scenario planning, and policy design. Future research should explore alternative AI models and validation methods, higher levels of functional aggregation, and longitudinal analyses to advance the study of energy ecosystems.

title: Biogas production from Co-digestion of chicken litter, swine manure, and whey: A comparative study of batch and semi-continuous regimes

Not all mining is equal: The impact of lithium production technology on land, water, and emissions footprints through 2040
abstract: As electrification accelerates, global lithium demand is rising. Lithium production pathways—hard rock mining, brine evaporation, and direct lithium extraction (DLE)—exhibit distinct land, water, and greenhouse gas footprints. We analyze how adoption of DLE, an emerging extraction technology, could reshape these impacts through 2040 under three global supply scenarios. Using Benchmark Mineral Intelligence 2024 supply projections, we constructed a business-as-usual (BAU), a moderately aggressive DLE, and an aggressive DLE scenario. The amount of lithium carbonate equivalent (LCE; a standard measure that expresses lithium content across different compounds in terms of lithium carbonate) produced each year was constant across scenarios. We mapped footprints of operational hard-rock mines and evaporation facilities and combined these with literature-derived impact factors (CO 2 emissions and freshwater consumption per ton of LCE) and representative DLE facility data to estimate future land use, freshwater consumption, and CO 2 emissions. Under BAU, hard rock and evaporation have similar current footprints (∼300 km 2 ) and together add ∼600 km 2 by 2040, while DLE's facility footprint is minimal (50 km 2 added under BAU). Shifting to DLE (moderate/aggressive scenarios) could avoid 141–381 km 2 of land conversion (20-50% reduction), reduce total freshwater use by ∼11% −32%, and lower CO 2 emissions by ∼9%-44%, respectively. Deployment of DLE technologies offers a technically plausible pathway to substantially reduce the land, water, and climate footprints of lithium supply, though realized benefits will depend strongly on DLE technology choice, site reinjection practices, energy sources, and the rate at which DLE can scale and displace other lithium production pathways.

Modelling the performance of emerging last-mile modes in 90 European pedestrian zones
abstract: This article compares the operational performance and sustainability of drones, autonomous delivery robots (ADRs), and electric cargo e-bikes through a simulation framework developed for pedestrian zones in 90 European cities. For each city, 200 parcels were assigned to evaluate mode-specific routing, energy use, cost, and service performance. Multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) was used to incorporate stakeholder perspectives. E-bikes combine the lowest energy demand with the low unit cost. ADRs offer the quietest, most space-efficient ground operation, halving drone energy use while matching bike cost, though their pedestrian speed lengthens service time. Drones deliver the shortest point-to-point travel time, 6–11 % quicker than bikes, but at higher externalities. Stakeholder-weighted MCDA scores average 0.83 for bikes, 0.61 for ADRs and 0.18 for drones, placing each mode first in one core attribute: overall sustainability (bike), low-impact night delivery (ADR) and urgent response (drone). The findings suggest policy mixes that fund cargo-bike infrastructure for routine flows, license ADR fleets for quiet off-peak distribution, and reserve drones for time-critical or topographically constrained drops. Such differentiated deployment can support decarbonisation, protect pedestrian comfort and maintain service quality in Europe's historic urban cores.

Assessing container glass production decarbonization through amine scrubbing, calcium looping and electrification: a comparative techno-economic analysis
abstract: This study performs a techno-economic assessment of decarbonization pathways for container glass production. A reference glass plant with a capacity of 250 t/day is modelled in Aspen Plus, implementing an end-fired regenerative furnace. Three alternative and decarbonized configurations are explored: (i) post-combustion CO 2 capture via calcium looping (Case 1), (ii) CO 2 absorption using monoethanolamine solvents (Case 2), (iii) system electrification through a modular approach involving two cold top vertical melting furnaces of 140 t/day each (Case 3). The energy, environmental and economic performances of the processes are compared aiming at identifying the most promising solutions for sector decarbonization in the short and long terms. Carbon capture by calcium looping cycles significantly increases energy consumption (from 7.5 to 10.1 GJ/t glass ), whereas MEA scrubbing results in a moderate increase (7.9 GJ/t glass ) due to extensive heat recovery for solvent regeneration. The fully electric configuration drastically reduces natural gas consumption but increases electricity demand (from 1.24 to 3.8 GJ/t glass ). All options reduce direct CO 2 emissions by more than 76% compared with the reference case. In a medium-term scenario, MEA scrubbing emerges as the most economically competitive option under current energy prices and CO 2 tax of 100 €/t CO2 , with a cost penalty of only 18 €/t glass . In contrast, full electrification could achieve economic attractiveness in a long-term scenario, involving higher natural gas prices, lower electricity costs and higher carbon tax.

title: Beyond performance-cost trade-off: Engineered Geopolymer Composites (EGC) incorporating ultra-high-volume coal gangue wastes
Integrated bioprocessing of garlic peel waste: Dual valorization through prodigiosin production using Serratia marcescens NITDPER1 and sustainable nanocarbon dots synthesis
End-of-life biodegradation and enzymatic hydrolysis kinetics of regenerated cellulose soft electronics: Influence of silver nanowires, silver ions, and substrate composition
abstract: The rapid growth of electronic devices use has intensified concerns over electronic waste, emphasizing the need for biodegradable alternatives that align with cleaner production and circular economy principles. Regenerated cellulose films (RCFs) are renewable substrates with demonstrated biodegradability, but the environmental compatibility of complete electronic devices remains uncertain when additives and conductive materials are incorporated. Here, we investigate the end-of-life behavior of RCF-based soft electronics with screen-printed silver nanowires (AgNWs), combining ISO 14851 closed-bottle respirometry aquatic biodegradation with controlled enzymatic hydrolysis. Biodegradation profiles were quantitatively evaluated using the Gompertz model, which confirmed that glycerol and PEGDE (Poly(ethylene glycol) diglycidyl ether) modifications enhanced microbial mineralization of RCFs, while the addition of AgNWs slightly lowered the average ultimate extent of biodegradation; however, the cellulose films remained biodegradable, generally reaching more than 60% extent of biodegradation within 28 days. Enzymatic hydrolysis kinetics were fitted with the Chrastil model, revealing diffusion-limited behavior in crystalline microcrystalline cellulose (MCC) and higher accessibility in amorphous RCFs. Comparative assays showed strong inhibition by ionic silver, particularly in MCC, where the product concentration decreased by up to 50%. In contrast, RCFs maintained high hydrolysis yields (78–84%) and only slight reductions in hydrolysis rates. Visual analysis indicated in situ reduction of silver ions into metallic nanoparticles, with color variations attributed to nanoparticle aggregation and substrate crystallinity. Overall, RCF-based devices incorporating screen-printed AgNWs remained biodegradable, though overall biodegradation performance depended on silver form and coverage. By integrating mechanistic insights, kinetic modeling, and standardized biodegradation metrics, this work highlights how additives and conductive materials influence cellulose degradation and provides a framework for assessing the environmental fate of biodegradable soft electronics, supporting circular end-of-life management.

title: Compatibility assessment and comprehensive evaluation model for co-production of natural gas hydrate and shallow gas
Uncovering the interaction between surface water heavy metal pollution and industry-induced pressures in Chinese cities
Sufficiency in principle and practice: An operational definition and typology
abstract: Sufficiency is emerging as a necessary concept as safe and just Earth system boundaries are increasingly transgressed, yet its definition and operationalisation remain fragmented. In this paper, we provide an operational definition for the concept, defining sufficiency as a state of enoughness that avoids both deficiency and excess in relation to fair social and ecological limits. Then, we develop a typology for the classification and analysis of practical sufficiency measures through a theory-informed content analysis of 1,101 proposed measures drawn from three diverse datasets. The resulting typology identifies five distinct types of sufficiency measures: quantitative, qualitative, use, sharing, and steering. To demonstrate the applicability of our typology, we test it against 33 policies presented in the “Sufficiency Manifesto” for the European Union, classifying policies based on the sufficiency measure type and whether they targeted the household, private, or public sector. Our analysis shows that all five types of sufficiency measures were present, though unevenly, with sharing measures least represented. This demonstrates how the typology can reveal patterns or gaps in current approaches and highlight opportunities for more comprehensive strategies. By developing an operational definition of sufficiency, clarifying its implications in both principle and practice, and offering a typological tool for analysing sufficiency measures across sectors and scales, this study advances the conceptual foundations and operationalisation of sufficiency, providing an empirically grounded framework for its systematic application.

title: Electrolysis with ultrafiltration membrane as a pretreatment for seawater desalination
abstract: The work explores the feasibility of applying membrane electrolysis incorporated with a low-cost ultrafiltration (UF) membrane as an alternative seawater pretreatment process. For the first time, this study evaluates the potential of replacing anolyte Na 2 SO 4 with seawater in both UF membrane electrolysis chamber, eliminating chemical anolyte requirement, paving the way for a chemical-free pretreatment. Likewise, the novel approach of incorporating activated carbon (AC) submerged in the electrolysis chamber as a supplementary flow electrode material is examined. The combination of dual chamber seawater UF membrane electrolysis incorporated with AC removed up to 99% of Ca 2+ and Mg 2+ , while also efficiently removing boron and bromide. Dispersed AC provides high-surface-area adsorption sites and functions as a network of conductive micro-electrodes. This adsorption-electrochemical interaction synergy enabled 60% boron removal in the catholyte, against 38% without AC. AC also improved anode-side bromide oxidation, attaining 99.5% removal while inhibiting the chlorine evolution reaction (CER), increasing selectivity and overall process efficiency. Operating at a reduced current density of 4 mA cm −2 resulted in comparable seawater ion removal efficiency within 5 h as that at 8 mA cm −2 , with 51% lower energy consumption. Also, Ca and Mg can be recovered as Ca(OH) 2 and Mg(OH) 2 , providing a low-carbon route to raw limestone mining for cement feedstock production. These findings establish that AC-assisted UF membrane electrolysis as an alternative low chemical and scalable pretreatment platform for seawater pretreatment.

title: Integrative design process for structural optimization: A life cycle assessment-driven approach for sustainable office building design
Manure and sewage dominate nitrate sources in runoff from key headwaters area in China
Integrating circularity and lifecycle assessment for building renovation: A multicycle framework
abstract: There exist different circularity indicators and lifecycle assessment (LCA) methodologies to calculate resource efficiency and environmental impacts of the building sector. But they largely operate within single-lifecycle boundaries and lack a consistent approach for assessing material across multiple lifecycles in existing buildings. This study addresses this gap by adapting the Material Circularity Indicator (MCI) assessment approach for the renovation of buildings (MCI RENO ), which accounts for successive lifecycles of the materials generated from the renovation. The MCI RENO is integrated with the Circular Footprint Formula (CFF) to provide a methodological operational unified framework for evaluating circularity and environmental impacts. Using a systematic selection process, seven end-of-life-cycle allocation methodologies were compared to identify the CFF's point of integration with MCI RENO . In the framework, the MCI RENO incorporates extended lifetimes and reuse potential, while CFF allocates environmental burdens and credits across multiple loops using standardized factors. The framework is validated with an empirical example of façade brick using seven scenarios and probabilistic uncertainty analysis of key parameters. The analyses reveal that material recoverability drives the degree of circularity and is sensitive towards varying scenarios. Similarly, environmental outcomes remain scenario-dependent and primarily driven by avoided virgin material production. The combined results are sensitive to contextual and scenario-specific assumptions. The approach offers a structured framework to jointly evaluate multicycle circularity and environmental impacts of inert materials. Future research across heterogeneous materials and renovation complexity can strengthen the robustness of the proposed framework.

title: Linking land cover changes to carbon storage in Hunan Province, China: Insights from multi-task learning
abstract: Long-term land cover dynamics are a key regulator of regional carbon storage, yet most assessments still rely on a few temporal snapshots and therefore overlook how land transitions unfold over time. Here we reconstruct annual land cover in Hunan Province, China, from 1990 to 2023 using a multi-task deep learning framework, and combine it with climate-corrected carbon accounting, driver attribution and future scenario simulation. Although total carbon storage increased from 2122.74 Mt in 1990 to 2209.98 Mt in 2023 in Hunan, this net gain masked pronounced spatial heterogeneity and distinct carbon responses to land cover transition frequency and pathways. Trajectory analysis further showed that different change frequencies and transition pathways produced distinct carbon consequences, with return-type pathways tending toward near-neutral responses and directional pathways leading to clearer carbon gains or losses. The dominant drivers of carbon storage were also not stationary, with vegetation condition prevailing in 2000 and 2020, whereas population density became most important in 2010. Interactions among vegetation condition, topography, and population density mainly shaped spatial heterogeneity in carbon storage. Historical-trend simulation further indicates that regional carbon storage growth may decelerate sharply by 2030, with only a marginal increase of 1.35 Mt relative to 2020. These findings are particularly concerning because the potential to offset the carbon costs of continued urban expansion through land conversion alone may be increasingly limited, making the protection of existing high-carbon ecological spaces more urgent.

title: Hybrid fiber-reinforced shield muck-slag-based engineered geopolymer composites: multiscale thermomechanical behavior and sustainability assessment
Optimizing CO2 absorption and desorption in water-based nanofluids: Predictive modeling and analysis of multifactor interactions
Completing the puzzle of aged microplastics towards microalgae at environmental concentration: effects of polymer type, size, aging method, and aging duration
Sustainability assessment of advanced calcium looping solutions for the decarbonization of the iron and steel industry
abstract: Achieving the 1.5°C climate target by 2050 requires urgent action in the steelmaking sector, as it contributes by about 7% to global CO 2 emissions. With Electric Arc Furnace (EAF) routes representing 30% of global production, their decarbonization is critical to sector-wide emission reductions. The current study evaluates the environmental implications of an EAF equipped with a Calcium Looping (CaL) based carbon capture unit via Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) methodology. The environmental analysis follows a cradle-to-gate approach and it is conducted using the ReCiPe 2016 assessment method. Four distinct CaL configurations featuring variations such as intermediate solid storage and/or calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH) 2 , injection were investigated, each assessed under two alternative CO 2 transportation scenarios: T1 – onshore pipeline followed by offshore shipping, and T2 – onshore truck transportation followed by offshore shipping. The findings suggest more than 63% Global Warming Potential (GWP) reduction in the advanced CaL configurations as against standard strategies, primarily due to Ca(OH) 2 injection (i.e., enhanced CO 2 capture efficiency) and CO 2 purification unit (CPU) vent gas recirculation. However, these improvements are offset by higher impacts in Fossil Depletion Potential (FDP), Mineral Depletion Potential (MDP), Photochemical Oxidant Formation Potential ecosystem (POFP ecosystem ), Photochemical Oxidant Formation Potential human health (POFP human-health ), Stratospheric Ozone Depletion Potential (ODP), and Terrestrial Ecotoxicity Potential (TETP). Of the two CO 2 transportation pathways, T1 and T2 show similar values in five indicators (i.e., Freshwater Ecotoxicity Potential – FETP, Freshwater Eutrophication Potential – FEP, Human Toxicity Potential cancer – HTP cancer , MDP, and HTP non-cancer ), yet T1 outperforms T2 in terms of GWP, FDP, POFP ecosystem , POFP human-health , ODP, and TETP. Of all scenarios, the advanced CaL configuration with two intermediate storage tanks coupled with T1 exhibits the best overall environmental performance. A detailed analysis reveals that the CO 2 transportation contributes around 16.8 kg CO2 eq. /t CO2 captured , emphasizing the importance of developing alternative transport strategies to reduce associated emissions.

Enhancing microbial oils production from food waste-derived short-chain fatty acids via gas-permeable membrane nitrogen recovery
abstract: Short-chain fatty acids-rich fermentation liquids from food waste acidogenic fermentation contain high nitrogen concentrations that hinder lipid accumulation in yeast. Thus, achieving high carbon/nitrogen (C/N) ratio remains a key challenge for the valorization of fermentation liquors for microbial oils production. This work demonstrates the integration of nitrogen recovery using a gas-permeable membrane (GPM) with lipid production by oleaginous yeast. This nitrogen recovery from the fermentation liquids increased the C/N in fermentation broths, thereby boosting lipid accumulation. Specifically, GPM was able to recover 97 % of ammoniacal nitrogen in fermentation liquids, doubling the C/N and increasing lipid content by 2-3-fold in shake flask cultivations. Scaling up the process to a lab-scale bioreactor further increased lipid accumulation, reaching up to 30 % w/w lipids (4-fold increase) due to more controlled operational conditions. The study also evaluated the ability of Yarrowia lipolytica to metabolize organic and inorganic nitrogen sources, which is important to understand how the C/N influences microbial oils production. Although Y. lipolytica showed a preference for inorganic nitrogen ( i.e. , ammonium sulfate), bovine serum albumin was also consumed, though at approximately half the consumption rate. Overall, these finding prove that nitrogen recovery via GPM is an effective strategy to increase the C/N of fermentation liquids and promote lipid accumulation in yeast, therefore contributing to the development of an integrated waste-to-resource system within a circular economy framework.

title: Evaluating the sustainability of Montado farm's pastures: Insights from emergy and nitrogen footprint assessments of pastures with reduced productivity
abstract: The Montado ecosystem, a Mediterranean agro-silvo-pastoral system, plays a vital role in sustainable livestock production, yet faces increasing challenges from climate variability and pasture productivity decline. This study evaluates the sustainability of two Montado farms integrating cattle and sheep production by applying emergy and nitrogen footprint assessment under three different pasture productivity scenarios. Emergy indicators highlight the reliance on external resources during droughts, while nitrogen (N) footprint analysis underscores the potential environmental costs of maintaining livestock productivity under such conditions. Results indicate that cattle production is more emergy-efficient under regular pasture productivity, whereas sheep production consistently exhibits lower N losses and lower sensitivity to pasture decline. Integrating emergy and N footprint assessments reveals that increasing reliance on external feed to compensate for pasture reduction leads to higher resource dependence and N losses, particularly in cattle systems. These findings support management strategies that prioritize pasture-based feeding, promote legume-rich pastures to enhance N efficiency, and encourage mixed sheep–cattle systems as a means to buffer sustainability trade-offs under increasing climatic variability.

title: Exploring necessary and sufficient values in driving consumers’ willingness to pay premiums and purchase intentions for green food
Labor and education factors' empirical enlightenment on environmental-economic decoupling: Evidence from China
Tracking the carbon footprint of the iron and steel industry along the supply chain: From the urban agglomeration level
Closed-loop recycling of End-of-Life tires via devulcanized rubber: Life Cycle Assessment and circularity evaluation with durability trade-offs
abstract: More than 3 million tons of End-of-Life Tires (ELTs) are generated annually in Europe, with 91–95% currently managed through down-cycling processes for energy or material recovery. An Italian consortium has recently developed a closed-loop recycling process that enables the use of ELTs for producing new heavy-transportation tires. The baseline formulation has been validated through large-scale road testing, demonstrating performance comparable to traditional tires. This study evaluates the environmental performance and circularity of tread compounds incorporating devulcanized elastomer obtained from ELTs. Using Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) and the Material Circularity Indicator (MCI), four formulations were assessed: a traditional virgin compound and three containing 20%, 30%, and 50% recycled elastomer (20R–80V, 30R–70V, and 50R–50V, respectively, where R and V indicate recycled and virgin rubber content). The LCA results show that natural rubber is the main contributor to the environmental impacts, accounting for more than half of the burdens in most categories. Partial substitution with devulcanized elastomer leads to consistent impact reductions, with global warming potential decreasing by 13% in the validated 20R–80V formulation. Higher recycled-content formulations offer greater potential benefits; however, sensitivity analysis highlights that these benefits strongly depend on durability. Reductions in performance can significantly offset the environmental gains, indicating that durability represents a critical threshold parameter. The circularity assessment further confirms the advantages of both material substitution and recycling pathways: the MCI increases from 0.46 for a virgin tread sent to energy recovery, to 0.73 when recycled, and up to 0.79 when devulcanized elastomer is incorporated. Overall, devulcanized elastomer can effectively improve both environmental performance and circularity, provided that adequate durability is maintained.

Recycling of vanadium-extraction tailings by controllable aluminothermic reduction process
Operational cost impacts of tertiary treatment in wastewater treatment plants: An inverse optimization approach
abstract: Wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) are critical infrastructure in urban water management. However, their operation entails substantial costs that must be accurately assessed to support informed policy and regulatory decision-making. Directive (EU) 2024/3019 introduces more stringent nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) removal requirements for WWTPs, with potentially significant economic implications. This study develops and applies a novel methodological framework to estimate the increase in operational expenditure (OPEX) required for WWTPs to comply with these new standards while preserving their existing techno-economic efficiency. The proposed framework is based on inverse data envelopment analysis and enables the quantification of plant-specific compliance costs. An empirical application to 74 Spanish WWTPs reveals substantial heterogeneity in both current efficiency levels and the additional OPEX required to meet regulatory targets. On average, compliance with Directive (EU) 2024/3019 increases total OPEX by 25.9%, corresponding to an average increase of approximately 0.134 €/m 3 , although cost impacts vary widely across facilities and are not systematically related to plant size or baseline efficiency. While most WWTPs can achieve the required N and P removal levels without efficiency losses, the largest fully efficient plants face structural constraints that limit further performance improvements. Overall, the proposed framework provides a transferable, plant-level tool to support ex-ante regulatory impact assessments and informed investment and tariff decisions under evolving environmental policy frameworks.

title: Assessment of cost and environmental impacts of single point incremental forming and deep drawing for a range of production volumes
A practical framework for evaluating phosphorus redistribution after dewatering in tailings dry disposal
Toward green and sustainable pad-dyeing of polyester: a microcapsule-enabled low-water and recyclable process
Partial oxidation for blue hydrogen production: Techno-economic assessment of low-temperature carbon capture technologies
abstract: Hydrogen produced by partial oxidation (POx) integrated with carbon capture systems (CCS) remains critically underexplored compared to steam methane reforming (SMR), despite its inherent advantages of higher natural gas conversion and reduced external heating requirements. This study fills that gap by presenting the first comprehensive environmental and techno-economic assessment of POx coupled with cryogenic carbon capture (CCC) and amine-based absorption (ABS) at capture rates of 95% and 98%, at a production scale of 600 MWth. Six hydrogen production configurations are evaluated: a baseline SMR, unabated POx, and four POx-CCS variants (POx-CCC-95, POx-CCC-98, POx-ABS-95, POx-ABS-98) not previously assessed together in the literature. Performance is benchmarked across net efficiency, specific CO 2 emissions, capital and operating costs, levelised cost of hydrogen (LCOH), cost of CO 2 avoided (CCA), and investment payback periods. Our findings reveal, for the first time, that POx-CCC integrated systems show higher efficiency (∼59%) than amine-based CCS (∼55–56%). Integrating CCS cuts emissions from 93.91 gCO 2 eq/MJ (H 2 ) in unabated POx to 18.66–21.20 gCO 2 eq/MJ (H 2 ) for CCC and 27.34–29.12 gCO 2 eq/MJ (H 2 ) for amine-based, with only CCC (at 98% capture rate) meeting the UK Low Carbon Hydrogen Standard, a regulatory threshold not previously evaluated in this technology context. We further demonstrate that CCS integration increases the LCOH by 13–20% relative to unabated POx. Sensitivity analysis identifies natural-gas price as the main driver of LCOH, while plant cost most strongly affects CCA. Meanwhile, increasing carbon price reduces the CCA across all CCS cases.

title: Framework for assessing sustainability from an organizational perspective in early chemical product and process design
abstract: This work presents a framework for sustainability assessment during the early design stages of chemical products and processes from an organizational perspective by incorporating prioritization factors. The framework follows a progressive approach, beginning with a set of sustainability principles at a strategic level. These are gradually translated into specific criteria, providing guidance for designers when comparing different alternatives, which are subsequently evaluated through indicators, calculated based on specific system properties or operating conditions. This hierarchical approach helps information transfer from the strategic to the operational level, where technical design occurs, allowing the designers to align engineering decisions with the organization's sustainability objectives. The framework is applied in four stages: i) definition of principles and criteria according to organizational priorities; ii) identification of alternatives and information gathering; iii) assessment of alternatives through a multicriteria decision analysis method (MCDA); and iv) Decision-making. Two case studies are presented: the selection of a chemical route to produce a chemical product (i.e. ethyl acetate) and the design of structured product (i.e. cosmetic) containing it. In this case, the MCDA was conducted by using MAUT method. Utility functions were defined considering the meaning of the indicators, as interpreted through principles from the organizational context. The proposed methodology could be further used in the design of products and processes for different industries.

title: The balance of complexation and decomposition determines the sequestration behaviors of heavy metals from acidic wastewater by chelating captures
Digital content for environmental change: The roles of credibility, usefulness, entertainment, and emotions in driving pro-environmental behaviours across education level
Compliance over performance in sustainable public procurement? Evidence from regulatory reforms in Slovakia
A numerical model for quantifying the hydrological performance of clogged permeable brick pavement based on pilot-scale experiments
Guiding sustainable waste management: LCA-based evaluation of trade-offs in high-quality recycling of paper and board from lightweight packaging waste
abstract: The expanding global market of fiber-based composite packaging and rising recycling targets necessitate high-quality recycling routes, which involve the reutilization of fibers in comparable applications. As existing treatment routes for paper and board (PB) from German lightweight packaging waste are limited to thermal recovery and low-quality recycling abroad, a novel process for high-quality recycling has been developed. This raises the question: Can high-quality recycling in Germany enhance recycling rates while simultaneously reducing environmental impacts compared with existing treatment routes? To address this question, we conducted a comparative life cycle assessment (LCA) with the functional unit “Treatment of 1 ton PB”. Analyzed scenarios were incineration, low-quality recycling abroad and novel high- and low-quality domestic recycling processes. We used primary data from technical assessments to establish a comprehensive model foundation for our study. Our results indicate that the main contributors to global warming potential (GWP), cumulative energy demand (CED), land occupation potential (LOP), and water consumption potential (WCP) are transport, stock preparation, and thermal treatment across all scenarios. For high-quality recycling, GWP decreased from 148 to 93 kg CO 2 -Eq/t compared with recycling abroad but increased compared with incineration with 51 kg CO 2 -Eq/t. CED and LOP decreased from −483 to −2,533 MJ-Eq/t and from −83 to −156 m 2 ∗a crop-Eq/t, respectively, when comparing high-quality recycling with recycling abroad. No significant differences were found for WCP. These findings provide essential guidance for developing circular economy strategies and legal frameworks by highlighting the importance of LCA in minimizing trade-offs and burden shifting in waste management.

title: Valorization of allelochemical-rich olive pomace: Comprehensive effect microbial nutrient release and ursolic acid-enhanced uptake improve crop growth and quality
abstract: Biomass can be recycled into organic fertilizers, but allelochemicals in some residues restrict their safe use. Using olive pomace (OP) as an example, we prepared an Olive Pomace Microbial Organic Fertilizer (OPMOF) through microbial fermentation. Pot experiments showed that, compared with a commercial organic fertilizer applied at the same rate, OPMOF increased Brassica chinensis yield by 27.5%. Effective microorganisms enhanced soil available nutrients and crop quality, and increased gram-negative bacteria, generating more C 12 -AHL to promote lateral root development. Importantly, this study demonstrated the concentration-dependent physiological effects of ursolic acid (UA) in OPMOF and provided evidence for these effects: low UA upregulated the expression of root respiratory-chain genes, was associated with enhanced ATP synthesis, and improved nutrient uptake in multiple crops, whereas high UA inhibited growth. However, the in situ interaction between microbial activity and UA effects remains to be experimentally verified. Overall, this study provides a promising strategy for the high-value utilization of allelochemical-rich agricultural wastes and highlights the potential of allelochemicals in developing plant growth-promoting products.

title: A perspective on the role of multi-criteria decision-making in assessing the sustainability of alternative shipping fuels
abstract: According to the fourth “International Maritime Organization greenhouse gas study”, the combustion of fossil fuels such as heavy fuel oil in the shipping sector was responsible for 2.9% of global anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions in 2018. These emissions can potentially be reduced through alternative fuels with low or zero-carbon footprints. Of issue, however, is the high financial investment and lead in time for development of facilities to produce these fuels, and the assessment of which of the fuel systems should be prioritised. Multi-Criteria Decision Making (MCDM) methods can aid decision-makers in comparing alternative fuels from technical and sustainability perspectives. MCDM provides methodologies to deal with multiple, often conflicting, criteria with varying degrees of importance. This paper provides a perspective on the use of the MCDM methods for comparing alternative shipping fuels. The work indicates that: 1) future research must use Life Cycle Assessment for a more holistic approach to assessing the environmental impact of each fuel; 2) process simulation software can be used to develop the data required for comparing different fuel production pathways; 3) objective weighting methods can be used more in future research; 4) input from port stakeholders must be considered in future research; and 5) to generate a robust comparison, infrastructural requirements must be considered.

title: From barns to atmosphere: Pakistan's livestock manure-derived NH3, N2O, and CH4 emissions (1961–2022) and cleaner production pathways
Synergistic acid–sodium bisulfite pretreatment of banana straw for enhancing cellulose utilization: A comprehensive physicochemical and multivariate mechanism analysis
Enhancing treatment performance for agricultural runoff in ecological ditches through synergistic effects of denitrifying phosphate-accumulating bacteria and natural/synthetic media
Sustainable pre-reduced sinter production: Recycling carbon-bearing dust and reducing CO2 emissions
Designing low-carbon lithium carbonate production: An ex-ante life cycle assessment of CO2-Based precipitation pathways
Strategic role of integrated agricultural systems in alleviating land-use competition and accelerating climate mitigation
abstract: Integrated and agroforestry systems (IS/AS) are increasingly recognised as pivotal pathways to reconcile agricultural productivity, ecosystem services, and climate mitigation. This study assesses the system-level contribution of IS/AS to land-use dynamics and greenhouse gas mitigation in Brazil using the Brazilian Land Use and Energy System (BLUES) integrated assessment model (IAM). Distinct from previous global assessments, we developed and explicitly represented eleven region-specific IS/AS production systems – two Integration-Livestock-Forest (ILF) systems, five Integration-Crop-Livestock (ICL) systems, two Integration-Crop-Livestock-Native Forest (ICLFn) systems and two Integration-Crop-Livestock-Commercial Forestry (eucalyptus/pine) systems – to capture heterogeneous productivity, input intensity, and carbon dynamics across diverse biomes. Our findings demonstrate that IS/AS are not only economically viable but also strategically superior to conventional practices, with their large-scale deployment primarily driven by their systemic expansion potential rather than marginal costs. Under 1.5°C-consistent scenarios, IS/AS substantially abate agricultural emissions, particularly methane (22 MtCO 2 e) and nitrous oxide (35 MtCO 2 e), while accelerating carbon sequestration in soils and biomass (15 MtCO 2 e). Crucially, their adoption alleviates land-use competition by minimising the need for extensive industrial carbon capture and storage (CCS), reforestation and pasture recovery – reductions of 86, 216 and 439 MtCO 2 e, respectively – thereby securing food and bioenergy production. These results underscore the role of IS/AS as foundational structural components of sustainable land-use strategies, providing a benchmark for climate policy in nations with extensive degraded agricultural landscapes.

title: Measurement of competitive water-use pressure across multi-regional sectors in China: A perspective considering economic-benefits
Environmental and thermo-economic assessment of industrial heat recovery retrofits with integrated waste heat and multiple utility systems
abstract: Retrofitting industrial heat recovery systems is a key pathway toward low-carbon and resource-efficient manufacturing. Integrating waste heat recovery (WR) with multiple utility (MU) networks can significantly improve energy efficiency, but also creates strong coupling between process heat recovery, waste heat utilisation, and utility allocation. However, existing approaches often address these elements separately or sequentially, limiting the ability to identify optimal system-level retrofit solutions. This study aims to develop a system-level optimisation framework to resolve trade-offs between waste heat recovery and multiple utility integration in industrial retrofit. The framework allows for (i) modifying existing exchangers, (ii) installing new process-to-process units to enhance heat recovery, (iii) integrating waste heat recovery systems for generating high-pressure steam, low-pressure steam, and hot water, and (iv) incorporating optimal utilisation of multiple utilities. The framework is validated through two large-scale industrial case studies. In Case 1, WR and MU integration reduce utility cost to 9.8E+06 $/y (64.6% below the original design) and GHG emissions from 1.7E+08 to 1.2E+08 kg/y CO 2 (30.3% reduction), with hot water generation contributing 82.7% of savings. In Case 2, the same strategy achieves a 45.6% GHG reduction relative to the baseline and lowers operation costs by 28.9%. This work provides a practical, system-level retrofit framework to support sustainable production and low-carbon transition in industrial processes.

title: Firm-level evaluation of the environmental Kuznets curve: thresholds in cross-sectional data from small, medium and mid-sized enterprises
abstract: In a context of insufficient global regulation, a substantial proportion of firms set voluntary greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets. This study draws on a new dataset of about 1000 GHG Protocol-compliant assessments from a thousand Europe and US-based small and medium enterprises and mid-sized firms between 2019 and 2024 to investigate how emissions metrics compare across as companies grow and consolidate their productivity. Moving beyond the conflicting environmental Kuznets curve evidence and the traditional focus on large enterprises, we uncover a new, untheorized link between emissions and firm productivity. Using competing polynomial and threshold regression models, and addressing endogeneity, selection bias and omitted variable bias by relying on Granger causality, Hausman instruments, poststratification, Oster sensitivity tests and split sample testing, we establish that contrary to the classic inverted U shape of the EKC, corporate emissions and emissions intensities do not show a clear turning point but instead stabilize once over a critical threshold in revenue per employee. We find raising productivity can halve per revenue intensities despite simultaneous fourfold and twofold surges in absolute and per-employee emissions. This structural influence of financial productivity challenges the fairness of corporate net-zero targets that assume comparable baseline intensities across firms.

title: A novel-method of 3D-Gaussian fitting with DOM-EEMs of small sample sizes to identifying components compared with parallel factor analysis
Uncovering environmental and economic hotspots of nuclear research reactors: A life cycle perspective
abstract: Nuclear research reactors provide essential services for health, industry and science, yet systematic evidence on how to operate these facilities within cleaner-production principles remains limited. This study applies an integrated Life Cycle Assessment (Environmental Footprint 3.1) and Life Cycle Costing framework to quantify environmental and economic hotspots associated with the IEA-R1 research reactor, an open-pool, light-water-moderated facility operated by IPEN in Brazil. One hour of operation at full power defines the functional unit. Long-lived infrastructure and the nuclear fuel cycle emerge as dominant contributors to environmental burdens. Infrastructure accounts for most land use (approximately 73%), water use (approximately 83%) and carcinogenic human toxicity (approximately 78%), indicating opportunities for material optimization and extended component lifetimes. Uranium enrichment, modeled with low-enriched uranium below 20% U-235, drives ionizing radiation and fossil resource depletion. Auxiliary diesel generators add combustion-related impacts, including eutrophication, photochemical oxidants, particulate matter and ozone-depleting emissions. Sensitivity analyses confirm the stability of hotspot patterns despite proxy fuel inventories, underscoring the need for more complete nuclear life-cycle datasets. The economic assessment indicates a negative net operational cost, consistent with the public-service mandate of research reactors. Overall, the integrated framework clarifies priority levers for impact prevention and resource efficiency, supporting evidence-based modernization pathways and strengthening the sustainability governance of research reactor operations.

title: High-intensity intermittent aeration with multi-stage descending rates enhances oxygen uptake to mitigate nitrogen emissions and promote humification in composting
EcoLLM: A lightweight ReAct-SFT framework for document-driven LCI extraction and automated LCIA in metal additive manufacturing
Applying a consumption-based perspective to nitrogen and phosphorus discharges in the Liao River Basin
Global accessibility of food ecosystem services under economic inequality, food production, and infrastructure shocks
abstract: Reconciling food ecosystem service (ES) supply and demand requires understanding not only food production capacity but also the transport infrastructure connecting resources to people. Economic and transport disparities cause inequalities in access to food ES, making the global food system vulnerable to disruptions. To evaluate global transport network efficiency in delivering food ES, we developed a spatial accessibility analysis method to assess the balance between food supply and demand. Our framework includes case analyses under the following scenarios: uniform transport costs, economic disparities, and regional shocks, including production disruptions and infrastructure damage caused by hazards in North America, Eastern Europe, and East Asia. Our results show that current state of transport infrastructure and food production distribution lead to unmet demand, particularly in Asia and Africa. Comparisons between equal and economic analysis show that economic differences between regions further exacerbate the ES supply-demand mismatch. Accounting for economic costs increases supply surpluses across most sub-regions, particularly in Southeast and South Asia, Africa, and Eastern Europe, while unmet demand also increases. About two-thirds of the global unmet demand is concentrated in Asia. This coexistence of surplus supply and unmet demand suggests transport bottlenecks and network inefficiencies, meaning that although food is available it cannot be effectively delivered to all the locations where it is needed. Among all scenarios analyzed, economic inequality has the greatest impact on food accessibility. Alongside food production, the structure and cost of transport are important factors in global food accessibility, even without considering trade relations and geopolitical influences.
