Natural gas purification with complete CO2 capture using ionic liquids: Process optimization and multi-criteria evaluation
Reduced-energy processing of PLA/Talc biocomposites: Comparing in-mold crystallization and IR annealing
abstract: PLA is a promising bio-based alternative to fossil-based plastics, but its slow crystallization during injection molding often requires high mold temperatures, increasing cycle time and energy demand. This study evaluates two manufacturing routes for obtaining highly crystalline PLA/talc injection-molded parts: (i) high mold temperature molding at 100 °C and (ii) low mold temperature molding at 30 °C followed by infrared post-molding annealing. The comparison integrates manufacturability, crystallinity, surface quality, thermomechanical/mechanical response, and gate-to-gate specific energy consumption. Samples molded at 100 °C with a cooling time of 35 s (HM(35)) reached a crystallinity of 54.12 ± 0.65%, whereas samples molded at 30 °C (LM) showed 25.0 ± 0.23%. A 1-min IR treatment increased the crystallinity of LM-IR to approximately 54%. Under optimized annealing utilization and similar crystallinity, LM-IR reduced specific energy consumption by about 45% relative to HM(35). Ejection force measurements showed lower ejection demand during the high mold temperature molding, while surface roughness parameters including Ra, Rz, Rv, and Rp showed lower values at 100 °C. Maximum tensile strength was 48.98 ± 0.42 MPa for LM, compared to 44.66 ± 1.44 MPa for HM(35) and 43.50 ± 0.83 MPa for LM-IR. Heat deflection temperature increased from 55.0 ± 0.2 °C for LM to 145.81 ± 0.42 °C for HM(35) and 134.6 ± 1.4 °C for LM-IR. Overall, the study provides an integrated gate-to-gate comparison of two established routes for the investigated commercial PLA/talc composite and quantifies the process-property-energy trade-offs that govern route selection in similar nucleated PLA systems.

Analysis of sustainable printing materials using computed tomography and tensile testing for aeronautical applications
abstract: Material extrusion is a well-established strategy for producing multiple parts for aeronautics applications. The process primarily consumes thermoplastic materials, which are a significant environmental risk. Thus, there is a need to develop sustainable printing strategies that achieve the expected benefits without compromising the environment's future. This manuscript analyzes three materials: conventional polylactic acid (PLA) and two potential PLA substitutes: recycled PLA and lightweight PLA. The specimens were then tested to determine the maximum tensile stress for two printing orientations: vertical and horizontal. The results show that PLA and recycled PLA exhibit similar behavior in tensile testing, with lower tensile strength observed in the vertical orientation. Using a lightweight PLA resulted in lower tensile stress but allowed higher strains. Computed tomography enabled a precise assessment of printing quality. Specifically, computed tomography enabled identification of how the cross-sectional area varied across the gauge section and revealed that Lw_PLA specimens exhibited significant expansion compared with their respective models. Finally, it was noted that the tensile strength calculated from computed tomography can vary by up to 8% relative to that calculated from the nominal cross-section for PLA and r-PLA. For Lw-PLA, this difference ranges from 25% to 30%.

title: Climate and anthropogenic drivers of spatiotemporal variation in ecosystem regulation service value across China (2000-2023)
abstract: Ecosystem service values (ESV) are utilized by many nations to guide investments in ecological conservation and restoration. However, the relative contributions of natural and anthropogenic factors to the spatiotemporal variations in ESV under the combined pressures of reclamation, urbanization, and ecological restoration remain poorly understood, with an increasing number of cases failing to achieve expected value realization. This paper quantifies the ecosystem regulation service value (ERSV) in China from 2000 to 2023, performing pixel-level trend analysis, identifying major contributing factors using the ARIMA time series method, and differentiating responses of ERSV to climate change, reclamation, urbanization, and ecological restoration. Our results indicate an overall upward trend in the average ERSV in China. Areas where precipitation and evapotranspiration are the primary contributing factors constitute over 65% of the land area, exhibiting distinctive zonal distribution patterns. Within regions experiencing Land Cover (LC) changes, a substantial proportion of ERSV variation remains primarily climate-driven. Climate-induced fluctuations account for over 81% of the total terrestrial area and ERSV. The gains in ERSV from ecological restoration projects reached 1236.70 billion yuan in 2023, which have compensated for and even exceeded the losses due to reclamation and urbanization. The study identifies and quantifies the impacts of natural and anthropogenic factors on changes in ERSV, while assessing the balance between ecological depletion losses and ecological restoration gains on human well-being, providing data support for the precise implementation of future ecological conservation policies.

title: A novel integrated risk assessment approach based on a two-dimensional water quality model and Bayesian networks: A case study in the Yangtze River basin
Between refuse and recycle: asymmetric polarization in circular economy representations
abstract: The concept of the circular economy ( CE ) has gained increasing prominence over the past decade, yet its meaning remains ambiguous and often diverges from the original vision of early CE pioneers. Understanding how this ambiguity shapes public perceptions is critical for the effective design and implementation of CE policies. Drawing on a survey of 1281 respondents in France, this study examines individuals' familiarity with CE , their spontaneous definitions, and their prioritization of circular strategies using the 5R hierarchy (refuse, reduce, reuse, repair, recycle). The results reveal a strong and asymmetric polarization of CE representations, structured around the acceptance or rejection of the refuse (sufficiency) lever. Recycling and reuse dominate spontaneous definitions, while reuse and recycling are prioritized when respondents explicitly rank CE levers. By contrast, refuse remains marginal despite its central role in strong circularity approaches. Socio-economic characteristics do not robustly explain this polarization. However, respondents whose preferences align more closely with strong circularity—consistent with the pioneers’ vision—report higher levels of pro-environmental behaviors and stronger support for CE-related public policies. These findings highlight a persistent gap between weak and strong circularity representations and suggest important implications for CE communication strategies and public policymaking.

title: Multi-objective design optimization of bio-based oriented strand boards from urban and orchard pruning residues via support vector machine and genetic algorithm
Exploring the spatiotemporal coupling mechanism of livestock carbon emissions intensity and ecological vulnerability in inner Mongolia: An ensemble learning approach
A comprehensive LCA CO2 emission inventory for passenger car fleet in Europe and future trends
abstract: Europe, countries worldwide and several organizations account systematically the emissions from road transport in various applications ranging from official sectorial targets setting to territorial inventories and monitoring statistics. However, this paper argues that the ongoing shift to electrification challenges the adequacy of these activities in revealing true climatic impacts of road transport. The current focus on Tank-to-Wheel (TTW) emissions that narrows the accounting boundaries to on-road operation would benefit from additional elements that would take into consideration upstream and end-of-life emissions of vehicles and fuels, similar to the approaches adopted in Life Cycle Assessment (LCA). To support efforts for more holistic emission inventorying in Europe, this paper compiles a comprehensive lifecycle CO 2 inventory for the passenger-car fleet of EU-27 countries using a fleet-based method. The inventory is “comprehensive” in the sense that it represents the entire fleet at an increased level of detail, covering all fuel types and vehicle size classes, instead of emphasizing individual vehicle performance. It is also based on actual data for fleet composition, vehicle characteristics and activity patterns. Up-to-date emission factors are used to account for the fleet emission performance across all lifecycle stages. Projections for the future are made in all elements, considering a realistic fleet electrification pathway in response to official EU CO 2 targets. In addition, to ensure consistency and comparison with TTW regulated emissions reporting practices, the inventory builds upon COPERT, which is widely used for TTW inventorying in Europe, and enriches it with lifecycle system boundaries. Results achieved with this extended inventory have practical meaning as they answer questions on how much the total greenhouse emissions of the fleet are, and how far the global picture from the TTW is, given that targets for road transport are set on TTW basis in EU. Results show that electrification can bring true net-zero CO 2 results, which can only be assessed with an LCA-equivalent method.

title: Decomposing capital-endogenized emissions: A comprehensive accounting analysis of Korea's carbon emissions
abstract: Conventional carbon accounting methods for production-based emissions (PBE) or consumption-based emissions (CBE) treat investment as an exogenous final demand category, without accounting for the fact that capital goods are emission-intensive inputs to production. Using Korea's 2020 benchmark input–output table, we construct and compare PBE, CBE, and a capital-endogenized consumption-based measure (CBEk). We further decompose CBEk into emissions induced by household consumption, government demand, investment, and imports. The results show that endogenizing capital fundamentally reshapes the sectoral distribution of emissions. Relative to conventional CBE, emissions attributed to the Construction sector decline by 64.4%, while those for capital-using sectors increase markedly, with emissions in the Dwelling sector rising by 227.4%, ICT & Communications by 21.6%, and Service by 17.4%. Applying a novel decomposition method that fully attributes emissions to final demand, including those embodied in intermediate imports, we find that household consumption-induced emissions amount to 58.5% of total emissions under CBEk. These findings underscore the importance of endogenizing capital in national carbon accounting standards and in shifting policy attention toward demand-side mitigation strategies.

title: Parametric sensitivity analysis of design and operation for a methanol synthesis process
abstract: Methanol is a key chemical molecule and energy carrier whose importance is expected to grow as a cornerstone of future energy systems and carbon recycling strategies. Its sustainable production is tightly linked to the availability of renewable hydrogen, making the efficient and flexible use of syngas a critical challenge. This work presents a reactor-level parametric assessment of the flexibility and performance of an industrial boiling water-cooled multitubular methanol synthesis reactor. A pseudo-homogeneous model was developed to evaluate the combined effects of syngas quality, expressed through the Carbon Oxide Ratio (COR) and the Stoichiometric Number (SN), and syngas quantity, represented by the Gas Hourly Space Velocity (GHSV). Results show that a favorable operating region of COR value exists in the range 0.05–0.2, with operation below this range (CO-rich feeds) leading to steep losses in methanol yield and conversion. In contrast, a slight CO 2 surplus has less impact, making CO 2 -rich operation more robust to variations in inlet feed composition. The SN most favorable region depends strongly on feed composition: values below 2 (SN ≈ 1–1.3) maximize methanol yield while reducing hydrogen demand for mixed CO/ CO 2 feeds, whereas CO 2 -rich feeds require higher SN values ( ≈ 2.5–3). GHSV critically affects performance, with lower values extending residence time and increasing yield, while higher values amplify sensitivity to feed composition. Flexibility analysis highlights that both operational and design strategies, such as reactor volume increase, can mitigate off-optimal performance. Overall, the study demonstrates that methanol synthesis reactors are highly sensitive to the balance between syngas composition and reactor load. Beyond identifying favorable steady-state operating windows, the results provide reactor-level guidelines for exploiting operational and design flexibility to improve carbon utilization and reduce renewable hydrogen demand. The proposed maps may support the preliminary design and control-oriented interpretation of methanol synthesis units into power-to-methanol schemes and renewable-based CO 2 valorization pathways.

Thermal selection of microbial consortia modulates copper corrosion toward mineral stabilization
abstract: Copper corrosion can be strongly modulated by microbial activity despite the intrinsic toxicity of copper ions to most microorganisms. This study investigates the corrosion behavior of high-purity copper (Cu ≥ 99.9 wt%) exposed to thermophilic bacteria and methanogenic archaea collected from a biological methanation plant. Batch experiments were conducted at 45 °C for 15 days, using the inoculum as-is (biotic), or after three distinct treatments: 1) boiling (120 min), which did not significantly alter the overall-community-level diversity and structure; 2) double autoclaving (121 °C, 20 min), which selectively enriched thermotolerant populations, and 3) sterilization, only achieved by combining autoclaving (121 °C, 60 min), filtration (Φ = 0.22 μm), and UV exposure. Microbial communities were characterized by 16S rRNA gene sequencing; corrosion was monitored by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and Raman spectroscopy. Results reveal a time-dependent transition from microbially influenced corrosion (MIC) to microbial corrosion-inhibition (MICI). Bacterial-dominated communities transiently perturbed interfacial electrochemistry and delayed passivation but did not produce the highest cumulative copper dissolution (3,1, 3,73, 3,09 mg L −1 , for biotic, boiled, and autoclaved inoculum, respectively). Two distinct MICI pathways were identified: Cu 2 O barrier stabilization under archaeal-dominated inoculum (autoclaved), and diffusion resistance through porous phosphates precipitation in mixed bacterial-archaeal communities (biotic, boiled inoculum). Sterile conditions exhibited uninhibited chloride-driven localized corrosion and the highest copper release (7.1 mg L −1 ). Overall, the microbial community exerts a net moderating influence on copper dissolution, and thermal selection of community composition determines which MICI mechanism prevails.

A governance-sensitive blue economy index for ports: Benchmarking sustainability and transition readiness in Spanish ports
abstract: Ports occupy a critical role in supporting sustainability transitions within the contemporary Blue Economy, yet existing evaluation frameworks remain fragmented and not aligned with governance and transition-related challenges. This article introduces a governance-sensitive composite index designed to evaluate port performance across five core dimensions: Economic, Environmental, Social, Innovation & Technology, and Governance & Regulation. The framework consists of 26 indicators aggregated through a seven-step methodology that includes Delphi validation, min-max normalization, and weighted aggregation. The empirical application focuses on four anonymized Spanish ports representing different functional profiles across both the Mediterranean and Atlantic façades. The empirical results reveal substantial heterogeneities in sustainability performance and institutional readiness, with Blue Economy Index (BEI) scores ranging from 62.3 to 89.7. For instance, Mediterranean ports obtained the highest overall scores, driven primarily by innovation and governance dimensions, whereas lower-performing nodes exhibited greater structural weaknesses and limited adaptive capacity. To complement the static assessment, two forward-looking indicators were incorporated: the Forward Capacity Index (FCI), associated with institutional and innovation readiness, and the Blue Transition Risk Index (BTRI), designed to identify latent vulnerabilities related to sustainability alignment. The findings suggest that governance capacity and innovation dynamics play a central role in shaping long-term sustainability performance and transition preparedness in port systems. The resulting index can support benchmarking, strategic planning, and governance-sensitive sustainability evaluation within Blue Economy contexts.

title: Food waste-sludge co-fermentation liquid drives efficient partial denitrification: Kinetics, microbial community, and metabolic insights

Risky purchases – A study of consumers’ risk perceptions of plant-based leather alternatives
abstract: Luxury fashion brands are increasingly using plant-based leather alternatives to reduce their environmental impact. However, consumers tend to perceive significant risk with unfamiliar stimuli, such as products made from these materials, which can negatively influence their purchase intentions. Hence, understanding consumers’ perceived risk of luxury fashion products made from plant-based leather alternatives is key to encouraging their consumption. However, as new materials, there is a gap in the literature on them, which is crucial to address, given their projected growth. Through 24 semi-structured interviews, we addressed this gap and explored consumers’ perceived risk of luxury fashion products made from plant-based leather alternatives and their influence on their purchase intentions. Our findings suggest that financial and functional risks are significant concerns, particularly due to the waste and plastic content of plant-based leather alternatives. Social and sanitary risks also play a notable role in influencing consumers’ purchase behaviour, while perceived aesthetic risk was low and psychological risk was not evident. Moreover, we found that perceived risk influences purchase intentions differently across product categories. This research provides original theoretical contributions by extending the concept of perceived risk within environmentally sustainable luxury consumption and uncovering entirely new risk dimensions and subthemes not previously explored in literature. It offers practical implications for luxury fashion brands and plant-based leather alternative manufacturers to improve their marketing and product development strategies.

title: Conversational AI for real-time life cycle assessment
abstract: Life cycle assessment (LCA) remains underused in early-stage design due to slow computation, complex interfaces, and reliance on expert interpretation. This study presents an AI-augmented LCA framework that couples a lightweight real-time computational engine with a conversational large language model to support rapid, standards-aligned exploration. Implemented in a modular Python–Flask architecture with CSV-based inventories, the system generates EN 15804–compliant A1–A5 results while maintaining sub-second recalculation. Users can conduct interactive scenario comparisons and one-factor-at-a-time sensitivity tests to probe the influence of material, transport, and energy assumptions. The conversational interface translates user queries into model operations and returns explanations using a complexity-adjustment mechanism intended to support both novice and expert users. In a pilot usability study (n = 14), the platform achieved an overall mean System Usability Scale score of 65.18, while experienced participants rated usability highly (SUS ≈ 92.5), suggesting additional onboarding and interpretive improvement are needed for novice users. Overall, the results establish computational fidelity and real-time exploratory capability within defined system boundaries, indicating the platform's potential for early-stage decision support while motivating broader benchmarking against rapid-LCA tools and larger, longitudinal user validation.

title: Multi-scenario carbon storage prediction in high groundwater table coal-grain complex area under land use change
abstract: Land use/land cover (LULC) changes exert a significant influence on regional carbon sequestration capacity, essential for combating global climate change and supporting China's carbon neutrality objectives. Nonetheless, the effects of LULC on carbon storage (CS) in the high groundwater table coal-grain complex area (HGT CGCA) of eastern China have not been thoroughly examined. This study innovatively incorporates the constraints of regional policy planning along with the effects of underground mining subsidence. It integrates the GMOP, PLUS, mining subsidence prediction system (MSPS), and InVEST models to analyze the historical and future changes in CS. The geographical detector model based on optimal parameters (OPGD) is utilized to explore the driving mechanisms underlying the spatial heterogeneity of CS. The findings revealed that: (1) From 1985 to 2020, the major types of LULC included farmland, construction land, and water bodies. Farmland experienced the most significant area of conversion, with transitions primarily occurring to construction land and water bodies, which comprised 92.07% and 6.12% of the total converted area. (2) The spatial distribution of CS within the study area displayed a pattern characterized by lower values in the central region and elevated values in the northern region. Significant changes in CS were primarily observed around underground coal mining areas, where coal extraction transformed previously terrestrial land into water bodies. Over the past 35 years, the total reduction in CS amounted to 393.81 & times; 104 t. (3) Compared to the other three scenarios, the concurrent mining and reclamation scenario (CMRS) demonstrated the most favorable overall performance regarding carbon sequestration capacity and the holistic benefits of land use. The decline in CS was effectively managed, resulting in a reduction of only 70.01 & times; 104 t.(4)The driving analysis revealed that topography and anthropogenic activities were the primary factors influencing changes in CS. Revealing a distinct carbon loss pathway in HGT CGCA, characterized by "coal mining subsidence -* rise in groundwater levels -* evaporation and salt accumulation -* loss of CS". The research results offer new perspectives on the carbon cycling mechanisms that contribute to ecological degradation in the HGT CGCA. They also provide essential data and theoretical insights for optimizing land management and developing diversified ecological compensation mechanisms within the region.

title: Cost-sharing mechanisms for safeguarding water quality in inter-basin water transfer projects: A Stackelberg–evolutionary game analytical framework
Prioritizing and managing ecological zones on the northeastern Qinghai-Tibet plateau using static and dynamic ecosystem service supply-demand analysis
Integrating circularity indicators with life cycle assessment for plastic packaging: A refill-and-reuse system case study
abstract: This study addresses the lack of methodological consensus for nano-level Circular Economy (CE) assessments of plastic packaging. Existing approaches are reviewed to identify relevant methods. The outcome is the application of an ISO 59020 oriented, integrated Circular Life Cycle Assessment (Circular-LCA) that combines LCA with Material Circularity Indicator (MCI) and Product Circularity Indicator (PCI). Applied to a use case comparing a conventional single-use detergent bottle with a concentrate pouch in a refill-and-reuse system, indicator informativeness, system boundaries, and sensitive parameters are critically examined. Three complementary scopes are applied: packaging-only, a packaging + product transport scope to consider the packaging's volumes transported, and a full-product scope including detergent production and use. Results show mostly gains from transitioning to refill-and-reuse: even one refill mostly reduces packaging-related impacts by on average 35% and substantially increases circularity. The original MCI peaks at one reuse, while its adapted version integrating reduced mass peaks at five reuses and then declines due to the pouch's dominant virgin feedstock. Introducing recyclate content for refill packaging would mitigate this trade-off. Reduce, Reuse, and Recycle emerge as primary levers with net benefits and limited trade-offs, while Recover offers supplementary advantages. In the full-product scope, packaging improvements are overshadowed by impacts from detergent production and use, underscoring the need for holistic evaluation. The study demonstrates the value of combining life-cycle methods with circularity indicators, identifies sensitive parameters, and thereby offers guidance for practitioners navigating the implementation of Packaging & Packaging Waste Regulation, ISO 59000, and Digital Product Passports.

title: Dual-stream valorization of spent LFP black mass via microwave-assisted NaHCO3 treatment: lithium phosphate-rich leachate and reusable iron-rich residue
abstract: The recycling of valuable elements and compounds from lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries remains challenging due to the low economic value of Fe–P components and the limitations of conventional pyrometallurgical, hydrometallurgical, and alkaline-based processes, which are often energy-intensive or reagent-demanding. In this work, a novel and sustainable treatment for LFP black mass is proposed, based on the synergistic combination of microwave irradiation in the presence of sodium bicarbonate. This approach promotes the controlled decomposition of the LFP structure under relatively mild conditions, inducing the simultaneous formation of water-leachable lithium and phosphorus species and the transformation of iron into stable oxide phases. NaHCO 3 decomposition (CO 2 release) further contributes to structural modification and enhanced reactivity. A subsequent water-leaching step enables the selective separation of a liquid fraction enriched in Li + and PO 4 3− from a solid residue mainly composed of iron oxides. Under the investigated conditions, a lithium leaching efficiency of up to 45% was achieved with an 88% recovery of PO 4 3− . Compared to conventional routes, the proposed process offers a low-temperature, low-reagent alternative that combines selective lithium extraction with the potential valorization of iron-rich residues, highlighting its dual functionality and providing a basis for further optimization toward higher recovery yields.

title: Operationalising regenerative entrepreneurship through practice theory and life cycle thinking
abstract: This paper develops and applies a qualitative framework to examine how regenerative entrepreneurship is enacted in everyday business practice across value chains. Drawing on practice theory and Life Cycle Thinking, we conceptualize regenerative entrepreneurship as an ongoing process in which intent, routines, value-chain positioning, and perceived socio-ecological effects are continually related, rather than as a fixed business model or set of metrics. The framework distinguishes four interrelated dimensions: regenerative intent, practice enactment, life cycle situatedness, and socio-ecological effects, which are used as sensitizing concepts to guide empirical analysis rather than as prescriptive categories. We apply this theory informed, practice based framework in two in-depth case studies of Dutch SMEs in materially intensive sectors: a locally embedded food and beverage company that seeks to restore biodiversity through herb polycultures and inclusive employment, and a bamboo products company that links global sourcing, land restoration, and long-term farmer finance. The analysis shows how regenerative ambitions become selective, situated configurations of practices, shaped by organizational history, available resources, value-chain leverage points, and place-based relations. Across both cases, the framework makes regenerative practices more visible and discussable, surfacing tensions (e.g. between local depth and global reach, or between experimentation and formalization) and revealing where regenerative intent is strong, muted, or contested along the life cycle. We argue that this practice- and life-cycle-oriented view advances regenerative entrepreneurship research by shifting attention from idealized models and impact claims to the concrete ways in which firms organise for socio-ecological regeneration, and by offering practitioners a structured, non-metric approach for reflection and learning.

Boundary-resolved dynamic assessment of mitigation in forest–wood product systems
abstract: Forest–wood systems are increasingly positioned as climate mitigation instruments, yet reported carbon payback times range from near-instantaneous benefit to multi-decade debt. This divergence shapes carbon markets, offset protocols and investment decisions, but it remains unresolved whether it reflects differences in system physics or differences in accounting design. Here we show that reported mitigation outcomes are boundary-conditioned properties of attribution rather than intrinsic properties of forest–product systems. We develop a Boundary-Resolved Dynamic Ledger (BRDL) that applies alternative reporting operators to a single conserved carbon ledger, enabling direct comparison of full-ledger and disturbance-rebased framings without altering underlying biophysical fluxes. In a mill-scale case study with total anthropogenic emissions of 676.09 kg CO 2 eq m −3 , apparent “instant” payback emerges only when inherited forest stock accumulation is commingled with post-disturbance change; rebasing to the disturbance year yields a carbon payback of 6 years under identical carbon dynamics. Residue routing modifies early atmospheric trajectories but does not overturn the regrowth-dominated control of long-horizon magnitude. When mitigation is temporally distributed but costs are front-loaded, discounting structurally amplifies economic thresholds, revealing that feasibility is governed by the geometry of credited abatement rather than by physical removal alone. By separating carbon conservation from claim construction, BRDL reframes forest-based mitigation as a problem of attribution architecture, providing a transparent basis for evaluating what counts, when it counts, and under what liability.

title: Fintech-driven sustainability: Examining the pathways to sustainable performance through innovation and circular practices in emerging market SMEs
abstract: Small and medium-sized enterprises in emerging economies face persistent sustainability constraints due to limited financial access, weak digital infrastructure, and mounting regulatory pressures. FinTech adoption emerges as a strategic enabler for sustainable performance, yet the operational mechanisms through which digital finance translates into sustainability outcomes remain underexplored. Grounded in innovation diffusion theory and the resource-based view, this research examines how FinTech adoption influences sustainable performance through green innovation, sustainable supply chain management, and circular economy practices, with digital transformation as a boundary condition. Analysis of survey data from 394 managerial respondents in Pakistan demonstrates that FinTech adoption significantly enhances sustainable performance through direct (β = 0.095, p < 0.05) and indirect pathways. Green innovation, sustainable supply chain management, and circular economy practices collectively mediate this relationship, with indirect effects ranging from β = 0.037 to 0.156 (p < 0.05). Digital transformation amplifies these pathways, yielding interaction effects between β = 0.156 and 0.209 (p < 0.05). The framework explains 58.4% of the variance in sustainable performance (R 2 = 0.584) and demonstrates predictive relevance (Q 2 = 0.286). The findings suggest that FinTech adoption alone is insufficient to generate sustainability gains; rather, value realization depends on embedding digital financial tools within structured organizational capabilities and sustainability-oriented routines. This research advances theoretical discourse by resolving the direct-effect bias in digital sustainability literature and provides actionable guidance for policymakers and managers seeking to align financial innovation with operational sustainability in resource-constrained emerging markets.

title: Environmental and economic assessments of novel polyurethane prepolymer modified porous asphalt: A case study in Hong Kong
Interplay of consumer and municipality roles in developing e-waste separation behaviour: Moderating effects of objective knowledge
abstract: Consumer e-waste separation involves sorting, dumping into recycling bins, transporting to waste centres, or finding e-waste storage spaces. The process needs careful handling because some e-waste may contain harmful toxic chemicals, bad for consumers/the environment. Despite the danger, inappropriate and inadequate e-waste handling is reported in some African countries. Therefore, the contributions of consumer objective knowledge and municipality support are needed in the process but rarely studied. Borrowing from two theories, this study examined how much consumers’ perceptions of ability and usefulness, low and high objective knowledge, and municipality support help/hinder perceived consumer effectiveness (PCE), e-waste separation willingness (WTS), and actual behaviour. The municipal support and two objective knowledge levels were also tested as moderators. Quantitative data was collected from 350 South-African consumers. Structural equation modelling results revealed that performance expectancy (PE) and perceived ease of use (PEU) significantly impacted PCE, which with PE and PEU, significantly drove WTS domestic e-waste, all at p < 0.01. WTS strongly impacted actual e-waste separation behaviour. Municipal support played negative roles on WTS and a significant but negative moderating role in the PCE- WTS relationship. Multigroup analyses revealed that at low levels of objective knowledge, the negative impact of municipality support on how WTS drove actual behaviour increased. At high levels of objective knowledge, the impact of PE on PCE increased. Thus, while objective knowledge of environmental issues played positive moderating roles in two instances, municipal support was a hindrance. Practical implications are provided for policymakers, social marketers, and municipal management dealing with waste management .

title: Anthropogenic activities drive variability in Dissolved Organic Matter composition and characteristics among and within reservoirs
Life cycle assessment of Solar Power Towers: A systematic review
abstract: Solar power towers (SPTs) are a promising class of concentrated solar power (CSP) technologies capable of producing dispatchable renewable electricity with significantly lower greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions than fossil fuel-based systems. This review aims to critically analyse the environmental performance of SPT systems through life cycle assessment (LCA) studies reported in the literature, identifying a substantial gap in the systematic evaluation of key environmental impact categories. Additional sustainability indicators such as water consumption, energy payback time (EPBT), cost, and avian mortality are also examined. A systematic search identified 23 relevant studies evaluating these parameters across the entire life cycle of SPT plants. Reported GHG emissions for SPT systems vary widely depending on system configuration and operational conditions, ranging from approximately 8 to 105 g CO 2 -eq/kWh, which is substantially lower than emissions from conventional fossil-fuel power generation. The review highlights that the manufacturing and operation phases account for the majority of environmental impacts (nearly 90% of GHG emissions), with heliostat production and material demand being major contributors. Furthermore, the results indicate that the operation and maintenance phase accounts for approximately 70% of the total water consumption of these systems. The study identifies key knowledge gaps and proposes strategies to reduce environmental burdens, including heliostat design optimization, improved heat transfer fluids, water-efficient cooling technologies, and enhanced site selection. Overall, the findings provide insights for researchers, industry stakeholders, and policymakers to support the development of more environmentally sustainable solar power tower systems.

title: Corrigendum to “Enhancing the resistance of hyperaccumulator with arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi in cadmium-contaminated saline soil: A physiological and transcriptional mechanistic study” [J. Clean. Prod. 501 (2025) 145330]
Treatment Trains vs. Single-stage Systems: Nutrient removal and economic tradeoffs of biochar-enhanced woodchip bioreactor systems
abstract: Biochar has been widely used as a soil amendment and also as a cost-effective adsorbent for pollutant treatment. Herein, we reexamined the system design and interactions between biochar and woodchip bioreactors (WBRs) to achieve synergies and minimize trade-offs, providing the first integrated assessment of treatment configuration, mechanistic interactions, and techno-economic performance in biochar-enhanced WBR systems. Three types of biochar-enhanced WBRs were evaluated: a single-stage system (biochar-woodchip mixture, W+B) and two treatment trains (WBRs followed by biochar systems, W-B, and biochar systems equipped with secondary WBRs, B-W). The results indicated that all types of biochar-enhanced WBRs exhibited simultaneous removal of nitrate and dissolved reactive phosphorus (DRP). Single-stage W + B systems achieved the highest reductions in DRP and nitrate but resulted in the highest amount of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) leaching. Meanwhile, the treatment train design with a downstream biochar system effectively mitigated byproduct leaching from upstream WBRs while maintaining stable nitrate removal. DRP removal showed similar trends across the three types of biochar-enhanced WBRs, with a gradual decrease in removal efficiency over time. Microbial analysis revealed that the interaction between biochar and woodchip amendments selectively supported the growth of microbes that facilitate denitrification and organic matter decomposition, while reducing microbial diversity in W+B systems, which likely reflects system functional specialization towards denitrification. Furthermore, techno-economic analysis identified W-B systems as most cost-effective, achieving $187.9 ± 160.0/kg DRP and $5.7 ± 1.7/kg N per year. The relatively higher uncertainty associated with DRP removal costs was primarily attributed to variability in influent DRP loading and removal efficiency. In contrast, the W+B system, despite higher removal performance, exhibited higher unit costs due to decreased treatment capacity. Overall, our findings highlight the importance of infrastructure design and media interaction for advancing biochar application into WBRs to enhance their feasibility, effectiveness, and sustainability in water quality management.

title: Techno-economic analysis of microalgae and microalgae–bacteria polyhydroxyalkanoate (PHA) production: A decision-making framework
abstract: Microalgae are a promising feedstock for polyhydroxyalkanoate (PHA)-based biodegradable plastics, as they can directly accumulate PHAs intracellularly and provide fermentable sugars for bacterial PHA production. Despite numerous studies on microalgal PHA accumulation, the commercial viability of such processes remains unclear. This study evaluated the production cost of PHAs from microalgae under three scenarios, each with two cases: (1) microalgal PHA accumulation with residual biomass used for bacterial PHA production (base and lower-productivity cases), (2) microalgal PHA accumulation only (base and lower-productivity cases), and (3) bacterial PHA production from microalgae-derived substrates only (base and wet biomass processing cases). Estimated base-case costs were US$ 11.70, US$ 9.94, and US$ 33.06 kg −1 PHA for scenarios 1–3, respectively, whereas the costs for alternative cases were US$ 14.61, US$ 13.63, and US$ 29.75 kg −1 PHA, respectively. Sensitivity analysis revealed that production cost was most influenced by the overall PHA yield. Scenario 2 was the most economical when microalgal PHA content exceeded 20 % (wt/wt dry mass), with cost of US$ 3.43-35.36 kg −1 PHA depending on biomass productivity and PHA content. At lower PHA contents, Scenario 1 became more competitive, with costs of US$ 4.30–27.06 kg −1 PHA depending on biomass productivity, algal PHA content, and PHA yield of bacterial process. A decision-boundary framework is proposed to guide the selection between Scenarios 1 and 2 based on microalgal PHA content and bacterial process yield. This work provides the first techno-economic comparison and prioritisation tool for direct and indirect microalgae-based PHA production routes.

title: How to account for the unaccounted? An analysis of governance barriers to consumption-based carbon accounting in European cities
Seasonal estrogenic exposure in reclaimed-water systems: Microbial community associations, functional pathway responses, and cellular tolerance signatures
Artificial intelligence and digital product passports: Data governance infrastructures enabling circular business model innovation
abstract: Digital Product Passports have emerged as a central regulatory instrument within the European Union's Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation, aiming to enhance transparency, traceability, and circularity across product value chains. While prior research has examined digital traceability systems, artificial intelligence, and circular business models in isolation, integrative frameworks explaining how these elements jointly enable systemic circular transitions remain underdeveloped. This article addresses this gap by developing an integrative conceptual framework informed by a PRISMA-guided systematic review and bibliometric mapping, which positions Digital Product Passports (DPPs) as data-governance infrastructures whose circular potential is realised through the interaction between AI-enabled analytics and dynamic capabilities at both organisational and ecosystem levels. The analysis shows how structured DPP data can support AI-driven sensing, seizing, and transforming processes, thereby reducing information asymmetries and enabling circular business model innovation. It further demonstrates that the effectiveness of AI–DPP integration is contingent upon robust data governance arrangements, interoperability standards, and coordinated multi-actor participation, while also revealing tensions related to data sovereignty, unequal access to digital infrastructures, and the environmental footprint of digital technologies. By linking regulatory design, technological capabilities, and business model transformation, this article advances theory on digitally enabled circularity and provides policy and managerial insights for fostering scalable and inclusive circular transitions.

title: From machine centred to productivity based sustainability assessments of machine tools
abstract: Manufacturing-related carbon footprint assessments increasingly require product-oriented environmental indicators that consistently reflect productive output. This study presents a productivity-based sustainability assessment framework for machine tools that allocates operational and infrastructure-related impacts to manufactured parts based on productive manufacturing output. The methodology integrates setup activities, utilization, cycle times, batch structures, and auxiliary systems into a unified allocation approach. The framework is applied to seven industrial case studies covering grinding, milling, wire EDM, and highly automated positioning systems. The results show that productivity-related operational characteristics strongly influence part-specific carbon footprints and may lead to substantially different sustainability interpretations compared to machine-centred assessment approaches, with utilization-related variations causing changes of up to 40 % across the investigated case studies. The study contributes a transparent allocation methodology for machine-tool-related foreground sustainability data and improves the comparability of manufacturing-related carbon footprints across heterogeneous industrial production systems.

title: A digital-enabled circular recovery system for post-consumer inhalers: Linking material recovery, behaviour, and carbon reduction
Analyzing the emergence of territorialized value chains based on the circular economy: Circular Value Chain Canvas (CVCC) and its application to the recycling of diffuse metals deposits
abstract: The circular economy (CE) plays a key role in the sustainable transformation of territories, particularly through the emergence of territorialized value chains. However, few tools currently exist that can simultaneously capture the systemic complexity of these chains and the interactions between actors with heterogeneous strategies and resources. This article proposes the Circular Value Chain Canvas (CVCC), a methodological approach for analyzing the conditions for the emergence and structuring of these value chains. The CVCC facilitates the formulation and evaluation of organizational scenarios, the identification of levers for action, and collective decision-making. As part of a systemic and multi-level approach to innovation dynamics, the CVCC offers an integrative analytical framework linking economic, technical, environmental, and institutional dimensions. A case study on copper recovery in the Hauts-de-France region (France) illustrates the relevance of this approach for analyzing and supporting the development of territorialized circular value chains in the service of sustainability.

Process design and techno-economic-assessment of the sorption enhanced methanol synthesis over zeolite 3A
abstract: The current effort towards sustainable methanol production is fostering research into the development of new small-scale processes that can adapt to the decentralized nature of most renewable electricity production sources. The production of methanol from electrolytic H 2 and C O 2 requires the development of new chemical routes that account for the many limitations present in small-scale applications. Among these, the most relevant is the low pressure (<30 bar) at which H 2 is normally delivered from electrolysis. In this context, the exploitation of sorption-enhancement may be of interest as it shifts the thermodynamic equilibrium, requiring lower synthesis pressure. This work delivers a comprehensive model of the sorption-enhanced methanol synthesis process, including both the reaction and the regeneration phase in the simulation. An economic assessment is performed to determine the levelized cost of methanol (LCMeOH) and compare it with that of a benchmark methanol plant. In every scenario analyzed, the configuration with the sorption-enhanced reactor shows better economic performance. Nevertheless, costs related to the production of hydrogen, representing 50.60% of capital expenditures and 76.40% of operational expenditures, make this solution not competitive compared to the traditional, fossil-based production process. As the electricity cost is dominant in the total process costs, the LCMeOH can be reduced by considering the self-production of electricity from photovoltaic panels, decreasing the LCMeOH by 28.71%, settling it at 1785 $ / t o n . With an increase in the operating hours. it could be possible to achieve an additional reduction by 29,54% of the levelized cost, to 1250 $ / t o n .

title: Synchronous separation and rejuvenation systems for reclaimed asphalt pavement based on a deconstruction-reconstruction strategy

Environmental impact of the total chemical synthesis of barettin
abstract: The development of a sustainable bioeconomy depends on ensuring that novel bio-based products incur a smaller environmental footprint than the conventional counterparts they replace. Benchmarking the environmental burdens of emerging production routes against established synthetic baselines is critical to avoid "burden shifting". This study presents the first prospective attributional Life Cycle Assessment of the total chemical synthesis of barettin, a bioactive alkaloid originally isolated from the deep-sea marine sponge Geodia barretti - with promising pharmaceutical and antifouling applications. The assessment covers four main reaction steps and incorporates 32 separate inventories for intermediate molecules. Environmental performance was evaluated across sixteen impact categories and four process maturity scenarios: laboratory, scaled-up, scaled-up optimised, and a future decarbonisation scenario. The results indicate a climate change burden ranging from 1884 to 13,970 kg CO 2 equivalents per kg of barettin. Organic solvent use (specifically ethyl acetate, dichloromethane, and diethyl ether) was identified as the principal environmental hotspot, driving impacts across almost all categories. The findings demonstrate that transitioning from waste incineration to 95% solvent recycling is the most effective mitigation lever, achieving impact reductions ranging between 32% and 95% across all 16 impact categories assessed. This study establishes a critical environmental baseline against which future bio-based production routes, such as sponge cell culture or wild harvesting, can be rigorously benchmarked. It provides actionable evidence for researchers and decision-makers in the pharmaceutical and bioeconomy sectors to guide the sustainable scale-up of marine-derived metabolites.

title: A critical review of emerging technologies for direct lithium extraction from brines: Current industrial practices, challenges for sustainable process integration, and a view of current commercialization status

Comparative life cycle assessment of stainless steel and single-use bioreactor units: A laboratory scale case study
abstract: In recent years, the biopharmaceutical industry has witnessed a surge in the adoption of Single-Use technologies; however, concerns about environmental sustainability have arisen due to the substantial amount of solid plastic waste generated by implementing such technologies. This study presents a comparative Life Cycle Assessment grounded in an industrially applied case study at a pharmaceutical facility in Italy, using primary operational data. The assessment evaluates two distinct laboratory scale bioreactor units reflecting the actual equipment configuration at the facility: a conventional stainless-steel bioreactor (SSB) and a single-use bioreactor (SUB). The assessment followed a cradle-to-grave approach over a 20-year operational horizon, normalising the results to the functional unit of 1 g of protein produced in a bioreactor. Five end-of-life scenarios for the single-use bioreactor were explored: landfill, incineration, incineration with energy recovery (IER), recycling and a combined recycling with IER scenario. Results across all 16 evaluated impact categories consistently show that the SSB exhibits a higher environmental burden than the SUB. In the Climate Change impact category, producing 1 g of protein in the SSB emitted 14.9 kg of CO 2 -eq., whereas the SUB emitted 8.7 kg of CO 2 -eq, assuming landfill as the base case disposal method. Electricity consumption was identified as the dominant environmental driver for both systems. The study also demonstrates that end-of-life management is not a marginal factor. The environmental profile of the SUB varied across disposal scenarios, with IER providing the most ecological benefits. These findings confirm that the disposal of plastic components emerges as a critical factor in assessing the environmental sustainability of single-use technologies.

Stratification enhances yet self-limits carbon sequestration through microbial necromass accumulation at reservoir sediment–water interfaces
abstract: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) includes a substantial recalcitrant fraction that constitutes a major form of long-term carbon storage in sediments, yet the processes controlling its stabilization at reservoir sediment–water interfaces (SWIs) under climate-driven stratification remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated temperate stratified reservoirs using high-resolution mass spectrometry and multi-omics to resolve how stratification reshapes DOM transformation at SWIs. During summer stratification, recalcitrant dissolved organic matter (RDOM) concentration and total dissolved organic carbon (TDOC) increased by 50.7% and 37.8%, respectively. Stratification enhanced nitrogen mineralization and suppressed ammonium oxidation at SWIs, promoting amino sugar biosynthesis and microbial necromass accumulation associated with DOM recalcitrance. The summer plateau in RDOM accumulation further suggests a necromass-associated substrate-supply constraint that self-limits continued carbon sequestration under prolonged stratification. Short-term hydrodynamic disturbances from natural events or human-induced intermittent mixing temporarily relieve this constraint and sustain DOM transformation. These findings uncover a climate-sensitive, internally regulated feedback that governs carbon sequestration efficiency at reservoir SWIs, with implications for predicting inland-water carbon storage under a warming climate.

title: Impact of sustainable product development tools through intermediaries: A multi-actor study of pathways and conditions
abstract: This study provides an empirically grounded, multi-actor investigation of how industrial impact of sustainable product development (SPD) tools forms along the pathway from academic tool development, through intermediary adoption and adaptation, to client application, and under what conditions impact unfolds over time. A multi-actor, multiple-case design, combining an embedded consultancy case with cross-sector client cases was employed, using interviews and follow-up questionnaires to explore how consultants adopt and adapt academically developed SPD tools and how clients experience and assess their application and impact. The analysis shows that adoption by consultants is enabled when tools are proven useable and time-effective in early phases, provide clear visualizations and credible traceability, and can be customized to sector language and practices. Across client cases, the application of SPD tools was perceived primarily as an enabler for innovation and competitiveness, together with increased ability to meet customer needs and improved reputation. The findings indicate a multi-layered and time-phased pattern of impact where impacts were reported most consistently at organizational level, including mindset change, cross-functional dialogue, and prioritization routines, whereas more technical and measurable outcomes emerged more selectively, with time delay, and depended on enabling conditions beyond tool use, e.g., governance and leadership, supplier capability and openness, policy and market signals. System-level change is discussed as a potential downstream pathway when SPD tool use is paired with deliberate work on enabling conditions. The study synthesizes these insights into seven multi-actor recommendations for researchers, consultants, and firms on designing, translating, and embedding SPD tools to maximize impact.

title: A field-scale model using an integrated framework for evaluating food and water dynamics in agrivoltaics in three-dimensional space
Beyond Kaolinite: Unlocking the performance of diverse calcined clays as sustainable cement replacement
abstract: “Greening” cement with supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs) is considered as an effective strategy to mitigate CO 2 emissions from the cement industry, with calcined clays (CCs) emerging as promising alternatives. However, the performance of such low-carbon cements highly depends on the nature of the clay utilized. Existing studies have mainly focused on kaolinitic clays which are relatively scarce in Europe, where illitic, smectitic, and mixed-layered clays predominate. The recent industrial implementation of low-carbon calcined clay cements in Europe, such as Futurecem™, further highlights the growing practical relevance of non-kaolinitic CCs. In this study, locally available non-kaolinitic calcined smectitic, illitic, and common (mix-layered) clays from Germany were investigated in comparison with a commercial metakaolin. Ordinary Portland cement (OPC) was replaced by 30 wt% or 50 wt% with CCs, their rheological behavior, flow behavior, workability retention, mechanical properties, environmental impact, and cost efficiency of the OPC/CC blends were systematically evaluated. The results demonstrate that calcined illitic and smectitic clays significantly increased water demand, impaired PCE efficiency and slump retention, even in the presence of high-range water-reducing admixtures. In contrast, the calcined common clay (CMC) exhibited a rheological behavior comparable to OPC, substantially better than the other non-kaolinitic clays. Although metakaolin exhibited superior strength development, CMC demonstrated the best balance between workability, environmental benefit, and cost effectiveness. This work highlights the critical role of specific surface area and mineralogy of CCs used in calcined clay cement blends, and demonstrates the potential of non-kaolinitic clays as viable low-carbon SCMs for sustainable cement formulations.

title: The multilayered toxic effects of cadmium on earthworms are driven by both cadmium content and soil properties: The potential mediating role of microbiota
Biostimulant-enriched anaerobic digestate as a sustainable nitrogen fertiliser for enhancing wheat growth, drought resilience and soil health
abstract: Climate change is driving farmers to adopt sustainable, eco-friendly fertilisers that enhance crop resilience. Anaerobic digestate, a nutrient-rich byproduct of biogas production, offers a promising biofertiliser option. However, its agronomic performance and interaction with biostimulants under water stress remain insufficiently understood. This study evaluated the effect of substituting inorganic nitrogen (N) fertilisers with anaerobic digestate, with or without biostimulants (plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria and humic substances), on the growth and drought resilience of common wheat ( Triticum aestivum ). A long-term pot experiment comprising sixteen treatments was conducted, supplying 100 kg N/ha through varying ratios of digestate and diammonium phosphate/urea. Biostimulants were applied at standard agronomic rates– Bacillus spp. (20 L/ha), humic acid (10 L/ha), and fulvic acid (500 g/ha). A drought condition was simulated during stem elongation. Plant biometrics, soil physicochemical properties, and post-harvest microbial communities were analysed. Wheat growth was comparable across treatments, indicating the digestate's potential to replace inorganic fertilisers. Under drought conditions, treatments receiving ≥85% digestate N combined with biostimulants showed improved soil moisture retention, thereby enhancing drought tolerance. The application of digestate (40–85% N) containing biostimulants, enriched soil nutrients, optimised N and potassium uptake, and reduced phytotoxicity. Specifically, digestate-based fertilisation (100% N) with biostimulant supplementation reduced potentially pathogenic Clostridia while promoting beneficial taxa, including drought-tolerant Bacillus licheniformis and Alphaproteobacteria associated with nutrient cycling. Thus, integrating anaerobic digestate with biostimulants showed enhanced wheat drought resilience and improved soil health compared to inorganic fertilisers, supporting the sustainable recycling of waste into effective biofertilisers.

Life cycle and economic assessment of inverted p-i-n perovskite solar cells
abstract: Photovoltaic technologies hold significant potential for meeting the world's growing energy demands. Among emerging alternatives to conventional silicon-based solar cells, perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have attracted increasing attention for their promising efficiency and cost-effectiveness. This study aims to evaluate the sustainability performance of an inverted PSC, addressing a critical gap in the integrated assessment of this emerging technology. A cradle-to-grave life cycle assessment (LCA) was conducted, combined with energetic and economic analyses, evaluating energy payback time (EPBT), energy return on investment (EROI), and levelized cost of electricity (LCOE). A sensitivity analysis was performed to assess the influence of key operational parameters. The results show a carbon footprint of 0.20 kg CO 2 eq./kWh and a cumulative energy demand of 4.88 MJ/kWh. The system exhibits an EPBT of 0.53 years and an EROI of 9.50, while the LCOE is estimated at 0.29 €/kWh, for a PSC production cost at 0.67 €/cm 2 . The sensitivity analysis indicates that the PCE and degradation rates are the main drivers of energetic performance, whereas the LCOE remains relatively stable. Additionally, EPBT and EROI are strongly influenced by solar irradiance and local climatic conditions. These findings highlight that, despite the relatively low manufacturing impacts, improvements in PCE, operational lifetime, and degradation rates are essential for enhancing the overall sustainability and economic viability of PSCs. The main contribution of this work lies in providing a multidimensional (environmental, energetic, and economic) baseline assessment of inverted PSCs, offering novel insights into the key parameters that will determine their future commercial competitiveness.

title: Deconstructing the carbon spillover effects of foreign direct investment: Upstream-downstream production linkages perspective

Life-cycle environmental and cost implications of longer-life road infrastructure designs: A case study of California
abstract: Most state road agencies in the U.S. design rigid pavements for a 40-year design life based on specific performance criteria for fatigue cracking, longitudinal smoothness, and sometimes other distresses. Would there be reductions in life-cycle environmental impacts and economic gains if the design lives were 60 or even 100 years? To answer this question, a comprehensive analysis was conducted on three representative case studies, each designed for 40-, 60-, and 100-year lives, with data applicable to California. The pavement structural design showed that extending the design life from 40 to 60 years necessitated only a modest 15 mm (0.05 feet) increase in concrete thickness, corresponding to an approximate 5% increase in initial construction costs. The life-cycle cost analysis indicated a 3% reduction in life-cycle agency costs, while infrastructure life-cycle global warming potential was reduced by around 24% without discounting and around 5% using time-adjusted warming potential. Fewer life cycle construction closures for maintenance, rehabilitation, and reconstruction activities also reduced road user delay costs. In contrast, increasing the design life to 100 years provided diminishing returns. The minimal additional savings are attributed to the relatively high annual discount rate (3.2%), which drastically reduces the present value of far-future savings. Consequently, a 60-year design life emerges as the most balanced and beneficial alternative, offering significant sustainability gains and cost savings for a minimal upfront investment.

title: Scaling sustainable protein production: Integrating farmer knowledge with AI to optimize black soldier fly larvae cultivation
abstract: The transition toward a circular bio-economy requires scalable technologies for organic waste upcycling and sustainable protein production. Black Soldier Fly (BSF) farming has emerged as a promising approach for waste-to-resource conversion; however, its industrial expansion is constrained by biological variability and the lack of robust optimization tools suitable for decentralized production systems. This study presents a farmer-partnered Decision Support System (DSS) that applies machine learning to optimize larval biomass yield and nutritional quality, including protein and fat content, using real-world data collected across multiple farms. The proposed DSS follows a data-centric approach that integrates practitioner domain expertise with longitudinal experimental data while accounting for the biological variability inherent in organic side-streams. We evaluate cross-farm generalization compared to personalized modeling strategies and analyze how shared datasets can improve prediction reliability in heterogeneous farming environments. To support practical adoption, the system incorporates explainability and interactive visualizations that enable farmers to better understand how diet composition influences larval growth and nutrient outcomes. The results demonstrate that integrating data science with farmer knowledge can improve process consistency and resource efficiency in BSF production systems, contributing to reduced reliance on marine-derived feed inputs and supporting progress toward UN Sustainable Development Goals related to responsible production and environmental sustainability.

title: A comparative techno-economic and life cycle assessment of energy-from-waste technology integrated with carbon capture and storage
abstract: Rising urbanisation and global population growth are projected to nearly double municipal solid waste (MSW) generation by 2050. Energy-from-waste (EfW) technologies recover energy from mixed waste streams, generating electricity and heat. However, for every tonne of MSW incinerated, 0.7–1.7 tonnes of CO 2 is emitted. Integrating carbon capture and storage (CCS) into EfW (EfW + CCS) presents a promising pathway to mitigate these emissions yet remains constrained by high costs and decreased energy efficiency. This study presents a comprehensive assessment of EfW + CCS, using a combined techno-economic and life cycle assessments approach. A thermodynamic steady-state model was developed in Aspen Plus to evaluate mass and energy balances for both standalone EfW and EfW + CCS. Results show that an EfW + CCS system with 250 ktpa capacity and 80% capture rate incurs a 35% energy penalty and increases capital (CAPEX) and operating expenditure (OPEX) both by 30%. Additionally, the system results in a positive net present value, 2.7% return on investment and a levelised cost of electricity of £163/MWh, but extended payback period from 4.5 to 8.3 years compared to standalone EfW. The life cycle assessment results showed a 33% reduction in global warming potential (GWP), though monoethanolamine production and carbon capture infrastructure increased other impacts. This study suggests that the current carbon price of £49.4/t CO 2 is insufficient to incentivise CCS deployment, with a required subsidy estimated at £178/t CO 2 captured. Furthermore, ammonia use for NO x removal strongly influenced GWP and OPEX, with 60% NO x removal resulting in a reduction of 41% in GWP and increasing OPEX by 19% compared to standalone EfW.

title: A calcium-assisted route for humic-carbon enrichment in manure–straw biochar via mild hydrothermal pretreatment and low-temperature pyrolysis
Transition to a circular economy in pearl aquaculture: Environmental impacts, consumer preferences, and willingness to pay
abstract: The transition to a circular economy in pearl aquaculture is hindered by uncertainties regarding both environmental performance and consumer acceptance of sustainability premiums in this luxury sector, yet these two dimensions have rarely been examined together. This creates a critical gap in understanding whether environmentally beneficial recycling practices can also gain support from consumers. This study integrates Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) with a Discrete Choice Experiment (DCE) to estimate consumers’ willingness to pay (WTP) for pearl products associated with recycling-based reductions in the environmental impacts of discarded pearl aquaculture cages. The LCA results show that the Full Recycling scenario substantially reduces environmental impacts compared with the Partial and No Recycling scenarios, primarily through resource substitution effects. Based on the DCE administered to 600 Japanese consumers, the analysis estimated a median premium of JPY 1,438 per pearl among experienced consumers for upgrading from No Recycling to Full Recycling. Incremental premiums were estimated at JPY 494 for upgrading from No Recycling to Partial Recycling and JPY 944 for upgrading from Partial Recycling to Full Recycling. Latent class analysis further showed that demand for recycling-based sustainability was concentrated among Eco-conscious Balancers, whereas higher-income Aesthetic Seekers placed greater weight on conventional luxury attributes such as luster and size. Together, the results quantify the environmental benefits of recycling-based circular strategies in pearl aquaculture and consumers’ stated WTP for these sustainability improvements, while economic feasibility still depends on additional cost-side evidence and credible sustainability communication.

Circular economy strategies in metal production: A comparative environmental and economic analysis of primary lead and secondary lead smelting in China
Contributions of ecological engineering to sustainable development goals on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau
Towards an extended product value model for circular products
abstract: The adoption of circular products remains limited despite strong consumer support for sustainability. A key explanation is the persistent gap between consumers’ stated intentions and their actual purchasing behaviour. Existing research in the circular economy has largely focused on improving the tangible characteristics of products, while paying less attention to how consumers perceive value. This conceptual article argues that the intention–behaviour gap is partly rooted in how circular products are experienced and valued. It examines the role of intangible value dimensions, particularly trust, authenticity, and symbolic meaning, in shaping consumer decisions. To do this, it develops a synthesis of three complementary frameworks: the Golden Circle from strategy and leadership, the multidimensional framework of product value and authenticity, and the marketing mix. The resulting extended product value model shows how organisational purpose, operational practices, and product attributes interact to shape perceived value. The analysis suggests that circular products are more likely to be adopted when they are experienced as trustworthy, meaningful, and relevant, not only environmentally beneficial. The article therefore argues that firms need to move beyond a narrow focus on material sustainability and engage more directly with how value is constructed and communicated. By highlighting the role of intangible value in enabling sustainable consumption, the paper contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of persistent barriers to the adoption of circular products.

Assessing the industrial-scale recycling feasibility of paper, board and fiber-based composites from lightweight packaging waste for high-quality applications
abstract: Despite high recycling targets, paper and board (PB), including fiber-based composites from German lightweight packaging waste (LWP), are still predominantly subjected to thermal recovery or low-quality recycling due to technical and regulatory barriers. To overcome these barriers and support the development of sustainable, high-quality recycling pathways (i.e., reutilization in applications comparable to the original product), we conducted two production trials in an operational board mill. The trials aimed to demonstrate technical recycling feasibility on an industrial scale, while generating data to support regulatory adaptation and providing primary data for a subsequent comparative life cycle assessment. Using a tailored quality assessment, we evaluated the entire process chain, including dry mechanical sorting, defibration, wet mechanical processing with an additional hygienization step, and final board production. The results indicate that PB recycling from LWP for high-quality applications is technically feasible (under investigated conditions, feedstock share 12.5 wt%), provided that specific process adaptations are implemented. Based on the assessed quality parameters, a substitution coefficient of 0.75 was derived for PB from LWP in the newly developed recycling process, indicating near-equivalent recyclability to that of conventionally collected recovered PB. Overall, this study provides a comprehensive industrial-scale quality assessment of PB recycling from LWP, with a particular focus on primary data collection and high-quality material recovery. The results support the scientific basis for the development of sustainable recycling pathways.
