Quantitative social life cycle assessment of plastic, bioplastic, and paper packaging systems
abstract: Social impacts in packaging supply chains remain underexplored compared to environmental and economic aspects, despite their growing relevance in sustainability decision-making. This study applies Social Life Cycle Assessment (S-LCA) to evaluate the social sustainability of three carrier bag types: low-density polyethylene (LDPE) plastic, polylactic acid (PLA) bioplastic and kraft paper. The assessment is conducted using OpenLCA by integrating primary data with the SOCA V2 database, and focuses on four stakeholder groups, including Local Communities, Society, Value Chain Actors, and Workers. Social impacts are quantified across life cycle stages and stakeholder categories. Results are expressed as “medium risk hours,” a relative indicator used for comparative hotspot identification. The results indicate that Society and Value Chain Actors face high to very high risks (>40%) across all materials, highlighting potential areas for improvements. The PLA bioplastic bag exhibits the highest social impacts during raw material production, while the kraft paper bag performs worst in manufacturing and end-of life treatment. Overall social impacts rank PLA bioplastic highest (95.79 medium risk hours), followed by kraft paper (54.45), and LDPE plastic (35.15), a ranking that challenges common assumptions about the sustainability of bioplastics and paper alternatives. This quantitative social impact analysis provides clear, data-driven insights into social risk hotspots and improvement opportunities.

title: Physically consistent design of hybrid renewable energy systems for green methanol: A chained load modeling and techno-economic approach
Interactions between curbside collection and open-access street recycling systems: Evidence from a field experiment in Chile
ESG reporting and action in real estate: A case study of Australian Real Estate Investment Trusts
abstract: ESG (Environmental, Social and Governance) has emerged as the latest catchphrase to define sustainability in organisational practice. However, understanding what ESG means in practice and how it applies in the real estate sector remains mute. Building rating tools have significantly influenced market adoption of sustainable building practices. This paper explored ESG reporting and prevalence of sustainability rating tool use by Australian Real Estate Investment Trusts (AREITs), through a content analysis and comparison of 10 AREITs sustainability and/or annual reports. Findings revealed a higher emphasis on the Social component of ESG, mainly focused on aspects of Community and Customer relations, surpassing the Environmental and Governance criteria in terms of number of occurrences and investments disclosed. ESG strategies were found to be interconnected, with actions mainly defined by a combination of environmental, social and governance aspects. Leading AREITs, classified as frontrunners, were characterised by more detailed disclosure of their actions, alignment with global financial standards and a strong commitment to financial disclosures related to ESG and sustainability. Sustainability rating tools were commonly used to demonstrate ESG credentials, mostly focused on performance-based tools, yet an increasing focus was dedicated to social sustainability, especially in health and wellbeing of building occupants. Findings from this research help establish AREITs reporting practices of ESG and sustainability, albeit it should be acknowledged there is some disconnect between corporate sustainability and the asset portfolio's sustainability. It also provides the property industry with a better understanding of the profile of current ESG and sustainability characteristics in real estate, enabling prioritisation and reflection in the ESG consideration requirements under the International Valuation Standards.

title: Global vulnerability of coastal blue carbon ecosystems to climate and anthropogenic impacts: A spatiotemporal perspective
Navigating toward 2050 decarbonization: A design-constrained life cycle emission and costs assessment for sustainable marine fuel retrofits incorporating feedstock sources
abstract: This study contributes to the maritime industry's pathway toward the IMO 2050 net-zero objective through an integrated approach that links design-constrained retrofit evaluation and fuel feedstock sources with life-cycle and cost assessments. Two representative vessels, a 49 m Ro-Ro ship operating on medium range routes and an 87 m car ferry operating on longer routes, are evaluated, with propulsion configurations divided into ICE systems and electric motor systems. Retrofit scenarios include electric propulsion using lithium-ion batteries and hydrogen fuel cells, and ICE propulsion operating on methanol and ammonia, both recognized for their potential to deliver low or near-zero carbon emissions. Environmental performance is assessed through a well to wake life cycle assessment, while the cost analysis incorporates feedstock sources to evaluate long-term cost feasibility under future decarbonization pathways. The retrofit feasibility assessment shows that all alternatives except pure battery-electric propulsion are technically achievable, with battery energy density as the limiting factor. From a life cycle perspective, hybrid diesel–electric propulsion, fossil based hydrogen fuel cells, fossil based ammonia ICE, and renewable energy based methanol ICE offer viable mid-term mitigation options, while only renewable energy based ammonia and renewable energy based hydrogen enable net zero decarbonization consistent with long-term climate objectives. Integrating retrofit feasibility, environmental performance, and cost assessment, the study highlights ammonia-based ICE systems as particularly promising solutions for achieving IMO 2050 targets, offering both technical feasibility and economic robustness under time horizon and scenario of this study.

title: Risk control zoning optimization and source contribution identification of microplastics in wetland water under ecological risk threshold and uncertainty constraints

The economics of mine waste reduction: The case of ore-sand
abstract: Amid rising mineral demand for the renewable energy transition and a long-term decline in average metal ore grades, volumes of mine waste are expected to increase significantly. This paper presents an economic model to assess the private economic benefits of extracting large-volume by-products to reduce mine waste. Using the case of ore-sand-a type of manufactured sand that can be produced as a by-product of metal ore mining-this paper quantifies profitability across various adoption scenarios. The dynamic economic model is calibrated to a representative large-scale iron-ore operation covering a 30-year mine's life and uses Monte Carlo simulations to evaluate the different adoption scenarios. Simulations indicate significant economic incentives for ore-sand adoption though with substantial heterogeneity across factors such as the costs of waste management and rehabilitation costs, recovery rates, processing efficiency, and output prices. The findings highlight that, while ore-sand profitability is subject to important uncertainty in costs and final demand, cost savings in tailings waste management and mine rehabilitation from the primary operation provide robust economic incentives for adoption.

title: Integrating LCA and geospatial analysis to assess the environmental and logistical feasibility of sugarcane bagasse ash as supplementary cementitious material in Brazil
abstract: This study evaluates the environmental and logistical feasibility of replacing calcined clay (CC) with sugarcane bagasse ash (SCBA) as a supplementary cementitious material (SCM) in Brazilian Portland-blended cement, using an integrated approach that combines life cycle assessment (LCA) and geospatial analysis. Two formulations of Portland-blended cement were assessed: one containing 14% CC as the pozzolanic material, and another in which this pozzolanic fraction was fully replaced by SCBA. LCA results were used to determine the maximum transport distance over which SCBA can be delivered to cement plants without compromising the environmental benefits achieved relative to CC. Subsequently, all cement plants and sugarcane mills in Brazil were mapped and spatially integrated with these transport limits. Replacing CC with SCBA reduced environmental impacts in every category evaluated, reflecting the advantages of using an agricultural waste in place of an energy-intensive pozzolan. SCBA can be transported up to 2665 km considering the global warming category and up to 669 km for fine particulate matter emissions while maintaining net environmental benefits over CC. Spatial analysis revealed that from an environmental perspective, most Brazilian cement plants (91%) could incorporate SCBA as an SCM, and 70% are located within 300 km of a sugarcane mill. Annual CO 2 equivalent emissions could be reduced by approximately 1 Mt if 70% of Brazilian cement plants incorporate SCBA. Overall, the wide availability of SCBA and its environmental advantages support its large-scale adoption in the Brazilian cement industry.

title: Robust PROMETHEE II screening of nutrient recovery technologies for cleaner production in wastewater treatment
abstract: Wastewater nutrient recovery can support cleaner production by reducing dependence on primary fertilisers, but early-stage technology shortlisting remains difficult when evidence is drawn from heterogeneous studies and stakeholder priorities differ. This study develops a PROMETHEE II screening framework for seven pilot-to-near-market nutrient recovery configurations in wastewater treatment plants, covering air stripping, chemical precipitation, ion exchange with regeneration, and electrochemical systems. The alternatives are compared using a compact first-stage criterion set: total cost, potential climate-substitution benefit, and recovery efficiency, all expressed per unit of nutrient recovered. Ranking stability is examined across 405 PROMETHEE II runs combining three preference-function scenarios, five stakeholder weighting profiles, and 27 threshold combinations. The results do not identify a universally superior technology, but rather robust candidates within the assessed dataset, retained criteria, and modelling assumptions. Electrochemical struvite recovery is the most stable high-performing option, remaining in the Top-3 in all runs and ranking first in 65.2%, with 90% recovery efficiency and 3.30 kg CO 2 e avoided per kg nutrient. Air stripping on digestate ranks first in 34.8% of runs and represents the strongest cost-oriented candidate, with the lowest unit cost (€1.78 kg −1 ) and 90% efficiency, provided that concentrated digestate streams are available. The framework converts heterogeneous techno-economic evidence into reproducible early-stage shortlisting evidence, while final implementation requires site-specific techno-economic, regulatory, agronomic, operational, market, and life-cycle assessment.

title: Calculating balance of cumulative non-fossil methane emissions over consecutive or non-consecutive periods of livestock production
abstract: Methane (CH 4 ) emissions from livestock production are conventionally reported as annual methane emissions (AME) or converted to carbon dioxide equivalents. However, these assessments cannot determine the methane burden or removal in the atmosphere, as they do not account for continuous methane removal and short-term accumulation. Consequently, they may obscure the identification of livestock (sub)sectors or (sub)populations with methane burden or removal, thereby limiting optimal mitigation efforts. Here, a novel method is developed and demonstrated to calculate the balance of cumulative non-fossil methane emissions (BME) over consecutive or non-consecutive livestock production periods, considering the atmospheric methane decay. Two BME approaches are defined: BME with a chain base (BME C ), which allows comparison of two cumulative methane emissions (CME) in consecutive years i and i + 1; and BME with a fixed base (BME F ), which allows comparison of CME in year j (where j can range from -∞ to ∞) with a fixed CME in year i. The average BME F for Slovenian dairy cows and non-dairy cattle between 2018 and 2022, compared to the fixed year 2001, was −46.45 kt CH 4 and 19.76 kt CH 4 , indicating a long-term methane removal and burden, respectively, from these sectors. For practical use, BME C and BME F can be applied across livestock farming systems to assess and monitor short-term and long-term efficiency, respectively, in any (sub)sector or (sub)population. In addition, BME provides a template for developing novel tools for farmers and enables the incorporation of reduced AME through methane mitigation measures.

title: Land transfers, efficiency improves? The land–labor–capital synergy behind grain eco-efficiency gains in China
Carbon taxes, emissions trading, and policy mix effects on carbon intensity: Causal and distributional evidence from OECD countries
abstract: This study examines the comparative effectiveness of carbon pricing mechanisms, namely carbon taxes, emissions trading systems (ETS), and their combined use, in reducing carbon intensity across 38 OECD countries from 1990 to 2024. Addressing key methodological shortcomings in the existing literature, we utilize recent advances in staggered difference-in-differences methods to derive credible causal estimates that accommodate heterogeneous treatment effects across adoption cohorts and time. To further explore distributional variations in policy impacts, we employ method of moments quantile regression techniques. Our results indicate that all three policy configurations are associated with statistically significant reductions in carbon intensity, with combined instruments producing the strongest average effect (approximately 10.7%). Dynamic analysis shows that policy impacts intensify over time, with carbon taxes achieving a reduction of up to 16.7% and ETS up to 17.0% after 12–14 years. Quantile-based findings reveal notable heterogeneity: the association between carbon pricing adoption and carbon intensity reductions strengthens at higher quantiles, suggesting greater impact in countries with initially high carbon intensity. In contrast, combined policies exhibit stronger associations at lower quantiles, implying reinforcement of decarbonization trends in already cleaner economies. These insights offer practical guidance for policymakers seeking to tailor carbon pricing strategies to national contexts and long-term sustainability goals.

Biobased fertilisers from fishery side-streams: an environmentally friendly alternative to mineral fertilisers?
abstract: The replacement of mineral fertilisers by biobased fertilisers (BBFs) produced from organic waste streams is promoted by the European Union to reduce political dependencies and nutrient excess. Life cycle assessment (LCA) studies have so far been mainly conducted on BBFs produced from municipal biowaste, sewage sludge and animal manures, primarily considering their production phase. This LCA study compares for the first time environmental impacts of three BBFs produced from fishery side-streams against those of mineral fertilisers assessing both BBF production (per kg N) and application (per kg broccoli), assuming burden-free side-streams. Compared to mineral fertilisers, two BBFs (one from fish sludge, the other from fish frames and heads) had a 3-62% (per kg N) and 11% (per kg broccoli) lower global warming potential and a 1-12% (per kg N) and 7-13% (per kg broccoli) lower mineral resources use. However, the third BBF from fish viscera showed overall higher impacts than the mineral fertiliser highlighting the importance of optimising the production of BBFs and their agronomic performance. Levers for optimisation include establishing the BBF production close to the location of the side-stream, implementing energy-efficient drying technologies and appropriate BBF application techniques. Methodological challenges such as modelling field emissions of BBFs and lacking harmonization of LCA methodology for the assessment of BBFs are discussed. By considering both production and application of BBFs, this study shows that BBFs from fishery side-streams can provide environmental benefits when used as a substitute for mineral fertilisers and identifies optimisation potential along the life cycle.

title: A multi-source traceability and assessment framework for comprehensive environmental impacts in national parks: A case of Wuyishan National Park
How does carbon emissions trading affect renewable electricity consumption? City-level evidence and mechanisms from China
Alternative passenger car fleet decarbonisation pathways in Europe
abstract: Achieving rapid reductions in real-world CO 2 emissions from road transport requires not only ambitious CO 2 standards for new vehicles, but also policy designs that accelerate fleet turnover and promote electric driving under real-world conditions. An open question is whether passenger car fleet decarbonisation can be achieved solely through full electrification or also through plug-in hybrid powertrain configurations that operate predominantly in electric mode. While the European Union's (EU) current CO 2 standards focus on type-approval performance of new vehicles, their climate impacts depend critically on fleet turnover rates, fuel mix, as well as user behaviour, particularly during the transition period up to 2040 when the displacement of internal combustion engine vehicles is most critical. This study uses a scenario-based assessment framework to examine alternative decarbonisation pathways for the EU passenger car fleet up to 2050. Two scenarios are compared: a baseline pathway consistent with the current EU CO 2 standards, and an alternative stylised pathway reflecting possible market responses to the European Commission's Automotive Package. Particular attention is given to the role of plug-in range-extended electric vehicles (PREVs), together with conventional plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs), as complementary technologies to pure electric vehicles (PEVs) that may support faster fleet renewal under regulatory flexibility supporting technological neutrality. Results indicate that under favourable conditions, the alternative pathway leads to lower cumulative tailpipe CO 2 emissions than the baseline pathway with reductions of about 8% between 2028 and 2040. However, the results show that these benefits are highly sensitive to real-world use. If PREVs are operated with electric driving shares similar to current use of PHEVs, the gains are substantially reduced and can reverse beyond 2040 in the longer term. Differences relative to the current standards pathway remain limited up to 2040 because older internal combustion engine vehicles still dominate fleet emissions during much of the transition. The results also indicate persistent demand for liquid fuels in mixed electrification pathways, highlighting the importance for achieving decarbonisation targets of low-carbon fuel supply for road transport alongside electrification. Overall, these findings suggest that regulatory flexibility allowing technological neutrality over the next decade does not automatically accelerate or delay decarbonisation. Its effectiveness depends largely on the conditions under which it is implemented, especially real-world electric driving, fleet-turnover dynamics and supporting fuel and electricity pathways, with prudent assumptions suggesting that until 2040 decarbonisation would not be slowed.

title: Digital-twin driven thermo-mechanical coupled modeling for temperature-prediction in reheating furnaces

Does the market assign a premium to environmental resource efficiency? The synergistic impact of water and energy performance on firm value in an emerging economy
abstract: As climate change continues to progress, corporate sustainability transitions are increasingly relevant, though their financial viability within capital-constrained emerging markets remains a subject of ongoing debate. Anchored in the Natural-Resource-Based View (NRBV), this study investigates whether financial markets assign valuation premiums to corporate environmental resource efficiencies, specifically examining the combined effects of water and energy management on overall company value. Using panel data from 66 socially responsible companies listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange from 2013 to 2021, the study employs a dynamic two-step system generalized method of moments, complemented by omitted variable, propensity score matching, Lind-Mehlum non-linear, and Dumitrescu-Hurlin causality robustness checks. The findings suggest that isolated water conservation is associated with marginal benefits (short-run β = 0.0438, long-run β = 0.0521; p < 0.10), while standalone energy transitions show a persistent negative relationship with market valuation (short-run β = −0.2125, long-run β = −0.2530; p < 0.01). These results indicate that the market may associate isolated environmental expenditures with linear sunk costs rather than value-adding investments. However, the concurrent integration of water and energy strategies is associated with a statistically significant, positive impact on firm valuation (short-run β = 0.4498, long-run β = 0.5355; p < 0.01). Furthermore, causality evaluations map a bidirectional sustainability feedback loop, suggesting that integrated resource management is positively associated with market valuation, which subsequently could help finance further integrated operations. Consequently, it is suggested that corporate executives consider transitioning from fragmented compliance toward integrated environmental management systems to unlock sustained competitive advantage. Furthermore, policymakers might explore structuring fiscal incentives for holistic resource strategies rather than isolated environmental targets, which may help align corporate sustainability with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and economic growth.

Demand-driven environmental responsibility in livestock systems: Integrating trade-linked land-use change and consumption-based accounting
abstract: Livestock systems contribute substantially to greenhouse-gas emissions, land-use change, and biodiversity pressures, yet responsibility for these impacts is often obscured by fragmented accounting frameworks and globally dispersed supply chains. Territorial inventories frequently separate environmental pressures from the consumption patterns that drive production across regions. This study develops a harmonized livestock-focused accounting framework combining trade-linked land-use-change attribution with consumption-based environmentally extended multi-regional input–output accounting. Livestock-related land-use-change emissions were quantified for 2018–2022 using the Singh et al. hybrid trade-flow database and FAOSTAT feed-use shares, while consumption-based terrestrial animal-product supply-chain emissions were quantified for 2020–2022 using EXIOBASE 3.9.6 MRIO tables and World Bank population statistics. Results show that livestock-related land-use-change emissions were dominated by pasture-linked ruminant systems, with Brazil representing the largest producer-location hotspot. Consumption-based attribution further showed that both domestic demand within producer economies and internationally traded demand contributed substantially to livestock-related land-use-change responsibility. Consumption-based terrestrial animal-product emissions revealed strong regional inequality: Global North economies maintained substantially higher per-capita emissions, while China accounted for the largest aggregate national emissions due to population scale and rising demand for animal-source foods. These findings demonstrate that livestock-related environmental responsibility is jointly shaped by producer-location hotspots, international trade, demographic scale, and consumption intensity. Interpretations of responsibility therefore depend strongly on accounting boundaries and producer–consumer relationships within globally interconnected supply chains. By integrating producer-location and consumption-based perspectives, the framework provides a more comprehensive basis for understanding livestock-related environmental pressures and informing cleaner production, demand-side mitigation, and food-system governance strategies.

title: The relationship between income inequality and energy poverty in the context of sustainable development goals: A micro-instrumental variables estimation in Türkiye
abstract: Energy poverty has adverse consequences on individuals’ lives. It endangers their health, interrupts their education, and may even undermine equality both within and between them. Since income inequality remains a significant problem on the path to achieving sustainable development in Türkiye, identifying its determinants on a micro scale is of great importance. In this regard, this study analysed the relationship of energy poverty to personal income inequality in Türkiye, utilising the TurkStat 2017-2020 income and living conditions survey micro-panel dataset. Instrumental variables estimation was used, and robustness checks were applied to achieve this aim. According to this, energy poverty is negatively related to personal income inequality. To check for heterogeneity, this relationship was re-examined within three income groups. The findings suggested that while energy poverty is positively related to personal income inequality at the bottom of the income distribution, it is negatively related to personal income inequality at the top of the income distribution. This study mainly contributes to the literature by providing the first micro-level evidence on the relationship between income inequality and energy poverty. A combination of targeted social and energy policies is required to tackle both energy poverty and income inequality on the micro scale in Türkiye.

The role of central actors in improving the circular economy adoption in born-sustainable industries: Case of the offshore wind industry
abstract: Industries are increasingly shifting from linear to circular economy (CE) practices in response to growing resource pressures. Traditional industries, however, find this transition costly and difficult because their value creation models are long established, which creates rigidities that slow change. One way to avoid these barriers is for emerging sectors in the green transition to be born-sustainable. These sectors are designed around sustainability principles from the outset and continuously innovate to improve their environmental performance. Many of them are adopting CE practices to reduce reliance on virgin materials during manufacturing and to minimise waste at the end of life. Despite these intentions, overall CE adoption in born-sustainable industries remains limited. This study argues that the complexity of value chain structures plays a central role, since numerous stakeholders are involved and some hold more influence than others in driving progress. The research examines how central actors contribute to CE adoption in born-sustainable sectors through a case study of the offshore wind industry, supported by insights from the Solar PV and EV battery sectors. The analysis identifies regulatory bodies, asset owners and component manufacturers as central actors. It also shows that these actors need to engage in two types of collective-oriented governance collaborations, both within their industry and beyond industry boundaries. They are considered central because they can influence regulation, shape cross-industry CE initiatives, and build the collaborations needed to advance CE from a systemic perspective.

Touch performance and microfiber pollution potentials of commercial fleece fabrics
abstract: This paper aims to measure the skin touch comfort parameters and microfiber shedding potentials of commercially produced three-thread fleece (3 TF) fabrics objectively and quantitatively, which have not been presented before. Four different 3 TF fabrics – straight, double tuck, 3-butt diagonal, and 4-butt diagonal - were produced in an industrial setup using the same types of yarns, under identical knitting and finishing conditions with a cotton-polyester blend ratio of 70:30. The skin touch sensation of these fabrics was tested using the latest Fabric Touch Tester (FTT) from SDL ATLAS, initially developed by Hong Kong Research Institute of Textile and Apparel (HKRITA) and the Honk Kong Polytechnique University. To evaluate the microfiber shedding tendency of these fabrics, the material loss from the fleece fabrics during washing was determined following the BS EN ISO 4484-1:2023 and fiber shedding by mechanical abrasion was tested using an industrially practiced method known as pilling box-syringe test. Findings show that double tuck structure performs the best when the touch comfort properties and microfiber pollution potential are considered jointly. It also shows that the industrially practised pilling box-syringe method for testing fiber shedding suffers from limitations and needs further improvement.

Transitioning to a circular economy: A framework of economic analysis and measures of circularity
abstract: The transition to a circular economy (CE) is crucial for addressing the complex challenges of population growth, climate change, and the need to boost production in food, feed, fiber, and bioenergy amidst depleting natural resources. Even though circular economic systems comprise both market mechanisms and material flow systems and their feasibility and sustainability depend largely on their economic viability, the role of markets and the economics associated with their functioning have largely been ignored by the relevant literature. This paper presents a general, empirically relevant, integrated multimarket framework of analysis of the supply chain transition to a more circular system. The framework explicitly accounts for imperfectly competitive market structures at the various stages of the supply chain and for the joint production and disposability when modeling the relevant production technologies in the supply chain of interest. The framework can also be utilized to examine the market and welfare impacts of a number of changes in the demand and/or supply conditions due to increased circularity (like changes in consumer preferences, production technologies, costs and market structure), identify potential market failures and rebound effects, and inform the design of policies and strategies that can induce the system transition to a more socially desirable level of circularity.

title: Power play: A multi-criteria analysis of present and future battery technologies
abstract: Advancing electrification requires batteries that combine high performance with sustainability, cost-effectiveness, and supply-chain resilience.Post lithium-ion batteries (PLIBs) such as sodium-ion (SIB), lithium-sulfur (LSB), and solid-state batteries (SSB) are widely discussed as alternatives to today's lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), yet discussion of their technical and sustainability benefits and drawbacks remains fragmented.Here we present an integrated, multi-criteria assessment of twelve battery chemistries, combining cradle-to-gate life cycle, raw material criticality and material cost analyses with performance metrics, specific energy and energy density into a unified comparison.On average, PLIBs exhibit 114 % higher global warming potential and up to 461 % higher material costs than LIBs, particularly when lithium metal or specialty lithium chemicals are required.SIBs achieve 94 % lower criticality and slightly lower cost than LIBs, although their specific energy and energy density remain comparatively low.SSBs deliver the highest specific energy, outperforming LIBs, but depend on costly and less scalable materials.LSBs exploit abundant sulfur and offer high theoretical specific energy, but today's reliance on lithium foil and electrolyte-intensive designs lead to elevated cost, criticality, and carbon footprint.A sensitivity analysis demonstrates how improvements in specific energies enhance PLIB competitiveness.By linking sustainability, cost and criticality hotspots with performance, this study identifies targeted areas of improvement to guide next-generation battery development.

title: Sustainable lactic acid production from lignocellulosic biomass via circular salt recycling: Techno-economic and life cycle assessment
Agents of the circular ecosystem engaged in Preparation for Reuse (PfR) activities: a set of best practices for circularity
abstract: Preparation for Reuse (PfR) encompasses activities such as reuse, repair, refurbishment, remanufacturing, and repurposing, occupying a priority position within the waste management hierarchy by enabling the extension of the useful life of products and materials with lower additional consumption of resources and energy when compared to recycling and energy recovery. Despite its relevance, PfR remains underrepresented in public policies, monitoring instruments, and consolidated operational models, which limits its adoption on a broader scale. In this context, this article aimed to propose a set of best practices for the incorporation of PfR by organizations, thereby contributing to the transition toward a Circular Economy. To this end, this study adopts a qualitative multiple-case study research design and a systematic literature review, guided by an abductive analytical approach, systematic combining, which blends deductive and inductive elements across three interconnected phases. The results show that, although heterogeneous, these organizations share convergent patterns in operational, managerial, and institutional aspects. Based on these findings, the study systematizes best practices in a framework structured around five analytical dimensions – collection and logistics, operations and technical aspects, governance and management, financial sustainability, and social and educational practices – and in an operational flowchart that visualizes their application along the material trajectory. This framework supports the identification of bottlenecks, the prioritization of actions, and organizational self-diagnosis, helping organizations recognize which practices they already perform and which represent opportunities for development. Thus, the study contributes by providing applicable instruments that bring PfR closer to its concrete implementation as a Circular Economy strategy.

Nuclear cogeneration in district heating systems: optimal pathways to decarbonization
abstract: Nuclear cogeneration—the use of nuclear plants in cogeneration mode to produce both heat and electricity—is a proven technology for decarbonized electricity generation and has already been employed in a number of district heating (DH) networks worldwide. However, despite its promises as an option for low-carbon residential and commercial space heating, expanding the use of nuclear technology requires substantial investment, whereas more established conventional low-carbon heat energy sources such as biomass and large-scale heat pumps are already available. At this juncture, the potential role of nuclear cogeneration demands thoughtful assessment. This paper aims to identify key factors influencing the optimal transition pathways to low-carbon DH systems with the potential to include nuclear cogeneration plants. We explore how nuclear cogeneration can fit into an optimized heat production mix at local scale alongside conventional low-carbon technologies. We develop scenarios to quantify the benefits of nuclear cogeneration in optimal multi-year DH network decarbonization pathways in various local-scale configurations and exogenous economic and policy conditions. Transport of heat produced is a pivotal factor in both the modeling and the economic evaluation. Our results suggest that integrating a nuclear cogeneration plant (NCP) into the set of technologies available to the DH planner could significantly reduce overall DH system costs, with larger and closer networks benefiting more from NCP availability. The economic competitiveness of nuclear cogeneration depends primarily on NCP-to-DH network distance, annual consumption of the DH network, and discount rate, rather than on carbon emissions caps or the prices of conventional fuel sources. We find that when it is cost-competitive to include nuclear cogeneration in the production mix, the NCP can largely replace conventional low-carbon heat generators and cover the bulk of district heat demand.

Shifting to bio-based plastics in Austria: An assessment of options within the bioeconomy under land constraints
abstract: Bio-based plastics are promoted as a sustainable alternative to fossil-based plastics to reduce emissions, fossil fuel dependency, and environmental pollution. However, increasing bio-based plastic production can intensify land-use pressures through competition with food, feed, and bioenergy. By incorporating a detailed representation of bio-based plastics production into the mass-balanced accounting model FoodClim, we analyze an option space consisting of 432 scenarios for 2050 to explore the potential for a shift to bio-based plastics without expanding agricultural land and compromising food security in Austria. These scenarios combine assumptions for bio-based plastic demand with changes in diets, bioenergy consumption, trade patterns, and food losses. We find that a full substitution with bio-based plastics, assuming no other systemic changes, would increase the cropland embodied in domestic biomass inputs (domestic extraction and imports) into the Austrian bioeconomy by 0.29 megahectares (Mha), or 6.6%, under an ambitious plastic demand reduction scenario. In contrast, in the absence of any plastic demand reduction, this increase would rise to 0.41 Mha, or 11.2%, compared to the 2050 reference scenario. The option space reveals that 14.6% of the scenarios remain within domestic and global agricultural land limits, as defined by the 2020 baseline. These scenarios require at least shifts to less land-intensive diets, limited bioenergy demand, and improved food system efficiency, with the majority also involving a significant reduction in plastic demand. Without these systemic changes, a shift to bio-based plastics could result in land-use changes, posing risks to biodiversity and food security.

A hybrid machine learning framework for enhanced day-ahead solar forecasting in large scale systems
abstract: Accurate solar power forecasting is becoming increasingly crucial for the efficient planning and operation of modern power systems as solar energy constitutes a growing share of the energy mix. This work evaluates the performance of various artificial neural network (ANN) models for day-ahead solar power forecasting. Through two case studies, it examines the impact of seasonal and weather-related variations on large-scale distributed solar generation. The analysis draws on solar power generation and weather data from the Imperial Irrigation District (IID) and the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power (LADWP) in the United States from January 2019 to December 2022, with over 20,000 h of operational data. The bidirectional long short-term memory (Bi-LSTM) model demonstrated the highest accuracy in day-ahead solar power forecasting and was selected as the baseline for comparison. To further improve prediction accuracy, two ensemble approaches, namely weighted averaging and multi-input, were explored. The results show that both approaches improve forecasting performance relative to the baseline, yielding positive MAE-based skill score improvements on the order of several percent across seasons. In particular, weighted averaging provides stronger and more consistent gains in the IID case study, with skill score improvements reaching approximately 11% in favorable seasons, whereas the multi-input ensemble demonstrates more consistently favorable performance in the LADWP case study, achieving skill score improvements of up to about 13%. These findings suggest that ensemble formulations provide a practical framework for improving day-ahead solar power forecasting in large-scale distributed PV systems. The results further indicate that performance depends on regional characteristics and the structure of available meteorological inputs.

title: Prediction of breakthrough time in hydrogen purification from coke oven gas using deep learning model
Biodiversity at risk when businesses rely on narrow indicators
abstract: Businesses are major drivers of biodiversity loss and face increasing pressure to assess and disclose risks to biodiversity from their activities. Yet it remains unclear which indicators businesses rely on to measure biodiversity, and whether these indicators represent biodiversity broadly enough to support robust decision-making. We reviewed which indicators Global Fortune 500 businesses in high-impact sectors have reported using and assessed how well these indicators represent biodiversity. As of 2025, only 9% of assessed businesses had reported using biodiversity indicators. Businesses that reported indicators rarely applied more than one simultaneously, and these indicators captured only a narrow scope of biodiversity. Spatial correlations among the indicators were often weak, and sometimes negative, indicating that decisions based on avoiding high-value areas for one indicator, such as ecosystem integrity measured by Mean Species Abundance (MSA), may still degrade areas important for another, such as threatened-species importance measured by the STAR metric. We further identified ecoregions where comprehensive biodiversity assessments are especially critical because high values of multiple indicators, most notably threatened-species importance, coincide with areas projected to undergo high habitat loss by 2050. In 33 of the world's 846 terrestrial ecoregions, more than half of the aggregated value of each assessed indicator was concentrated in such high-risk areas, rising to at least 80% in 10 ecoregions. Most of these ecoregions occur in the tropics, where agricultural expansion and deforestation are the primary drivers of projected habitat loss. Composites integrating multiple indicators can reduce the risk of overlooking important values, but applying multiple individual indicators in parallel remains the most robust way to retain information on each biodiversity aspect.

An integrated life-cycle assessment of three different propulsion pathways for medium-sized wheel loaders under Nordic quarry conditions: A case study
abstract: Non-road mobile machinery (NRMM) represents a hard-to-abate segment because of high power demand, long operating hours, and limited charging or refuelling flexibility. To address the limited evidence linking life-cycle climate performance and economic competitiveness in NRMM, this study applies an integrated life-cycle assessment (LCA) and techno-economic assessment (TEA) to three propulsion pathways for medium-sized wheel loaders operating under Nordic quarry conditions: diesel internal-combustion engines, battery-electric drivetrains, and hydrogen fuel-cell electric systems. Environmental performance is evaluated using a work-normalised functional unit (kg CO 2 -eq t −1 moved), while economic performance is assessed using relative-adjusted total cost of ownership (RA–TCO, € t −1 moved), complemented by net present cost and Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis. Under the assessed Nordic electricity, energy-price, utilisation, and quarry-duty assumptions, battery-electric wheel loaders achieve the lowest life-cycle greenhouse-gas emissions and RA–TCO across the four countries considered. This outcome is driven by high drivetrain efficiency, comparatively low grid-carbon intensity, and lower energy expenditure per unit of productive work. Hydrogen results are strongly dependent on the production pathway and upstream electricity supply. Renewable hydrogen can reduce life-cycle emissions relative to diesel under low-carbon electricity conditions, but remains cost-disadvantaged in the modelled cases, whereas grid-based electrolytic hydrogen can exceed diesel impacts when supplied by carbon-intensive electricity. Investment support and shared infrastructure improve battery-electric economics, while the hydrogen pathways remain more sensitive to fuel price and infrastructure utilisation. The findings indicate that battery-electric propulsion is the most robust option for the medium-sized wheel-loader application and Nordic quarry conditions evaluated in this study. The results should not be interpreted as a universal ranking for all NRMM applications, duty cycles, electricity systems, or regional markets.

title: Towards a circular water economy in Southeast Asian cities
abstract: Water supply continuity and quality are significant policy challenges in developing countries, exposing shortcomings in resourcing, infrastructure, and governance capacity. At the same time, water policy often remains embedded in a command-and-control paradigm that relies on perpetual technological innovation and infrastructure investment to offset increasingly unsustainable demand patterns and management inefficiencies. This article explores the opportunities and challenges of integrating a circular-based perspective at the urban scale to overcome exploitive and inefficient patterns of water management, focusing on Southeast Asia. Emerging from the realm of industrial production, the circular economy emphasizes waste reduction and reuse. The circular water economy can be used a means for addressing supply scarcity. While a physical circular water economy would still primarily be local or national in scale, we posit that policy coordination, knowledge exchange, and institutional learning across Southeast Asia urban areas can complement localized circular water practices by generating a community of practice. The article concludes with six practical pathways to realizing this ambition.

Study on the impact of recycled plastic introduction methods on the performance of asphalt mixtures
abstract: Each year, millions of tons of waste plastic are produced, yet the recycling rate remains low. Incorporating recycled plastics into asphalt pavement construction is a promising approach to utilizing waste plastics beneficially. Various methods exist for introducing recycled plastics into asphalt mixtures; however, most past studies have focused on laboratory-produced plastics-modified asphalt mixtures. Plant production conditions differ significantly from those in laboratory settings and may therefore affect the performance of plastic-modified asphalt mixtures. This study evaluated how plant- and laboratory-based introduction methods of recycled plastics influence asphalt mixture performance, particularly at high application rates. Recycled plastics, a blend of high-density polyethylene (HDPE) and low-density polyethylene (LDPE), were introduced into plant-produced loose asphalt mixtures in the plant and laboratory, respectively. Recycled PE was added at rates of 0%, 0.75%, and 1.5% of the total asphalt mixture mass, respectively. The results showed that the introduction methods had a significant influence on asphalt mixture performance in terms of rutting and fatigue cracking resistance. The addition of 1.5% plastics resulted in a 45.5% increase in cracking resistance for laboratory-introduced mixtures, whereas a 24.4% reduction was observed for plant-introduced mixtures. The absorption of maltenes by recycled PE and the reinforcing effects of recycled plastics are believed to play key roles in performance outcomes. This study demonstrated the importance of using realistic production conditions when evaluating the performance of recycled plastics-modified asphalt mixtures.

Enhancing mechanical performance and environmental sustainability of poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate) biopolymers using modified bio-oils: A comparative study
abstract: Poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV) is a promising biodegradable polymer for sustainable packaging applications; however, its inherent brittleness and limited flexibility restrict its wider use. Bio-based plasticizers have the potential to improve the performance of this material while reducing dependence on fossil-derived additives. Therefore, this study investigates the effects of different modified bio-oils on the mechanical performance and environmental sustainability of plasticized PHBV materials, with Mesamoll® included as a synthetic plasticizer reference for comparison. Mechanical performance was evaluated through tensile and Charpy impact tests, while thermal properties were analyzed using differential scanning calorimetry. In addition, a cradle-to-grave life cycle assessment was performed using the Environmental Footprint (EF) v3.1 method to compare the environmental impacts of bio-based and synthetic plasticizers. The results showed that bio-based plasticizers significantly improved the processability and mechanical performance of the polymer. Among the investigated formulations, the material containing 20 wt% sunflower and soybean oil epoxidized ester achieved a tensile strength of 24.6 MPa and a strain at break of 2.2%, showing performance comparable to that of the synthetic plasticizer Mesamoll®. The addition of modified bio-oils reduced processing torque and temperature, indicating improved flowability during processing. Thermal analysis revealed changes in melting temperature and crystallinity depending on the type and concentration of plasticizer. The life cycle assessment demonstrated that bio-plasticized materials generally exhibited environmental impacts comparable to or lower than those of the synthetic reference in several impact categories. However, sunflower and soybean oil epoxidized ester showed higher impacts in categories related to fertilizer use, land occupation, and land transformation. The study demonstrates that modified bio-oils are promising alternatives to conventional plasticizers for biodegradable packaging applications. Future research should focus on optimizing bio-oil production and processing routes to further improve material performance and reduce environmental impacts, thereby supporting cleaner production and sustainable material development.

pH-mediated mechanisms and optimization of electrocoagulation for treating authentic Fe-rich acid mine drainage
abstract: Acid mine drainage (AMD) containing high Fe concentrations of 1–10 g L −1 is characterized by strong acidity, complex redox cycling, and unstable mineral precipitation, making remediation more challenging than for low-Fe AMD. Here, electrocoagulation (EC) was systematically evaluated for treating authentic Fe-rich AMD collected from two pyrite mines, focusing on pH-mediated transformation pathways by electrode combinations of Fe (anode) and stainless steel (cathode). An optimal current density of 30 mA cm −2 was identified. Experimental results indicate that an initial pH 5 serves as a practical threshold for EC applicability. Below pH 5, initial metal concentration is the dominant control on purification efficiency. Solid-phase analysis revealed interconnected transformation of Fe reduction, hydrolysis, and co-precipitation. The metal removal pathway exhibits a distinct temporal evolution under experimental conditions. Mechanistically, three pH-mediated removal stages were identified, with Fe-(oxy)hydroxide precipitation, subsequent surface complexation, and co-precipitation acting as the dominant pathways for the removal of Cu, Zn, and Mn. Under high ionic strength, pH elevation was suppressed and energy efficiency decreased, limiting the effectiveness of standalone EC-based AMD treatment. An integrated neutralization-EC configuration addressed these limitations, achieving over 97.5% removal of all target metals while reducing wet sludge production by 32%. The results demonstrate that neutralization-EC is an effective and practical strategy for treating authentic Fe-rich AMD.

A hybrid particle swarm optimization (PSO)-based framework for green diesel production under the water-energy-food nexus paradigm
authors: Mauro Antonio da Silva Sá Ravagnani
abstract: The energy transition toward renewable fuels is essential to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and decrease reliance on fossil resources. This manuscript presents a hybrid framework for designing a green diesel supply chain under the water-energy-food (WEF) nexus. The framework integrates data reduction techniques, simulation-based surrogate models generated from Aspen Plus simulations, and a multi-objective optimization model solved using Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). The surrogate models, coded as Optimized Baselined Regressors (OBR), enable efficient estimation of process performance and their integration into large-scale optimization. The OBR achieved adjusted R 2 values above 0.99, validated through 5-fold cross-validation, confirming their robustness and predictive accuracy. The case study focuses on Paraná, Brazil. A scoring and selection procedure reduces the number of municipalities from 399 to 24 representative nodes. Results show that green diesel production from soybean oil can reach about 180 m 3 per hour, equivalent to roughly half of the conventional diesel demand in the region, without violating WEF constraints. The optimal configuration results in total greenhouse gas emissions of 178.5 million t-CO 2 per year, a total annual cost of 41.5 MMUSD per year, and freshwater consumption of 79.79 hm 3 per year. The findings demonstrate that combining OBR surrogates with a PSO-based optimization model provides an effective way to balance cost, emissions, water use, and fuel output in biofuel supply chain planning. This is the first integration of PSO with OBR surrogates for simultaneous supply chain design and WEF nexus analysis in green diesel production.

title: Parametric life cycle assessment of asphalt pavements with probabilistic lifetimes and traffic
abstract: This study develops a parametric life cycle assessment (LCA) framework to evaluate the environmental impacts of asphalt pavements, integrating probabilistic lifetimes and traffic volumes. The attributional LCA method (cut-off approach) is applied to five asphalt pavement types, incorporating seven key parameters and statistical modeling based on Norwegian road data. Results indicate that binder type, asphalt plant efficiency, and transport distances are dominant contributors to environmental impacts, with stone mastic asphalt (SMA) showing the highest burden due to its polymer-modified bitumen content. By incorporating probabilistic lifetimes and traffic loads into the functional unit, the study reshapes environmental rankings, revealing that longer pavement lifetimes do not always equate to lower environmental burdens. These findings underscore the importance of real-world performance factors in LCA and provide data-driven insights for reducing the environmental impacts of road construction and maintenance.

From Kaizen to sustainability: How operational lean tools drive the Triple Bottom Line
abstract: The manufacturing industry seeks to achieve operational efficiency and sustainability through lean manufacturing; however, the literature has not fully established their relationship, as prior studies have examined them in isolation and have not modeled Kaizen (KAI) as a philosophical driver that governs another Operational Lean Tool (OLT). This study proposes a structural equation model (SEM) assuming KAI as an umbrella that enforces three OLTs, namely 5S, Gemba Walking (GEM), and Muda (MUD) identification, to obtain Sustainability (SUS), operationalized as a second-order formative construct according to the Triple Bottom Line (TBL) framework. The SEM was validated using data from 834 responses to a survey applied to professionals in the manufacturing industry, employing the Partial Least Squares approach in WarpPLS v.8 and the Warp3 algorithm to detect nonlinear relationships, where eight of nine hypotheses were supported. Kaizen influences all three OLTs (5S: β = 0.513; GEM: β = 0.431; MUD: β = 0.227) and had the strongest direct effect on SUS (β = 0.540); however, the GEM→SUS relationship was rejected (β = 0.013, p = 0.357) indicating that GEM improves SUS only through the waste identification (indirect effect: β = 0.154). The model explains 73.6% of the variance in SUS. Beyond validating the hierarchical logic of the Toyota Production System (TPS), this study contributes a formative second-order conceptualization of TBL sustainability as a methodological advance. Two practical implications emerge from this study: building Kaizen as an organizational culture before deploying specific tools and redesigning Gemba Walks as structured dialogues rather than observation exercises.

Life cycle assessment of battery minerals to 2040: contribution of voluntary sustainability initiatives
abstract: The expansion of electric mobility is intensifying demand for lithium, nickel, and manganese, increasing the environmental burdens of mineral extraction and processing. Voluntary sustainability initiatives (VSIs) have emerged to encourage improved environmental management, yet their long-term effectiveness remains uncertain. This study explores a proof-of-concept of how VSI-aligned operational interventions could influence the future environmental performance of battery mineral supply chains, using a scenario-based prospective environmental assessment informed by life cycle modelling. By integrating Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) with VSI-aligned process measures such as air pollution control devices (APCDs), we assess midpoint impacts including climate change, particulate matter formation, and human toxicity. Results show that systemic background decarbonization dominates reductions, while VSI-inspired interventions deliver complementary benefits, including up to ∼75% reductions in particulate matter formation for nickel beneficiation and localized process-level reductions of up to ∼90%. These findings highlight how coupling systemic and operational measures can improve resource efficiency and environmental performance in battery-mineral supply chains.

An operational decision framework for energy–carbon trade-offs in hemp-derived biochar systems
authors: Thiago Luccas Correa dos Santos Gomes
abstract: Industrial hemp ( Cannabis sativa L.) is increasingly discussed as a multipurpose lignocellulosic feedstock for renewable energy, carbon sequestration, and circular bioeconomy strategies. However, current evidence on hemp-derived biochar remains dispersed across agronomy, thermochemical conversion, environmental assessment, techno-economic analysis, and regulatory readiness, limiting transparent decision-making for process selection and scale-up. This study develops an operational decision framework for hemp-derived biochar systems through a structured evidence synthesis and scenario-oriented classification of thermochemical pathways. Peer-reviewed literature on hemp biomass, biochar production, thermochemical conversion, integrated assessment, and regulatory constraints was screened and coded to define three decision dimensions: energy recovery, carbon retention, and operational feasibility. These dimensions were translated into carbon-oriented, balanced, and energy-oriented regimes and operationalized through an ordinal scenario-screening matrix for comparing low-, intermediate-, and high-temperature conversion pathways. The analysis indicates that thermochemical conditions, especially temperature and residence time, control the core trade-off between stable carbon retention and recoverable energy products. Lower-temperature regimes generally favor biochar yield and carbon stability, whereas higher-temperature regimes increase energy carrier production but reduce the solid carbon fraction. Intermediate regimes provide the strongest basis for multiproduct circular bioeconomy configurations. The framework does not replace life-cycle assessment, techno-economic analysis, or multi-criteria decision analysis; instead, it provides an upstream operational layer for defining system objectives, selecting conversion regimes, and identifying where detailed quantitative assessment is required. By linking process parameters, energy–carbon performance, environmental applications, logistics, and regulatory constraints, the study offers a practical decision-oriented contribution to cleaner biomass valorization and hemp-based bioeconomy design. Statement of novelty This study proposes an operational decision framework for hemp-derived biochar systems by explicitly linking thermochemical process conditions with energy recovery, carbon retention, environmental applications, and feasibility constraints. Unlike conventional descriptive syntheses, the framework organizes dispersed evidence into an energy–carbon decision space and classifies conversion pathways according to their dominant functional objectives. The contribution differs from LCA, TEA, MCDA, and generic biochar assessment approaches by providing an upstream screening layer that helps define system objectives and select candidate thermochemical configurations before more detailed quantitative assessments are conducted.

title: Integrated optimization of berth allocation, crane assignment, and onshore power supply with multi-source energy dispatch for green ports
Toward sustainable food systems: Circular economy practices and perspectives of small-scale producers in the Bega Valley
abstract: There is an increasing focus on transitioning to a circular economy within the agrifood industry for both human and planetary health. This study aimed to explore the perspectives of small-scale producers towards circularity and understand the barriers and enablers towards implementing more circular supply chains. Small agrifood producers in the Bega Valley region, a shire in regional Australia with a unique circularity focus, were recruited using purposive sampling. Guided interviews were recorded and transcribed verbatim. Reflexive, thematic analysis was used to identify key themes in the data, which are interpreted through a framework of four interacting dynamics: institutional, logistical, relational, and economic. Ten interviews were completed with producers from a range of areas: horticulture and market gardening (n = 4), food and beverage manufacture (n = 4); aquaculture (n = 1); and apiary (n = 1). The results reveal that producers engaged readily in reducing, reusing, and repurposing, while engagement in more complex recycling, repairing, and recovery was more limited. This uneven adoption reflected not individual motivation but how far institutional, logistical, relational, and economic conditions aligned, and varied with producers' scale, sector, and market position. As such, circularity in regional agrifood systems is framed as a challenge of ecosystem-level governance rather than -organisational level innovation. Advancing circularity therefore requires coordinated, ecosystem-level support, including shared infrastructure, mechanisms for knowledge exchange and collaboration, financial support for small producers, and alternative local food-system and labelling models, which are likely to be applicable across other regional agrifood systems internationally.

title: Amending soil with dredged nutrient-rich lake sediment and biostimulants to enhance plant growth and phosphorus recycling
abstract: Phosphorus (P) management in agriculture remains a global challenge due to its scarcity, geopolitical constraints, and its central role in maintaining crop yields, while driving freshwater eutrophication. The reuse of dredged P-rich lake sediments offers a dual opportunity to mitigate eutrophication and recover a recyclable P resource for crop production. This study evaluated dredged lake sediment as a recyclable P fertiliser, alone and in combination with P-solubilising biostimulants (PSB), on pea ( Pisum sativum L.) grown in a 45-day laboratory experiment. Treatments comprised the application of 30 kg P ha −1 as either lake sediment or conventional superphosphate fertiliser (positive control), alongside a negative control with no P added, each applied with and without PSB. We analysed a range of plant parameters (biomass and nutrient uptake) and rhizosphere soil attributes (Olsen P, cation-exchange capacity (CEC), water-holding capacity (WHC), total carbon, and enzyme activities). Lake sediment application produced biomass and P uptake comparable to the positive control, while increasing biomass by 45% and P uptake by 106% compared to the negative control. Compared with the positive control, lake sediment increased N, K, and Mg uptake by 7%, 43%, and 17%, respectively. It also enhanced rhizosphere functioning, increasing CEC (+15%) and WHC (+22%), alongside higher enzyme activities (acid phosphatase +16%, alkaline phosphatase +118%, and β-glucosidase +10%). In contrast, Olsen P was reduced by 12% relative to the positive control. Although lake sediment combined with PSB tended to result in higher nutrient uptake, particularly of N, K, and Mg, the statistical PSB effect was context-specific and not consistently observed across treatments. We conclude that lake sediment was the primary driver of improved plant nutrition and rhizosphere functioning, while PSB showed minor additional effect on nutrient mobilisation.

title: Navigating the global expanse of offshore floating photovoltaics: Techno-ecological-economic boundaries decoded by artificial intelligence
Optimal prosumer participation in dual peer-to-peer markets using multi-agent deep reinforcement learning, fuzzy satisfaction level, and blockchain settlement
Coordinated capacity configuration and techno-economic assessment of a grid-connected hydro–wind–solar–pumped storage complementary system for long-distance UHVDC power transmission

Dusty plasma actuators: “Powder-phobic” walls to mitigate clogging in granular flows
abstract: Clogging is a thornier problem for many production environments run by granular flows. The cure? Purging and cleaning the pipelines continuously. Although simple and certainly effective, such mechanical operations indicate that there is no pat answer to this challenge. Yet, stopping the line jeopardizes the reliability and predictability of production environments — two pivotal concerns for many industrial sectors, such as new energy systems based on granular media. Here, we propose the use of electric forces to clear the granular material adhered to the pipeline walls. The charge injected from the electrodes is transferred to the grains that eventually repel each other and the electrodes. To that end, we used a dielectric barrier discharge setup, with fine powders settling on the surface. Experiments monitored the powder mass ejected from the surface, exploring the role of the particle size (from 15 to 80 microns) and the frequency of the electric signal (from 2 to 500 Hz). The results left no doubt about the potential of these settings. All the tests, irrespective of the frequency and particle sizes, led to clean surfaces with no trace of particles — as general trend, higher frequencies result in faster cleaning. Particle size also plays a role; it modulates the powder removal rate. Importantly, we found an operational regime for frequencies of the electric stimulus around 100 Hz in which all the powder samples were thrust efficiently (in a minimal time window) and homogeneously (within similar time windows, regardless of the particle size). Undoubtedly, the practicality of using electrical forces to prevent particles from adhering to the pipeline walls opens new avenues for designing robust and reliable pumping systems — a long-standing demand for an ample palette of engineering processes that require transporting and storing cohesive granular media.
