Bayesian material flow analysis and life cycle assessment reveal decarbonisation and land use trade-off in England's cement and concrete sector
Co-inoculation of PGPB and AMF: Impacts on common bean yield, nutrition, and selective root taxon co-occurrence
abstract: Although inoculation with plant growth-promoting bacteria (PGPB) has shown promise for cleaner production with reduced reliance on synthetic fertilizers in common bean, field evidence regarding its combined use with arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) remains quite limited. This study investigated the effects of PGPB and their co-inoculation with the AMF Rhizophagus clarus on grain yield, plant nutrition, and microorganisms associated with common bean roots. The experiment was conducted in a randomized block design with an 8 x 2 factorial scheme and four replicates, and was repeated in the same plots over two winter cropping seasons. The treatments consisted of inoculation with the PGPBs Azospirillum brasilense, Azomonas macrocytogenes, Azotobacter beijerinckii, Bacillus amyloliquefaciens, Bacillus aryabhattai, Burkholderia vietnamiensis, Nitrospirillum amazonense , and an uninoculated control, combined or not with R. clarus . The results demonstrated that co-inoculation efficacy is highly context- and strain-dependent. significant increases in grain yield were achieved when R. clarus was applied alone. Furthermore, true synergistic increments were observed under co-inoculation with Bur. vietnamiensis , Az. brasilense , or Azot. beijerinckii . Significant grain biofortification was observed, with specific PGPBs enhancing nitrogen and magnesium export, while the AMF increased iron export. Conversely, the incompatibility of certain co-inoculations was evidenced by antagonistic effects, such as the reduction in yield following the co-inoculation of R. clarus + A. macrocytogenes . Finally, the analysis of the root-associated microbiome - restricted to a subset of three selected PGPB strains and their co-inoculations with R. clarus ( Az. brasilense, Bur. vietnamiensis, and N. amazonense ) - revealed that the inoculations did not alter the overall diversity but were observed in association with exclusive genera, driving specific qualitative changes in the microbial community without altering its global structure. In conclusion, under the conditions of this single cultivation site, this study demonstrates that R. clarus can benefit winter common bean by increasing yield and inducing qualitative changes in low-abundance root-associated taxa. Similarly, PGPB and their co-inoculations with AMF can benefit crop yield and nutrition, depending on the specific microbial combination.

title: From predictive accuracy to prescriptive value: A data-driven framework for sustainable multi-period electric vehicle battery recycling networks
Estimating the nutrition- and environment-attributable human health burden of the Spanish food consumption vs. Spanish dietary guidelines
abstract: Current dietary patterns in Spain contribute significantly to both chronic health burden and environmental degradation, which in turn has a health impact. Using disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) as a common metric, this study aimed to quantify and compare the dietary health burden among Spanish adults (referred to as nutDALYs) and the human health burden associated with the environmental impacts of food consumption (referred to as envDALYs). We analyzed current food consumption in Spain in 2022 and compared it with scenarios reflecting adherence to the 2022 Spanish Dietary Guidelines, and alternative, more plant-forward dietary guidelines. Their effects on morbidity and mortality were quantified through dietary comparative risk assessment (for nutDALY) and life cycle assessment (for envDALY). In 2022, Spanish adult diets were associated with 945,351 nutDALYs and 331,797 envDALYs, primarily driven by low intake of whole grains, fruits and legumes, and high consumption of red meat and ultra-processed foods. Adherence to the Spanish Dietary Guidelines could reduce nutDALYs by 78–96%, with further reductions under alternative, more plant-forward guidelines. These shifts would also improve nutritional adequacy, aligning intake with WHO recommendations—except for calcium and vitamin B12 in certain plant-based scenarios. Environmentally mediated health impacts showed more nuanced changes: compared to current diets, Spanish Dietary Guidelines adoption would reduce envDALYs by 3% to 27%, while alternative, more plant-forward guidelines would reduce envDALYs by up to 33%. This study underscores the dual potential of dietary transitions through sustainable dietary guidelines to improve direct and indirect human health, offering a realistic and inclusive pathway toward sustainable food systems.

title: Carbon continuum across Eastern Himalayan forests: Elevational shifts in productivity, storage and turnover
Synergistic enhancement of low-carbon cement-based materials and CO2 sequestration via graded carbonization and composite design of rice husk ash
Integrated nitrogen fertilizer management strategies for sustainable subtropical vegetable production: A multi-objective approach
Dynamic emission evolution and synergistic effect of heavy metals and primary air pollutants in China's iron and steel industry
Carbon footprints of RFID labels in mass production
Reducing the carbon footprint of asphalt production through crude oil selection guided by refining history
Data for circularity assessment: what, where, and how?
abstract: The growing need for circular economy (CE) assessment in manufacturing enterprises is driven by increasing regulatory and market pressures. However, existing approaches provide limited support for identifying and collecting the required data to compute circularity indicators. The main contribution of this paper is a structured method that links circularity indicators to collectable data and formalizes data collection as a decision problem. CE assessment is operationalized through a four-phase, data-driven approach comprising (1) an industrial diagnosis to define objectives, scope, and relevant information systems, (2) a systematic sense-making process to translate CE assessment resources into structured data requirements, (3) a decomposition of circularity indicators into data points, referred to as c-data, and (4) a mixed-integer linear programming model to determine an efficient data collection strategy. Applied to a medical radiology system manufacturer case study, 69 target indicators are decomposed into 91 c-data points distributed across eight information systems. Building on this, the optimization model shows that accessing only a limited subset of systems can be sufficient to compute a substantial share of indicators, thereby revealing trade-offs between implementation effort and assessment coverage. In this context, three alternative data collection strategies are identified for the company. Notably, one of these strategies demonstrates that accessing just one of eight information systems makes it possible to collect 13% of eligible data points, which in turn enables the computation of 25% of CE indicators. The approach supports the transition from high-level assessment requirements to actionable data sourcing strategies and is extendable to other sustainability assessment contexts.

title: Decarbonizing manufacturing through circularity and renewable electrification: A panel threshold analysis of production-based and consumption-based emissions in the EU-27
abstract: Decarbonizing manufacturing is central to the EU's 2050 climate-neutral agenda. However, production-based and consumption-based emission perspectives are rarely contrasted, and the conditions under which circularity and renewable electrification jointly reduce emissions remain underexplored. This study examines how circular material use, renewable energy share, and resource productivity affect production- and consumption-based emissions in the EU-27 panel, 2010-2024, combining cross-sectional dependence and unit-root diagnostics, Westerlund cointegration, Augmented Mean Group and Common Correlated Effects Mean Group estimators, Hansen panel threshold regression, Driscoll-Kraay robustness, and System GMM. The Hansen test locates a candidate breakpoint at a circular material use rate of 2.80%, with a positive coefficient below and a small negative coefficient above the threshold; the likelihood-ratio test does not reject linearity at conventional levels (p = 0.213), so this result is suggestive rather than confirmed. Per-capita income elasticity is strongly negative for production-based emission intensity (−0.97) but positive for consumption-based footprint (+0.27), consistent with carbon leakage, though the design cannot identify leakage causally. Resource productivity cointegrates negatively with emission intensity in both perspectives, while the renewable-energy channel reaches significance under Driscoll-Kraay fixed effects but not under the heterogeneous-slope estimators. Country-level decomposition shows that the pooled circularity effect is concentrated in a small number of economies rather than being uniform across the EU-27. Findings imply that the European Green Deal's 2030 circularity target exceeds the candidate threshold, and that the production-consumption asymmetry is a relevant consideration for Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism design. Policy implications are framed as conditional priorities for circularity planning, infrastructure financing, and standardized emission reporting.

title: In situ Zn-substituted CuFe2O4 for enhanced peroxymonosulfate activation and antibiotic degradation in real wastewater
Bioelectrochemical enhancement for polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons degradation in saline wastewater
Climate change impacts on designing the power system of Kenya in 2050
abstract: Africa’s economic growth in the coming decades will hinge on the strategic planning of national power systems to meet growing demand and ensure rural energy access. Renewable energy sources, particularly wind and solar, will be pivotal in the expansion and transition to a low-carbon energy system. However, the vulnerability of these renewable sources to climate change could introduce imponderability in the design of the energy mix. In this regard, this paper explores a climate-informed energy system pathway by integrating the future climate projections directly into the capacity expansion of Kenya’s power system within three scenarios towards 2050, to formulate future energy profiles under climate change. The PyPSA-Earth model is applied to calculate capacity expansion decisions of the Kenyan power system. The EC-Earth3-Veg Earth System Model projects future climate variables such as wind speed. The cooling demands with global warming are estimated based on Cooling Degree Days (CDDs) projected by the Multi-Climate Model ensemble. The capacity expansion optimization results reveal that temperature increase leads to a rise in cooling demand, resulting in capacity expansion by 12% to 52% larger than the cooling demand without global warming. The projected change in wind speed is complex, with the onshore wind speed declining and the offshore wind speed rising, which causes a jump in the share of offshore wind power, taking 9% to 19% of the total capacity. Life cycle assessment indicates that large-scale deployment of wind and solar has less 5% climate change mitigation potential, but has 35% more total system cost compared to the baseline. In Kenya, geothermal is expected to continue playing a critical role in the energy strategy. Besides solar power, offshore wind is forecasted to become an important renewable energy source for Kenya. However, climate models’ resolutions and accuracy need to be further improved for effective integration into energy system modelling.

title: Cleaner transportation through energy-oriented vehicle routing under disrupted arcs
Magnetic response associated enhancement of magneto-Fenton degradation of p-Nitrophenol over amorphous FeSiB
An integrated modelling framework for feedback-driven and mass-balanced circular economy analysis
abstract: Achieving a circular economy requires not only quantifying material stocks and flows but also understanding the dynamic processes that shape them over time. While Material Flow Analysis (MFA) is widely used to track physical stocks and flows, MFA has limited capacity to represent behavioral feedback, endogenous system responses, and temporal delays. System Dynamics (SD), by contrast, is well suited to capturing feedback structures and non-linear system behavior, but it does not inherently enforce mass conservation. Despite these fundamental differences, the two approaches are often applied without a clear conceptual distinction. Here, we compare and integrate MFA and SD to develop a modelling framework that is both mass balanced and feedback driven. Using three simplified models (MFA, SD, and integrated SD-MFA), we demonstrate that the integrated approach can simultaneously preserve mass balance and represent causal relationships, feedback loops, and time delays. The combined framework offers a more robust basis for analyzing circular economy transitions, enabling the assessment of not only how materials flow through systems, but also how socio-technical dynamics influence those flows over time.

title: Mechanistic insights into coupled Fe–S–N cycling in constructed wetlands: potential contributions of cable bacteria and their community associations
Is ESG always profitable? Sustainability transition and dimension-level evidence from an emerging market banking system
Evolution path of anti-involution in photovoltaic enterprises driven by digital twin technology
Urban organisms’ metabolic laws and policy effects: A weight-physique perspective
Unveiling the role of soil in urban vegetation greenness: City-scale evidence from field sampling across green spaces in Shanghai
Mechanistic insights into lidocaine degradation in UV/H2O2 and Fenton systems: A computational investigation of pathways, kinetics, and toxicity evolution
Effect of replacement rate on longevity and methane emissions for dairy herds in New Zealand
abstract: A high replacement rate in dairy herds is desirable to accelerate genetic gain. However, higher replacement costs are incurred, and average age and maturity of the herd is decreased, which can diminish overall herd productivity and profitability, but effects on methane emissions have not been reported. This study examines the relationship between herd replacement rate, longevity and methane emissions of the New Zealand dairy herd under grazing conditions. Three herd replacement scenarios were examined, low (13%), base (17%) and high (19.5%) using a farm model to quantify the annual metabolizable energy requirements for growth, maintenance, pregnancy and milk production for the national herd. Farm income was the sale of dairy products, culled cows and surplus calves, minus processing costs. Methane emissions were calculated using dry matter requirements and were expressed as CO 2-e . An increase in the replacement rate from 13% to 19.5% resulted in a reduction of 400 days in the life expectancy of a cow. The methane emission at the low replacement rate was 7.97 kg CO 2 -e/kg fat + protein, while methane emission at the high replacement rate was 8.81 kg CO 2 -e/kg fat + protein. By increasing the lifetime of the cow producing milk, the methane burden decreased from 3.0 kg total CH 4 /kg lactational CH 4 when the cow is 3 years old, to 2.1 kg CH 4 /kg CH 4 when the cow reaches 10-years. A better alignment between profitable production and consumer needs, animal welfare and an improved environment is needed.

title: Structure-guided tuning of the SiO2/Al2O3 mass ratio enables low-temperature fiberization of red mud slags
Manufacture or recycle? Strategies for green products in a closed-loop supply chain
Driving green ethical behaviour: the sequential effects of transformational leadership, ethical climate and co-worker ethical behaviour
The impact of green finance on the synergy between pollution control and carbon reduction: Exploring the moderating role of institutional environment and spatial spillover effects
Enhancing sustainable oil palm management through plantation age mapping and yield estimation
Doped NiFe2O4 spinel oxygen carriers for enhanced H2 production in photo-assisted chemical looping reforming with water splitting under mild conditions
Life cycle assessment of the Mekong Delta rice supply chain: emission inventory and mitigation pathways toward food security synergies
abstract: Despite growing pressure to mitigate greenhouse gas emissions in rice systems, supply chain assessments jointly addressing mitigation and food availability trade-offs within an explicit national policy framework remain limited. Vietnam's Mekong Delta, supplying approximately 10% of global rice trade while accounting for 48% of national agricultural emissions, represents a critical case study for evidence-based mitigation. We conducted an LCA drawing on 11 focus groups with rice farmers and 478 farmer and post-harvest stakeholder interviews to quantify cradle-to-market carbon intensities and evaluate mitigation scenarios and food security trade-offs under a cradle-to-dryer-gate boundary. Cradle-to-market carbon intensities were 2.96 and 2.93 kg CO 2 -eq kg −1 for market-ready milled rice in the domestic and export channels, respectively, with over 97% of emissions concentrated in cultivation, dominated by methane from flooded fields and anaerobic straw decomposition, the two highest-sensitivity parameters. We established a Business-as-Usual baseline (1.84 kg CO 2 -eq kg −1 dried paddy; 46.52 Mt CO 2 -eq yr −1 ) to enable scenario-based analysis across six intervention levers through single-lever, trade-off, and policy-aligned scenarios. Deep alternate wetting and drying and intensified straw removal achieved single-lever reductions of 14-26%. Trade-off analysis revealed two mitigation pathways: structural interventions, such as land transformation, achieved larger reductions but cut milled rice output by up to 18%, while efficiency-based interventions (food loss reduction, silo drying) reduced emissions while improving food availability. The integrated MI3 achieved a 31% reduction in total GHG emissions alongside a 1.75% increase in milled rice output, surpassing current policy targets and suggesting that ambitious mitigation need not reduce food availability under the modelled conditions. These findings demonstrate that mitigation and food security can be mutually reinforcing, offering actionable pathways for Vietnam's One Million Low-Emission Hectare Initiative and Nationally Determined Contributions.

title: Digital transformation and the diffusion of social sustainability practices in supply chains: Evidence from buyer–supplier dyads
A data mining-enhanced machine learning model considering breakpoint events for daily carbon dioxide emissions forecasting
BCT adoption for organic product deter counterfeiting: Tripartite evolutionary game with government involvement
Modeling sustainable development in resource-based regions: New evidence from an improved multivariate grey model
Assessing the impact of green certificate market transformation on China's carbon market under a multi-market coupling framework
Pyrolysis temperature controls long-term stability of heavy metals in sludge-derived biochar after soil application and oxidative aging
One-pot Cr3+-catalyzed alkaline oxidative hydrolysis for isolation of cellulose nanocrystals from waste paper towels
abstract: A one-pot Cr3+-catalyzed alkaline oxidative hydrolysis route was developed for the isolation of cellulose nanocrystal (CNC) from post-consumer waste paper towels (WPT), a cellulose-rich sanitary waste stream that remains largely underutilized. The process was conducted under mild conditions (75.00 °C, 30.00 min, dilute catalyst loading) and avoided concentrated mineral acids and multistep pretreatment. The study aimed to evaluate whether a sanitary paper waste feedstock could be converted into structurally robust CNC through a transition-metal-catalyzed oxidative pathway while maintaining low catalyst residue in the final product. A CNC yield of 63.00 ± 2.00% was obtained based on the dry cellulose-rich input. Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy confirmed retention of the cellulose backbone together with removal of non-cellulosic additives and formation of mildly oxidized surface groups, including carbonyl/carboxylate functionalities. Wide-angle X-ray scattering showed an increase in crystallinity index from 68.80 ± 0.40% for WPT to 82.20 ± 0.50% for CNC, indicating selective removal of amorphous contents. Transmission electron microscopy revealed rod-like CNC with average dimensions of 100.00 ± 20.00 nm in length and 8.00 ± 2.00 nm in width. Thermogravimetric analysis showed improved thermal stability, with a maximum degradation temperature of 372.00 °C for CNC compared with 330.00 °C for raw WPT. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy confirmed removal of calcium carbonate-rich surface additives and showed no detectable chromium on the CNC surface, while inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry confirmed that 98.80% of the introduced chromium was removed during purification. The main contribution of this work is the demonstration that pre-bleached sanitary paper waste can serve as a suitable feedstock for one-pot catalytic CNC production, yielding high-crystallinity and thermally stable nanocrystal without conventional strong-acid hydrolysis. The main limitation is that catalyst recovery, liquid-stream management, and process-level environmental assessment were not investigated in this laboratory-scale study and should be addressed in future scale-up, techno-economic, and life-cycle investigations.

title: Determining time- and region- specific electricity carbon emission factors with dynamic spatial zoning
Investigating the relationship between physical climate risk and green bonds: Disaggregated level evidence from the United States by novel quantile-based methods
Mn/Co-modified CaO pellets bound with mesoporous γ-Al2O3 for thermochemical energy storage: balancing energy-storage density, mechanical strength and solar absorptance
abstract: Low-cost and high-performance materials are needed for high-temperature thermochemical energy storage using concentrated solar energy and industrial waste heat. In this work, CaO pellets modified with Mn and/or Co and bound with mesoporous γ-Al 2 O 3 were prepared and evaluated as multifunctional materials combining thermochemical energy-storage performance, mechanical robustness, and solar absorptance. The incorporation of mesoporous γ-Al 2 O 3 (20 wt %) promoted the in-situ formation of mayenite (Ca 12 Al 14 O 33 ), which contributed to improved pellet strength. Among the tested formulations, the Mn-containing pellets, namely Ca20Mn/m-γ-Al 2 O 3 -80-20 and Ca20MnCo/m-γ-Al 2 O 3 -80-20, showed the most balanced performance, with average energy-storage densities of 1364 and 1179 kJ kg −1 , respectively, crushing strengths above 6 N throughout their full cycle life, and average solar absorptances above 50 %. These results are consistent with the presence of stabilizing Mn-containing mixed oxides together with mayenite and with the development of significant meso/macroporosity, which helped mitigate CaCO 3 sintering during cycling. As a result, Mn-containing pellets showed high and stable storage performance over 50 carbonation/decarbonation cycles. These materials are promising candidates for thermochemical energy storage systems coupled to concentrating solar irradiation or industrial waste-heat recovery.

title: An integrated chemical looping cycle for green ammonia and syngas co-production driven by staged oxidation of oxygen carrier: Process simulation and thermodynamic evaluation
When healthier eating emits more: Socioeconomic divergence in U.S. diet sustainability
abstract: Efforts to improve the sustainability of diets require a joint understanding of how nutritional quality and environmental impact vary across social and economic groups, and how they respond to policy levers, going beyond the now-standard “eat less meat” recommendation, too often repeated without asking who is actually able to change and how. Using nationally representative dietary data from the United States, we introduce a Data Envelopment Analysis framework that jointly scores how close each observed diet is to the best nutrition–emissions combinations already achievable in the population; we then combine this with regression and generalized additive models to identify how income, price, and education shape this nutrition–environment trade-off. We find that improvements in diet quality do not uniformly reduce environmental impact: among middle-income groups, income increase is associated with healthier diets but substantially higher emissions, whereas among high-income groups, further income gains reinforce both better nutritional profiles and lower emissions. Education exhibits a strongly nonlinear effect, with substantial gains in diet quality and large reductions in emissions emerging only at the highest educational levels. These findings show that sustainable diet policy cannot rely on a single dietary prescription. Targeted, equity-oriented food policies are needed to advance nutrition and climate goals jointly while accounting for differences in socioeconomic constraints, dietary baselines, and capacity to adopt low-emission, high-quality diets.

title: Predicting corporate environmental violations in China: Evidence from machine learning based on the Fraud Triangle Theory
Beyond a hydrological conduit: Highly reactive interfaces partition the capillary zone into a compartmentalized nitrogen bioreactor
Decoding China's low-carbon resilience: A discrete numerical integration approach to spatiotemporal dynamics and influencing factors
Integrated microalgal process for biogas upgrading, digestate bioremediation and astaxanthin production
abstract: The integration of photosynthetic biogas upgrading, anaerobic digestate bioremediation and astaxanthin biosynthesis by microalgae entails environmental and economic benefits. However, the toxicity of the H 2 S present in biogas and of the NH 3 in digestate challenges microalgal growth and the biosynthesis of added-value compounds. This study evaluated the combined effects of headspace composition and digestate dilution on the performance of Coelastrella sp. during biogas upgrading coupled to nutrient removal from digestate. In Test Series I, cultivation under biogas with different H 2 S concentrations (0, 600, and 5000 ppm v ) with digestate pre-treatments (untreated, pH-adjusted, and activated sludge-bioaugmented) showed that moderate H 2 S levels (600 ppm v ) supported high biomass growth (maximum concentration of 6.5 ± 0.1 g TSS L −1 ) and efficient CO 2 and nutrient removal. High H 2 S levels (5000 ppm v ) inhibited culture growth, although the inhibitory effect was treatment-dependent and was substantially mitigated by activated sludge bioaugmentation. In Test Series II, the influence of digestate dilutions (10, 50, and 100%) was investigated under 600 ppm v H 2 S. Diluted digestate (10-50%) enhanced Coelastrella sp. growth, CO 2 capture, and nitrogen assimilation compared to synthetic digestate and undiluted real digestate. While operation with 50% digestate mediated the highest biomass concentrations, 10-fold diluted digestate provided the most balanced performance, including total nitrogen and phosphate removal. A two-stage cultivation strategy was applied to foster carotenoid production under high-light stress. Lutein and β-carotene decreased after high light exposure, while astaxanthin showed a treatment-dependent response, with the highest accumulation (0.39 ± 0.07 mg g −1 ) under stress conditions, particularly at high digestate concentration. Optimization of digestate dilution and cultivation strategy is essential to balance process performance and metabolite production.

title: Life cycle assessment of high-tech vertical aquaponics for grape tomato and rainbow trout production
abstract: The adoption of innovative and combined cultivation practices, such as aquaponics, has gained traction as a pathway to intensify food output on limited land. However, the environmental performance of these intensive systems warrants systematic assessment. In this study, a pilot high-tech aquaponic system was developed for greenhouse grape tomato and rainbow trout production, and three fertilization regimes were evaluated: (i) standard hydroponic solution, (ii) trout effluent supplemented with mineral fertilizers, and (iii) trout effluent without additional fertilization. Life Cycle Assessment was performed using actual operational data by using SimaPro v.9.4.0.2 and EF v.3.0 method. Results showed that the complemented aquaponic system represented the most balanced aquaponic configuration, maintaining higher productivity compared to the non-supplemented system. The hydroponic treatment exhibited lower values across most midpoint categories due to the absence of aquaculture-related hotspots, such as electricity. An alternative scenario was further modelled with increased fish biomass, additional tanks, and photovoltaic integration, while the robustness of the results was examined through Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis and deterministic sensitivity analysis. Replacing grid electricity with photovoltaic energy led to a consistent reduction in environmental impacts across all energy-related categories. A comparative scenario showed that replacing rainwater with tap water and relocating the aquaculture unit increased water use (15.2 to 19.9 m 3 deprivation) and land use (70.0 to 153.0 Pt), highlighting that system design plays a key role in improving land and water efficiency. Consequently, on-site renewable energy sources and optimized system configuration appear as the most effective levers to improve sustainability. The approach provides a reproducible template for assessing and optimizing circular aquaponic systems under real operational conditions.

title: Machine learning advances volatile fatty acids production in anaerobic sludge fermentation: linking substrate traits to operation parameters
Optimized design of the bulge structure for alkaline electrolyzers based on response surface methodology
Farmers’ willingness to contribute to circular economy: A framed field experiment from Kenya
abstract: Tackling climate change requires scaling up circular economy practices. However, there is little guidance on how this can be done in resource-scarce settings such as sub-Saharan Africa, where most of the population relies on agriculture for livelihoods but faces challenges related to agricultural waste disposal. This study posits that an effective way of boosting circular economy practices is to promote conversion of biowaste to biochar and explores the acceptance of this idea among Kenyan smallholder tomato farmers. The study uses a randomized information-based intervention that conveys important facts about tomato biowaste and its conversion to biochar. Measured immediately after the intervention, the results show that farmers who received information about biochar are more likely to support relevant policies and the adoption of this practice, even if it is costly. Message framing plays an important role in shaping acceptance. Collective information more strongly increased policy support–a subsidy in particular, and public goods contributions, which capture intention to support collective biochar production. The individual framing significantly increased willingness to pay for own-farm biochar production. The implications of this study are twofold. First, it indicates a strong role of information and in particular collective message framing in eliciting support for public policies targeting circular economy and climate change. Second, this study reveals that at present, there is interest in both collective and individual biochar production from tomato biowaste in Kenya. However, investments in collective facilities require transparency in assessing personal gains from collective effort. These findings are useful for policy makers when devising policy instruments and gauging the costs of public investment in circular economy.

title: Assessing energy poverty alleviation, energy security enhancement, and decent work and economic growth in China under SDGs 7 and 8: A meta parallel two-stage dynamic SBM-DEA analysis
Recovery of rare earth elements from end-of-life permanent magnets via slag extraction and hydrometallurgical processing
abstract: This study demonstrates a one-step selective oxidation process for recovering rare earth elements (REEs) from end-of-life sintered Ce-containing NdFeB magnets using the CaO-Al 2 O 3 -REE 2 O 3 slag system. Pyrometallurgical treatment at 1700 °C enabled efficient separation of the Fe-rich metal phase and an REE-enriched slag, achieving over 98% REEs extraction when using Fe 2 O 3 or Al 2 O 3 as oxidants. The process was successfully scaled from 50 g to 1.35 kg of magnet feed, with slags containing approximately 19 wt% REE 2 O 3 . SEM-EDX and XRD analyses confirmed the presence of REE-rich τ2 (REECaAl 3 O 7 ), and REEAP (REEAlO 3 ) phases. The slag was subsequently ground and subjected to hydrometallurgical processing. Leaching tests using H 2 SO 4 and HCl showed maximum REEs recoveries of 93% and 97%, respectively, with HCl providing superior performance and avoiding CaSO 4 precipitation. Precipitation using oxalic acid enabled over 90% REEs recovery from HCl leachates. The integrated process achieved an overall REE recovery of approximately 85%, offering an effective route for REEs recycling from waste NdFeB magnets.

title: Upcycling waste plastic into carbon nanotubes-basalt fiber hybrids: synthesis, mechanism, and asphalt pavement application
A spare-share scenario framework for exploring biodiversity - onshore wind trade-offs in electricity system planning
abstract: Abstract Expanding wind energy to meet net-zero targets increasingly conflicts with biodiversity and landscape conservation, creating contested geographies where socio-ecological values compete. Existing spatial analyses identify ecologically preferable sites but lack representation of system constraints and trade-offs, while most energy system models optimize technology deployment under cost constraints by specifying regional capacity limits, rarely encoding which specific sites become available under different ecological priorities. We address this disconnect through a spare-share scenario framework coupling high-resolution biodiversity (247 bird species, 5 bat species) and infrastructure datasets with electricity system optimization for Norway's 2050 net-zero pathway. Spatial allocation strategies spanning infrastructure-proximate concentration (spare) to ecologically guided dispersion (share) including collision risk minimization, habitat protection, and infrastructure concentration are examined. Analysis reveals that only 7% of Norwegian land area remains consistently available across spare-share scenarios, while 67% exhibits flexible availability depending on ecological criteria prioritization, and 26% faces universal restrictions. Ecological restrictions reduce onshore wind capacity potential 11-fold, increasing electricity generation costs by 19–21% per MWh while investment and operational costs rise up to 6%. Despite targeting divergent ecological priorities, moderately restricted scenarios cluster within less than 1% cost increase variation, reflecting biodiversity hotspot overlap that creates functionally equivalent constraints while achieving better system integration. Findings demonstrate that for 67% of land, which is sensitive to ecological priorities, spatial allocation decisions are not a technical optimization problem but require inclusive stakeholder engagements to navigate competing ecological and infrastructure values. The framework provides transferable methodological insights for regions balancing renewable expansion with biodiversity preservation.

A comprehensive and inclusive decision-making framework for the end-of-life of built facilities
abstract: The construction industry generates more than a third of global waste, most of which is generated at the End-of-Life stage of built facilities and is disposed of in landfills. While decision-making models have been developed by previous studies, they have focused only on a subset of End-of-Life decisions and have lacked stakeholder diversity, which can lead to biased decisions. This study seeks to develop a comprehensive and inclusive decision-making model for the End-of-Life stage of built facilities. A framework of four End-of-Life sub-phases, related decision problems and alternatives was defined based on a systematic literature review. A set of 25 criteria was compiled and validated through semi-structured interviews with 25 stakeholders representing various roles in the End-of-Life. Criteria weights were assigned with an Analytical Hierarchical Process-based survey, conducted with 52 participants. Regulations were found to be the most important criterion, specifically pointing to the value of implementing circular construction regulations and financial incentives. Furthermore, by including diverse stakeholders, higher priority was given to certain social and material factors, particularly those related to safety. Logistical constraints were also found to be important, suggesting a need to streamline deconstruction and material handling at the End-of-Life to enable circular practices. These results offer actionable insights for policymakers, building owners, and contractors aiming to implement circular economy strategies in End-of-Life decision-making. The findings highlight the role of circular economy principles in guiding sustainable End-of-Life strategies by emphasizing regulatory levers, social safeguards, and logistical enablers essential for reuse and recovery.

title: Macroalgae for sustainable textile dyeing and functional finishing: Natural pigments and bioactive compounds driving eco-innovative materials
abstract: The textile industry contributes substantially to environmental degradation through the intensive use of water, energy, and synthetic chemicals in dyeing and finishing processes. Marine macroalgae have emerged as renewable sources of pigments, polysaccharides, and bioactive compounds with potential for sustainable textile coloring and functional finishing. This systematic review was structured according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines; the search and screening process identified 829 records, of which 179 studies were included in the qualitative synthesis. The review critically integrates evidence on macroalgal chemistry, extraction technologies, textile performance, life cycle assessment, and industrial scalability. The findings indicate that macroalgae-derived systems can provide coloring and additional functional properties, including antimicrobial, antioxidant, UV-protective, and broader bioactive effects. However, performance remains strongly dependent on species, extraction route, textile substrate, mordanting or fiber-modification strategy, and processing conditions. Selected studies report quantitative indicators such as color strength, fastness ratings, extraction yields, climate-change impacts, water-related indicators, and techno-economic metrics, including net present value, gross margin, and internal rate of return. Nevertheless, these parameters are not consistently reported across studies, limiting direct comparison among macroalgae-based textile systems. Recurrent bottlenecks include light fastness, batch-to-batch reproducibility, drying and extraction energy demand, solvent recovery, downstream purification, and limited industrial standardization. Collectively, macroalgae-derived systems should be considered multifunctional bio-based platforms rather than direct one-to-one substitutes for synthetic dyes. Further progress will require standardized extraction and dyeing protocols, improved extract characterization, textile durability assessment, LCA-guided process optimization, techno-economic validation, and scalable integration into cascade biorefineries.

title: Patent now, benefit later: Lagged relationships between green innovation, GHG emissions and efficiencies in the EU-27
abstract: Green innovation plays a key role in reducing emissions and increasing resource efficiencies, as suggested by pioneering definitions. However, there are still some gaps in the literature as few studies consider the effects of green innovation on emissions and resource efficiencies simultaneously, while also considering lagged effects by explicitly modelling the temporal lags between patent filing and observable environmental benefits. To address these gaps, this study analyses this relationship by incorporating greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, various measures of resource efficiency (energy and materials) and green patents across the 27 EU Member States for the period 1993–2017, using data from the European Patent Office (EPO) and other secondary sources. The results show that green innovation, captured through lagged associations of green patents, reduces emissions and increases resource efficiency. However, the relationships are not immediate and differ depending on the type of indicator. Policy implications should consider the differentiated effects of green technologies on these indicators in order to effectively address climate change.

Life cycle assessment of a fuel cell electric agricultural tractor with decentralised biogenic hydrogen supply
abstract: Agricultural tractors remain predominantly fossil-diesel-powered, yet the transition to zero-emission operation is technically challenging, and no life-cycle evidence exists to date for medium-power fuel cell electric tractors or their integration with decentralised biogenic hydrogen supply. This study presents the first cradle-to-grave life cycle assessment (LCA) of FCTRAC, a 95 kW fuel cell electric tractor prototype, combined with the BioH2Modul-prototype, a decentralised biomass gasification system producing high-purity hydrogen. Global Warming Potential (GWP) and Cumulative Energy Demand (CED) are assessed in accordance with ISO 14040/ISO 14044, using 1 kWh of mechanical energy at tractor service level as the functional unit. FCTRAC yields a life-cycle GWP of 349 gCO 2 /kWh and a CED of 9.90 kWh/kWh, with 90 % from renewable sources. The hydrogen supply chain dominates life-cycle GWP (84 %), driven by electricity demand for BioH2Modul auxiliaries (38 %) and hydrogen refuelling station compression (20 %). Under an energy scenario with renewable wood chips logistics and renewable electricity, the BioH2Modul delivers hydrogen at 21 gCO 2 /kWh H2 , reducing total life-cycle GWP to 125 gCO 2 /kWh – a 90 % reduction relative to conventional diesel operation. Vehicle production of FCTRAC (18.2 tCO 2 ) exceeds that of the diesel reference (10.5 tCO 2 ), with carbon-fibre hydrogen storage vessels as a hotspot. Life-cycle GWP and CED are primarily governed by the hydrogen production pathway rather than vehicle lifetime or load profile. Under renewable conditions, the BioH2Modul achieves GWP values competitive with renewable-electricity-based electrolysis, indicating that decentralised biogenic hydrogen can potentially become a GWP-competitive pathway for zero-emission agricultural mechanization.

title: Techno-economic assessment of an integrated biorefinery for the production of advanced biofuels from the organic fraction of municipal solid waste
abstract: The organic fraction of municipal solid waste (OFMSW) is an abundant feedstock whose techno-economic potential remains poorly characterised: most published assessments rely on process simulation rather than operational data and omit general plant expenditures unavoidable at commercial scale. This work assesses a commercial-scale (49,500 t yr −1 ) integrated biorefinery co-producing lipids, advanced bioethanol, and biogas. Process performance is scaled from a demonstration plant on source-separated household food waste, and capital, process, and general plant expenditures are explicitly modelled. A 25-year discounted cash flow model is combined with break-even mapping, deterministic sensitivity on fifteen parameters, levelised cost estimation, and Monte Carlo simulation on the eight dominant parameters. Capital investment is 16.68 M€ and annual operating expenditure 4.17 M€ yr −1 , with drying alone contributing 39.6% of OPEX. The project is not viable under market-only operation (NPV −15.50 M€); under a reference scenario of a 30 €/t gate fee and a 30% CAPEX subsidy it delivers a positive NPV of +8.42 M€ and an IRR of 11.74%. The levelised costs of 2.34 €/kg for lipids, 1.26 €/L for bioethanol, and 110 €/MWh for biogas-derived electricity place biogas in a competitive position, bioethanol within reach of the 2030 EU advanced-bioethanol price projection, and lipids above the used cooking oil benchmark. Thermal energy price and drying specific energy consumption emerge as the dominant drivers of project economics. Reducing the drying thermal demand, through high-efficiency dryers or industrial waste-heat symbiosis, is therefore the most impactful pathway to cleaner production for OFMSW biorefineries.

Phosphorus recovery from sewage sludge ash by wet acid extraction in technical scale: Potential for reducing acid consumption
abstract: Phosphorus recovery from sewage sludge ash has become increasingly important in view of resource criticality and evolving regulatory requirements. In this study, the transferability of wet acid phosphorus extraction from laboratory to pilot/semi-technical scale was investigated. Moreover, strategies to reduce acid consumption while maintaining high phosphorus extraction efficiency (PEE) were developed. The extraction efficiency of elements from a pilot-scale plant with PARFORCE® technology correlates strongly with the laboratory results (R 2 = 0.90). This outcome confirms the transferability between laboratory-scale and technical-scale conditions. However, PEE at the pilot scale was 4-5% higher, primarily due to an intensified washing step for the ash residue. Two new empirical models were developed and validated in this study. The literature-based model (Model L, n = 219) can robustly predict the PEE (R 2 = 0.74, RMSE = 11.05) but shows limitations at PEE above 80%. The project-area-specific model (Model P, n = 68) demonstrated greater robustness and accuracy in predicting PEE (R 2 = 0.91, RMSE = 3.58). Model P demonstrated greater robustness than standard machine-learning benchmarks in quantifying parameter influence. The model result identified the liquid-to-solid ratio (L/S) as the dominant process parameter at a higher range of HCl concentration (C HCl ). Increased C HCl provided only marginal benefits within the range investigated, as confirmed by validation in the technical setup. By optimizing these process parameters, it is also feasible to reduce the specific consumption of hydrochloric acid as the extraction agent by 10%, highlighting significant potential for optimization in technical-scale operation.

title: Predicting worker-level particulate matter exposure categories at a renovation site using multi-source monitoring and machine learning
abstract: Construction activities are a major source of airborne particulate matter (PM), exposing workers to elevated concentrations of PM10, PM2.5, and PM1 that pose serious health risks. However, current monitoring practices focus primarily on ambient or fixed-site concentrations and often fail to capture the dynamic, task- and location-dependent nature of worker exposure. This study developed a high-resolution, multi-source dataset at an active renovation site by combining helmet-mounted sensors, fixed-point monitors, meteorological measurements, and detailed worker activity and location records. Using a machine-learning-based prediction framework, worker PM measurements were assigned to five ordered exposure categories, and four machine-learning models—deep neural network (DNN), random forest (RF), XGBoost, and LightGBM—were evaluated under the observed imbalanced category distributions. Results show that DNN provided the most balanced overall performance across the nine worker–PM prediction tasks, with its clearest and most consistent advantage observed for PM10. For PM10, DNN achieved Accuracy values of 0.44–0.51 and Macro F1 values of 0.40–0.46, compared with 0.17–0.22 and below 0.13, respectively, for the tree-based models. For PM1, high Accuracy coexisted with low Macro-level performance across all four models, reflecting the dominance of the Good category. Feature-importance analyses using PFI and SHAP consistently identified monitored worker activity and meteorological conditions as leading contributors to the model predictions, although their relative importance varied among workers. Fixed outdoor PM measurements generally made the smallest contribution. This study provides field-based evidence that high-frequency, multi-source data can support worker-level PM exposure classification and establishes a methodological foundation for the development of adaptive, worker-centred exposure monitoring and management systems.

A dynamic goal programming approach for sustainable product design: Balancing multi-dimensional sustainability objectives under uncertainty
abstract: This study develops a Dynamic Goal Programming (DGP) model for sustainable new product design that simultaneously optimizes economic, environmental, social, and material sustainability goals under real-world operational constraints. The model employs a rolling-horizon approach to handle stochastic demand and to dynamically recalibrate goal targets and objective weights across planning periods. A comprehensive Sustainability Index (SI) integrates weighted criteria including renewable energy use, hazardous material reduction, greenhouse gas emissions, customer satisfaction, and design usability. The specific contributions of this work are: (1) integration of material sustainability as a fourth optimization objective via hazardous material coefficients (hj), a dimension absent from all prior SNPD-GP studies documented in the literature; (2) a rolling-horizon DGP formulation in which goal targets, bound values, and objective weights are recalibrated at each planning period in response to updated demand and stock data; (3) direct embedding of the SI into the optimization objective rather than post-hoc evaluation, enabling sustainability metrics to govern production and material selection decisions in real time; and (4) a quantified Pareto frontier (α ∈ [0.1, 1.0]) enabling transparent managerial navigation of sustainability–profitability trade-offs, validated in the furniture manufacturing sector using 44 months of real production data. The results demonstrate that the model maintains strict economic viability (positive profit in all ten periods) while providing decision-makers with a controllable trade-off mechanism between aggregate SI (0.535 at α = 0.1 to 0.443 at α = 1.0) and total profit (42,165 TRY to 163,156 TRY on average).

title: Towards high-resolution energy performance monitoring in ceramic tile manufacturing: Coupling production and energy metering data for detailed KPI construction
abstract: Improving energy performance monitoring in ceramic tile manufacturing requires industrial datasets with sufficient granularity to distinguish productive from non-productive energy consumption and to enable efficiency assessment at the level of specific tile formats. Conventional reference datasets typically rely on monthly aggregated production and energy records, which limits their suitability for detailed operational analysis and the identification of cleaner production opportunities. This study proposes a data-driven methodology to construct a detailed industrial dataset by coupling daily production records with electrical and thermal energy metering data from five ceramic tile factories. Energy consumption is allocated to individual production records using a time-based correlation approach, and a hierarchical data curation procedure, combining interquartile range filtering, robust Huber regression, and Mahalanobis distance analysis, is applied to identify and remove non-representative observations. A consistency check at monthly scale confirms that the reconstructed energy consumption preserves the overall distributional characteristics of the reference data, while providing substantially higher operational resolution. The resulting cleaned detailed dataset enables the estimation of format-specific energy key performance indicators (KPIs) that are less affected by non-productive consumption than traditional aggregated metrics. These format-level KPIs provide a consistent basis for more detailed energy performance assessment and illustrate how routinely available industrial data can be transformed into operationally meaningful information to support cleaner production practices in the ceramic tile industry. The format-level granularity of the curated dataset enables operational comparisons that are not achievable with conventional monthly aggregated data, such as the detection of systematic differences in specific energy consumption between factories producing the same tile format under otherwise comparable conditions.

Price models as the missing link between sustainable business models and Scope 3 decarbonisation: Evidence from timber transportation
abstract: Scope 3 decarbonisation requires more than corporate sustainability ambitions, reporting systems, or cleaner technologies. It also depends on the contractual and economic mechanisms through which supply-chain activities are governed. This paper examines price models as such mechanisms and investigates whether, and how, corporate Scope 3 ambitions are translated into the purchasing and contracting of timber transportation in the Swedish forest industry. Drawing on the Price Model Equaliser, the study analyses how the dominant price model structures value sharing, incentives, risks, and responsibilities between forest companies and external hauliers. Empirical data were collected through 39 semi-structured and in-depth interviews with 26 interviewees, complemented by archival material, annual reports, and participation in industry conferences. The findings reveal a clear disconnect: large forest companies articulate Scope 3 ambitions in public sustainability communication, but these ambitions are largely absent from the standardised price model used to purchase timber transportation. The current model rewards tonnes, distance, and short-term flexibility, while reinforcing cost pressure rather than incentivising lower emissions. The paper contributes to cleaner production research by showing that Scope 3 decarbonisation depends on price models that make lower-emission practices economically actionable. It contributes to sustainable supply-chain governance by conceptualising price models as micro-level contractual governance mechanisms, and to sustainable business model research by specifying the price model as a missing link between sustainability-oriented business model claims and the concrete contractual arrangements that shape behaviour in activity systems.

From fossil fuel infrastructure to sustainable land use: agrivoltaics on oil and gas pipelines in Alberta, Canada
abstract: This study investigates re-purposing the 60 m wide oil and gas pipeline buffer zones for agrivoltaic applications. A case study of Alberta's oil pipelines is presented that maps them with solar irradiance to estimate available photovoltaic production. The results found that agrivoltaic electricity generation on the oil pipeline buffers would pay for themselves under 11 years, could theoretically generate between CAD $1.3 (single axis tracker for wheat) and CAD $6.6 trillion (fixed tilt for sheep grazing) in electricity over 30 years under full build-out conditions compared to oil pipelines' CAD $5.2 trillion. This could provide more than twice Canada's electricity needs, cut all electrical-related greenhouse gas emissions and provide more food (CAD $1.6 billion of wheat or CAD $1.0 billion in extra sheep meat/year), though actual utilization may be constrained by grid capacity, storage, and transmission infrastructure. The results show that oil and gas pipeline corridors can be transformed from long-term environmental liabilities into economically and environmentally productive assets that simultaneously advance climate mitigation, energy security, agricultural resilience, employment and land restoration.

title: On track but too slow? The dynamics of EU decarbonization
abstract: Despite the strong commitment of European countries to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050, the extent to which key policies and drivers jointly shape emissions dynamics remains insufficiently investigated. The study suggests that the interaction among circular economy, energy transition, emissions trading systems, carbon tax, and digitalization policies creates structural constraints on CO 2 emissions in the European countries. Using annual data from 2000 to 2023, the analysis integrates exploratory causal discovery, time-varying dependence modeling, and machine learning methods to unravel system-level causal structure, dynamic connectedness, and future emission trajectories. The results indicate that resource productivity emerges as a central transmission channel within the system, linking upstream factors (material footprint) and digitalization to downstream emission outcomes. Lagged disequilibrium shocks propagate through resource use as a mediating channel. Time-varying copula models indicate significant heterogeneity and evolving dependence among key factors, highlighting the dynamic nature of policy and relationships over time. Forecasting results, based on a Support Vector Regression model under the European Union's 2030 climate policy framework, indicate a persistently declining emission trajectory, but at a pace insufficient to meet the EU's 2030 target. Sensitivity analysis suggests that this gap does not primarily reflect a policy failure, but the structural limitations in how policy interactions translate into decarbonization outcomes. These findings highlight the need to improve the effectiveness of policy instruments by strengthening resource productivity and accelerating progress toward the targets.

A living lab approach to urban water reuse: Coupling plant growth monitoring and social acceptance in university buildings
abstract: This study presents a socio-technical assessment of treated wastewater (TWW) reuse for indoor irrigation, integrating plant growth monitoring based on projected leaf area with user acceptance analysis in a real-world educational environment. Unlike prior studies relying on hypothetical exposure, this living lab links continuous system performance with user perception under real operational conditions, addressing a key gap in the literature. Plant growth was monitored over one year using non-invasive image-based analysis, while social acceptance was assessed among 186 students through the Perception and Acceptance of Water Reuse (PAWR) index (Cronbach's α = 0.878). Four classroom environments were considered: a green classroom (GR) incorporating a nature-based solution with living plants irrigated with either TWW or drinking water (DW); a biophilic design classroom (BDR) featuring visual nature imagery; and two neutral classrooms (NR) without biophilic elements, serving as controls. TWW supported plant growth at levels comparable to DW across most species, with no adverse effects observed; only one species (Scindapsus aureus) showed significantly greater growth under TWW (p = 0.006). The overall PAWR index (3.9 ± 0.5) indicated generally high acceptance of water reuse, particularly among students with water-related academic backgrounds, while the physical classroom environment showed limited overall influence, though responses were more favourable in the GR for specific reuse applications. By integrating plant growth monitoring and behavioural analysis within a living lab setting, this study provides a transferable socio-technical framework for evaluating water reuse systems in institutional buildings, supporting freshwater conservation and evidence-based circular water strategies in higher education institutions.

title: Research on the coordination between agricultural carbon emission efficiency and food security in Hebei province based on the coupling framework of “Water-Land-Energy-Carbon”
Comparative assessment of photovoltaic waste generation across European countries
abstract: During the 2000s, photovoltaic (PV) solar energy began a period of sustained development in many European countries. The lifespan of PV panels, which is 25-35 years, will present a significant challenge for waste management in all these countries in the coming years. This study examines photovoltaic deployment in the European countries with the highest solar PV capacity—Germany, Italy, Spain, France, and the Netherlands—and introduces a waste generation model to estimate photovoltaic waste streams up to 2035. This model is based on a Weibull distribution, and its specific parameters are discussed in order to improve the current estimations. These estimations are too outdated to include the latest PV installations, and they were developed without considering the significant increase in waste generation that began in 2018. The proposed model showed good agreement with the observed data for all analysed countries, with the exception of Spain, where the later development of photovoltaic technologies resulted in an outlying behaviour. The analysis considers the challenges and opportunities that lie ahead. By 2035, it is estimated that 230,000 tonnes of PV waste will be generated in Germany, 100,000 in Italy, 44,000 in Spain, 30,000 in France, and lastly 5000 tonnes in the Netherlands. These findings highlight the need to boost current collection rates and drive the development of recycling techniques to improve the circularity of the sector. This would foster the recovery of significant quantities of glass, Ag, Al, Cu, and Si, as well as contribute to the supply needs of the European Union.

Unlocking a decarbonized future: Institutional barriers and governance innovations in China's circular economy transition for the built environment
abstract: China's deep decarbonization of the built environment is hindered by institutional lock-ins in the circular economy transition. Applying Scott's three pillars of institutions and using document analysis, semi-structured interviews, and comparative case studies, this research diagnoses how fragmented regulations, cost-driven industry norms, and cognitive biases mutually reinforce stagnation. Successful projects demonstrate that alignment across pillars enables circular practices, while failures stem from misalignment. To break institutional lock-ins, governance innovations must shift green standards from voluntary to mandatory, embed circularity into financial and performance metrics, and establish multi-stakeholder platforms. These findings contribute a dynamic institutional explanation and contextualize transition barriers within China's strong state–strong market configuration, offering pathways for coordinated policy, market, and cultural change toward a low-carbon circular built environment.

title: Integrated process development and comparative assessment of CO2-to-sustainable aviation fuel production via thermochemical and electrochemical pathways
Cost-saving and decarbonization-oriented coordinated optimization for copper metallurgy integrated energy system under material–energy–carbon coupling constraints
abstract: As energy-intensive industries move toward deep decarbonization, copper metallurgy remains constrained by tightly coupled multi-energy flows, limited process flexibility, and high carbon intensity. These characteristics hinder the coordinated regulation of production and energy systems and complicate the simultaneous pursuit of economic and low-carbon operation. This study develops an economic low-carbon coordinated optimization framework for a copper metallurgy integrated energy system (CMIES). A unified CMIES model is established to capture the coupling of electricity, heat, gas, material, and carbon flows, and a decoupling mechanism based on anode copper storage is introduced to separate continuous smelting from flexible electrolytic refining, thereby releasing process-side scheduling flexibility. On this basis, a bi-objective optimization model is formulated to minimize total operating cost and total carbon emissions. To obtain implementable operating strategies, the solution framework combines NSGA-II for Pareto search, hypervolume (HV) and spacing for solution-quality evaluation, and knee-point identification and TOPSIS for preference-based decision-making. Case studies show that the proposed flexible scheduling mechanism reduces total operating cost by 7.36%, while carbon capture and storage (CCS) reduces carbon emissions by more than 50%. When process flexibility and CCS are jointly coordinated, the system achieves a balanced improvement in economic and environmental performance. This study provides a practical pathway for low-carbon operation and decision support in energy-intensive process industries.

Optimization of energy transition pathways in the lime industry: A superstructure approach
abstract: Lime manufacturing is a hard-to-abate industry, owing to high-temperature heat requirements and process-related CO2 emissions from limestone calcination. Although numerous mitigation technologies have been proposed, existing studies generally evaluate individual options or rely on predefined economic scenarios, providing limited guidance for technology selection under uncertain future energy and carbon prices. This study presents a systematic techno-economic assessment of multiple decarbonization options, including fuel switching, electrification, and CO2 capture (CC) with storage or utilization. A unified superstructure model is coupled with scenario analysis and a parameter sweep of key energy and CO2 prices to assess robustness under market volatility. Results show that the fuel switching alone achieves only 18% CO2 emission reduction, making CC implementation inevitable for deep decarbonization. Implementing CC enables up to 78% emission reduction for fossil-based routes and net-negative emissions down to −0.22 tCO2/tlime for biomass-based configurations, at the expense of an energy penalty of 1.4–6.2 GJ/tlime. Current economic conditions favor unabated and bioenergy-based production (€147–176/tlime vs. €257–380/tlime with CC), whereas CC becomes competitive only under high CO2 pricing, achieving cost reductions up to 45% compared to the base case. Electrification and hydrogen-based production require very low-cost (≤€62/MWh) low-carbon energy to become competitive, whereas CCU remains constrained by its high energy demand (12.2 GJ/tlime). Finally, oxycombustion appears as the most promising decarbonization pathway, as it consistently provides the best trade-off between energy penalty, CO2 emissions, total cost, and robustness to market fluctuations, outperforming amine-based capture across all pricing scenarios.
