Techno-economic design of integrated infrastructure for CO2 transportation to sequestration and utilisation sites
abstract: Efficient CO 2 transport pathways are essential for reducing emissions and completing carbon capture and utilisation (CCU), carbon capture and sequestration (CCS), and carbon dioxide removal (CDR) chains. This study presents a techno-economic assessment of integrated CO 2 infrastructure for two key emitters in Finland, a pulp and paper mill and a cement plant, covering capture, conditioning, multimodal transport, and end use. Utilisation in the form of e-methanol synthesis is assumed in Oulu, Finland and Spain, while offshore and onshore sequestration are considered in Norway and Iceland. Aspen HYSYS was used for modelling and costs are presented as levelised costs of utilisation/sequestration for 2030-2050. Results indicate that shipping is the cheapest transportation option for long routes. Among sequestration scenarios, rail transport to port followed by shipping to Norway for offshore injection is the cheapest option. Despite higher injection costs in Norway (15-16.8 €/tCO 2 ) compared to mineralisation in basaltic rocks in Iceland (7.9-10.2 €/tCO 2 ), the shorter distance results in lower overall costs. For utilisation, shipping CO 2 to Spain for solar photovoltaics-based e-methanol synthesis results in lower costs than pipeline transport within Finland for wind power-based production, highlighting the stronger impact of electricity costs over transport costs. Overall, hybrid pipeline–shipping systems offer cost-efficient and flexible CO 2 transport solutions for future carbon management strategies in Northern Europe.

title: Influencing factors and hierarchical pathways of structural quality in concrete modular integrated construction: A dematel–ism case study in Hong Kong
Eco-Construction from the sea: assessment of mollusk shells by-products as sustainable building materials
abstract: This paper describes the development of novel bio-composite mortars made by reusing waste from the fish canning industry, namely mussel, clam, and oyster shells, as recycled aggregates to achieve a complete (100%) replacement of conventional sand. For each shell type, different granulometric fractions (0.00–1.00 mm, 1.00–2.00 mm, 2.00–4.00 mm, and a calibrated 0.00–4.00 mm blend) were investigated. Several waste-based cement mixes were tested and compared with conventional OPC mortar. Chemical-physical properties and the functional and engineering performance of the new bio-composite mortars were evaluated to explore their potential for construction applications. Main results indicated a strong dependence of mortar performance on both shell type and particle size distribution. In particular, oyster- and clam-shell mortars significantly improved the mechanical properties, achieving increases of up to 120% in flexural strength and 60% in compressive strength compared with the reference mortar, whereas mussel-shell formulations generally exhibited lower mechanical performance; opposite behaviours were observed for the mussel shell. Nevertheless, developed mixes were analysed in light of EN 998-1 and EN 998-2, for plastering and masonry application respectively, demonstrating potentials for uses in construction, including ordinary and lightweight structures and plasters. In addition, with an average 30% reduction in bulk density and a 40% increase in energy behaviour, the bio-composite mortars resulted particularly suitable for improved energy-saving applications. Finally, accelerated aging tests based on salt (4% NaCl) crystallization and exposure to high thermal loads (up to 800 °C), permitted to simulate exposure to prolonged stress and preliminary investigate the evolution of degradation phenomena, suggesting long life span. In conclusion, the use of sole bio-waste aggregate offers a sustainable alternative to conventional landfill disposal of the waste and makes these mortars promising candidates for Minimum Environmental Criteria certification, in line with the European Green Deal and Circular Economy principles.

title: Efficiency measures recommended for industrial facilities: Environmental and economic perspectives
Proof-of-concept investigation of an integrated multi-effect and forced-circulation adsorption water treatment system
In-situ hydrogen generation via water-gas shift reaction over Ni-Fe3O4/USY: A sustainable pathway for efficient polypropylene hydrogenolysis
Single-step fast decomposition of high-strength organophosphorus in industrial aqueous waste using DC water plasma
Decision-making in electrification transformation under dual-subsidy policy: Insights from digital investment and cost threshold analysis
Sustainability assessment of concrete pavement overlays reinforced with hybrid recycled and manufactured steel fibers
From waste to thermal regulator: Upcycling preservative-treated wood into multifunctional composite phase change materials for sustainable thermal management
Compound environmental exposures and age-stratified vulnerability: Nationwide evidence from U.S. county-level mortality among older adults
Green in situ construction of a macadamia waste-derived biochar/UiO-66-NH2 hybrid for high-efficiency removal of congo red and methyl orange from wastewater
Green finance and the efficiency of energy transition policies: An integrated MCDA and SHAP approach for OECD countries
abstract: This study examines how green finance strategies influence energy transition performance in 31 OECD countries. It combines a structured, literature-based indicator framework with WSM, TOPSIS, SMAA robustness analysis, and interpretable machine learning via Random Forest, XGBoost, and SHAP, and double machine learning for orthogonalized effect estimation. The results reveal significant differences among countries, with Denmark ranking as the top performer and several others constrained by fossil fuel dependence and structural barriers. The XGBoost model predicts the SMAA-based country ranking with an R² value of 0.447. SHAP analysis identifies real GDP per capita, renewable energy public RD&D, and green patents as the three strongest predictors of transition performance rankings, followed by environmentally related tax revenues and energy productivity. Double machine learning shows that environmental tax revenues carry a robust orthogonalized effect on the transition rank, stable across nuisance learners and control sets. The 31 OECD countries fall into three strategic profiles: 8 renewable-dominant, 8 intermediate-transition, and 15 fossil-dominant. These findings demonstrate that effective green finance strategies require coherence among fiscal instruments, innovation support, energy productivity, and country-specific structural conditions. The study provides a comparative framework for designing differentiated policy strategies aligned with national transition capacities.

title: Structural and operational optimization of cold storage system for enhanced energy efficiency, rapid cold release and economic benefits
Average photon energy based solar spectrum reconstruction for building-oriented TMY databases
Developing a phased implementation strategy for greenhouse gas mitigation in Korea's cement industry with the MESSAGEix model
Interfacial electron redistribution stabilizes Cu-centered redox cycling for efficient Fenton-like catalysis
Supply chain carbon penalties of U.S. carbon capture deployment: An EEIO-based assessment of net abatement performance
abstract: Carbon capture and storage (CCS) is increasingly viewed as an essential option for decarbonizing emissions-intensive sectors, yet its net abatement value depends not only on captured emissions at host facilities but also on the economy-wide effects induced by deployment spending. Existing studies rarely integrate output propagation, supply-chain emissions added, emissions removed, and net performance indicators within a single U.S.-wide high-resolution framework. This study addresses that gap by developing an environmentally extended input-output model to quantify the economy-wide production impacts, supply chain carbon penalties, and net performance of CCS deployment in the United States. Annualized capital and operating expenditures for CCS were represented as an exogenous final-demand shock and mapped into the 402-sector USEEIO v2.5 framework, while emissions were evaluated using sector-specific capture fractions. For the modeled 90% capture scenario in electricity, lime and gypsum products, cement, and iron and steel, gross CO 2 removal reached 1.14 Gt, supply-chain activity added 0.08 Gt CO 2 , and net abatement remained substantial at 1.06 Gt CO 2 . The corresponding emission penalty ratio was around 67 kg CO 2 added per ton removed, and the net abatement cost was 73 $/tCO 2 . Scenario analysis showed that a 20% reduction in total CCS cost lowered the emission penalty ratio by 19% and the net abatement cost by 20%, whereas a 90% reduction in electricity-sector CO 2 intensity lowered the penalty ratio by 59% while producing only a marginal reduction in net abatement cost. These results indicate that CCS can deliver substantial net abatement, with cost reductions primarily improving economic performance and electricity-sector decarbonization providing greater leverage for reducing the upstream carbon penalty. Because the analysis uses a static national EEIO structure, it does not resolve regional heterogeneity, facility-level technological differences, or endogenous changes in economic and production relationships over time.

title: Annual energy use and economic performance of rice-based cropping systems: A three-year field study in Southwest China
Toward circular biochar systems from waste-derived precursors: multi-analytical and multivariate insights into adsorption and heterogeneous Fenton-like oxidation performance
abstract: Understanding how waste-derived resources can be transformed into functional materials is essential for advancing circular economy strategies and sustainable water treatment technologies. In this work, a combined multi-analytical and multivariate framework is developed to elucidate how waste-derived precursor type, pyrolysis temperature, and iron functionalization collectively control adsorption and heterogeneous Fenton-like oxidation in biochar-based systems. Biochars were produced from 4 waste-derived precursors: spent coffee grounds, olive pomace, olive pomace stones, and sewage sludge, at three pyrolysis temperatures (450, 550, and 650 °C), generating 12 pristine materials and, after iron functionalization, a total of 24 materials. This design enables a systematic evaluation of waste-to-resource pathways and the decoupling of compositional and structural effects. Advanced characterization was combined with I-optimal response surface methodology (RSM) and principal component analysis (PCA) to provide complementary information: RSM was used to optimize material and process variables, whereas PCA was applied to interpret structure-property-performance relationships and identify the main descriptors controlling adsorption and heterogeneous Fenton-like oxidation. Equilibrium adsorption data were better described by the Freundlich model (R 2 ≥ 0.97), indicating that surface heterogeneity was a dominant factor, while Langmuir-derived Qmax values were used only as comparative capacity indicators. Lignocellulosic biochars were governed by surface area and aromaticity, whereas sewage-sludge-derived biochars showed enhanced affinity due to their mineral-rich matrices and oxygenated functionalities. Iron functionalization significantly improved performance, with Fe-SSBC450 showing the highest Langmuir-derived adsorption capacity (Qmax = 6.57 mg g −1 ) and oxidation efficiency (∼76% phenol removal). Oxidation proceeded via • OH-driven mechanisms following pseudo-second-order kinetics. This work demonstrates how waste-derived precursors can be valorised into high-value materials for environmental remediation, supporting circular economy strategies through resource-efficient water purification.

title: Towards cleaner rare earth metal production: Techno-economic and life cycle assessment of direct Nd2O3 pyroelectroreduction in low-temperature chloride-based molten salt
A decision-support framework for structuring and assessing photovoltaic panel recycling costs in emerging economies
abstract: The rapid expansion of solar energy systems has intensified concerns about the sustainable management of photovoltaic panels at the end of its life cycle, particularly recycling and resource recovery. Despite the growing volume of end-of-life solar equipment, significant uncertainties persist regarding recycling costs, especially in emerging economies, where structured economic assessment approaches remain limited. This study proposes a structured decision-support framework to support the assessment and management of recycling costs associated with end-of-life photovoltaic panels. A Systematic Literature Review was conducted to identify cost components related to photovoltaic recycling, which were then structured using the Function Analysis System Technique. Expert evaluation was used to validate cost relevance and structure. The Fuzzy Delphi method and Mean Rank Position were applied to reach consensus on cost relevance, while the Stepwise Weight Assessment Ratio Analysis method was used to assign weights to cost categories. The resulting framework consolidates consensual cost components into weighted functional clusters, providing a structured basis for economic assessment and supporting decision-making in photovoltaic panel recycling initiatives. The proposed framework contributes to resource conservation and circular economy strategies by supporting managers, investors, and policymakers in structuring and comparing the cost dimensions associated with photovoltaic panel recycling in emerging economies.

title: Global perspectives on the curricular integration of nature-based solutions in hydrology and water resources management education
abstract: Nature-based Solutions (NbS) are strongly advocated in international environmental discourse and policy agendas for climate risk management. However, a critical knowledge gap remains regarding the extent to which NbS concepts are systematically integrated into higher education curricula, despite the role of universities as institutional settings for developing and disseminating knowledge relevant to NbS. In this study, we examined the degree of curricular integration of NbS within university study programs in water resources management (WRM) and hydrology at the undergraduate, master's, and doctoral levels across 25 countries in 8 geographic regions. Data were collected through a structured survey, and curricula analysis was conducted, in which the proportion of NbS content within each course was categorized into Major (core focus), Moderate (partial coverage), Minor (peripheral inclusion), or NA (no explicit content). Our findings reveal significant regional and disciplinary contrasts. Countries with research-active disciplines, such as engineering and environmental science, and those with formal NbS policy frameworks, such as in the EU, show earlier or more extensive NbS curricular integration. Contrary to the interdisciplinary nature of NbS, we find that NbS are predominantly, yet sporadically, embedded in civil and environmental engineering and natural sciences, with minimal contributions from other disciplines, such as social sciences. Moreover, NbS concept remains insufficiently represented at the undergraduate level as 45.9% of the courses contain Minor content and 33.9% have no explicit NbS content, which represents a missed opportunity for NbS exposure during foundational professional study and training. More substantive NbS content appears in master's and doctoral programs, suggesting that NbS remains a specialized, research-oriented topic rather than foundational curriculum content. Faculty-led NbS teaching initiatives, identified through the survey, though encouraging, reveal a misalignment between high NbS research activity and their low curricular integration, where 31–41% of lecturers in courses with NA and Minor NbS integration do publish NbS-related research. Without explicit NbS framing in WRM and hydrology curricula, study programs may remain confined to specific disciplinary silos, potentially limiting students' overall engagement with NbS concepts. These findings collectively suggest that advancing comprehensive NbS integration in higher education may require deliberate and coordinated curricular reform across institutional levels, highlighting the importance of a whole-institution approach that systematically integrates NbS into curriculum, governance structures, and campus infrastructure.

title: Decision-making for enhancing thermal resilience: Identifying and prioritising intervention domains across social, economic, ecological, and technological systems
abstract: The compounding effects of climate change and urbanisation have intensified heatwave frequency and the urban heat island effect, posing growing risks to thermal comfort and public health. Enhancing thermal resilience requires coordinated interventions across social, economic, ecological, and technological systems. However, existing studies remain limited in clearly identifying key intervention domains and in understanding how these domains interact within an integrated systems perspective. Therefore, the overarching aim of this research is to identify key thermal resilience interventions, examine expert-perceived interrelationships among them, and develop an expert-informed decision-support analytical framework for interpreting and prioritising interventions. Focus groups with experts from China and the UK were conducted using a modified Problem Tree Analysis approach to elicit intervention-related problems, perceived causes and effects. A subsequent web-based survey was used to assess the perceived influence relationships among the identified intervention domains. These relationships were analysed using the Decision-Making Trial and Evaluation Laboratory-based Analytic Network Process (DANP) method. The results reveal distinct expert-perceived influence structures among intervention domains across Social-Economic-Ecological-Technological (SEET) system dimensions, while also highlighting the central role of policy development and planning and economic feasibility in shaping the implementation of intervention domains. The key contribution of this study is the development of an expert-informed decision-support analytical framework that systematically captures cross-dimensional influence relationships and supports the prioritisation of thermal resilience interventions. The findings provide an expert-informed analytical basis for supporting context-sensitive decision-making in urban heat adaptation under climate change.

title: Pressure-aware multi-modal CO2 transport planning for industrial decarbonization: A case study of Germany's steel sector to 2050
abstract: Multi-modal CO 2 transport networks involve coupled decisions on operating pressure, mode-switching equipment, and infrastructure deployment timing, yet existing optimization studies typically treat the associated compression, liquefaction, and heat exchange as post-processing assumptions. This study develops a pressure-aware mixed-integer linear programming framework for multi-modal CO 2 transport planning that couples mode selection with pressure-state-dependent conditioning, allowing pressure regimes and mode transitions to be optimized jointly. The framework integrates phased deployment across three time horizons (2030, 2040, 2050) under three decarbonization pathways, carbon pricing for uncaptured emissions, and selective reuse of existing pipelines within a single optimization. Seven mode-pressure variants are considered, with mode-transition costs derived from a 49-transition simulation matrix. The framework is applied to twelve major German steel emitters connected to the Northern Lights offshore storage site via three candidate ports. The cost-optimal network shifts from truck-and-rail logistics in the early, low-volume stage to a dense-phase pipeline backbone as captured volumes grow. Unit transport costs remain within 15–18 €/tCO 2 across the scenarios. The marginal cost of expanding transport and conditioning capacity stabilizes at 13–14 €/tCO 2 from 2040 onward. These figures indicate that transport is not the binding economic constraint on scaling up capture ambition, rather than that CCUS as a whole is inexpensive. Existing pipeline reuse is found to be capacity- and stage-dependent: sufficiently large reused assets can reduce new-build requirements. The framework offers a transferable approach for cleaner industrial logistics design, supporting the transition to low-carbon hard-to-abate sectors in Europe and beyond.

title: Interface interaction between yeast and β-glucan drives soil aggregate stabilization: molecular mechanisms and bioremediation functions
Uncovering the burden shifting of data center cooling: System-level water-energy-carbon optimization for urban infrastructure
abstract: The rapid growth of data centers (DCs), driven by artificial intelligence and cloud computing, presents a critical resource challenge for urban infrastructure planning across the water-energy-carbon nexus. Traditional energy models often treat DC integration merely as an isolated electrical load, failing to capture weather-dependent cooling demands and the resulting "burden-shifting" between direct on-site water consumption and the indirect water footprint of the regional grid. To bridge this gap, this study introduces a multi-scale mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) optimization framework for urban capacity expansion planning that explicitly integrates hourly climate data with the Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) and Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE) of distinct DC cooling architectures. Applied to a representative urban microgrid, the model simulates a multi-year horizon at an hourly resolution to evaluate two contrasting DC cooling strategies: evaporative cooling and closed-loop air chillers. Our results reveal a critical trade-off: optimizing exclusively for zero on-site water use via air chillers inadvertently shifts the resource burden upstream to the regional electrical grid, demanding substantial increases in low-carbon generation, energy storage, and total infrastructure costs. Ultimately, moving beyond facility-specific metrics to evaluate holistic, system-wide Pareto trade-offs is essential for developing sustainable urban energy strategies.

title: Fewer children, higher carbon intensity? Exploring household carbon emission intensity in low-fertility contexts
Machine learning prediction and analysis for LFL of C0-C2 combustible gases and blends under wide operating conditions
Resilience and reconfiguration: A CPD-STERGM analysis of structural breaks in the BRI LIB trade network
Green efficiency under heterogeneous technologies: Evidence from Indian manufacturing industry
Understanding consumer reactions and corporate reputation in corporate sustainability crises: The role of blame, harm, and CSR relevance
abstract: This study investigates how consumers' behavioral responses vary across different types of corporate sustainability crises characterized by differences in potential harm, attribution of blame, and relevance to Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR). We also examine the moderating role of pre-crisis corporate reputation in shaping these responses. An experimental full factorial design is employed based on a representative sample of U.S. adults (N = 680). Situational Crisis Communication Theory (SCCT) posits that stakeholders' attributions of responsibility are influenced by an organization's crisis history, stakeholder relationships, and reputation. Extending SCCT, the findings indicate that when a firm's pre-crisis reputation is low, consumers' behavioral responses are not significantly influenced by the crisis's potential for harm, CSR relevance, or attribution of blame. In contrast, when pre-crisis reputation is high, both potential harm and attribution of blame exert a significant effect on consumer behavior, whereas CSR relevance does not. This study makes a novel contribution by examining a comprehensive set of sustainability-related crisis types, including industry-wide collective crises, product-harm crises, and CSR-related tensions. Theoretical and managerial implications are discussed.

title: Modified lignosulfonate-assisted in situ synthesis of Co3Mo3N/CoMo2S4 heterojunction electrocatalyst with strong interfacial interactions for efficient overall water splitting
Regulating interface charge separation to unlock photocatalytic non-radical pathways: Construction of BiOCl/COF S-scheme heterojunction for efficient antibiotic remediation
Investigating the regulatory effects of surfactants to design high-performance and eco-friendly soybean oil-based emulsions for the manufacturing industry
Sustainable salt recovery from DMF-containing industrial brines through integrated nanofiltration and space-confined catalytic ozonation
Life cycle assessment of growing media: a baseline dataset for European horticulture
abstract: Growing media underpin a substantial and growing share of European food and ornamental production, with 116 million cubic metres used globally per year. Their environmental footprint has become a focus of regulatory and commercial attention, but comparative assessments to date have been fragmented in scope and rely on outdated data, limiting their value for research and industry. This study presents a Life Cycle Assessment of twelve constituents and thirty mixes (covering seven applications) representative of European horticulture. The study follows a cradle-to-gate scope, including use-phase emissions for all organic materials. Climate change impact and single score (weighted impact of 16 categories) are presented per functional unit (1 m 3 ) at the constituent and mix levels. Wood fibre (15 kg CO 2 eq/m 3 ) and expanded perlite (33 kg CO 2 eq/m 3 ) had the lowest climate change impact; white peat (219 kg CO 2 eq/m 3 ), green compost (249 kg CO 2 eq/m 3 ), and black peat (390 kg CO 2 eq/m 3 ) had the highest. Single score results show a reversal in ranking for white peat (7.7 mPt/m 3 ) and coir constituents (9.0 to 10.5 mPt/m 3 ), emphasising the need for multi-indicator assessments to minimise the risk of shifting environmental burdens. Green compost presents a high climate change impact and single score result (21.3 mPt/m 3 ), but substantial uncertainty of this estimate highlights the need for further inventory data improvement. Mix-level results indicate that substantial carbon savings can be achieved by strategic formulation of mixes in the sectors of fruiting vegetables, potted plants and ornamentals, and tree nurseries. Assessment at the application level is identified as the next methodological priority to define strategies for efficient use of growing media resources.

title: Cradle to grave life cycle assessment of retreaded truck tyres: an industrial case study in Italy
abstract: The transition to climate-neutrality by 2050 requires decarbonizing mobility and among the different materials used in this sector there is the urgent need to decarbonize tyres. Despite the problems related to the recycling of tyres, retreading is a technology already available on the market that, prolonging the useful service life of tyres, allows considerable environmental advantages. However, its diffusion is still limited and concentrated in the truck sector with a decreasing trend in the last decade. This study presents for the first time a cradle to grave Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) that compares the environmental performance of two product systems, i.e. retreaded truck tyres and virgin truck tyres. The study is based on primary data, when available, and on secondary data or estimations, when necessary. The results show that retreading allows a considerable reduction in the environmental impact of tyres: up to 50 % in the climate change impact category, 52 % in the fossil fuels consumption, 49 % in the consumption of natural resources, 55 % in the water use, 37 % in the PM 10 emission and 10 % in the PM 2.5 emissions. Moreover, retreading allows for a reduction up to 46 % in the use of natural rubber (EU is 100 % import-reliant on this material). These findings highlight the urgent need for policies that can promote the diffusion of retreading on a larger scale in case of truck tyres and that support the creation of a dedicated supply chain for the retreading of car tyres.

title: Delay-consistent adaptive incentive governance for circular beverage packaging systems: distinguishing structural and algorithmic limits in PET and returnable glass recovery in Mexico
abstract: Mexico's 2030 target of 80% PET-container recovery under the ANNEP agreement remains 16 percentage points above the current national recovery rate, with returnable glass already operating near its infrastructure asymptote. Whether adaptive incentive governance can close this gap depends on distinguishing the mechanism sources of policy performance: the adaptive feedback timing itself, the average incentive intensity at which policies operate, or the underlying behavioral response of the recovery system. This paper investigates the distinction using a delay-consistent adaptive proportional–integral controller embedded in a system-dynamics closed-loop supply chain calibrated against four independent empirical sources for the Mexican beverage-container context. Four policies are compared in a 216-cell balanced factorial design: a no-incentive baseline, a constant deposit-refund, an adaptive proportional–integral controller, and a quarterly threshold rule. A new stratified matched-budget identification experiment decomposes policy performance into three analytically distinct levels — algorithmic effects, operating-point effects, and structural constraints — by comparing the adaptive controller against an equivalent-intensity fixed benchmark across baseline, demand-dip, and demand-whiplash regimes. The matched-budget analysis indicates that the adaptive controller and the equivalent-intensity fixed policy converge to essentially identical steady-state return rates (approximately 0.759) under all three demand regimes; the previously observed adaptive advantage is attributable to operating-point effects rather than to feedback timing. This identification supports interpreting the 2.1-percentage-point gap between the observed ceiling and the 0.78 composite target as structural rather than algorithmic in origin: the ceiling reflects the saturating Michaelis–Menten behavioral response of the recovery system, not a limitation of the control algorithm. Closing this gap requires policy instruments capable of expanding the behavioral elasticity envelope itself — reverse-vending densification, extended producer responsibility, informal-sector formalization, and consumer information campaigns — rather than stronger deposit-refund incentives alone. • Matched-budget identification experiment isolates algorithmic from operating-point effects in deposit-refund governance. • Adaptive controller and equivalent-intensity fixed policy converge to identical return rates across three demand regimes. • The 0.759 composite return-rate ceiling is structural, not algorithmic — reflecting behavioral elasticity limits. • Structural ceiling stops recovery 2.1 percentage points below Mexico's 0.78 composite target under current elasticities. • Closing the gap requires elasticity-envelope expansion, not stronger deposit-refund incentives.

title: Evaluating and advancing large language models for soil and water conservation tasks: Case study of the black soil region
A polymer-modified bentonite stabilizer for cadmium- and arsenic-contaminated soils: Simultaneous microbial diversity enhancement, nutrient enrichment, and plant growth promotion
Release of multilayered constraints drives metabolic and regulatory evolutionary strategies for polyethylene biodegradation
Estimating consumption-based electricity carbon emission intensity from public data: A cleaner production framework for the Tokyo Metropolitan Area
abstract: This study develops a reproducible framework to estimate synthetic 30-min electricity-related CO 2 emissions intensity (CEI) across 14 zones in the Tokyo Metropolitan Area (TMA), addressing gaps in urban emission accounting for decarbonization planning. The primary contribution is an economic dispatch-based electricity carbon emission (ED-CE) model implemented under both Monthly and Intra-day demand allocation approaches using publicly available data. The ED-CE model combines a merit-order dispatch algorithm with a neighbor-priority allocation approach in which surplus electricity is redistributed to the closest zones based on geographical proximity. The Intra-day approach incorporates synthetic half-hourly demand profiles to represent short-term electricity consumption variability. To assess robustness, a network-constrained electricity carbon emission (NC-CE) model is implemented using power-flow information. Results show that while system-level CEI estimates are consistent across ED-CE and NC-CE, spatial patterns are more sensitive to allocation assumptions under ED-CE, whereas NC-CE produces comparatively smoother spatial variability due to power flow constraints and flow-traced emission attribution. In addition, a sensitivity analysis using random surplus allocation indicates that major emission hotspots are generally robust, although absolute zonal magnitudes remain uncertain. The results reveal spatial and temporal heterogeneity in electricity-related emissions and annual emissions (33.2 MtCO 2 /year), increasing 37.0 MtCO 2 /year under the Intra-day approach, while suburban regions show lower or redistributed emissions under intra-day allocation. Southern Ibaraki maintains the lowest CEI (0.26 kgCO 2 /kWh) across all model configurations, indicating a robust low-carbon supply pattern. Industrial and commercial emissions exceed Tokyo Cap-and-Trade value due to differing boundaries and methods, while electricity CEI shows temporal variability from renewables.

title: Electricity-carbon traceability settlement model based on contract and power flow distribution under the new-type power system
Regulating CoOx/Ni inverse structure to enhance magnetocatalytic purification of VOCs emitted from intermittent sources
Towards eco-friendly biofuel design: Atmospheric transformation and divergent ecological risk assessment of dimethylbutanol isomers
Data-driven multi-ion synergistic regulation for cleaner copper electrorefining: Enhancing energy and resource efficiency
Techno-economic and risk-adjusted assessment of PV–wind–hydrogen hybrid energy systems in Morocco: Towards cost-effective low-carbon electricity supply
Structuring co-creation for circular ecosystem emergence: The minimum viable circular ecosystem framework
abstract: Circular economy transitions require coordinated action among multiple interdependent actors across value chains. While research on circular ecosystems has expanded rapidly, two interrelated gaps persist: existing frameworks remain largely conceptual and provide limited process-level guidance for orchestrators, and the field lacks a theoretical account of how circular ecosystem emergence unfolds through co-creation; what orchestration activities are required at each stage and through what mechanisms they shape alignment and value creation outcomes. This study addresses both gaps by developing the Minimum Viable Circular Ecosystem (MVCE) framework through a design science research approach combining a literature synthesis, fifteen semi-structured expert interviews, and three multi-actor workshops conducted in the context of emerging reusable packaging ecosystems. The MVCE framework conceptualises circular ecosystem emergence as an iterative co-creation process unfolding through four interrelated phases: visioning, ecosystem framing, experimentation and learning, and structuring and governance, each operationalised through a dedicated boundary tool supporting collective sensemaking, ecosystem configuration, hypothesis-driven experimentation, and collaborative governance. While prior ecosystem frameworks address individual functions such as actor mapping, readiness assessment, or governance design in isolation, to our knowledge, prior frameworks have not integrated all four functions within a single co-creation process architecture operationalised through complementary boundary tools. The study advances four theoretical contributions: a theoretically grounded process framework for circular ecosystem emergence; the operationalisation of distributed orchestration through boundary objects; an account of value co-creation at the ecosystem emergence level; and a nascent design theory for circular ecosystem orchestration. Together, these contributions advance understanding of how circular ecosystems can be deliberately designed, aligned, and validated through structured co-creation.

title: Can digital transportation contribute to mitigating environmental pollution? Evidence from the Chinese Context
AI-driven multi-objective decision framework for flare gas valorization pathway selection: Regional comparative analysis for Iran and the Kurdistan Region of Iraq
Natural sciences for post-growth in practice: low-tech iron oxide reduction under a concentrated light flux using urine-derived ammonia and hydrogen as reducers
abstract: A telling example of the green growth sociotechnical imaginary in natural sciences is the future of ‘green’ steel production, envisaged to grow based on a hypothetical massive deployment of low-carbon electricity. In this article, we show how a post-growth, low-tech framework can open up new innovation pathways towards sustainable futures of ironmaking. The low-tech processes that we envision aim at converting iron oxide into iron using readily available and renewable sources of reducing agents and energy: ammonia and hydrogen from urine, and concentrated sunlight. In our study, a solar concentrator simulator and synthetic urea were used as models to assess two ways of generating ammonia from urea for iron oxide reduction: i) the pyrolysis of solid urea inside the reduction reactor under concentrated light flux, and ii) the biocatalysed hydrolysis of urea by addition of urease-rich plant seeds – like soybeans or watermelon seeds – to an aqueous solution of urea mimicking urine. During the reduction of iron oxide, in situ mass spectrometry confirmed the decomposition of ammonia into hydrogen in presence of iron species. X-ray diffraction analysis of the resulting samples showed that the reduction yield successfully reached 90–98%. The global level of production of iron of such a process would be limited by urine production; estimates are provided and discussed. Parting from the green growth imaginary, our interdisciplinary work aims at reintegrating chemical processes into natural cycles, independent from both electricity and fossil fuels, and also at participating in opening up research to more diverse visions of the future.

title: A low-energy natural carbonation pathway for fully recycled self-compacting concrete: mechanical performance and life-cycle carbon assessment
Quantitative sustainability assessment of bioactive ingredients lipophilization
abstract: Bioactive compounds exhibit diverse biological activities, including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anti-microbial, photoprotective, and anti-aging effects, making them highly attractive ingredients in cosmetic formulations. However, despite their multifunctional potential, the practical application of many natural compounds is often limited by poor chemical stability, low aqueous or lipid solubility, and poor compatibility with formulation matrices. This work critically evaluates the sustainability of recent lipophilization (bio)catalytic strategies for the functional upgrading of bioactive compounds for cosmetic applications, especially those with antioxidant properties, with particular emphasis on reaction media design and materials efficiency. The analysis covers processes carried out in volatile organic solvents (VOSs), ionic liquids (ILs), deep eutectic solvents (DESs) and solvent-free media, including self-DES and “2-in-1” systems. Representative case studies are compared using a “gate-to-gate” sustainability assessment (comprising product synthesis and purification), or a strictly upstream analysis when the workup has not been addressed. A quantitative assessment was enabled by selected Green Metrics, CHEM21 solvent selection guide and the Modified Green Star Area. Results unveil the following rank of median Environmental factor values: organic solvents (72.6) > ILs (32.7) > DESs (7.0) > Solvent-free (4.6). These data underscore that non-reusable solvents are the main source of waste and carbon emissions, with product workup identifying as a critical bottleneck. Although product purity is vital for the cosmetic industry, this step is often neglected, creating a major gap in successful industrial scalability. To address this, solvent-free systems are crucial, as they facilitate the streamlined utilization of products with minimal environmental and health impacts.

title: Unravelling the atmospheric occurrence and partitioning of emerging PAH derivatives from the coking industry: Mechanistic insights into 9,10-anthraquinone formation
Does repair improve environmental performance? Integrating temporal dynamics into environmental assessment of circular strategies
abstract: Growing electronic waste and rising demand for critical materials have intensified interest in circular economy strategies that keep products, components and materials in use for longer. Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) is the most widely used method for assessing environmental impacts, but it is a static methodology and does not inherently incorporate the timing of circular interventions. This is particularly relevant for time-sensitive products exposed to component failure, technological obsolescence or performance decline, where repair benefits can depend on when failure occurs during the product's service life. This study develops a time-explicit, LCIA-derived threshold metric to assess whether repair or replacement is environmentally preferable under different component-failure scenarios. The metric is demonstrated through a mobile device case study comparing replacement with battery, display and printed wiring board repair across selected LCIA impact categories. The results show that repair is not uniformly preferable: the threshold between repair and replacement depends on the environmental burden of the failed component repair, failure timing and the impact category assessed. Components with higher repair-to-product burden ratios reach the replacement-preferable threshold earlier in the product's service life, while lower ratios extend the range of service life in which repair remains environmentally preferable. The findings demonstrate that environmental assessments of circular strategies can produce oversimplified conclusions when failure timing is not represented explicitly. The proposed metric provides a transparent approach for incorporating temporal dynamics into repair-versus-replacement assessment for consumer electronics and may be extended to other time-sensitive product categories, such as electric mobility components and renewable energy technologies.

title: Blockchain enabled closed-loop supply chain for EV batteries with environmental tax and reward penalty policy
You can't improve what you don't measure: empirical evidence from Australian businesses around industrial decarbonisation
abstract: Industrial decarbonisation is central to achieving Net Zero emissions in manufacturing, and its success depends not only on technological implementation but also on firms’ ability to measure performance. Despite growing attention to sustainability reporting, little focus has been placed on measuring decarbonisation performance at firm level. To address this gap, this study develops a framework for assessing decarbonisation performance integrating Triple Bottom Line of sustainability, followed by an exploratory investigation among 217 Australian manufacturing firms in measuring their decarbonisation performance. Findings reveal significant gaps and uneven trends in current decarbonisation performance measurement practices. Of 49 indicators examined, 17 were not reported by respondents as being measured, mainly those related to pollution control, carbon pricing, and cost competitiveness. Moreover, the indicators not reported as being measured comprised 10 of the 25 economic indicators (40%), 5 of the 20 environmental indicators (25.0%), and 2 of the 4 social indicators (50%). In the investigated sample, larger firms omitted 51% of indicators compared to 36.7% in Small- and Medium-sized Enterprises. Sectoral analysis also showed comparatively high proportions of indicators not reported as being measured across food (65.3%), beverages (65.3%), wood (57.1%), chemicals (67.3%), machinery (63.2%), textiles (67.3%) and other industries including pulp & paper, fabricated metal products, and transport equipment (63.2%). This study finds that manufacturing firms do not comprehensively measure decarbonisation performance yet. Furthermore, noticeable differences were observed across firms, indicating uneven levels of engagement toward decarbonisation performance measurement practices. The findings suggest implications for policy and managerial practice, calling for a paradigm shift that embeds decarbonisation measurement within business strategy.

Integrated digital framework for wastewater treatment performance and sustainability assessment in low-income countries
abstract: Modelling and simulation are widely used to optimise biological wastewater treatment processes, while life cycle assessment (LCA) is well established for evaluating environmental impacts. However, integrated modelling-LCA approaches have largely been developed for data-rich and well-resourced settings, limiting their practical application in developing countries where reliable operational data, technical capacity, and resources are often constrained. Moreover, few studies have demonstrated such integrated approaches using field-measured data and validated their recommendations through full-scale implementation. To address these gaps, an integrated digital framework linking metabolic activated sludge model (META-ASM) with LCA was developed and applied to optimise the Santa Catarina wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) in Cape Verde. The framework integrates systematic data collection and reconciliation, field-data-driven dynamic simulation, scenario-based optimisation, sensitivity analysis, and sustainability assessment. Model predictions were evaluated against observed plant performance, and operational and structural scenarios were sequentially assessed to identify improvements across individual treatment units. The recommended operational strategies were subsequently implemented at full scale, with field monitoring confirming reductions in effluent total chemical oxygen demand (COD Tot ), total suspended solids (TSS), total phosphorus (P Tot ), and total nitrogen (N Tot ) of 51.4%, 58.7%, 44.4%, and 21.5%, respectively, compared with baseline operation. LCA further demonstrated reductions of approximately 30% in human toxicity, freshwater ecotoxicity, and marine ecotoxicity, and 36% in eutrophication potential. Beyond improving treatment and environmental performance, the framework incorporates practical data-management tools, capacity building, and context-specific operational considerations. This field-validated, data-adaptive approach provides a scalable and transferable pathway for applying digital process modelling and sustainability assessment to WWTP optimisation in resource-constrained developing country contexts.

Environmental impact of manufacturing and use of ceramic matrix composites for aerospace propulsion applications
abstract: Ceramic Matrix Composites (CMCs) have emerged as promising materials with exceptional mechanical properties, making them appealing for aerospace applications. Notable contenders among various CMC formulations, including Al 2 O 3 /SiO 2 , Al 2 O 3 /B4C, and SiC/SiC, show great potential for replacing traditional materials in the production of aircraft components, such as turbine blades. However, environmental evidence to support such substitution remains limited, and no consistent basis exists for comparing CMCs with established materials across their full life cycle. This paper presents a cradle-to-grave Life Cycle Assessment that compares five candidate blade materials under a common functional unit and a single blade geometry, so that differences in impact are attributable to the material and its manufacturing route. The study covers Al 2 O 3 /SiO 2 manufactured by sol-gel infiltration, Al 2 O 3 /B 4 C manufactured by sintering, and SiC/SiC manufactured by chemical vapour infiltration, pyrolysis of a preceramic polymer, or melt infiltration, alongside the nickel superalloys Inconel 625 and Hastelloy X manufactured by powder metallurgy. An aircraft turbine blade is selected as the case study, with material quantities defined from the blade design criteria and impacts assessed across the manufacturing, use, and end-of-life phases. Variation in the underlying inventory and operational assumptions is examined to test how firmly the comparison holds and which parameters drive it. The results provide a quantified basis for material and process selection in turbine blade design, identifying the life cycle stages and manufacturing parameters that govern the environmental performance of each option.

Pulsed electric field pretreatment enhances anaerobic digestion of cashew apple bagasse by increasing methane yield and energy recovery
abstract: To avoid the high energy demand and inhibitory compounds associated with conventional methods, pulsed electric field (PEF) pretreatment was investigated as a low-energy strategy to enhance the anaerobic digestion (AD) of cashew apple bagasse, a lignocellulosic residue with limited biodegradability. Two stirred tank reactors (4.3 L) were operated for 42 days under mesophilic conditions (36 °C) with a hydraulic retention time (HRT) of 25.8 days: a control reactor fed with untreated bagasse and a PEF reactor initially fed with PEF-pretreated biomass. During the semi-continuous phase, both reactors were subsequently fed with untreated bagasse. PEF processing promoted complete cell disintegration (Z = 1) and induced structural modifications, as indicated by Fourier-Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FT-IR) and Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), thereby enhancing substrate accessibility by disrupting the fibers' physical barriers and significantly increasing the available surface area for AD. As a result, cumulative biogas production in the PEF reactor increased by 37.67% compared to the control (75.47 L vs. 54.82 L), while methane yield increased by 22.01%, reaching 235.23 L CH 4 per kg of volatile solids. The methane concentration in the biogas remained similar (∼70%) in both reactors, suggesting that PEF primarily enhanced hydrolysis efficiency rather than altering methanogenic pathways. Dynamic volatile fatty acids (VFA) monitoring showed PEF accelerated intermediate consumption, especially of butyric acid. The system maintained low propionic/acetic acid ratios (≤0.37), ensuring stability without toxicity and enhancing methanogenic activity. Despite the additional energy input required for PEF pretreatment (22.52 kJ per kg), the overall energy balance remained positive, resulting in higher net electricity (70.55 kWh per t) and heat (634.91 MJ per t) generation. Greenhouse gas mitigation increased to 38.27 kg CO 2 -eq per t of biomass in the PEF scenario. A preliminary techno-economic assessment estimated that PEF integration could double annual cash flow and reduce the estimated payback period from 6.7 to 3.3 years under the evaluated assumptions. A univariate sensitivity analysis (±30%) shows that both configurations are sensitive to changes in heat prices, but the PEF scenario offers greater economic stability, with a payback period of 5.1 years even under a 30% drop in thermal energy prices. These results indicate that PEF is an effective pretreatment for improving methane production, energy recovery, and the sustainability of AD of cashew apple bagasse.

Environmental and Economic Life Cycle Assessment of low-tech digesters coupled with gasification technology implemented in a small-scale dairy farm
abstract: Improving organic waste management while strengthening the circular bioeconomy and providing clean energy remains a key challenge for small-scale farms in low- and middle-income countries. This study assessed the potential environmental and economic impacts of low-tech digesters coupled with gasification technology in a small-scale farm producing dairy products in Colombia, using the Life Cycle Assessment and the Life Cycle Costing tools. Three scenarios were considered: i) a baseline scenario based on conventional waste management and fossil energy use, ii) a scenario with a low-tech digester, and iii) a scenario with a digester coupled with a gasifier. The selected functional unit was 1 kg of produced cheese. The system boundaries (i.e. cradle to grave) included the emissions associated with waste management, the construction and operation of the low-tech digester and gasifier, and the use of fuels, synthetic fertilisers and/or digestate in agriculture. The results showed that adopting low-tech digesters to co-digest cattle manure with waste generated from dairy processing (i.e. cheese whey) reduced the environmental impacts associated with eutrophication, climate change and fossil resource scarcity (up to 17% reduction compared to the baseline scenario). Moreover, coupling the digester with gasification further increased bioenergy production and completely replaced fossil fuel consumption. From an economic point of view, the synergies between low-tech digesters and gasification technology reduced the total costs associated with cheese production by 56% compared to the baseline scenario. Overall, the study demonstrated the potential of decentralised, low-tech bioenergy solutions to support circular bioeconomy and sustainability in small-scale dairy farms in low-income countries.

Organic vs. conventional wine production: a comparative multi-year environmental LCA study in central Italy
abstract: Comparative assessments of organic and conventional wine have reported divergent results and are largely based on single production years. This study evaluates and compares the environmental impacts of a 0.75 L bottle of conventional and of organic wine over three consecutive years. Using Life Cycle Assessment, the analysis covers all phases from raw material production to the farm gate. Primary data were collected from an Italian winery for 2022–2024, years with different climatic conditions, levels of field operations and grape yields. On average, the organic bottle shows higher impacts than the conventional one in 14 out of 18 impact categories considered. Differences are modest but systematic and mainly reflect more field operations, higher diesel use and lower yields in the organic vineyard. In both systems, glass bottle production is the dominant hotspot in most of the impact categories. Organic viticulture shows a clear advantage in terrestrial ecotoxicity, due to the absence of specific synthetic fungicides. For marine ecotoxicity and human non-carcinogenic toxicity, differences are marginal, indicating broadly comparable performance. The comparison further shows that the gap between systems varies with climatic conditions, input profiles and yields, with rainier years associated with more field operations but not necessarily with higher impacts when management is adjusted. Overall, neither production system is environmentally superior across all impact categories. Organic management improves toxicity-related indicators but performs worse in climate- and resource-related categories, while conventional management shows the opposite pattern, highlighting the value of multi-year, multi-indicator LCAs to capture trade-offs in viticulture.

title: Construction of a promising self-sedimenting industrial chassis strain EGMS of Euglena gracilis with high paramylon yield via EMS mutagenesis combined with dark-heterotrophic screening
Comprehensiveness or equalization? Rethinking urban-rural integration through a dual-dimension framework and its sustainable development implications in Northeast China

Emission forecasting based spatial-temporal carbon response: A multi-agent attention-enhanced deep learning framework
abstract: As a major contributor to carbon emissions, the decarbonization of power systems has garnered significant societal attention. Nodal carbon intensity (NCI), a critical factor in carbon-oriented demand response, has traditionally been determined through ex-post calculations. However, this ex-post approach introduces latency in low-carbon dispatch. To address this, this paper presents a proactive ex-ante spatial-temporal carbon response framework. At its core, we develop a novel deep learning-based hierarchical design, enhanced by a dual-stage attention mechanism and a large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent cooperation system, to accurately forecast day-ahead NCI. This design effectively mitigates the impact of renewable energy uncertainty and enhances predictive resilience. On the demand side, the framework proposes a spatial-temporal carbon scheduling model that integrates geographically dispatchable loads (GDLs), including mobile energy storage systems (MESSs) and distributed data centers (DDCs). Leveraging high-accuracy day-ahead NCI predictions, the framework can effectively reduce system emissions by quickly responding to carbon intensity fluctuations. The proposed framework is tested on the modified IEEE 33-bus system. According to the simulation results, the impacts of proposed framework on dispatching latency and emission outcomes are analyzed. The results demonstrate that under a one-hour reduction in carbon scheduling latency, the proposed model and methodology can achieve over 30% emission reduction. This research breaks through the limitations of passive carbon accounting, advancing toward proactive carbon management. It offers an intelligent solution that accelerates the transition to cleaner power systems while directly supporting sustainable production goals.

Spain's realistic potential for ocean alkalinity enhancement: Carbon dioxide removal through industrial integration
abstract: A common challenge for carbon dioxide removal (CDR) approaches, including those falling under ocean alkalinity enhancement (OAE), is the need to develop new global industries and supply chains to underpin their sustainable scale-up. To facilitate roll-out, OAE approaches could be incorporated into existing industries, notably by: i) partially substituting silica sand in existing beach nourishment projects with (ultra)mafic (e.g., olivine-rich) sand for carbon dioxide drawdown through coastal enhanced weathering; ii) using the spare capacity of the cement industry to produce slaked lime for ocean liming; and iii) producing sodium hydroxide from waste desalination brines through electrochemical brine splitting. Here, the gross CDR capacities of these OAE approaches were examined for Spain by considering spare capacities, technical constraints, and engineering restrictions and challenges. Prospective life cycle assessment (pLCA) revealed their net-negativity and their sensitivity to future climate scenarios and particularly technology maturity. Spain's gross/net CDR capacity via OAE amounted to 13.52/8.27, 38.35/26.50, and 40.54/38.13 Mt CO 2 yr −1 in 2030, 2040, and 2050, respectively. Future decarbonisation and improved technology readiness levels and spare capacities drive this increase. Therefore, technological maturity and decarbonised economies, particularly decarbonised energy, are needed for CDR technologies to achieve their full potential. Finally, we considered how complex social, regulatory, and governance factors may impinge on the feasibility of these three OAE approaches. Regulatory clarity and innovation, governance frameworks, and social acceptance are needed, which also requires robust efforts to consult and engage communities. Overall, OAE could underpin national long-term strategies and form an essential part of climate-neutrality strategies.

Rubberized Engineered/Strain-Hardening Geopolymer Composites (EGC/SHGC) with low fiber content to enhance strength and ductility efficiencies
Are environmental standards unsustainable? A discussion through the regulatory uncertainty of double materiality
abstract: Although environmental standards are intended to support ecological transition, the regulatory uncertainty surrounding their implementation may paradoxically reinforce the neoliberal logics of the very financial capitalism they claim to challenge. This article examines to what extent, and through which mechanisms, the uncertainty associated with double materiality transforms environmental reporting mechanisms into (counter-)performative tools. We analyse 812 CSR reports issued between 2016 and 2022 by the largest French listed firms (SBF120). Using a structured content analysis, we identify four reporting profiles and show a marked phase of instability between 2017 and 2019, during which time dominant firms in the field test and recombine registers of legitimation while concrete requirements remain unclear. Our results suggest that uncertainty is not merely an obstacle to compliance, but can become a strategic lever through which dominant actors reappropriate the (critical) language embedded in emerging sustainability standards, prioritise communication over action, and produce symbolic reports. In this sense, double materiality risks operating as a counter-performative standard, enabling reporting to be deployed as an instrument of legitimation that renews and reinforces neoliberal logics, potentially to the benefit of the most polluting firms. We thus expand the debate on the political role of quantification mechanisms and underscore the need to rethink the institutional and political conditions under which double materiality can become a genuine lever for environmental change rather than a language that fuels the capitalist machine.

title: Machine learning-based integration of plant growth regulators and overcompensation enhances microalgal protein production from wastewater
abstract: Photoautotrophic wastewater valorization represents a sustainable route for carbon-neutral nutrient upcycling into bioproducts. However, its practical implementation is often constrained by wastewater-induced growth inhibition. Besides, the distribution of metabolic flux across competing pathways may further restrict nutrient allocation towards target product. In this study, we propose a combined strategy integrating plant growth regulators (PGRs) with a nitrogen overcompensation strategy to enhance microalgal performance during potato starch wastewater treatment. Gibberellic acid (GA 3 ) and naphthaleneacetic acid (NAA) both alleviated wastewater inhibition and enhanced nutrient recovery in Chlorella pyrenoidosa , achieving up to 79.9% total nitrogen removal. Notably, supplementation with 10 mg L −1 GA 3 resulted in a 26.2% increase in biomass compared to controls. The random forest model identified candidate high-response concentrations of approximately 10.5 ± 1 mg L −1 for GA 3 and 10.2 ± 1 mg L −1 for NAA and suggested declining biomass responses at higher NAA concentrations, whereas GA 3 showed a broader model-predicted growth-promoting range. Under the nitrogen starvation–repletion condition, PGR-supplemented cultures achieved maximum biomass and protein concentrations of up to 1.58 g L −1 and 594.82 mg L −1 , respectively, together with over 90% removal of COD, total phosphorus, and ammonium. Transcriptomic profiling indicated that GA 3 induced significant upregulation of genes involved in photosynthetic apparatus function, ribosomal biogenesis, and transmembrane transport processes compared to NAA. This work establishes a strategy that integrates PGRs with nitrogen overcompensation to overcome wastewater-induced stress. The proposed approach provides a practical strategy for improving microalgal productivity and nutrient recovery from high-strength wastewater, advancing the development of carbon-neutral biorefinery systems.

title: Sludge-derived biochar-activated peroxymonosulfate as a waste-to-resource pretreatment for sustainable membrane fouling control: Adsorption-oxidation interplay and thermodynamic insights
Synergetic activation of slag by sodium sulphate and magnesium oxide: Strength, hydration, and microstructure
abstract: Sodium sulphate-activated slag has been recognised as an eco-friendly binder, although it faces issues of slow setting and strength development. In this study, magnesium oxide (MgO) is introduced as a co-activator alongside sodium sulphate (SST) to tackle these challenges. The results demonstrate that SST-MgO-activated slag (SSTMS) pastes exhibit favourable fresh and mechanical properties, with the fastest setting time of around 12 h and compressive strength of up to 55 MPa at 28 days. During hydration, MgO partially dissolves and primarily provides an alkaline environment to initiate slag dissolution. Afterwards, SST actively participates in the alkali-activation process by reacting with Ca 2+ and Al(OH) 4 - ions released from slag to form ettringite at early ages. This not only promotes self-alkalinisation for accelerating slag dissolution, but also enhances strength through the pore-filling and bridging effects of ettringite. However, the competition for aluminium sources between ettringite and C-A-S-H gel results in some retardation of the initial gel polymerisation. As the pore solution alkalinity exceeds a level aborting ettringite precipitation, the hydration of SSTMS paste gradually resembles that of MgO-incorporated alkali-activated slag (AAS) paste. The excess Al(OH) 4 - ions then tend to react with Mg 2+ ions, leading to the generation of hydrotalcite at a later stage. Overall, understanding the hydration mechanism for the SSTMS system provides a theoretical basis for optimising its mechanical performance. The SSTMS paste, as a weakly AAS system, offers favourable long-term compressive strength and improved operational safety compared to conventional AAS systems.

title: Taxonomy of circular economy practices aimed at preventing and reducing food waste in retail
abstract: Food loss and waste (FLW) in food retail poses critical challenges at the intersection of environmental sustainability and circular economy (CE) transitions. Despite growing scholarly attention, approaches to preventing and reducing FLW remain fragmented, with uneven adoption across institutional contexts. This study develops a systematic taxonomy of CE practices and applies it in a comparative analysis of Brazil and Spain, two countries with contrasting institutional contexts for circular economy implementation. A systematic literature review identified 233 practices, which were consolidated into a taxonomy of 33 CE practices organized into five hierarchical categories based on value preservation: food surplus prevention, avoidable waste prevention, reuse, recycling, and recovery. An Importance–Performance Analysis (IPA) assessed specialists' perceptions of the strategic importance and implementation of each practice. The findings indicate that, although CE practices were consistently perceived as highly important in both countries, their implementation differed substantially. Higher implementation levels in Spain were associated with a more consolidated regulatory environment, technological infrastructure, and coordinated governance, whereas wider implementation gaps in Brazil were linked to technological limitations and institutional fragmentation. This study contributes by systematizing retail-oriented CE practices into an integrated taxonomy, operationalizing the distinction between food surplus prevention and avoidable waste prevention, and showing how institutional conditions shape the adoption of CE practices. The findings provide practical guidance for retailers in prioritizing circular interventions and inform policymakers on institutional actions needed to accelerate food waste prevention and support progress toward Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 12.3.

Economic viability of thermal flexibilization of agricultural anaerobic digesters under intermittent Power-to-Gas plant operation
abstract: Power-to-Gas systems in biogas plants complement volatile renewable energy systems by converting surplus electricity into an energy carrier suitable for long-term storage. Heat integration and sales support the economic performance especially for catalytic high-temperature technologies, but thermal storage is required to assure supply to the anaerobic degradation process in intermittent operation. This can be achieved by thermally flexibilizing the digesters avoiding additional heat storage. This study evaluates such thermal flexibilization in Power-to-Gas applications by comparing its total costs with various conventional constant-temperature alternatives. Detailed simulations of typical agricultural biogas facilities and intermittent Power-to-Gas plant operation provided data for the techno-economic assessment. The results indicate that thermal flexibilization is viable between 4,000 and 8,000 annual full-load hours of Power-to-Gas system operation. The relative economic improvement over the closest constant-temperature alternative is at least 5.7% and 6.6% for manure- and energy-crop-based biogas plants, respectively, even at low methane prices. If the influence of temperature on biogas production is neglected, thermal flexibilization becomes non-viable at 8,000 annual full-load hours. While savings in internal methane consumption alone are sufficient for a competitive thermal flexibilization in energy-crop-based biogas plants, manure-intensive facilities may require additional measures in the absence of waste-heat revenues, with necessity depending on Power-to-Gas plant configuration. In future intermittently operated catalytic Power-to-Gas plants, conventional waste-heat integration can reduce synthetic methane production costs by 8% and 5% for manure- and energy-crop-based biogas plants, respectively. Thermal flexibilization can provide further cost reductions of 2% and 1%, respectively.

Life-cycle modeling of integrated agro-industrial and urban waste biorefineries in Brazil
abstract: The shift toward a low-carbon circular economy requires transforming conventional wastewater and solid waste treatment systems into integrated biorefineries capable of recovering value-added products. Participatory approaches address the complexity of this transition by leveraging stakeholder expertise to guide the selection of feedstocks, technologies, and products suitable for integration into biorefinery systems. This study proposes a novel conceptual biorefinery design developed through participatory workshops and the collaborative process mapping of 33 Brazilian research initiatives focused on agro-industrial and urban-source wastewater and waste streams. The analysis reveals a multi-product landscape dominated by low-value energy outputs, primarily generating biogas, methane, hydrogen, and syngas, followed by medium-value-added products, including volatile fatty acids, fertilizers, and biochar. Conversely, high-value bioproducts (polyhydroxyalkanoates, lactic acid, acetic acid, γ-valerolactone, mycelium-based materials) were identified less frequently. Based on this analysis, seven conceptual integrated biorefinery scenarios originating from local agro-industrial sectors and urban environmental services were proposed by combining: (i) feedstock-based integration, clustering by-products originating from the same production chain and functionally similar wastes from different sources within defined sectors; (ii) technological integration, emphasizing mass/energy integration and process intensification; and (iii) product integration, utilizing a value-oriented cascading logic and zero-waste principles. Finally, although no quantitative Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) was performed, the study presents preliminary LCA modeling for a multifunctional scenario, with decision-support criteria and thresholds for constructing integrated biorefinery scenarios, providing practical guidelines for future multi-product life cycle modeling of these conceptual configurations through a scenario-based application of a five-step LCA decision framework.
