Life cycle optimization of an off-grid waste-to-energy-renewable-methanol coupled system considering economic-environmental trade-offs
abstract: Integrating waste-to-energy (WtE) with variable renewable energy and power-to-methanol technologies offers a promising pathway for waste valorization and low carbon fuel production. This study develops a high-fidelity life-cycle optimization (LCO) framework for an off-grid WtE-renewable-methanol coupled system by integrating Aspen Plus simulation, mixed-integer linear programming, and 18 midpoint indicators from ReCiPe 2016 (H). The framework jointly optimizes capacity allocation and representative daily dispatch for four regions in China under four weighting scenarios. Results show that the LCO framework captures region-specific configuration pathways and weighting-driven structural shifts in energy supply and buffering layers. The optimized systems achieve life-cycle emissions of 0.539-0.801 kg CO2 eq./kg MeOH and levelized costs of 438.2-644.6 $/t MeOH. Regional resource endowments strongly shape system design, with Inner Mongolia being wind dominated and most cost competitive, Guangdong relying on photovoltaic generation with higher flexibility needs, Xinjiang requiring stronger thermal and carbon buffering despite abundant resources, and Jiangsu exhibiting greater capacity redundancy under moderate resource conditions. Increasing environmental weightings reduces reliance on photovoltaic generation and electrochemical storage while favoring wind power, WtE, and thermal or material storage. Notably, the climate-priority scenario reduces climate impacts but aggravates toxicity, resource depletion, and air pollution, revealing environmental burden shifting, whereas the environment-priority scenario delivers the most balanced performance. These results highlight LCO as a robust decision-support tool for regional green methanol system planning.

title: Spatially explicit assessment of seawater intrusion in urbanized coastal aquifers using an integrated geophysical-hydrochemical approach
Smart carbon capture: Leveraging LSTM networks for hourly CO2 flow prediction in an industrial stack of a CO2 recovery plant
Environmental labeling in food services: Which strategy is the most effective?
abstract: Food prepared outside the home accounts for a significant portion of food-related greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. However, consumers have little information about the GHG emissions associated with their food choices. Environmental labels and information schemes (ELIS) could be a lever for steering these choices toward environmentally sustainable options. This experimental study examines the effectiveness of six types of ELIS formats (1 informative, 1 contextual, 2 interpretive, and 2 mixed) featured on restaurant menu cards. A hypothetical choice task experiment was designed to assess consumers' response to two successive choice tasks: without information and with general information (control) or with one of the 6 ELIS signaling the environmental sustainability of either separate dish options or a set table d'hôte. 2808 Canadian respondents were randomly assigned to one of the 14 experimental groups (2 contexts × 7 information conditions). All ELIS formats significantly increased the likelihood of choosing a meal with a lower environmental impact, although individual-level choice changes remained only partially explained. Mixed formats, combining visual elements and numerical data, were the most effective, in terms of shifting choices toward meals with a lower environmental impact and in terms of reduction in GHG emissions. By comparing six ELIS formats within a single experimental framework, this study provides novel empirical evidence on the relative effectiveness of environmental labeling strategies in food service settings. These results suggest that mixed formats could be integrated as tools in public policy or food service differentiation strategies to promote more environmentally sustainable eating. However, future research in real-world conditions is needed to confirm these effects.

title: Integration of geothermal energy in RO desalination plant: Flexible design meeting variable water demand with cleaning and maintenance schedule
abstract: Desalination technologies are being used to meet the world's growing demand for freshwater but are extremely energy intensive whether it is a thermal or a membrane based process. As global fossil fuel-based energy supplies have been going through a turmoil in recent years due to war in several parts of the world, consideration of alternative and renewable energy sources for desalination is extremely important. In this work, potential for low-enthalpy geothermal resources to provide a part of the required energy in a 3-stage Reverse Osmosis (RO) desalination plant to supply freshwater to a population of 40,000 people in the city of El Masdar in UAE is investigated. As the demand for freshwater changes throughout the day and throughout the year, the plant is flexibly designed with storage tanks and also using disconnected pressure vessels (PVs) to be cleaned and serviced (schedule maintenance) throughout the year without the need for shutting down the plant at any time. To prevent the use of enormous storage tanks, RO plant operates to produce minimum excess water at the end of every month allowing cleaning of storage tanks at least once in each month. ASPEN HYSYS software is used to design the Organic Rankine Cycle (ORC) plant, which produces 1 MW of electricity using the geothermal field in El-Masdar city with 10% efficiency, which is then used to supply part of the RO plant's electrical demand. The investigation indicates that integrating low-enthalpy geothermal energy in RO plant can decrease dependence on fossil fuels by offsetting the external power required to operate the RO system. The findings showed that geothermal energy can provide considerable offsets of fossil fuel, reaching 28.87% of the required external energy during peak water-demand months and 55% during low water-demand months.

title: Farmers' income increase and environmental win-win: How China's digital industry cluster policies balance economic development with ecological efficiency
Zero-residue valorization of chrysotile asbestos tailings via oxygen-free NaOH roasting: Stepwise recovery of SiO2 and MgO with chromium stabilization
Optimization of filter bag structure for metal dust removal system based on multi-physical field simulation of high-temperature flue gas
Beyond compliance: How sustainability assurance achieves value creation under resource scarcity
Multidimensional energy poverty assessment and behavioral scenarios: An interpretable analytics approach
abstract: Energy poverty is a multidimensional socioeconomic and sustainability challenge that extends beyond affordability to include inadequate thermal comfort, limited access to energy services, and adverse health and well-being effects. This study examines how multidimensional energy-poverty assessment can be integrated with interpretable analytics to identify household vulnerability drivers and explore the model-based implications of changes in selected behavioral practices. The framework is applied to pilot survey data from households in Portugal and Denmark. An adapted multidimensional energy poverty index (MEPI) is constructed using four dimensions: heating and cooling comfort, financial strain, access to energy-efficient appliances, and health and well-being. The resulting MEPI-based classification is then linked to socioeconomic, behavioral, dwelling-related, and policy-related predictors through recursive feature elimination with cross-validation, logistic regression, and the Shapley additive explanations. Robustness is examined through regularized-model comparisons, repeated cross-validation, calibration assessment, and country-held-out validation. Energy-saving beliefs, power-saving practices, and selected resource-efficient behaviors are associated with lower predicted energy-poverty vulnerability, whereas larger household size and reported policy or subsidy support are associated with higher predicted risk. The latter may reflect support being targeted towards households already experiencing vulnerability. Exploratory scenarios indicate that hypothetical increases in several negatively associated behavioral practices correspond to lower model-predicted energy-poverty prevalence, although the uncertainty intervals are wide and the results noncausal. The study contributes an integrated workflow for multidimensional identification, transparent driver analysis, and exploratory behavioral scenario assessment. Despite the limited pilot sample, the framework supports the development of policy hypotheses for testing in larger and more representative datasets.

Life cycle analysis on United States titanium dioxide and titanium metal products based on global titanium supply chain datasets
abstract: Complexity of global supply chain of titanium makes accurate analysis on the life cycle of titanium products challenging. To address this need, life cycle inventory datasets for titanium dioxide and titanium metal powder are collected using trade databases published by the United States International Trade Commission and the World Bank. Then, leveraging those global supply chain datasets of raw and intermediate titanium feedstocks for the final titanium products, the greenhouse gas emissions for titanium metal powder and titanium dioxide produced in the United States are assessed using the R&D Greenhouse gases, Regulated Emissions, and Energy use in Technologies (R&D GREET) database. The potential changes in greenhouse gas emissions intensity of titanium dioxide and metal powder produced in the United States are estimated for multiple scenarios, assuming changes in the domestic production share of titanium feedstocks and types of energy and material resources used for final titanium products. The results show that increasing domestic production of titanium sponge metal or titanium slag can achieve about 2-7% (current) and 5-15% (2035 projection) reduction in the greenhouse gas emissions intensity of titanium metal powder. However, more emissions reduction (about 19% for titanium metal powder and about 30% for titanium dioxide) is expected by replacing fossil fuel energy sources (e.g., coal) with lower emitting sources (such as nuclear or renewable electricity) for chlorination or by replacing the average grid electricity with nuclear or renewable energy to produce key material inputs (e.g., sodium hydroxide) required for the chlorination process.

title: Multi-objective optimization for sizing of residential hybrid renewable systems with battery storage: Balancing economic, environmental, and energy autonomy perspectives

How can higher education become climate-proof?
abstract: Higher education institutions (HEIs) are increasingly exposed to climate-related risks, including extreme weather events, infrastructure disruptions, and related social and economic impacts. At the same time, they are expected to play a leading role in advancing sustainability and decarbonisation efforts. In this context, this paper aims to assess how HEIs are preparing to become climate-proof and to identify the institutional strategies, barriers, and priorities that shape the transition towards climate-resilient and sustainable higher education. Adopting a mixed-methods approach, the research combines comparative case studies of universities implementing climate adaptation and mitigation measures with a global online survey of 404 respondents from 83 countries, making it one of the largest studies on the topic undertaken to date. The case studies show three main typologies of institutional response, i.e., comprehensive integration, operational emphasis, and social–educational engagement, illustrating varying levels of maturity and coordination. The survey findings reveal that although more than half of assessed institutions have initiated inventories or decarbonisation strategies, implementation remains fragmented. Operational measures concentrate on energy systems and waste management, while systemic integration across curricula, governance, and community engagement is less common. Key barriers include limited financial capacity, fragmented institutional priorities, and insufficient stakeholder participation. The study shows that climate-proofing higher education requires transformative and cross-sectoral governance, aligning decarbonisation, education, governance and equity objectives.

title: Sustainable production of bio-methanol via integrated CO2-Assisted catalytic pyrolysis process: A comprehensive energy, economic, and environmental analysis
Towards a holistic sustainability assessment of organic and conventional wine production systems in Germany via AHP-MCDA
abstract: Sustainable viticulture requires balancing competing economic, environmental, and social objectives, yet comprehensive tools for holistically evaluating alternative management strategies remain limited. This study addresses this gap by developing a multi-dimensional evaluation framework based on Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis using the Analytic Hierarchy Process (MCDA-AHP) to aggregate heterogeneous sustainability indicators into a unified evaluation structure. The framework is tested in a case study from the Rheingau Valley, comparing organic and conventional wine production systems across six sustainability indicators and multiple stakeholder groups. Indicators were selected based on their ability to represent key sustainability aspects while remaining feasible for practical implementation in operational decision-making. AHP results showed that, despite variations in individual preference intensities, stakeholder groups displayed distinct weighting patterns reflecting differences in their sustainability priorities. Institutional stakeholders and academic researchers assigned high importance to economic performance and producers and academic researchers also place high importance on human health risks. Environmental criteria, particularly carbon footprint, received comparatively lower weights across most groups. Across all stakeholder groups, organic production is consistently preferred over conventional production but the overall difference between scenarios is small . This stable ranking reflects the slightly better performance of the organic system in five of six indicators and the limited differences between the assessed systems. The case study serves to demonstrate the operational feasibility of the MCDA-AHP framework and the selected indictors and does not aim to provide a generalized comparison of organic and conventional viticulture. Overall, the findings underscore the importance of incorporating diverse stakeholder inputs when developing tools for holistic sustainability assessments.

title: Car self-repair and online access to spare parts: Evidence from French motorized households
abstract: Repair plays a central role in circular economy strategies, yet most studies of self-repair focus on low- or medium-involvement products, such as clothing, household appliances, or consumer electronics. This article examines car self-repair, a high-involvement product context in which repair decisions are shaped by cost, technical complexity, safety concerns, and dependence on automobility. It analyses the relationship between car self-repair and online access to spare parts using a 2019 survey of 5004 French motorized households. A bivariate probit model is used to jointly estimate two binary decisions: purchasing automotive spare parts online and engaging in self-repair, either directly or through one's close social circle. The results show that the two practices are statistically interdependent. Prior online shopping experience, vehicle mileage, the number of vehicles owned, and delayed maintenance are positively associated with both behaviours. Lower-income households are more likely to engage in self-repair, while online spare-parts purchasing is more strongly associated with prior e-commerce experience and middle-aged groups. The findings suggest that online access to spare parts should be understood as a repair-support infrastructure rather than as a direct causal trigger of self-repair. The article contributes to circular economy research by showing that, for high-involvement products, self-repair may reflect not only environmental or expressive motivations but also economic necessity, asset preservation, and unequal access to professional repair services. It highlights the limits of self-repair in digitalized vehicles and points to the need for hybrid repair services that combine online information and spare-part sourcing with professional diagnosis, assistance, and safety expertise.

title: TINeXt-G: A dual encoding ConvNeXt-powered time-to-image representation framework for electricity load forecasting
Potential of agrivoltaics in Mexico: Opportunities and challenges for energy and agricultural sustainability
authors: Naomi Akane Saguchi Pérez de Alva
abstract: Agrivoltaics, defined as the co-location of agricultural production and photovoltaic electricity generation on the same land, has emerged as a promising strategy for expanding renewable energy while maintaining productive agricultural use. This study presents a national-scale screening of the theoretical upper-bound agrivoltaic electricity potential in Mexico and identifies the main opportunities and challenges for future implementation. The assessment combines cultivated area, state-level average solar irradiation, photovoltaic efficiency, and literature-derived agrivoltaic density scenarios for crops cultivated in Mexico with documented agrivoltaic relevance. Results show that maize presents the highest theoretical electricity estimate at the national level (9219.89 TWh yr −1 ), followed by wheat (809.12 TWh yr −1 ) and green chili (435.07 TWh yr −1 ), mainly due to their cultivated area and adopted density assumptions. On a per-hectare basis, strawberry, raspberry, green chili, and tomato show the highest estimates, ranging from 2.04 to 2.73 GWh yr −1 ha −1 under the reference-density scenario. Crop classification by agrivoltaic density and rotation compatibility indicates that crop management constraints should be considered when moving from national estimates to site-specific planning. Under an unconstrained upper-bound scenario, allocating an equivalent area corresponding to 1% of the selected agricultural land would correspond to 14.79% of national electricity consumption and an avoided emission estimate of 22.38 million tons of CO 2 per year. The results provide a screening-level reference for prioritizing regions, crops, and research pathways, while technical, economic, spatial, and social challenges require site-specific assessment before implementation. • Theoretical agrivoltaic electricity potential is estimated for Mexico. • Solar resource, crop area, PV efficiency, and agrivoltaic density are integrated. • Sinaloa, Chiapas, and Jalisco show the highest state-level estimates. • Maize, wheat, and green chili show the highest national estimates. • Strawberry, raspberry, green chili, and tomato lead per-hectare estimates.

title: Drivers of online pre-owned product purchases across different product categories
abstract: This study investigates consumers’ motives and barriers for purchasing pre-owned products in online re-commerce across three major product categories: books, consumer electronics, and apparel. Building on the Theory of Planned Behaviour and extending the multidimensional motivation scale proposed by Guiot and Roux (2010) to the online context, this research develops and tests a structural equation model that integrates green value, hedonic and economic motivations, perceived risk, and TPB constructs to explain attitudes and purchase intentions. The PLS-multigroup analysis demonstrates substantial explanatory power for both attitude and purchase intention and indicates that the relevance of drivers is markedly category-specific. Green value consistently enhances attitudes but only predicts purchase intentions in the socially visible apparel category, indicating a category-contingent intention-behaviour gap. In contrast, economic and hedonic motivations emerge as strong and stable predictors of both attitudes and intentions across all categories, suggesting re-commerce functions as a hybrid consumption phenomenon in which sustainability is closely intertwined with price and experiential benefits. The findings advance theory on second-hand consumption and imply that retailers should highlight economic and hedonic benefits across all categories, stress green aspects especially for apparel, and reduce perceived risk through guarantees and transparent product information.

title: Spillover effects of green infrastructure on the supply–demand utility of flood regulation services: A telecoupling perspective
Toward trustworthy AI-based emission assessment for cleaner residential biomass heating: The role of validation strategy
abstract: Small-scale residential biomass combustion remains a significant source of gaseous pollutants, particularly under transient and manually operated conditions, contributing to local air quality degradation despite the renewable nature of biomass fuels. Reliable prediction of emission dynamics is therefore essential for supporting cleaner and more environmentally responsible residential heating practices. This study investigates machine learning-based prediction of CO, CO 2 , NO x , and organic gaseous compound (OGC) emissions from controlled combustion experiments using beech wood logs and densified briquettes. Time-resolved operational parameters and emission concentrations were analyzed using neural (MLP) and boosting-based (LightGBM, XGBoost) regression models. A central objective was to assess the influence of validation strategy on model robustness in transient combustion datasets. Two approaches were compared: stratified splitting, preserving statistical balance across fuels and combustion phases, and chronological-by-fuel splitting, preserving temporal order of combustion cycles. While stratified validation yielded very high predictive accuracy for all pollutants (R 2 up to .9961 for CO 2 ), chronological validation revealed substantial performance degradation for incomplete combustion indicators, particularly OGC and, to a lesser extent, CO. In contrast, CO 2 and NO x retained comparatively stable predictability across validation schemes. Cross-validation error dispersion and phase-resolved evaluation showed that balanced data splits may overestimate model generalization by favoring interpolation within similar combustion regimes. Chronological validation exposed sensitivity to temporal distribution shifts and combustion regime transitions, particularly for regime-sensitive pollutants. SHAP-based interpretability analysis confirmed that oxygen concentration and flue gas temperature were the dominant predictors across pollutants, although feature contributions were more heterogeneous for regime-sensitive emissions. The results demonstrate that validation strategy strongly influences the perceived predictive performance and apparent generalization capability of data-driven models in biomass combustion studies. The findings highlight the importance of validation-aware model assessment and support the development of more trustworthy AI tools for emission monitoring and cleaner operation of residential biomass heating systems.

title: Environmental life cycle assessment of hybrid steel construction featuring metal additive manufacturing
abstract: Hybrid manufacturing, featuring the addition of steel material onto hot-rolled structural steel members through direct energy deposition arc (DED-arc) – a type of metal additive manufacturing (AM) – has recently been demonstrated as a viable means to produce hybrid steel members with considerably enhanced structural performance and material efficiency. The enhanced performance stems from the optimised deposition location and/or the high strength of the DED-arc additions. This underscores its potential for reducing both the material consumption and the environmental impacts of steel construction, thereby improving overall sustainability. In the present study, the environmental impacts associated with the production of hybrid DED-arc-hot-rolled steel I-section beams are investigated through a cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment (LCA), with beams making up approximately 70% of the mass of typical building structures. A unit-mass analysis was first conducted whereby unit mass (i.e., 1 kg) productions of hot-rolled and DED-arc steels were examined. The results of this unit-mass analysis were then used to evaluate the environmental impacts of a series of hybrid beam specimens investigated in previous experimental studies. Finally, a comprehensive parametric study, covering a wide range of I-section profiles and steel beam design scenarios, is presented. The findings demonstrate that the hybrid DED-arc-hot-rolling manufacturing strategy is capable of reducing the overall embodied carbon associated with steel beams by, on average, 11% and 14% for normal and high strength steel additions to S355 steel profiles, and up to approximately 40%, for some typical loading conditions. For S275 steel profiles, which are likely to feature prominently in retrofitting and re-use scenarios, the savings in embodied carbon are even greater, up to 45%.

title: How does digital industry agglomeration affect the environmental efficiency of power systems in China
Renewable energy integration and grid stability: Heterogeneous effects of virtual power plants across Chinese provinces
Life cycle assessment and improvement of industrial nanocellulose production via mild peracetic acid treatment
abstract: This study presents a prospective life cycle assessment of cellulose nanofibre production via a mild peracetic acid treatment route at industrial scale, aiming to identify environmental hotspots and improvement opportunities. An existing scale-up framework, integrated with IDEF0 process modelling, is applied to quantify cradle-to-gate environmental impacts per 1 kg of cellulose nanofibre, extrapolated from laboratory-scale data. Peracetic acid treatment emerges as the dominant contributor across all impact categories in the baseline: global warming potential (17.52 kg CO 2 eq.), acidification (0.0451 kg SO 2 eq.), freshwater eutrophication (6.48 × 10 −3 kg P eq.), marine eutrophication (1.29 × 10 −3 kg P eq.), and cumulative energy demand (504.04 MJ). Three improvement scenarios are evaluated, with continuous peracetic acid addition combined with chemical recovery achieving the greatest reductions — 74.9% in global warming potential, 72.0% in acidification, 73.8% in freshwater eutrophication, 52.5% in marine eutrophication, and 76.5% in energy demand. Sensitivity analysis under ±20% input variation confirms robustness of these findings. Substitution of a bio-based acetic acid-derived peracetic acid pathway further underscores the influence of upstream inventory assumptions on overall environmental performance. These findings offer process specific guidance for sustainable industrial scale-up of nanocellulose production via the peracetic acid route.

title: Reconsidering Limits to Growth: Integrating energy transition and circular economy in an extended World3 framework
abstract: The 1972 study The Limits to Growth highlighted the risk of systemic overshoot and steep decline due to resource constraints, but was criticized for underestimating technological adaptation. This paper revisits that thesis by extending the World3 model to incorporate two major contemporary transformation strategies: the energy transition (ET) towards renewable energy sources and the circular economy (CE). It asks to what extent combined CE and ET strategies alter overshoot-and-collapse dynamics and whether they can prevent, rather than merely delay, systemic decline. To enable this analysis, the aggregated stock of non-renewable resources is disaggregated into distinct energy and material flow components. The CE module represents material life cycles, including durability constraints and a maximum recyclability rate of 90%. The ET module simulates renewable energy expansion under economic, environmental, and resource feedback constraints. Under the World3 model structure and the selected scenario assumptions, the results indicate that CE and ET individually delay systemic decline, but do not prevent it within the explored parameter space. Instead, resource pressures shift between the energy and material domains. The ET pathway alleviates the depletion of fossil energy, but accelerates the material demand for renewable infrastructure. In contrast, CE reduces primary material extraction but increases energy requirements. The combined CE & ET scenario exhibits the highest resilience, extending population stability and industrial output relative to the individual strategies. However, the system’s fundamental overshoot-and-decline dynamics persist. More broadly, the simulations should be understood as exploratory scenario experiments rather than predictive forecasts. These findings reaffirm the core message of the original study under the assumptions explored here: technologies and efficiency-oriented strategies alone are insufficient when continued exponential growth on a finite planet outweighs gains in resource productivity. This study contributes to the cleaner production literature by quantifying rebound effects, burden shifting, resource-efficiency limits, and energy–material trade-offs within an integrated system dynamics framework.

title: Do green innovation and advertising intensity enhance financial performance? Firm-level evidence from the global chemical sector
Detailed breakdown of companies carbon footprints per origin of emissions using distributed input output analysis
Decomposing ship carbon intensity under fuel-intensity regulation: Separating fuel decarbonization from operational energy efficiency
abstract: International shipping requires performance indicators that distinguish reductions in operational energy demand from reductions in the life-cycle greenhouse gas (GHG) intensity of marine fuels. The Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) is emission-based but is often interpreted as a proxy for operational energy efficiency, an interpretation that becomes less reliable as alternative fuels, onshore power supply, and well-to-wake accounting gain importance. This study develops an integrated Data Collection System (DCS)–Greenhouse Gas Fuel Intensity (GFI) framework for comparing emission-based and energy-based ship performance indicators. An emission-based CII-type indicator is decomposed into transport energy intensity (TEI), defined as energy use per unit of transport work, and the energy-weighted average GHG intensity of the fuel mix. Annual operational data from five structured ship-operation cases are analysed. In controlled Bio30 and methanol comparisons, transport work, total energy use, and operating profile are held constant, fixing TEI while varying only fuel GHG intensity. Bio30 and methanol reduce the emission-based indicator by 12.8% and 20.4%, respectively, whereas the energy-based indicator remains unchanged. Thus, an apparent improvement in an emission-based carbon-intensity metric may reflect fuel decarbonization rather than lower energy use per unit of transport work. The findings support separate but complementary assessment of fuel decarbonization and operational energy efficiency. A dual structure in which the GFI addresses life-cycle fuel GHG intensity and an energy-based operational indicator monitors TEI could provide clearer regulatory signals for maritime decarbonization and energy productivity.

Economic and environmental right-sizing of battery-electric haulage fleets in open-pit mines
abstract: This paper presents a flow-based optimisation framework for right-sizing battery-electric vehicle (BEV) haulage fleets in open-pit mines and assessing their economic and environmental performance against a diesel baseline. Fleet design is formulated as a mixed-integer linear program (MILP) over an extended state network that captures truck load state, battery state of charge, production targets, charging-station capacity, and endogenous traffic congestion through delay curves calibrated via Bayesian inference. For each candidate truck class and battery capacity, the framework optimises fleet size and flows, then evaluates operational electricity-related CO 2 e emissions, battery embodied emissions, active-fleet battery capacity, and installed charging capacity within a stated environmental boundary. Experiments on three mine-scale maps show that omitting charging or congestion underestimates fleet cost and that cost-minimising designs need not be the lowest-emission alternatives in the evaluated design grid. Under the model-consistent diesel baseline and base grid-emission factor of 0.25 kgCO 2 e/kWh, the class-matched BEV designs reduce operational CO 2 e by 61.7%–63.5% (57.4%–62.4% including battery embodied emissions). The operational break-even grid intensity is 0.653–0.685 kgCO 2 e/kWh. Electrification also avoids the associated local NO x , particulate-matter, and black-carbon emissions. Under the base cost coefficients, these reductions come at a small, infrastructure-conditional cost premium of about −1% to ＋7.4% relative to the diesel cost minima. This range covers class-matching and charging-infrastructure-cost scenarios, and the BEV fleets require 7.5%–18.2% more active trucks. All results derive from synthetic mine layouts, a simplified traction-energy model, and a model-consistent rather than field-calibrated diesel baseline. The environmental accounting is a bounded CO 2 e evaluation rather than a full life-cycle assessment. These findings highlight the need to consider truck class, battery capacity, charging infrastructure, congestion, and electricity carbon intensity together when designing cleaner battery-electric haul fleets.

abstract: Rural Alaskan communities face extreme energy costs and energy insecurity due to logistical isolation and dependence on imported diesel fuel. This study evaluates long term decarbonization pathways for the Shungnak microgrid using a dual planning and operational framework. Tools for Energy Model Optimization and Analysis (Temoa) optimizes capacity expansion from 2025 to 2045, while a rolling horizon Unit Commitment Model (UCM) screens portfolios for hourly dispatch feasibility, generator commitment, ramping, and battery state of charge continuity. The UCM is an operational screening model rather than a complete grid stability assessment and does not represent dynamic frequency response, voltage behavior, or inertia. The constrained Business-As-Usual Reference (BAU) pathway remains diesel dependent, producing 853.9 tons of CO 2 in 2045 at a cumulative discounted system cost of 24.66 million USD. Allowing wind and hydropower shifts the least cost pathway toward a diversified renewable and storage portfolio, with all five alternative core scenarios reaching zero modeled operational emissions by 2040 under baseline resource assumptions. Sensitivity tests show that discounted cost is most responsive to wind capacity factor, ranging from 12.4% below to 17.0% above Unrestrained Reference (BAU-UR), followed by hydropower availability, ranging from 9.8% below to 10.8% above. A ± 30 % variation in battery capital cost changes system cost by 2.3% below to 2.0% above. Capital support tests locate cost parity between 6% and 7%, with an interpolated threshold of 6.34%. Findings are specific to Shungnak, while the open source framework may be adapted to other isolated systems after local calibration.

Spectroscopic and machine learning strategies for automated classification and quantification of textile blends: Enabling material recovery and circular economy in the textile sector
abstract: Accurate identification and classification of textile materials are vital for improving recycling efficiency, ensuring quality control, and advancing circular economy practices in the textile industry. Traditional sorting technologies struggle to differentiate between complex textile blends, particularly when compositions contain low-percentage additives or chemically similar fibers. This study investigates the integration of Near-Infrared Spectroscopy (NIRS) with machine learning techniques to classify and quantify both pure and blended textile fibers across diverse composition ratios. The dataset encompasses pure fibers including Cotton, Polyester, Polyamide, Modal, Lyocell, Viscose, Wool, Silk, Linen, Polypropylene, Acrylic, and Elastane alongside binary blends (e.g., Cotton–Elastane, Cotton–Modal, Cotton–Polyester, Polyester–Elastane, and Polyamide–Elastane). Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random Forests (RF), and k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) were evaluated for classification, while SVR, RF Regression, and k-NN Regression were applied to predict blend ratios, supported by Principal Component Analysis (PCA) for spectral feature exploration. Comparative evaluations revealed complementary model strengths rather than a single dominant architecture: while SVM achieved superior performance in primary fiber classification tasks (reaching up to 97% accuracy under external validation and 96% under Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation), ensemble-based RF and distance-driven k-NN exhibited marked advantages in handling non-linear blend dynamics, imbalanced minority classes, and challenging low-concentration additives (2–10% elastane). For quantitative composition prediction, Random Forest Regression achieved exceptional precision with R 2 values exceeding 0.99 (e.g., for Polyester–Elastane blends), confirming its efficacy for compositional quantification. These findings demonstrate that integrating NIRS with tailored machine learning architectures enables both reliable automated identification and precise quantitative sorting, offering a robust framework for high-throughput sensor-based sorting systems essential for circular material recovery.

title: Road to sustainable development: How does green finance affect cultivated land green and low-carbon use efficiency?
The bright prospect of China's photovoltaic under the double carbon goal: A potential assessment based on the life cycle of photovoltaic power plants
Corporate sustainability strategies for decarbonization in the automotive supply chain: Comparative analysis of emissions hotspots, decarbonization targets and measures of global automotive suppliers
abstract: The automotive value chain is facing increasing pressure to decarbonize due to its substantial contribution to greenhouse gas emissions in the transportation sector. However, extant research, with its predominant focus on decarbonizing the original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) in the automotive industry, generates only limited insights into the decarbonization potential and activities along the automotive supply chain upstream of the OEMs. Addressing the gap, this is the first study to identify emission hotspots and analyze decarbonization targets and mitigation measures across 44 international automotive suppliers using a comparative approach differentiated by region and firm revenue. Based on a systematic assessment of publicly available carbon accounting data and sustainability reports, the results revealed substantial heterogeneity in carbon accounting maturity, decarbonization target setting, and disclosed mitigation measures. Regional patterns are observed to be non-uniform across dimensions, with higher-revenue suppliers tending to disclose more comprehensive carbon accounting and management practices. Building on these findings, the study proposed the “Supplier Decarbonization Archetype Typology” as a framework for understanding the decarbonization strategies and actions of automotive suppliers. The typology distinguished between Disclosure Maturity and Action Intensity and enabled the synthesis of the investigated automotive suppliers into four archetypal supplier types. Study findings underscored the importance of clearer regulatory frameworks, strengthened OEM–supplier collaboration, and improved carbon accounting standards to enable effective, supply-chain-embedded decarbonization. The study contributed conceptually and practically to research and practice on automotive supply-chain decarbonization and provided actionable insights for policymakers, OEMs, and automotive suppliers seeking to accelerate sustainability transitions.

title: An integrated manufacturing-process optimization method for tubular heat exchangers considering carbon emissions
Is natural always greener? Evaluating the environmental performance of lab-scale biopolymer adsorbents
abstract: Bio-based materials are widely assumed to provide sustainable alternatives to conventional synthetic technologies. However, whether this assumption holds when evaluated across production and processing pathways remains largely untested. Here, we present a systematic assessment of biopolymer-based adsorbents for water treatment by integrating synthesis analysis with partial life-cycle assessment and a performance-normalized environmental index (EPI). We analyze 49 representative biopolymer systems across six material classes and benchmark them against synthetic counterparts. The functional unit of each adsorbent was determined by their adsorption capacity alongside the number of operating cycles. Our results reveal a fundamental eco-efficiency trade-off: the environmental advantages of biopolymers are frequently offset by energy-intensive processing and the use of auxiliary chemicals, leading to environmental impacts comparable to or exceeding those of synthetic materials. Moreover, their adsorption performance does not consistently surpass conventional alternatives, resulting in limited environmental efficiency when normalized to function across multiple uses. Consequently, both lab-scale synthetic adsorbents (median EPI of 0.00535) and mature commercial benchmarks (EPI ranging from 0.00029 to 0.00084) achieved superior (lower) EPI scores compared to the median efficiencies of widely researched lab-scale biopolymers like cellulose and starch (0.023 and 0.0185 respectively). These findings challenge the prevailing assumption that material origin determines sustainability and demonstrate that process-level considerations could dominate environmental outcomes. We show that material-centric choice is not enough and therefore system-level evaluation is vital. We suggest that research transitioning from laboratory to industrial scale should prioritize environmental efficiency over feedstock origin, for sustainable technologies generally and water treatment applications specifically.

title: A conceptual framework for uncertainty-informed system boundary expansion in life cycle assessment
Impact of pre-decarbonization on biogas-to-hydrogen performance: A combined catalysis and simulation approach for economic analysis
Fueling the future of ethanol: An IETB-based multi-criteria analysis in leading producer countries and regions
Water footprint and sustainability assessment of sustainable aviation fuel production from castor oil, soybean, switchgrass, and corn stover in the Tongliao region
Mapping and balancing tensions, conflicts and trade-offs in the European extractive sector in its sustainability transition: Insights from a multi-actor Delphi study
abstract: The European extractive sector operates within a dense socio-technical and regulatory environment where rising mineral demand, sustainability expectations and geopolitical pressures intersect. These dynamics generate persistent tensions, conflicts and trade-offs that limit the sector's contribution to a climate-neutral and strategically resilient European economy. Previous research has addressed individual challenges, but integrative assessments across economic, environmental, social and governance dimensions remain limited. This study addresses this gap by applying a Delphi method with a heterogeneous panel of European experts to identify, prioritise and contextualise these frictions through the SUMEX (Sustainable Management in Extractive Industries) sustainability framework. Results indicate a clear hierarchy of frictions. Social legitimacy appears to be the most influential source of disputes, followed by governance and permitting aspects, economic feasibility constraints, land-use conflicts and local environmental impacts. The panel identified mutually reinforcing frictions, such as those between social legitimacy concerns and permitting complexity, that were perceived as influencing the feasibility of the sector's sustainability transformation. The study concludes that technological optimisation and incremental policy adjustments alone are insufficient for this transformation. The findings suggest that addressing these frictions requires long-term, systemic and governance-centred strategies that strengthen social legitimacy, enhance institutional capacity, support credible and co-produced evidence, and embed benefit-sharing more systematically in project development.

Biochar cathodes for power-to-protein: a circular approach for anaerobic digestion side-product valorisation
abstract: Power-to-Protein is considered an innovative approach to store renewable energy by producing Single-Cell Protein as an alternative protein source to feed the growing global population, while lowering production impacts and recovering industrial side-streams such as CO 2 and NH 3 . Nevertheless, a win-win approach should balance protein yield with cost reduction. Three different biochar-functionalized cathodes were tested in Microbial Electrosynthesis Cells at a cathode potential of −1.2 V vs. Ag/AgCl for the recovery of CO 2 and NH 3 from anaerobic digestion. One biochar was activated with CO 2 , while the other two underwent imidazole impregnation and subsequent pyrolysis. The biochar application on the cathode led to improved performance compared to bare carbon cloth control in terms of protein productivity, protein content on dry matter, and nitrogen capture efficiency. However, the biochar post-treatments (i.e., nitrogen doping with imidazole and second-round pyrolysis) did not provide any additional benefit with respect to the key performance indicators considered. In particular, the untreated biochar achieved 47% and 59% higher protein space-time yield compared to the two post-treated biochars. Regarding relative protein content and amino acid profile, no significant differences were observed among the biochar-functionalized cathodes, all of which exhibited a satisfactory proportion of essential amino acids (39 - 41% of total amino acids). The protein-rich biomass obtained in this study shows protein contents and essential amino acid proportions comparable to those reported for soybean, highlighting the potential of Power-to-Protein as a sustainable biotechnological route for future feed and food applications supporting energy transition and applying circular economy approach.

title: Empowering networks: Social capital as informal insurance against energy poverty
abstract: Research on energy poverty has mainly focused on socioeconomic and structural determinants, while the role of social capital has received much less attention. This is particularly relevant for highly disadvantaged households, for whom informal support networks may represent an important source of protection when formal policy support is limited. We draw on the Journeys Home survey, a unique longitudinal dataset of Australians experiencing severe economic disadvantage, to examine whether social capital affects the dynamics of energy poverty. To account for state dependence, we estimate dynamic models based on Wooldridge's conditional likelihood approach for binary outcomes and complementary two-step GMM specifications. Considering two complementary measures of individual social capital, we find that a one-standard-deviation increase in perceived informal support reduces the probability of experiencing energy poverty by 4.8 percentage points, while an equivalent increase in social connectedness is associated with a 2.6 percentage-point reduction. These findings suggest that social capital can complement conventional policy measures in reducing energy poverty among vulnerable households.

title: Life-cycle and carbon-cost trade-offs in configuration and operation choices of a solid oxide fuel cell integrated hybrid desiccant cooling trigeneration system
Environmental and carbon footprint performance of biochar-augmented concrete: A cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment
abstract: This study conducts a cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment (LCA) of biochar-augmented concrete to evaluate its environmental performance and carbon mitigation potential. However, existing LCAs of biochar-containing concert remain limited and vary considerably in system boundaries, functional units, regional inventory data, impact-assessment methods, and treatment of biogenic carbon. No comprehensive study has evaluated biochar-and SCM-containing concrete under Australian conditions sing the ALCAS Best practice method together with carbon-stability, allocation, electricity, and transport sensitivity analysis. To address this gap, the study uses SimaPro with ecoinvent v3.11 and AusLCI datasets, the evaluation adheres to ISO 14040/44 standards and the ALCAS Best Practice v2.06, as well as the IPCC 2021 GWP100 and Eco-indicator 99 (H) methods. Three concrete series incorporating wood-derived biochar (3% and 5%) and supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs), including fly ash and ground granulated blast-furnace slag (GGBS) were modelled. Biochar exhibited net-negative global warming potential (−1.91 kg CO 2 -eq/kg), highlighting its strong carbon-sink capacity. Results showed consistent reductions in environmental impacts compared with conventional concrete: global warming potential (GWP) decreased by 6-12% within each series and by up to 41% overall when biochar and SCMs were combined; fossil-fuel depletion and acidification declined by 34% and 31%, respectively. However, photochemical oxidation potential increased by 15-25% with biochar addition. Sensitivity analysis showed that reducing the assumed stable-carbon fraction from 80% to 50% increased GWP by approximately 2.0-4.3%. Minor yet consistent reductions were also observed in particulate matter formation, eutrophication, and water use categories, indicating broader environmental co-benefits. Scenario analysis revealed that adopting an 82% renewable electricity grid and rail-based transport could further reduce impacts by 44%. The results represent an environmental comparison of nominal 32 MPa concrete mix designs; the exact biochar–SCM mixtures were not experimentally validated for mechanical performance or durability. Within these limitations, the findings indicate that biochar-augmented concrete has potential as a low-carbon and resource-efficient construction material, supporting Australia's circular economy and net-zero objectives.

title: Assessing recycling potential of critical materials in European electric vehicle fleet
abstract: The rapid expansion of electric mobility in the European Union (EU) is driving a significant increase in end-of-life (EoL) lithium-ion battery (LiB) flows. This study develops a dynamic material flow analysis (MFA) framework to quantify the future recycling potential of critical materials from electric vehicles (EVs) and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs). A temporally explicit stock-flow model is constructed, integrating vehicle adoption projections, survival functions (including cross-border dynamics), and battery characteristics (chemistry shares and material intensities) to estimate in-use stocks and resulting material flows. EoL pathways include second-life allocation to stationary storage and recycling processes. Results indicate a sharp rise in recoverable materials by the late 2020s, driven by the temporal mismatch between rapid EV uptake and delayed battery retirement. However, even under optimistic assumptions, EU targets for recycled content in new batteries (for the years 2031/2036) are unlikely to be met under current assumptions and without additional policy intervention, particularly for cobalt. Scenarios with extended second-life use further delay material recovery, reducing near-term recycling outputs by up to 20%–25%. The findings highlight critical timing and capacity gaps in recycling infrastructure, providing actionable insights for industry and policymakers to support strategic planning and alignment with EU circular economy objectives.

title: System archetypes shaping e-waste circular economy transitions: A participatory system dynamics study
abstract: Socio-technical transitions in e-waste systems are increasingly recognised as a distinct class of technological change, in which the co-evolution of reverse logistics infrastructure, extended producer responsibility regimes, and informal recovery networks determines the pace and direction of circular economy diffusion. Understanding how feedback structures within these systems accelerate or obstruct the scaling of circular technologies is therefore central to designing effective transition interventions. This study examines circular economy transition pathways in Brazil's e-waste sector through the lens of socio-technical change, employing a participatory System Dynamics methodology that integrates co-created causal loop diagrams (CLDs), backcasting exercises anchored to a 2030 normative vision, and archetype analysis. CLDs were developed in a participatory workshop engaging heterogeneous stakeholder groups, including manufacturers, waste cooperatives, policymakers, and industry practitioners operating across Brazil's hybrid extended producer responsibility and informal governance landscape. The diagrams were further validated through multi-round interviews with the same stakeholders. The analysis spans the full product life cycle, from circular design and manufacturing to reverse logistics and end-of-life recovery. This study develops participatory causal loop diagrams that capture how stakeholders represent circular economy dynamics across the manufacturing, policy, and recycling subsystems of the Brazilian e-waste system. It moves beyond causal mapping by identifying system archetypes such as Limits to Growth, Shifting the Burden, Fixes That Fail, and Success to the Successful, which reveal recurrent feedback structures associated with transition bottlenecks, unintended consequences, and persistent coordination failures. Finally, it derives subsystem-specific policy and management implications, showing that circular economy interventions need to be aligned with the distinct structural dynamics that shape each part of the system.

title: Reducing the idle times of forest machines: A scenario analysis with machine big data in Finland
abstract: The idling of forest machines reduces the energy and cost efficiencies of logging operations. This study aimed to estimate the idle times and fuel consumption during idling using automatically collected machine big data. Furthermore, a scenario approach was used to describe the influence of idle times on the volume and price of carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) emissions. The dataset included monthly data from 2021 to 2024, covering 10 logging enterprises with a total of 28 harvesters and 23 forwarders. The results showed that the proportion of idle time of harvesters and forwarders regarding the total operating hours was 14.0% and 11.1%, respectively. Average fuel consumption during idling was 4.28 L h −1 for harvesters and 3.38 L h −1 for forwarders. Annual idle-related CO 2 emissions for wood-harvesting machines in Finland were roughly estimated at around 11,000 metric tonnes (t) with costs equivalent to approximately €50 million. Reduction in idling by 25–50% could cut emissions by around 3000–5000 t CO 2 and generate additional revenue roughly up to €55 million when the reduced idle engine hours were transferred into productive hours. This study concluded that understanding, as well as acknowledging, the influence of idling has a positive impact on energy and cost-efficiencies, while also ensuring more environmentally friendly logging operations. While more research is needed regarding the effects of idling in non-road machinery, this study provides a solid foundation for promoting low emissions non-road machinery operations.

title: Demand-side drivers for low-carbon concrete: Provenance, certification and cultural legitimacy for construction uptake

3D-printed polymeric cryogel for tetracycline adsorption
abstract: The removal of emerging contaminants from aqueous systems remains a significant environmental challenge. Among the adsorbent materials explored for water treatment, cryogels based on natural polymers have emerged as promising candidates due to their interconnected macroporous structure, enhanced mass-transfer properties, and environmentally friendly composition. In this study, a 3D-printed cryogel composed of gelatin, carboxymethylcellulose, and sodium alginate, and crosslinked with Fe 3+ was developed for tetracycline (TC) adsorption in aqueous solution. The Fe-crosslinked cryogel (Cryogel-Fe) was characterized regarding its microstructure, porosity, surface area, and physical, chemical, rheological, thermal, and adsorption properties. The material exhibited a hierarchical macroporous structure with porosity of approximately 91%, as well as stability and swelling capacity in aqueous media, good thermal stability, and excellent rheological properties. The Cryogel-Fe reached a maximum experimental adsorption capacity of 336.45 mg g −1 for TC, while the Langmuir model yielded a theoretical maximum capacity (q max ) of 445.61 mg g −1 . Adsorption analysis indicated that TC removal was governed by a combination of adsorption and diffusion processes, while FTIR, Raman, and XPS results supported the involvement of hydrogen bonding, electrostatic interactions, and possible Fe-assisted interactions. Furthermore, Cryogel-Fe retained more than 80% of its adsorption efficiency after three reuse cycles and maintained high TC removal efficiency in the presence of common coexisting ions and in real water samples. These results demonstrate that the combination of 3D printing, natural polymers, and Fe 3+ crosslinking provides an effective strategy for developing sustainable adsorbents for antibiotic removal.

title: Supply chain network design and food loss in the U.S. fresh produce system
abstract: The U.S. food supply chain provides year-round access to a diverse range of fresh fruits and vegetables, but the perishability of these products makes food loss a persistent sustainability challenge. While previous studies have primarily focused on food loss occurring at the production and consumption stages, less attention has been given to losses arising from aggregation, handling, and transportation activities within the supply chain. This study develops a national-scale optimization model to evaluate how supply chain network design influences food loss and to quantify the trade-offs between economic efficiency and food loss reduction. The model integrates facility location decisions, economies of scale, transportation flows, and transportation-related food loss for eleven fresh produce categories across the continental United States. Results show that transportation-related food loss can be reduced by approximately 78 million pounds without increasing total system costs through strategic reconfiguration of facility locations and product flows. Additional reductions of up to 10% can be achieved through a more spatially dispersed network structure with shorter transportation distances, although at the expense of higher operating costs and reduced economies of scale. The findings demonstrate that food loss is strongly influenced by supply chain configuration and that substantial reductions can be achieved through strategic network redesign. The proposed framework provides a decision-support tool for evaluating trade-offs among economic performance, resource efficiency, and food loss mitigation in fresh produce supply chains.

title: Redox-assisted electrosorption pathways for nickel removal and recovery using carbon nanotubes modified iron based MOF in capacitive deionization
Assessing absolute sustainability: An analysis of impact assessment tools
abstract: Impact investors require information on whether a company's impacts are consistent with global environmental and social limits, yet the impact assessment tools (IATs) available for this purpose remain methodologically heterogeneous and rarely reflect absolute sustainability. In this paper, we address this gap in two steps. First, we conduct a systematic literature review on absolute sustainability to derive criteria for how absolute sustainability should be reflected in IATs conceptually for investment decision-making. Second, we translate these criteria into an analytical framework comprising a descriptive and an evaluative layer, with the latter specifying 12 criteria across 5 dimensions with a four-level scale. We apply this framework to 15 IATs. We find that IATs differ substantially in methodological rigor and rarely integrate a full life cycle perspective, absolute global thresholds and their allocation, as well as temporal dynamics or evidence of causal contribution. We further identify interdependencies between IATs, indicating that they are complementary rather than substitutable. Because IATs pursue different objectives, the descriptive layer represents this variation, implying that the results should be interpreted as alignment with the concept of absolute sustainability rather than as a universal quality ranking. We conclude that IATs are not yet adequately equipped to support capital allocation aligned with absolute sustainability, and that closing this gap requires operationalizing thresholds, allocation, and causal attribution at the company level.

title: Household water consumption patterns revealed through high-resolution fixture-level monitoring in a Swedish living lab
abstract: Detailed knowledge of household water use, at the level of individual fixtures, at high time resolution and in shared housing, remains scarce, limiting the design of water- and energy-efficient buildings. This study draws on a rare three-year dataset from the HSB Living Lab, a purpose-built residential facility in Gothenburg, Sweden combining two housing typologies: communal shared-living clusters and conventional self-contained apartments. Every fixture was metered individually by 214 m at 1-litre resolution and a fixed 10-min reporting interval, with hot and cold supply lines metered separately, allowing consumption to be characterised from 10 min to three years, decomposed by end use and compared between housing types within one building, climate and metering system. Residential consumption was 94–110 L/person/day, below the Swedish average of 140. Showers were the largest end use (30.5%); 38.3% of residential water and 64.4% of shower water were hot. The building's most distinctive features, a high shared-space share and a late-evening peak, proved specific to the communal clusters, whereas the conventional apartments behaved much like mainstream housing, clarifying which findings transfer beyond student living. Three results apply directly to water–energy management: peak-demand factors for system sizing (peak hour factor 1.53; daily peak-to-mean 4.40, or 2.49 on a 99th-percentile-day basis); a ranking of end uses by coupled water–energy intensity identifying showers as the highest-leverage retrofit target, where a low-flow measure would save an estimated 110 m 3 of water and 3900 kW h per year; and evidence that hybrid metering and billing suits shared housing, where much consumption is collective.

title: Circular carbon materials from organic waste: Life cycle comparison with fossil-derived carbon
Linking land use structure to ecosystem service enhancement potential: Implications for sustainable land management in the Poyang Lake Basin
A scenario-based robust multi-objective framework for climate-resilient water-energy systems in conflict-affected regions
SCADA-informed surrogate modeling and evolutionary optimization for simultaneous exergy, cost, and vibration management in gas turbine systems
Industrial thermal energy supply options: A multifactor evaluation framework
abstract: Industrial heat production represents approximately 50% of U.S. manufacturing sector energy needs and related emissions, yet emission reduction strategies for this sector remain underexplored relative to power and transportation. This study applies the open-source LiAISON (Life cycle Assessment Integration into Scalable Open-source Numerical models) framework, integrating for the first time the Global Change Assessment Model (GCAM) into a prospective LCA framework, to evaluate 189 unique configurations of low-temperature (100–500°C) industrial heat supply technologies across nine environmental impact categories from 2020 to 2100. Technologies evaluated include electrification (resistive heaters and heat pumps), hydrogen-based heating, biofuels, solar thermal, and carbon capture and storage (CCS)-integrated systems, assessed under both a business-as-usual (SSP2 Baseline) and a climate-target (SSP2 RCP2.6) scenario. Results demonstrate that under the climate-target scenario, all alternative heat sources reach global warming potential (GWP) parity with conventional natural gas by 2050, with heat pumps and solar thermal performing best across most impact categories. However, significant trade-offs emerge across other environmental dimensions: renewable electrification increases material supply chain burdens; hydrogen pathways involve elevated toxicity and upstream emissions; biobased heating raises marine eutrophication and water consumption concerns; and CCS-integrated systems require additional energy inputs and resources. A systems-level analysis projects cumulative GWP savings of 56.5 billion tons of CO 2 -eq. over 2030–2100 under the climate-target scenario but accompanied by a 4.5-fold increase in freshwater ecotoxicity relative to the baseline. Disability-adjusted life year (DALY) analysis reveals a short-term increase in health burdens through 2040, followed by net improvements as GWP reductions dominate. These findings underscore that relying solely on carbon metrics risks shifting environmental burdens to other domains, and that a multi-indicator, prospective systems framework is essential for identifying balanced industrial decarbonization pathways.

Sustainable collaborative planning of green hydrogen refueling networks in urban agglomerations: A three-stage framework integrating geospatially explicit screening, fuzzy MCDM, and stochastic optimization
abstract: Urban agglomerations, as strategic units for transportation decarbonization, face systemic challenges in their hydrogen refueling station (HRS) networks, including misalignment of wind-solar resources, highly heterogeneous hydrogen demand, and isolated station operations. Existing research, limited to single-station static planning, struggles to support green hydrogen transportation systems, thereby impeding sustainable urban mobility development. This study proposes a three-stage collaborative planning framework: Geospatial analysis, fuzzy MCDM, and stochastic optimization addressing site selection, optimization, configuration, and scheduling for HRSs. A combination method based on spatial analysis realizes coupling of wind-solar resources and transportation demand. A hybrid decision model quantifies expert’ fuzzy cognition and uncovers causal networks of indicators. Seasonal scenarios are generated through gaussian kernel density estimation and LHS, with NSGA-III solving the economic-environmental objective collaborative model for dynamic multi-station hydrogen synergy. Empirical results from a wind-solar-rich urban agglomerations (Urumqi-Changji-Shihezi) identify eight optimal sites. The results show that with a total annual cost of 366.24 million CNY, the lifecycle carbon emissions are 4766.5 tons, achieving carbon reductions of 28.36% and 40.28% compared to gray and black hydrogen, respectively. Collaborative scheduling reduces the system’s supply-demand gap by an average of 87%, significantly enhancing network resilience. The wind-solar hybrid configuration reduces costs by 25.3% and carbon emissions by 50.6% compared to single-energy solutions. This study provides a reusable collaborative HRSs planning paradigm for wind-solar resource-rich regions and enhances hydrogen infrastructure planning theory from the perspectives of spatial adaptation and dynamic coordination, offering valuable insights for the sustainable development of green transportation networks in global urban agglomerations.

Carbon balance in the Brazilian tropical dairy farming system
abstract: The expected increase in the global population is projected to raise the demand for milk and dairy products by 2050, highlighting the need to improve production efficiency while mitigating environmental impacts. This study evaluated the carbon balance of Brazilian tropical dairy farming systems by integrating greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and removals into a single farm-scale assessment, focusing on two milk production levels during lactation: high (HPS, ≥8500 kg milk cow −1 year −1 ) and medium production potential (MPS, <8500 kg milk cow −1 year −1 ). Emissions and removals were estimated following the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change and the Livestock Environmental Assessment and Performance Partnership guidelines. Compared with MPS, HPS showed larger areas, herd sizes, and milk production, reflecting greater productive efficiency associated with more effective management. Consequently, HPS exhibited lower GHG emission intensity from enteric fermentation, manure management, and feed, resulting in a lower overall emission intensity. In contrast, MPS attained higher GHG removal intensity, mainly through soil carbon sequestration associated with land-use change and tree biomass. Despite this greater removal capacity, the higher emission intensity of MPS resulted in a less favorable overall carbon balance than HPS. Both systems therefore contribute to low-carbon dairy development through complementary pathways: HPS primarily by reducing emissions per unit of product, and MPS primarily by enhancing carbon removals. Integrating emission-reduction strategies with practices that enhance carbon sequestration is required to advance low-carbon milk production and support the sector's mitigation goals.

Integration of multispectral imaging and explainable AI for alfalfa seed priming optimization under saline-alkali stress
abstract: Soil salinization poses an increasingly severe threat to sustainable agriculture globally, while conventional seed priming optimization remains time- and resource-intensive, limiting its widespread adoption. This study developed an innovative smart seed priming framework that seamlessly combined multispectral imaging technology with explainable machine learning algorithms to optimize alfalfa seed priming under saline-alkali stress (75 mM Na 2 SO 4 ). Through systematic evaluation of six distinct priming agents (gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), ascorbic acid (AsA), melatonin (MT), salicylic acid (SA), spermidine (Spd), and sodium sulfate (Na 2 SO 4 ), our sophisticated stacking ensemble model demonstrated exceptional performance in both priming parameter classification (accuracy: 0.812-0.920, ROC-AUC: 0.941-0.994) and effect prediction (accuracy: 0.820-0.950, ROC-AUC: 0.928-0.960). Comprehensive SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis identified critical spectral features across multiple analytical scales: the parameter model highlighted wavelengths at 570 nm and 970 nm as key indicators of moisture content and flavonoid compositional changes; for priming effects assessment, wavelengths at 850 nm (associated with storage materials) and 490 nm exhibited significant negative synergistic effects specifically on the ‘first’ category of MT priming; detailed individual seed analysis revealed complex nonlinear relationships between priming agent concentration, treatment duration, and corresponding spectral variations. The developed smart seed priming framework enabled rapid and efficient non-destructive optimization of seed priming, significantly accelerating priming technology development processes and advancing sustainable agricultural practices by providing personalized priming solutions under various stress conditions, particularly in regions affected by soil salinization.

title: Assessing energy security and sustainable development goal 7 performance in EU - A meta four-parallel two-stage undesirable dynamic DDF model
A remote sensing–GIS decision-support framework for mapping woody biochar potential and logistics-constrained application suitability on degraded rural land
abstract: Land degradation represents a major environmental challenge affecting soil productivity, ecosystem services, and climate regulation. Biochar application gained increasing attention as a potential response because it can improve soil properties while contributing to carbon dioxide removal. However, its large-scale deployment for restoration purposes remains constrained by the lack of spatially explicit assessments integrating biomass availability, production potential, logistical constraints, and land restoration needs. This study develops a remote sensing–GIS decision-support framework to assess whether the valorization of residual woody biomass could support degraded rural areas restoration. The framework objectives are to estimate biomass residue availability, biochar production potential, and logistics-constrained biochar application suitability on degraded rural land of the Veneto Region (Italy). Approximately 169,200 ha of degraded rural land were identified across the region, while useable residual biomass was estimated at about 10.2 million t yr −1 , corresponding to a theoretical biochar production potential of approximately 3.1 million t yr −1 . Despite this, spatial and logistical constraints strongly limited its effective deployment, with about 2% of degraded land treated even under the most viable scenario. Lower biochar application rates combined with short transportation distances provided the greatest territorial coverage. These findings demonstrate that biomass abundance alone does not determine restoration potential; rather, effective biochar deployment depends on the spatial alignment of biomass supply, production infrastructure, transportation feasibility, and restoration demand. The proposed framework provides a transferable approach for identifying where biomass valorization can realistically contribute to land restoration and complement with circular bioeconomy and restoration measures into regional planning.

title: Complexation-assisted regulatory mechanism: Insights into microscale interactions and macroscale oxidation kinetics
abstract: Abstract The formation of antibiotic-metal complexes (AMCs) via organic pollutant-metal ion binding is ubiquitous in transition metal-based Fenton-like processes. However, the regulatory mechanisms of binding interactions on oxidative degradation remain underexplored. In this study, tetracycline (TET) was selected as a model organic pollutant, and the impact of TET-Cu(II) micro-complexation on macroscale degradation in the Cu(II)/H 2 O 2 system was systematically elucidated, integrating in-situ spectroscopy, ex-situ characterization, hydrogen nuclear magnetic resonance ( 1 H NMR), electrochemistry, and electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) techniques. Results suggested that Cu(II) rapidly formed a TET-Cu(II) complex with TET’s dimethylamino, amino, and hydroxyl groups at a 1:1 ratio, with a complexation constant of 98036.7 L⋅mol − 1 , which had been confirmed to significantly promoted the macroscopic degradation of TET. Additionally, the bound TET was proved degraded preferentially over free TET, and the dissociation rates significantly exceeded binding rates during oxidation via time-resolved fluorescence scan analysis. The binding interaction promoted the formation of an TET ± -Cu(II)-OOH⁻ intermediate, which further enhanced Cu(II)/Cu(I) cycling and accelerated the generation of the dominant reactive species (hydroxyl radicals (•OH)), while O 2 inhibited reactions by consuming Cu(I) to generate superoxide radicals (•O 2 ⁻). Based on the Benesi-Hildebrand equation, the bound fractions of both TET and Cu(II) were accurately calculated, indicating that the bound TET in the system accounted for more than 90%. Furthermore, the binding model was constructed to accurately predict the degradation rate constants ( k obs ), with an R 2 of 0.96 against experimental values. This study uncovered the intrinsic link between microscale complexation and macroscale degradation, providing theoretical support for efficient composite pollution treatment.
