Economic vs. green complexity: Distinguishing their roles in monetary policy and energy vulnerability
abstract: It is essential to understand the effect of monetary policy and green complexity on energy vulnerability. We analyze the distinct roles of Green Complexity Index (GCI) and the Economic Complexity Index (ECI) in 28 middle-income countries from 2000 to 2019 and find that GCI exerts a non-linear, inverted U-shaped impact on energy vulnerability, acting as a structural catalyst for energy transition only after reaching specific technological thresholds. In contrast, ECI demonstrates a direct, linear, and positive influence without such non-linear moderations. We further find that expansionary monetary policy consistently exerts a negative impact on energy vulnerability across the conditional distribution and that this mitigating effect of monetary policy is significantly amplified as the level of GCI increases, identifying GCI as a sophisticated moderator of monetary transmission. This positive moderation is most pronounced in high-vulnerability economies; in these contexts, increased GCI capacity effectively doubles the marginal efficacy of monetary policy in curbing energy vulnerability. We conclude that prioritizing targeted green industrial strategies—integrated with strategic monetary policy—provides a substantially more effective lever for enhancing energy resilience than pursuing either general broad-based industrial growth or the reliance on traditional economic complexity (ECI) alone.

title: Investigating the hydrogen-based reduction of industrial BF-grade iron ore pellets: Reduction behavior and microstructural insights towards sustainable ironmaking
abstract: Conventional carbon-based ironmaking processes are a major source of global CO 2 emissions, which can be significantly mitigated by hydrogen-based direct reduction (H 2 -DR). Significant industrial and research efforts are underway to adapt processes for hydrogen utilization. However, a fundamental understanding of the complex interplay between reduction kinetics, microstructural evolution, and structural integrity remains elusive. This gap is particularly important for understanding how abundant, lower-cost BF-grade pellets behave compared with premium DR-grade pellets. This study investigates the hydrogen reduction of industrial BF-grade iron ore pellets at 700–1000 °C. Thermogravimetric analysis and multiscale microstructural characterization linked phase transformations, pore evolution, and metallic iron morphology to global reduction behavior. Results show that increasing temperature from 700 °C to 1000 °C accelerates reduction kinetics, decreasing the time to reach 93% metallization by 77%. This acceleration is accompanied by significant, temperature-dependent microstructural evolution. At lower temperatures, a stable, fine-pored structure is formed, while temperatures above 900 °C lead to significant pore coarsening and severe cracking. Microstructural analysis confirms a topochemical reduction pattern. A critical challenge emerges at 700 °C, where complete core metallization is impeded by the formation of a dense iron layer around unreduced FeO particles. At higher temperatures (≥800 °C), metallization is more pervasive throughout the pellet. The study highlights the interplay between temperature, kinetics, and microstructure during the hydrogen reduction of BF-grade pellets, providing insights crucial for optimizing H 2 -DR processes for a wider range of raw materials.

title: Evaluation and further development of the VERA multi-farm approach to test emission mitigation measures for floor systems in naturally ventilated dairy barns
abstract: Emissions from dairy barns should be reduced, given their environmental and climatic impacts. To assess potential mitigation measures comparative measurements are required. In order to achieve comparable results, the VERA test protocol was developed. Should the preferred case-control approach not be implementable, the multi-farm approach may be used as an alternative. However, recent studies have highlighted the question of whether increased variances between the calculated emissions of the barns prevent clear conclusions. The aim of this study is to evaluate the suitability of the multi-farm approach of the VERA test protocol for detecting emission mitigation effects of different floor systems under practical dairy barn conditions. The primary focus was the performance of the study design, rather than an assessment of the mitigation effect. To validate the method 4 b were equipped with a reduction measure and examined in terms of their methane (CH 4 ) and ammonia (NH 3 ) emissions. The concentrations of carbon dioxide (CO 2 ), CH 4 and NH 3 were measured using a Fourier-transform infrared spectrometer. Annual emissions were calculated by conducting measurements across seasons. The determined average annual emissions of the investigated dairy barns were 2.3 – 13.7 kg NH 3 -N and 180.6 – 356.5 kg CH 4 per animal place and year. The wide ranges of the estimated emissions indicate that the multi-farm approach presents statistical challenges due to individual barn variations. The analysis could be improved by including more barns.

title: AI to the rescue: A novel approach to measure plate leftovers
abstract: Assessment of household food waste has mainly relied on surveys, diaries, or waste bin composition analyses, each challenged by representativeness, completeness, validity, and/or measurement error. Photographing food waste is a promising alternative but manual coding requires time and effort. We demonstrate how recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) can be used to analyze photographed leftovers. Based on 469 photos of leftover dinner plates, we use GPT4o to obtain a reliable estimate of the type and quantity of visible remnants on plates. Based on our prompt development, we provide insights on how to use AI. We validate our findings, and assess the impact of measurement error by respondents, with 93 pictures collected by experts. The use of this novel approach severely reduces the effort associated with photo coding, while maintaining high precision and allowing for easy up-scaling.

Territory, cleaner production practices and firm performance: evidence from the Spanish wine industry
abstract: The transition towards environmentally responsible production systems is reshaping strategic priorities across the global wine industry, requiring wineries to reconcile ecological objectives with economic competitiveness. The interaction between cleaner production practices and territorial governance structures remains only partially understood in geographically embedded agri-food industries. The analysis investigates the relationship between formal environmental sustainability practices and firm performance in the Spanish wine industry, with particular attention to the role of territory, identified through Protected Designations of Origin (PDOs). Drawing from a dataset comprising 318 Spanish wineries observed between 2014 and 2022, the study analyses whether environmental sustainability engagement and place-based dynamics are associated with differences in economic performance and adoption patterns. Sustainability engagement is identified through the variable certification, which captures externally verified certifications and other formal, observable signals of environmental sustainability practices, while economic performance is measured through return on assets (ROA), return on sales (ROS) and labour productivity indicators. Empirical evidence reveals that wineries with formal environmental sustainability practices displayed significantly higher economic performance in the post-adoption window than those without practices, with average ROA values of 5.3% compared with 2.1% of non-engaged wineries ( p < 0.001). Firm size was significantly associated with formal sustainability engagement (χ 2 = 7.507; p = 0.023). In addition, adoption differed significantly across PDO territorial structures (χ 2 = 14.383; p = 0.006), highlighting the relevance of institutional and geographical embeddedness in sustainability transitions. The study contributes empirical evidence on the business case for sustainability in agri-food systems and advances a territorial perspective on cleaner production practices in the wine industry.

Exploring sustainable food procurement strategy – the case of farmed fish
abstract: Sustainable food procurement faces complex challenges, including balancing environmental goals with economic constraints, ensuring consistent supply, and meeting consumer expectations. This study explores how Sweden's major grocery retailers (ICA, Coop, and Axfood) approach the procurement of locally produced fish amid growing concerns about food system vulnerabilities. Focusing on consumer preferences, branding, and sustainability commitments, the study uses a qualitative case study design based on interviews with procurement managers and secondary data from annual and sustainability reports. Guided by frameworks on product branding and sustainable food procurement strategy, the analysis reveals a gap between sustainability ambitions and actual procurement practices. Despite strong sustainability messaging, Swedish fish remains underrepresented due to high prices, limited availability, and unpredictable demand. Consumers show interest in local, sustainable fish but tend to buy familiar, accessible options like salmon and cod. Nevertheless, retailers are taking steps through supplier collaboration, cost management, and gradual product integration. The findings offer insights into how branding and sustainability commitments shape procurement strategies and highlight key barriers and opportunities for strengthening local sourcing.

Circularity of different plastic product sectors in Germany: Product interaction with surrounding infrastructure
abstract: Circular Economy potential has often been classified based on individual aspects such as recyclability of materials. This fails to capture the complex interaction between products and the surrounding infrastructure, which stems from country-, product- and material-specific regulations and market conditions. Therefore, this study assesses the circularity of different product categories in Germany resulting from this interaction using a Material Flow Analysis and the Material Circularity Indicator. Different levers are discussed: i) applied polymer types, ii) product design, iii) waste collection systems and iv) product-specific regulations. The results show large differences in circularity of different product categories and reveal untapped Circular Economy potentials. They indicate that most applied polymers are technically recyclable, but circularity is limited by product design from a product perspective and waste collection systems and missing regulations for recyclate use from an infrastructure perspective. A successful Circular Economy implementation requires for both perspectives to be considered.

Evaluating Critical Raw Materials in the energy sector through an energy criticality index
abstract: The deployment of clean energy technologies to meet global decarbonization targets is driving an increase in the demand for Critical Raw Materials: for the energy sector alone, reaching net-zero emissions by 2050 requires up to a sixfold increase of these materials. Despite the growing need of evaluating material criticality of energy technologies, existing methods also based on life cycle thinking approach currently lacks a universally accepted framework that considers different aspects of “criticality.” To address this gap, the study proposes the Energy Criticality Index (ECI), a novel index developed within the Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) framework designed particularly for the energy sector. ECI integrates supply risk, economic importance, geological reserves, import reliance and recyclability into a single dimensionless parameter. To demonstrate its applicability, two hydrogen energy technologies at different stages of technological maturity are tested: a lab-scale alkaline electrolyser cell and an industrial-scale proton exchange membrane (PEM) fuel cell. The application to the two case studies shows that the ECI redistributes criticality: for the alkaline electrolyser, fluorspar (39%) and gallium (20%) emerge as primary hotspots, replacing the rare earth elements dominated profile (92%) of the SH2E (Sustainability assessment of Harmonized Hydrogen Energy systems) method, a criticality index used as benchmark for the same case study. For the fuel cell, gallium (44%) and tantalum (33%) are identified as dominant contributors despite their negligible mass. The index advances the state of the art by substituting annual consumption with geological reserves, introducing a vector magnitude formulation, combining supply risk and normalised economic importance. The same approach is replicable across different technologies for which a life cycle inventory is available.

Root-associated microbial community dynamics in tobacco following topping: implications for nicotine degradation
abstract: Agricultural topping is followed by rapid nicotine synthesis in tobacco roots, which may pose environmental risks due to nicotine accumulation in soil. Microbial degradation offers a promising remediation strategy, but the temporal associations between nicotine accumulation and root-associated microbiomes remain unclear. Here, we integrated multi-omics analysis and experimental validation to characterize the post-topping temporal dynamics of tobacco root-associated microbiomes and their potential roles in nicotine degradation. Amplicon sequencing revealed distinct temporal shifts in bacterial communities in bulk soil and rhizosphere (explaining 2.84% of bacterial variance), as well as the fungal community in the root endosphere following topping. Notably, this included enrichment of key nicotine-degrading microorganisms such as Paenarthrobacter , Streptomyces , Arthrobacter , Ensifer , and Nocardioides . Metabolomic profiling showed increased levels of nicotine, its biosynthetic precursor (putrescine), and microbial degradation products (6-hydroxynicotinine and 6-hydroxy-N-methylmyosmine) following topping. Integrated microbiome-metabolome analysis highlighted strong correlations between rhizosphere bacteria and nicotine-related alkaloids, particularly with nicotine-degrading genera such as Paenarthrobacter , Streptomyces , Arthrobacter , Ensifer , and Nocardioides . High-throughput cultivation yielded 221 and 197 nicotine-utilizing bacteria from rhizosphere and root, respectively. Functional validation of five representative strains demonstrated exceptional degradation efficiency, notably in Ensifer sp. A4 and Pseudomonas sp. B11. Given the absence of matched untopped controls in the field sampling scheme, our findings should be interpreted as temporal post-topping associations rather than causal evidence of topping effects. This study provides novel insights into the ecological patterns and temporal dynamics of tobacco root-associated microbiomes following topping, highlighting the potential role of specific microbes in nicotine degradation.

title: Supporting circular economy decisions in hospitality SMEs: A multi-criteria approach to strategy prioritization
abstract: Circular economy (CE) research has mainly focused on manufacturing and product-based sectors, while its application to service industries remains less understood. In services, circularity cannot be reduced to material loops, as it involves customer participation, organizational capabilities, service routines, and stakeholder coordination. Existing studies have widely examined CE practices, drivers, and barriers, but provide fewer tools for translating these elements into decision criteria, understood here as conditions used to compare the relative actionability of alternative circular strategies. This study develops and applies a multi-criteria decision support approach to Italian hospitality SMEs. Circular practices are classified into circular strategy options, while CE drivers and barriers are operationalized as economic-financial, technological-operational, stakeholder-related, and governance criteria that may facilitate or constrain implementation. By combining survey data collected from hospitality firms, expert-derived criteria weights, and stochastic multi-criteria acceptability analysis, the results indicate that reduction-oriented strategies show the most favourable average position across the four ranking methods, while asset renewal and life extension occupy comparatively favourable positions. Rethink, repurpose, and reuse have very similar expected ranks and cannot be meaningfully ordered. The study frames CE adoption in services as a prioritization process guided by predefined criteria and offers insights for resource efficiency, waste prevention, and cleaner service operations.

A framework for developing an emissions reduction roadmap for new residential buildings in urban Uganda: A demonstrative case study of detached bungalows
abstract: Considering the remaining global emissions budget is essential when regulating greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from the building sector, especially for emerging economies where the building stock is still undergoing rapid expansion. This study demonstrates a framework for developing an emissions reduction roadmap for detached bungalows in urban Uganda. A planetary boundary-based top-down benchmark for Uganda's housing emissions is derived. A hybrid life cycle GHG emissions assessment is conducted for a bungalow over 50 years. Context-specific emissions targets and reduction pathways are derived, forming the roadmap. The framework explores how a 71.6% emissions reduction requirement could be achieved over a 20-year period to remain below the 2°C warming threshold at an 83% risk-avoidance level. The demonstrative findings suggest that significant emissions reductions could be achieved by lowering embodied GHG emissions through sufficiency-oriented building design and low emissions-intensive construction materials and methods. Regulating dwelling stock growth and designing for optimal occupancy densities are identified as potentially important for achieving meaningful reductions. The framework highlights the importance of improving and scaling up Uganda's traditional earthen and bio-based materials to support reductions in embodied emissions. It further demonstrates the value of expressing assessment results using both floor area-based and per capita-based functional units to better account for house size in sufficiency-oriented design. The demonstrative application also highlights the importance of developing context-specific material life cycle inventory data and integrating emissions reduction strategies into Uganda's building policies to support refinement and implementation of the proposed reduction roadmap.

title: Estimating the economic and environmental impacts of critical infrastructure failure in the global natural gas industry: A case study of Nord Stream pipeline
Limits to achieving high circularity in PET bottle systems: Trade-offs, policy needs, and the role of multi-route recycling
abstract: Plastic beverage bottles remain a major environmental challenge, while most circular economy (CE) studies focus on isolated recycling pathways and rarely evaluate operational interactions among multiple recycling destinations. This study proposes a multi-route PET bottle CE network integrating bottle-to-bottle recycling with bottle-to-fiber, bottle-to-sheet, bottle-to-filament, and disposal pathways under operational, market, regulatory, and collection constraints. A multi-objective mixed-integer linear programming model is combined with Taguchi-based scenario analysis and the L p -metric method to evaluate economic, energy, circularity, and manpower performance under different decision-prioritization conditions. Results show that decision-prioritization directly reshapes recycling-route allocation, where circularity-oriented strategies improve material circulation but increase cost and energy burden (over 20%) nonlinearly, particularly beyond 60% circularity. Collection rate remains the strongest driver of circularity performance, while open-loop routes complement bottle-to-bottle recycling by absorbing material flows that are economically or operationally constrained. Restricting market acceptance of bottle-to-filament recycling—the outlet receiving the largest allocation in the examined case—reduced circularity by up to 55%, demonstrating how a route-specific demand shock can alter recycling-route allocation and redirect recyclable material toward disposal. Furthermore, mandatory r P E T -content regulation alone cannot significantly expand bottle-to-bottle recycling, while combining it with tax relief improves closed-loop recycling performance by 129–200%. The findings indicate that transitioning toward high-circularity PET bottle systems depends on operational maturity, collection stability, market acceptance, and flexible interaction between closed-loop and open-loop recycling pathways.

AI-driven granular LCA for apparel: Quantifying product-specific GHG emissions for sustainable design and circularity
abstract: Product-specific Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) for apparel is hindered by generalized data, failing to quantify unique environmental burdens crucial for sustainable production and consumption. This study addresses this challenge by proposing and validating an automated methodology using a Vision-Language Model (VLM) to extract product-specific details (e.g., fabric composition) from unstructured User-Generated Content (UGC) on consumer-to-consumer (C2C) platforms and subsequently calculate corresponding product-specific greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. The study seeks to demonstrate the significance of AI-enabled product-specific information as a tool for deriving insights into sustainable production, cleaner manufacturing, and resource efficiency. Applying this framework to 3500 apparel listings from a major C2C marketplace, our VLM demonstrated high accuracy in extracting physical attributes like garment size (92.3%) and fabric composition (81.6%). The subsequent LCA quantified an average emission of 11.9 kg-CO 2 eq/item. More importantly, by analyzing the product-related parameters required for these computations, we attempted to extract and structure data on product attributes and user behavior from unstructured UGC, enabling more effective estimation of product-specific GHG emissions. Although challenges remain in precisely inferring complex user behaviors from unstructured data, the successful granularization of material composition highlights the significant impact of material selection, providing actionable insights for sustainable eco-design and circularity. Ultimately, by significantly enhancing information transparency across the value chain, our work directly aligns with emerging global policies like the EU Digital Product Passport (DPP), fostering data-driven decision-making for cleaner production goals.

Deep eutectic solvent processing of seagrass biomass from beach wrack for sustainable polypropylene composites in large format additive manufacturing
abstract: Seagrass-rich beach wrack collected from the Bay of Cádiz (Spain) was valorized as a reinforcement for polypropylene (PP) composites manufactured by large-format additive manufacturing by fused granular fabrication (LFAM-FGF). Two delignification approaches were investigated with NaOH (SG-NaOH) and a deep eutectic solvent (DES) based on lactic acid and choline chloride (SG-DES). While SG-NaOH achieved greater lignin removal, SG-DES yielded a cellulose-rich material with higher crystallinity and a distinctive nanofibrillar morphology. When incorporated into PP at 15 wt%, untreated seagrass (SG-UT) and SG-NaOH resulted in a marked reduction in tensile strength and ductility. In contrast, composites reinforced with SG-DES exhibited a significant increase in Young's modulus while maintaining tensile strength comparable to neat PP and preserving high elongation at break. Thus, despite its lower delignification efficiency, the DES treatment produced the most effective reinforcement among the investigated formulations, highlighting that extensive lignin removal is not necessarily required to achieve high composite performance. In addition, all seagrass-filled formulations showed improved dimensional stability during LFAM-FGF printing, effectively suppressing the warping commonly observed in neat PP, enabling the fabrication of large-scale demonstrator parts which maintained their structural integrity after more than one year of outdoor exposure.

A model-driven simulation and requalification-decision framework for reuse of shelf-life-expired carbon-fibre prepregs in composite manufacturing
abstract: Circular composite manufacturing needs decision support that turns the uncertain condition of a recovered feedstock into production decisions. Shelf-life-expired carbon-fibre prepreg is a demanding case: each batch must be accepted, re-qualified under an adjusted process window, or rejected before it enters the line, and the information behind that decision is spread across organisations. This paper presents a model-based proof of concept of a simulation and requalification-decision framework. It couples an out-life degradation state model, a requalification and process-window decision layer, a mass-conserving material-flow model of eight unit operations and a first-time-right quality-risk module, and specifies the traceability service through which four partners share the records the decision needs. It is demonstrated on an Italian pilot reusing expired prepreg for drone components. The operational series and the out-life calibration data are synthetic, unit costs are illustrative and no part-level mechanical property was measured; 30 measured coupon-level requalification tests benchmark the out-life layer. Per 1000 kg of expired feedstock the reference case returns 149 kg of moulded output, 125 kg of it conforming, with the moulding conversion carried as a disclosed band of 0.21–0.79 (149–560 kg). For a proportional conversion, ratio results hold across that band: expired feedstock yields 84.0% of a virgin control, a value set by the admission rate, and a first-time-right cap reduces scrap by 40% for a 9% output loss under the stated parameters. In the measured tests, void content ordered the usability labels across four resin systems. Rising energy prices favour reuse in a directional screen.

Beating waste into value: Energy demand and technology of packaging paper production using post-consumer textiles
abstract: The increasing volume of post-consumer textile waste creates the necessity to develop alternative recycling pathways, beyond fibre-to-fibre applications. In this study, cellulose-rich textile waste (predominantly cotton) was mechanically processed, and the associated energy input was quantified. Textile fibres were refined at different levels of specific beating energy (SBE), fibre characteristics were investigated, and the resulting suspension was blended with industrial paper stock. Paper handsheets were produced, and the key properties were analysed. This study demonstrates that increasing SBE enhances tensile strength, short-span compression strength (SCT), density, and elastic modulus, while bending stiffness is comparatively less affected despite the associated densification and reduction in sheet thickness. Under realistic assumptions, the cumulative energy demand required to achieve industrially relevant fibre properties through refining was recorded at 748 kWh·t −1 at comparable dewatering resistance (Schopper-Riegler). This energy demand is well comparable to that of typical virgin fibre feedstocks utilised in packaging paper, such as mechanical pulp. A modelling approach demonstrated that the tensile index of fibre blends can be accurately predicted from the tensile properties of the pure components using a simple rule of mixtures approach. Furthermore, the tensile index was shown to be a suitable predictor of SCT. By combining these predictive models with the established energy benchmarks, this study provides a robust, data-driven roadmap for the industrial integration of textile waste into packaging paper production.

title: Major olive mill aqueous effluents as industrial sources of hydroxytyrosol, 3,4-dihydroxyphenylglycol and tyrosol for circular valorisation
abstract: The selective recovery of valuable chemicals from waste streams is a central objective of Green Chemistry, particularly when waste prevention and the use of renewable feedstocks can be combined. In two-phase olive oil extraction systems, several aqueous effluents are generated that are commonly treated as waste despite their significant organic and phenolic content. In this work, four industrial effluents—olive washing water (OWW), hopper drip water (HDW), vertical centrifuge water (VCW) and oil decanting water (ODW)—were systematically characterised in six olive oil mills over two consecutive production seasons to evaluate their potential as sources of bioactive phenolic compounds. HDW exhibited the highest phenolic concentration, reaching up to 3.5 g/L, together with elevated sugar contents, identifying it as the most promising stream for the recovery of hydroxytyrosol (HT) and 3,4-dihydroxyphenylglycol (DHPG). VCW, although more diluted, was generated in the largest volumes and contained substantial amounts of both compounds, while ODW showed an unusual predominance of DHPG over HT, enabling selective recovery. An industrial chromatographic process was optimised to maximise phenolic retention and HT purity in the most concentrated streams. Based on national production data, the valorisation of these effluents could enable the recovery of up to 80 t/year of HT and 56 t/year of DHPG. Overall, this study highlights the potential of phenolic recovery to support waste valorisation strategies and facilitate subsequent wastewater management within a circular-economy framework.

title: Consumer willingness to pay and farmers’ adoption intentions for pesticide-reducing technologies in European orchards
abstract: Reducing synthetic pesticide use remains an EU sustainability objective, yet uptake of pesticide-reducing technologies remains limited in high-input orchard systems. This study examines whether information on consumer willingness to pay (WTP) for products with reduced pesticides is associated with farmers' adoption intentions. We focus on four pesticide-reducing innovations: smart mapping variable rate (VRA) application systems, robotic weeders, bio-based solutions with low sulphur and copper formulations, and cover crops. Evidence is drawn from a structured survey experiment involving 354 olive and vine growers across five European Union countries. Using a within-subject design with randomised presentation order and a Cheap Talk script to mitigate hypothetical bias, we compare farmers' adoption intentions before and after exposure to estimated consumer WTP premiums for wine and olive oil produced with reduced pesticide use. Non-parametric tests and multinomial logit models indicate that consumer WTP information is positively associated with both partial and full adoption intentions across all four technologies, with stronger associations for smart mapping VRA and robotic weeders than for bio-solutions and cover crops. Farm structure and behavioural factors, including perceived costs, subjective norms, and perceived effectiveness of existing pest management practices, exhibited technology-specific associations with adoption intentions. Although the study design does not permit causal inference, the findings suggest that consumer-driven market signals could complement existing policy approaches to support the transition towards more sustainable agricultural production.

title: Village and farm ponds differ in contaminant retention and mobility: Implications for sustainable management of rural agricultural landscapes
Enhancing sustainability in greenhouse agriculture through chemical analysis–driven characterization of boiler biogas fuel strategies
abstract: Greenhouses can enhance sustainability and productivity by integrating renewable energy and CO 2 enrichment, which improves photosynthesis and reduces environmental impact. However, existing studies on biogas and methane combustion have not addressed how combustion-derived CO 2 can be strategically managed to meet the coupled thermal and photosynthetic demands of greenhouse crops. In this context, the present study is the first to conduct a parametric analysis of biogas utilization for greenhouse applications, offering a proposed adaptive fuel management strategy hypothesized to support both environmental and economic benefits. To achieve this, a counterflow flame configuration is employed to investigate the combustion characteristics of a greenhouse boiler operating with various methane–biogas fuel mixtures. The detailed Gas Research Institute Mechanism (GRI-Mech 3.0), comprising 53 species and 325 reactions, is utilized to model the reaction kinetics. Detailed thermophysical and transport properties based on fundamental thermodynamics are integrated to accurately capture flame structure and species transport. The model was validated against experimental methane/air flame data, demonstrating good agreement and confirming its predictive accuracy. The effects of (1) CO 2 enrichment, (2) operating pressure, and (3) strain rate on flame temperature and species concentrations (CO 2 , CO, NO, and NO 2 ) are systematically investigated. Findings demonstrate the potential of biogas as a sustainable fuel under characterized conditions: Biogas substitution lowers peak in-flame NO x and CO concentrations while increasing peak CO 2 concentration, highlighting its potential for CO 2 enrichment. A pressure-sensitivity analysis (1–10 atm) and a proposed adaptive diurnal fuel-switching strategy are also presented. Practical guidelines are proposed to support greenhouse growers in enhancing thermal efficiency and environmental performance.

title: Mine planning for responsible resource development: Integrated economic and sustainability-aware block valuation for open-pit to underground transition
abstract: Mine planning involves high-stakes decisions under geological, economic, operational, and sustainability-related uncertainties. Conventional optimization frameworks rely on simplified block economic value (BEV) models that omit geomechanical variability, metallurgical responses, multi-element contributions, and environmental and social externalities. This paper introduces the Comprehensive Net Block Value (CNBV) framework, which extends conventional block economic valuation through a comprehensive representation of block value. CNBV extends the conventional BEV formulation through five value-modifying modules: (i) a Rock Cost Index (RCI) for cost scaling based on material properties; (ii) an Extra Substance Impact Coefficient (ESIC) capturing recovery penalties from undesirable material content; (iii) penalty functions for deleterious elements under different mining and processing pathways; (iv) generalized by-product and co-product contributions; and (v) monetized environmental and social costs. The framework is applied to the transition from open-pit to block caving by extending the model of Badakhshan et al. (2024) and demonstrated on a large-scale copper deposit. The CNBV model identifies an optimal transition at 725 m, with a 22-year mine life, extracting 510 Mt at 0.50% grade, a stripping ratio of 1.22, and an NPV of USD 6.80 billion. In contrast, the BEV model suggests a deeper transition at 887.5 m, a higher stripping ratio of 1.64, a lower grade of 0.46%, and a higher NPV of USD 7.51 billion. The 162.5 m difference demonstrates the influence of incorporating additional value-modifying factors into block valuation. Sensitivity analysis shows that cost scaling and multi-element contributions most influence NPV, while environmental and social costs gain importance under stricter regulations.

title: One-pot maleic-acid-pretreated lignocellulose nanofibrils for UV-shielding and high-haze films

Legal-institutional inertia in circular electrification: Evidence from Swedish heavy-duty and off-road machinery
abstract: Electrifying heavy-duty and off-road machinery can cut operational emissions, but cleaner-production gains depend on circular battery and component flows, interoperable charging and useable data. Transition research explains policy mixes and socio-technical lock-in but often treats law as an external context. We ask which legal domains enable or obstruct circular electrification, how they create system inertia, and which legal design principles can reduce it. The study combines 29 semi-structured expert interviews in Sweden with hybrid thematic analysis and targeted doctrinal analysis of relevant EU and Swedish law. Eight connected domains emerge, spanning regulatory direction, permitting producer responsibility and product–waste status, standards, data governance, finance, contracts and procurement, and regulatory experimentation. Across them, ambiguity, fragmented authority and legacy-rule misfit increase coordination and transaction costs, delay decisions, shift risk to early movers and favour incumbent-led reconfiguration over more disruptive circular models. The central contribution is to specify legal-institutional inertia as a cross-domain regime mechanism that selects both transition pathway and actors. Connecting the multi-level perspective with institutional environmental governance and product-chain management, the paper derives a coordinated policy mix based on stable long-term direction, modular implementation, interoperability, proportional responsibility and experiments linked to scaling. Cleaner production policy must therefore align legal interfaces across the product chain, not only remove isolated barriers.

title: Operationalizing No Net Loss of biodiversity in tropical mining: A ten-step decision framework
Centralized versus conventional anaerobic digestion of sewage sludge: An environmental and economic assessment
abstract: High-solid anaerobic digestion (HSAD), in which dewatered sewage sludge from several small wastewater treatment plants is treated centrally, is an alternative to conventional low-solid anaerobic digestion (LSAD) for sludge stabilization and energy recovery from biogas. This work develops a modelling framework to compare centralized HSAD and decentralized LSAD through a coupled life cycle assessment (LCA) and economic analysis approach, supporting case-specific decision-making for sludge management under defined local boundary conditions. Four different sub-scenarios were modeled for both HSAD (S1.1-S1.4) and LSAD (S2.1-S2.4), forecasting different biogas uses, alternative sludge transportation routes, digestate valorization pathways, and ammonia extraction. The sub-scenarios were compared with the respective baselines (S1.0 for HSAD and S2.0 for LSAD), corresponding to full-scale Italian plant configurations. Under the investigated full-scale conditions, HSAD showed lower environmental impacts than conventional LSAD when transport distances were limited, due to higher credits generated by biogas and the avoided mineral fertilizer use in agriculture. However, input sludge/digestate transportation is a dominant driver of both environmental and economic impacts. Moreover, biogas upgrading to biomethane is environmentally preferable to electricity generation, but economically unfavourable at current market conditions. Overall, centralized HSAD can represent a favorable solution under regional-scale planning when logistics, digestate valorization, and gate-fee conditions are suitable, whereas optimized LSAD with dynamic sludge thickening can achieve comparable performance. Although the specific results are related to an Italian case study, this work provides a useful tool for decision-making among alternative sludge management solutions when local boundary conditions (sludge characteristics, transportation distances, HSAD/LSAD plant availability) are specified.

title: Assessment of carbon emissions and life cycle cost in railway infrastructure: comparison between steel slag ballast and natural aggregate
authors: Kathleen Dall Bello de Souza Risson
abstract: This paper evaluates the use of steel slag aggregates (SSA) as ballast for railways, from environmental and financial perspectives. The environmental assessment employs the Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) methodology framework to compare steel slag ballast (SSB) with natural aggregate ballast. The study focuses on the Global Warming Potential (GWP) impact category (also known as carbon footprint), measured in kg of CO 2 equivalent. The study considers a functional unit of 1 km of railway track over an 8-year reference service period, from a case study in the Southeast region of Brazil. The CO 2 uptake through the natural carbonation of the SSA was obtained through thermogravimetric analysis, resulting in an estimated uptake of 17.7 kg CO 2 /t SSA under the conditions considered, a value that was incorporated into the assessment. In addition to the environmental assessment, a Life Cycle Cost (LCC) analysis was conducted to evaluate the economic performance of the railway ballast alternatives over their life cycle. Within the defined system boundaries, the results showed that the railway with steel slag ballast showed a lower GWP than conventional ballast, primarily due to the estimated CO 2 uptake during natural carbonation. For the same 8-year reference service period, we calculated −4.82E+04 kgCO 2 e for the SSB (thus absorbing CO 2 ) and 1.30E+04 kgCO 2 e for the conventional ballast. A sensitivity analysis indicated that the SSB maintains its environmental advantage even with transportation distances of up to 470 km. From a financial standpoint, the LCC of the railway with SSB was 32% lower than that of conventional ballast. The study confirms the potential of SSB as an environmental and financial alternative for railway ballast, given the premises adopted in this research.

Environmental, circularity, and criticality assessment of end-of-life lithium-ion batteries: Implications for management strategies in Mexico
abstract: Mexico's rapid growth in battery electric vehicle (BEV) adoption has not been accompanied by a regulatory framework for the end-of-life management of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), creating environmental risks and limiting the recovery of strategic materials. This study evaluates four end-of-life management strategies for BEV LIBs in Mexico (controlled disposal, hydrometallurgical recycling, pyrometallurgical recycling, and repurposing) using an integrated framework that combines Life Cycle Assessment (LCA), the Material Circularity Indicator (MCI), and a criticality-weighted extension (MCI-c). The proposed MCI-c incorporates material criticality into the circularity assessment, allowing resource recovery to be evaluated not only in terms of material recirculation but also considering the strategic importance of recovered materials. Repurposing achieved the best overall environmental and circularity performance, while hydrometallurgical recycling consistently outperformed pyrometallurgical recycling among recycling alternatives. Incorporating criticality into the assessment altered the prioritization of management strategies under increasing lithium criticality, demonstrating that criticality can influence end-of-life management priorities. These findings highlight the importance of integrating environmental performance, material circularity, and criticality into the evaluation of end-of-life LIBs management strategies. For Mexico, they support the development of a dedicated regulatory framework that prioritizes higher-value recovery strategies and incorporates criticality into end-of-life decision-making. More broadly, the proposed framework provides a practical approach for evaluating end-of-life LIBs management in countries facing similar challenges in battery circularity and critical material supply.

title: A standardized energy performance certification framework for underground metro stations: Methodology development, seven-grade energy rating and energy-saving retrofit potential
Between symbols and substance: Voluntary impact reporting of funds
abstract: Impact investing has emerged as a prominent investment approach to addressing social and environmental challenges while generating financial returns. Given its dual mandate to generate impact and financial returns, impact investing faces heightened pressures on its legitimacy, making transparent impact reporting essential to counter allegations of impact-washing and to safeguard the credibility of the approach. Despite the growing relevance of impact reporting, little is known about the underlying motivations and reporting strategies of fund managers who voluntarily publish impact reports. Drawing on legitimacy theory, the paper investigates the motivations and reporting strategies behind voluntary impact reporting by fund managers using a sequential exploratory design. First, 13 semi-structured interviews with impact-reporting professionals were analyzed following Grounded Theory principles. Second, a qualitative content analysis of 141 publicly available impact reports was conducted to analyze how reporting strategies are implemented in practice. The findings of the interviews reveal that fund managers’ motivations are driven by a need to show the alignment of profit with purpose, move beyond institutional compliance, and foster impact reflexivity. These motivations are operationalized through six reporting strategies: rationalization, contextualization, verification, institutionalization, participation, and transformation, which cluster around the dimensions of justification, integration, and adaptation. The content analysis assesses the potential for more substantive forms of legitimation in individual reporting elements. The paper contributes to legitimacy theory in the context of reporting by demonstrating that reporting strategies are interdependent and to practice by offering practitioners and standard setters a starting point for critically reflecting on the design of impact reporting.

Environmental and economic assessment of olefin synthesis from waste as an emerging alternative to conventional light olefin production routes
abstract: Light olefins such as ethylene and propylene are essential petrochemical intermediates but remain highly energy- and carbon-intensive to produce using conventional fossil-based technologies. We conduct the life-cycle environmental and economic assessment (LCA/LCC) of seven olefin production pathways, such as coal-based, natural gas-based, shale gas-based, crude oil-based, bio-based, waste-to-olefins and waste-to-olefins with sorption-enhanced olefin synthesis, to understand trade-offs and identify decarbonisation opportunities. A cradle-to-gate LCA employs nine EF 3.1 midpoint indicators, using foreground data from industrial sources, Aspen Plus V14 modelling, and ecoinvent v3.10 inventories. Results show that coal-based olefin production exhibits the highest environmental burdens, particularly for climate change, freshwater ecotoxicity, eutrophication, and water use. Natural gas-based and crude oil-based routes perform better across non-climate categories but remain carbon-intensive. Bio-based olefin production route provides partial climate benefits but is penalised by large land and water requirements. In contrast, waste-to-olefins and waste-to-olefins with sorption-enhanced olefin synthesis achieve net-negative greenhouse gas emissions due to biogenic carbon uptake and integrated CO 2 capture. Sorption-enhanced olefin synthesis further reduces energy demand via in-situ water removal and process intensification, yielding lower GHG emissions (47%), reduced water use by 64%, and improved selectivity compared with conventional waste-to-olefin routes. However, higher impacts persist in ozone depletion and ionising radiation categories, driven by upstream electricity supply chains. Economic analysis indicates that gasification and CO 2 management dominate overall costs, while the sorption-enhanced synthesis adds only a modest incremental cost to waste-to-olefin pathways. Total life cycle costing for waste-to-olefins with sorption-enhanced olefin synthesis falls within EUR 2130 to 3550 t −1 olefin, including environmental cost, competitive with emerging green olefin pathways. Overall, the findings demonstrate that combining waste feedstocks, CO 2 capture, and sorption-enhanced process intensification offers a promising pathway for low-carbon, resource-efficient olefin production, especially within future decarbonised energy systems.

Future environmental impacts of EU permanent magnet demand: a combined prospective MFA-LCA assessment
abstract: Advancing climate change necessitates a transformation of the mobility and energy sector towards low-carbon technologies. Rare earth element-containing permanent magnets (PMs), a key component in efficient electric machines, are currently produced in only a few countries and not efficiently recycled, motivating efforts to diversify supply by establishing domestic recycling routes. This study inspects the projected environmental impacts of PM value chains, thereby providing context to transitioning from a geographically concentrated, linear value chain towards a circular value chain in the European Union. Combining material flow analysis (MFA) and prospective life cycle assessment (LCA), the emissions from 2025 to 2100 are estimated under alternative production and recycling scenarios. Results show that i) future impacts of PM production will increasingly depend on the footprint of the material, ii) guaranteeing high magnetic performance during the use phase is key to achieving environmental benefits of circular value chains, iii) end-of-life products can become a relevant source for PM materials if recycling technologies and value chains are developed, and iv) recycling material substitution rates strongly influence overall results. The article showcases how to meaningfully combine LCA and MFA in dynamic system studies and demonstrates the cumulative environmental benefits of diversifying PM supply. Findings support ongoing EU efforts to strengthen domestic critical raw material supply and circular economy strategies.
